This book is composed of entries made in a diary during the years 1915-18. It is not a narrative of either battles or heroic deeds, but of life far behind the front lines. It is a story of what went on in the “back-yards” of the war, and of those who died without their names being mentioned in the casualty lists,

I desire to express here my gratitude for the valuable assistance received in the preparation of this translation from my friend Herr Hans von Meixner, who himself spent more than five years in Russian captivity under conditions similar to those described here.

As I raised my sword to give my troopers the signal to attack, I was wounded for the first time. “ Forward; lances in position; attack,” I wanted to cry out, but I did not get beyond the first word. My troopers scattered like drops of water from a puddle struck by a down-coming heel. My mare, Zelle, reared straight up, hesitated a moment, then fell backwards.

I felt dully that all was at an end. Yet, although the desire to do so was strong within me, I did not call out for my mother. ** My God, why hast Thou forsaken me? ” I cried. Our religious teacher, Professor Schwarz, had explained this phrase to us as being a testimony to the humanity of the Son of God. It was no wonder that it came readily to my lips at this moment.

When I awoke, it seemed to me as though someone was sawing through both my legs. My mouth was full of crumbled earth. In my pain, while falling, I had bitten into the ploughed field. When I looked for my sword, I discovered that in the mean while I had been robbed. Field-glasses, watch, pocket-book, revolver — everything had been taken. “Captive ” —the word rang shrilly through my head. It was as though I had once more been hit —this time through the head.

Perhaps I could still save myself. My legs were paralysed, my back was stiff, and I could not alter my position. A heat burnt my thighs as if a fiery coal lay between them. I opened the flap of my trousers and inserted my hand. At the right, on the inner side of the thigh, four fingers slipped into a gaping hole; on the left, and farther down above the knee, only a single finger could be inserted into another wound.

“So you will bleed to death!” This knowledge scarcely grieved me any longer; for I had lost too much blood to be able to feel anything very intensely. “Perhaps this is even better than captivity,” I thought comfortingly to myself, gazing in surprise up at the blue sky. I turned my gaze upon something fluttering near by. It was only one of our lances on which the black and white pennon flapped in the breeze —as though crying for help.

After a time a troop of Cossacks came riding past. My sergeant was bound to their stirrups; his face was chalky, he limped, and as he panted by some five paces away, he saw that I was alive and pointed to me. Two Cossacks leapt from their horses and approached me. Seeing my bleeding body, one of them waved his hand, as if to say: “It is too late.” But they did not prevent Schmidt II from taking down my trousers in order to bandage me. I gazed in suspense upon my left thigh. If the blood were to gush forth, all would be over; but if it only oozes.... “It only oozes,” said Schmidt II, as if he knew what I was thinking. To my right and left lay a couple of dead troopers from my squadron. Schmidt went from one to the other, turned them over on their back$, and removed their rolls of bandages. Kneeling down with a groan beside me, he rolled — rolled —rolled. “Damn it,” he said gloomily, “it always comes through again.” Finally he and the Cossacks buttoned up my tunic and, supporting me under my arms, lifted me up. I placed my right arm around Schmidt’s shoulder, my left around the neck of a Cossack. My legs dangled like those of a marionette, filled with sawdust and jointless. “ Nu, pascholl,” cried the Cossacks, as they sprang with a clatter into their saddles. | ”

From the Windau—a small river in Kurland, which we crossed by means of a ford — Schmidt II gave me a drink. I emptied six cups in succession; it seemed as though it were only six drops. As we were looking for the ford, we passed by a dragoon half immersed in the river and transfixed by his own lance. It was Siidekum — a volunteer —I recognized him by his spectacles, which were held to his ears by wires. “ A stupid

fellow,” said Schmidt II, who had also recognized him. “He saw so badly without his spectacles that he was nearly blind whenever he lost them. He need never have volunteered, never once hit the target, and now he’s got it.”

On the farther bank of the Windau we encountered another troop of Cossacks. A couple of our horses were in their possession, and a dozen of my dragoons were their prisoners. Leaning against a dead horse was my sergeant major, Schnarrenberg — a pucka soldier decorated with the Iron Cross. His teeth protruded a little; he ground his jaws. “ You, too, Cornet? ” he grumbled in a disappointed tone.

Podbielski, Blank, Schmidt I, and Briinninghaus greeted me with their eyes. Nobody spoke. All had got their share. Three from the first squadron had been severely wounded by sabrecuts and thrusts from lances. My men had only bullet wounds. ** Well, devil take it! ” said Briinninghaus. “The war is at an end for us.”
‘Coward! ” murmured Schnarrenberg, grinding his jaws still more vigorously and looking as if he were chewing something hard.

The Cossacks were good-natured and in a good humour. Their unexpected victory had inspired them with kindly feelings. I understood them, in spite of their Siberian dialect, for my mother was a Russian, although we were never permitted to speak Russian in my father’s presence. How fortunate — I think to myself — that, when father was away at sea, I always asked mother to teach me her native language! And how wise it was of her to die before this war broke out! My God! what should I have done? She would never have got over it.... He, however.... It was a matter of course to my father that I should be among the first to volunteer for service. He is an officer.

After a time two Panje wagons came rumbling up, low vans with racks at the side, filled with straw. With the best intentions my troopers laid me first in the wagon. But the Cossacks were in a hurry, and they packed the whole dozen into the two wagons. Five men lay upon my wounded thighs. Their weight pressed me against the side rack, so that my face was jambed up against it as though against prison-bars. Close beside the rack the wheel turned and ground, and barely an inch separated forehead and mouth and chin from it. If the bars had broken, a single turn of the wheel would have torn the entire skin from my bones. I strained violently backwards, and this protracted exertion used up my last ounce of strength.

When the wagons stopped beside the Russian Divisional Staff Headquarters, I was so weak that I could not prevent the tears from rolling down my cheeks. Next to me lay Schnarrenberg. Being the undermost, we were left in the wagon; the others were laid beside it upon the grass. Some uttered smothered groans. Little Blank moaned. Schnarrenberg glanced at me. “ Damn it, Cornet!” he muttered angrily on seeing my tears. ““Smoke — that helps.” Customarily stingy —now he thrust a cigarette between my lips. Why? A gentle numbness overcame me. After three or four puffs my eyes were dry again.

A couple of Cossacks came galloping up. Over their saddles hung bleeding officers, whose bodies flopped like strips of rubber against the horses’ flanks. Their faces were terribly disfigured. A youthful Transbaikal officer stepped up to our wagon. He wore shining Wellingtons, blue silk breeches with yellow stripes, and a green silk sash. Schnarrenberg gave me a sharp and commanding punch in the ribs. “I protest against our treatment,” I said at once. “ We have been robbed of all but our shirts— contrary to the laws of war.” Schnarrenberg emitted a satisfied murmur. He did not know a word of Russian, but he understood the tone in my voice. The young officer only smiled. “ Is it not enough that life was left you? ” he asked gently. “ We Cossacks are not always accustomed to be so generous. In your place I would be satisfied.”

Presently a troika drove into the courtyard. Between two Russian officers of high rank I recognized a German dragoon uniform, a sharp familiar face in which a piece of glass glittered. “Captain Count Holcking —first squadron,” said Schnarrenberg, as though he were making an official report. The troika came to a standstill ten paces away from our wagon. Holcking alighted painfully, supported on either side by the Cossack officers. What? His sword was still hanging by his side? He took three or four steps, remained standing, fought for breath, shook his head — and looked as though he should long since have been dead. An officer hurried away, only to return immediately with an old General and his staff. “‘ Have a look, Cornet,” Schnarrenberg murmured excitedly, and I raised my head a little and heard someone report: “Colonel Beljajeff requests Your Excellency to leave his sword to this officer because of his valour.” Holcking did not know Russian — did not understand. What was there left for him to do? He drew his sword from its scabbard with nerveless fingers, held it aloft, shaking with emotion. Solemnly the old General saluted, bowed respectfully, and returned the sword to him with a polite gesture. Holcking stood like a man turned to stone. He seized the sword with his right hand, pressed his left upon his chest, and suddenly fell like a log upon the ground. “Is war not beautiful? ” said Schnarrenberg enthusiastically. ““ Damnation! that was something like! Let people talk as they like —that was something like! ”

Towards evening we were carried into an empty room in the Divisional Headquarters. About a hundred severely wounded men lay, one beside the other, on straw around the walls. Most of them groaned, several of them emitted the deathrattle, and a Cornet, who was still almost a child, called out unceasingly: “ Hildegard, Hildegard! ” “Have you no morphia?” I inquired of a passing surgeon. “ Morphia? Nitschewo....”

A broad table stood in the centre of the room, and on this the wounded were laid, one after another. A surgeon with rolled-up sleeves stood beside the table, while a Cossack held aloft a smoking lamp to light him at his work. Shadows moved back and forth across the whitewashed wall, and the surgeon’s knife looked large and long, like a Cossack’s sword. Almost everyone who was laid upon that table shrieked after a short time.

Above tall trees a pallid moon was shining. Across the windows came flying silhouettes of galloping Cossacks, with high fur caps, standing erect in the stirrups. The beating of hoofs announced their coming from afar off and, for the time being, deafened our cries of pain. From a great distance came the boom of cannon, while somewhere near by a house was in flames.

I was so weak that I could no longer raise my head. As dusk fell, I was seized by fever. All figures — the surgeon, the Cossack, the riders across the window, the other wounded —I saw only as shadow-pictures. Something mysterious and ghostlike enveloped them, and, though I did not as yet know what “Russia ” meant, I had a presentiment in these first quiet hours of my captivity that I was about to enter into a new, strange, incomprehensible world.

I was seized by a suffocating fear — and not I alone. It was to be seen upon all the faces around me, to be heard in each groan, yet did not come from our wounds or our miserable and hopeless plight. It came from the odour of the Cossacks, from the air of the room, from the sound of their language, from each of their quiet bear-like movements. Since he was carried into this room, even Schnarrenberg had not spoken a word. “ It will grind us to powder — this dark country! ” So thought we all. At midnight the door opened to admit a peasant girl. The lamplight fell upon her face — hers was the only figure I did not see as a silhouette. She carried an earthen jar, and a piece of

white bread was in one of her hands. After a few steps she stopped, contracted her shoulders as if she were freezing, and looked around her as though searching for help. “Go on, Mascha! ” said the surgeon. “ None of them can harm you any more! They will all eat out of your hand....” She passed down the rows of recumbent soldiers, remained standing at times, only to proceed again hesitatingly. It was easy to see that she had but one piece of bread, one jar of water, and that she wanted to give to him who had the greatest need. A few raised their hands. A few called: “Here.” The mutilated Cornet shrieked in a cracked voice: “ Hildegard, Hildegard! ” For an instant the Cossack held his lamp over his head in order that she might see better. Without having come to any decision, she returned to the door and began her way round again.

When for a second time she came to my feet, she stopped. I raised my head as far as I could, for I was indescribably tortured by thirst. Did my youthful face dispel her last doubt? She pushed my neighbour aside a little, stepped in between us, knelt down, laid her arm around my shoulders, and with her left hand placed her jar to my lips. I drank thirstily — the while my eyes remained fixed upon her. She was a flax-blonde, about eighteen years old, with a round childlike face and a motherly mouth. When the jar of milk was nearly empty, she soaked the bread in the remainder and pushed it piece by piece between my teeth. When the Cossack again held his lamp aloft, and its flickering light fell upon her face, I saw that large tears rolled down her cheeks. Slowly, almost tenderly, she laid me back upon the straw. I clung to her hands as a child clings to its mother. Had my fever gone? Or was it all only fever? “There are kind people everywhere! ” I thought. Something good and gentle had touched me and poured new life into my body. In my dying hour I shall see her before me.

Presently an officer came noisily into the room. He brought an order. The surgeon stopped his work at once — little Blank was at that moment under his butcher’s hands. Six or seven stretcher-bearers carried us away by our hands and legs. The pain of my wounds had for an hour past been unbearable. The bearers laid us down outside upon a meadow. The grass was tall and wet with dew. The sky above us was infinitely calm. “ They are taking us away,” grumbled Schnarrenberg. “ They are afraid, these swine, that tomorrow our comrades will liberate us if they leave us here.” I did not believe it. Neither did Briinninghaus, who said: “They only want to make room for the next lot.” After an hour had passed by, a train of wagons arrived — thirty or forty — each horse’s head tied to the wagon ahead. We were roughly thrown upon the straw in the vans; but this time we were not placed together — a Russian was laid next to each German. “So that we cannot escape,” Briinninghaus remarked sarcastically. The wagons were tiny and did not hold more than a couple of men apiece. A Russian officer was laid next to me. He was unconscious. “ It will go well with me,” I thought.

Slowly the column wound its way out of the village, escorted by a squadron of Cossacks. For a while the road ran across level country; then we entered an immense forest. It seemed to me as though the road was passing between two steep black walls reaching up to heaven. If they had come any nearer to each other, I should have been crushed between them. The road was full of holes. At times I was thrown against my companion; at others he was rolled over upon me. Nevertheless it might have been worse for me. In the wagon ahead the Russian screamed unceasingly — it sounded as though a dying dog were inside him. Every now and then the Cossacks came riding along the train of wagons; they were no longer good-natured and friendly. Perhaps Schnarrenberg was right after all; we had been victorious somewhere. Each time they rode past they made vicious thrusts at the Germans with their long lances. Couldn’t they hit, or didn’t they want to hit? Twice the sideboards of my
wagon, close beside my body, were splintered by the points of their lances.

When we reached the middle of the forest, the Russian officer in my wagon grew restless, uttered suppressed groans, and began throwing himself about. I turned my head and looked at him. He was a big bearded powerful man. The right side of his face and his chest were bandaged. “Oh!” he groaned, “ Oh! ” I moved aside a little to avoid hurting him. From the appearance of the left half of his face he seemed to be weeping. Presently he raised himself up and seized the bandages on his head with his hands. I sought to hold his hands in order to prevent him from tearing off the bandages. A fierce fight ensued. He grasped me by the throat. As I was trying to free myself from his grip, he tore the bandages from his head with a jerk. His cheek was cleft from the temple to the chin. Through his jaws I could see his white teeth grinning at me in the blackness of the night. At the same moment he began to rave. There was something peculiarly gruesome about his shrieks, which seemed to come, not from his mouth, but from the gaping slit in his cheek. He threw his arms about so violently that I was almost pushed out of the wagon, and I was forced to grasp the side with all my might in order to prevent myself from falling out. Gradually he began to pant and his breath came in gasps. I drew a sigh of relief. “He is dying,” I thought thankfully. The wagons rolled on unceasingly while in front of us the spavins of our horses rubbed monotonously against each other. The stars glittered hard and cold above our heads.

With the next jolt of the wagon the Russian rolled over on top of me, like a sack of flour, and his cleft cheek fell wet and cold against my lips. I distinctly tasted his blood in my mouth, and I thrust him violently away from me. I felt the hair rising upon my head, and my eyes seemed to be starting from their sockets, but, nevertheless, I turned round deliberately to gaze upon him. “ At last he is dead,” I thought to myself. “ What more can I ask? Is it not better than if he were still fighting with me?” It was not better. I could not keep my eyes away from his face—that unbelievably terrible moonlit face — from which the cheek, with a large piece of beard, hung down upon his chest. Yet it was less frightening to look at it than to imagine it beside me in the dark. His body was still warm; the cheek was already cold. Each time a jolt of the wagon caused it to fall across my face, I felt it. “Our Lord in heaven — hallowed be Thy name.... Thy trespass come upon us.... We forgive Thee... as Thou forgivest us....” I began to pray, and to hear voices — metallic voices that rang like great bells. Was I going mad?

I did not go mad. If morning had not come soon... ? The voices and the bells vanished with the fresh dawn. The body beside me lost its unnatural appearance. The morning was bright and sunny as the column came to a standstill in the market square of the village of Auts. A dozen peasant women went from wagon to wagon with pitchers and cups. When they reached the wagon.in which I lay, they clapped their hands to their faces. ‘‘ What is the matter? ” a Cossack called out, as he came quickly up to the wagon. “Have you killed him, you damned sausage-eater?” “No...no.” A peasant woman filled a cup with a red juice and held it to my lips. “ What — give him a drink, the dog! ” exclaimed the Cossack, dashing the cup from her hand. A small crowd gathered. Six or eight Cossacks came running up. “ Come along, you fellows! ” the first yelled out. “Let us water this little dog.” Beside the wagon stood a pump, at which they filled their mouths. Then, standing with swelled cheeks in a circle around me, and bending down grinning over my face, they promptly spat out the water in their mouths all over me. One had a nose that was a mass of ulcers, and the upper lip of another was swollen with syphilis. Ten to twelve times they went to the pump and returned to squirt out the water over me. Soon I was wet from head to foot,

while'the water ran down from the wagon in sputtering rivulets upon the pavement. A few peasant women began to cry. “I wish I could die now! ” the thought passed through my mind. “Must I be degraded still more deeply?” Finally some ambulance men came to place the dead Russian upon a stretcher and to bear him away to join a heap of dead from the other wagons. “Forward! Forward!” an officer called out. The Cossacks ran to mount their horses. A peasant woman wiped my face with her apron. A young girl put two cucumbers and a piece of black bread upon my chest. The horses started, and we began to move onwards. The sodden straw was pressed into a thin layer that no longer sufficed to deaden the jolting of the wagon. My tunic was filled with pus and blood. My two wounds seemed to be extending ever more deeply into my body. I was terribly cold.

In the afternoon we reached Mitau, where we were again carried into an empty room with a straw-covered floor. Two ambulance men brought a big cauldron of hot schtschi. Each of us was given a tin bowl and a wooden spoon. A stimulating odour of cabbage and meat-broth pervaded the room. We all fell to greedily. Podbielski had emptied his bowl before the ambulance man had even had time to fill it. “This infernal _ smell of cabbages!” he said plaintively. “This would be enough for a sparrow, but not for me.”

While the meal was in progress, stretcher-bearers came in and carried us away, one after another, upon stretchers, They laid me upon an operating-table in a bright room smelling strongly of iodine mingled with a heavy Russian perfume. A young doctor was working away with blood-stained instruments. A pretty nurse at once began to busy herself with my trousers. “Off with them! ” she said, with the peculiar intonation of the pure-blooded Russian. A flush spread over my cheeks, and I involuntarily placed both my hands between my thighs. “Darling,” she said in Russian, with a little laugh,

‘did you ever see a soldier who is so ashamed? ” The young doctor turned smilingly around. “No,” he said, and gave me a look. “ But this is not one. This is only a boy.” He came close to me and asked in German: “Is it already necessary in Germany to put children into the regiments? ” “I was a volunteer,” I replied stiffly. He frowned as he bent over my bandages. “Why so wet?” he asked abruptly. “Because your Cossacks ‘spat upon me!” J answered loudly. “Our soldiers are devils, Niki,” the nurse said indignantly, while she held her hands to my forehead to press me back in case I should struggle. Her precaution was scarcely necessary. My bandages were so sodden that the crusts had softened. “‘ Come on, little soldier,” the nurse said, when all was over. “ Put on this hospital-coat while I dry your clothes.” “Yes, do, Sonjuschka,” said the doctor, as he exchanged glances with her. “She must be his sweetheart,” I thought excitedly to myself. Encouraged by his looks, she rubbed my body dry, wrapped a red hospital-cloak around me, and placed a cigarette between my lips. “There! Now you are all right, aren’t you, little soldier? ” she asked in a motherly tone. | |

As evening came on, we were placed in a hospital train, in which the beds rose in three tiers above each other. There were white sheets, woollen horse-covers, and pillows. Everything was clean and quiet. A sister walked up and down. An orderly brought bottles and chambers. At the last moment the nurse from the bandaging-room arrived with my clothes. “Thank you, I said in fluent Russian. “ Please greet your friend from me.” She gave a little cry. ““ You know Russian? ” she asked in a frightened voice. “Yes,” I replied, “a little.” She laughed bashfully and ran off quickly. The train began to move. I looked out in silence. I stretched myself in my white sheets. I would have liked to have someone to love. My uniform lay across my feet, cleaned as well as possible, and dry. Did it not give forth an odour of a heavy Russian perfume?

Briinninghaus lay next to me, a slender man with a smooth clean-shaven face, neatly upturned moustache, and supple fingers. He gazed contentedly up at the ceiling with his hands beneath his head. “‘ Damnation! ” he said joyfully, “I should like to stay here until peace comes. Come here with the chamber, Russky comrade.” My sergeant major lay two beds farther away. “ Well, Cornet,” he said, “now it is possible to endure it. How did you fare during the night?” ” Oh!” I replied, “tolerably.” “I was not so lucky,” he said. “The fellow next to me wanted to take liberties, began to cling to me and to cry out for his mother. I kept on hitting him in the mouth until he saw his mistake and left me alone.”

As we entered Riga, night had fallen. For half an hour we were carried through dark streets until we were unloaded in the courtyard of a building with many windows. Hundreds lay about on stretchers. Not a soul took any notice of us. “ Organization, organization! ” growled Schnarrenberg. It was cool and the dew was falling. I distinctly heard my neighbour’s teeth chattering. If I had not had dry clothes now.... There - came a distinct rumbling as of thunder. The front was far distant. The sound must come from the sea. It must be the guns of a warship. “Tell me, Cornet,” inquired Schnarrenberg, “ isn’t your father a naval officer?” “ Yes,” I replied. “ Don’t you know where he is stationed at present? ” “In his last letter — truly, in his last letter there was something about a naval attack on Riga.” “ Good God, then it is they! ” He became excited and began to listen for each explosion. “ You will see. In three days Riga will have fallen. In three days we shall be free.” I made no reply. “ Perhaps he is right ” — the thought flashed through my mind—“ but... no!” I did not want to believe it, for it would have been too terrible if.... Nevertheless I found myself listening with him for each explosion. For the first time since I had been captured, my thoughts flew to my father. “ If he knew! ” I thought feverishly.

At last we were carried up many stairs and brought into a room the entrance to which was guarded by a barred prisondoor. Before the tiny door stood two sentries with fixed bayonets. At times one had believed that one was nothing more than a wounded soldier. Here for the first time we realized that we were prisoners. By chance I was given a bed which was still warm; the coverlet was smeared with blood. Schnarrenberg and Schmidt II were placed — still on their stretchers — in the aisle between the beds to the right and left of me. The mutilated Cornet was laid at my feet. Although he was still alive, his cries had sunk to mere gasps. He was so weak that he could not even call “ Hildegard” any more. Nor had he sufficient breath left to utter three syllables consecutively. We could only just hear him moaning “ Hil—Hil—” and every gasp he gave resembled this sound.

That night Schmidt II died. He was lying next to me, so I could witness all the stages of his dying. He was only slightly wounded — the slightest wound of us all — but he got tetanus; for we were not given any tetanus serum. For three or four hours he lay stiff, only his eyes were alive — eyes that regarded me unblinkingly. “ He has only a scratch, has only been grazed, yet has to die””—so the thought passed through my brain. “It was not even necessary to carry him; he saved me — and yet has to die.” If he had not chanced to come past that place? A terrible doubt stirred within me. Is everything chance? Is everything God? At last his eyes became fixed upon one spot, dimmed slowly, and became covered with a milky veil. Almost at the same instant the Cornet at my feet stretched himself out. “Give me his pocket-book,” I demanded hoarsely, “I will write to her.” As it was being handed over to me, a photograph dropped out —a girl, young, dark. On the back was written: “T pray for you every day. God is good.”
God is good? No—I wanted to sleep; I did not want to think of it. But it was not sleep that came after a while, it was

more of a falling down into dark depths, a sort of semiconsciousness due to exhaustion. Suddenly I became aware that all the doors were opening. A voice called out: “ Attention! ” A broad-shouldered naval officer came rapidly and with a light step into the room. He was followed at a respectful distance by his suite. From bed to bed he went, coming nearer all the time, until he suddenly stretched forth both arms. “Well, my dear boy? ” I started up. No one was standing before me. No familiar voice was speaking to me. Around me lay only the dying and the dead. Of my feverish dream nothing was true, except that at times the window panes rattled with the thunder of the distant cannonade. “ Might it be possible after all? ” I asked myself. “Have I a presentiment? ” I fell back in bed again. Once more the door opened — and again—and again. This continued until dawn, until the fever left me. Six or eight times I started up. “ Well, my dear boy....”

Morning had scarcely come before a crowd of orderlies noisily burst into our room. “Jdji, pascholl,” they cried excitedly. Before we had time to learn what was the matter, they had carried us out again through the great barred doorway. No one in whom was the least spark of life was left behind. From the doorway I cast a parting glance backwards into the room. Schmidt II and the Cornet had been rolled from their stretchers to make room for others. Both lay upon their stomachs in front of my bed, with their faces distorted by pain, as if they had been upon the rack. “The whole hospital is being evacuated,” whispered an infantryman with a shot in his pelvis. “It is said that only one railway line is open. All the others are already under the fire of our ships.” Schnarrenberg’s jaws were grinding while his bulldog face, with its prominent cheek-bones, brushed-up moustache, and low furrowed forehead, was green with excitement. “ Didn’t I say so, Cornet? Didn’t I say so? Oh, these swine — at the last moment.” I was quite apathetic. I no longer had strength enough left to be sorry or glad. I only wanted quiet — quiet at last for weeks, months, years. Certainly I pictured to myself how it might have been but.... Undoubtedly he would have brought me to Kiel on board his ship in the beautiful cabin in which my mother’s portrait hung.

A broad flat landscape flew past the windows of our hospital ‘train. At times we still heard the rumble of the cannonade. At times the wheels ran with a grating rattle across the catchpoints — every jerk and jolt stung as though red-hot needles were being thrust into our wounds — and with each revolution we were borne farther away from our hope. The feeling that at this last moment we had been forced to go away —that we had, so to speak, in this hour been taken captive for a second time — was a torturing thought to us all. Even the buoyant Briinninghaus, who adapts himself to all situations, had fallen silent. Podbielski could have been restored to his high spirits by a good dinner, but in the haste of departure food had been forgotten. And my sergeant? Schnarrenberg cursed without ceasing. His bile rose into-his sharp-cut face, and he looked as yellow as saffron.

It was again night when we reached Moscow. Once more we were left to lie for hours on the platform before we were finally carried into specially arranged tram-cars to be driven, rattling and jerking, through the poorly lighted streets. Once more we were borne through high barred gates, at which heavily armed sentries stood, and set down in the broad central corridor of a building resembling barracks. In a side corridor forty to fifty dead bodies had been heaped up, one above the other; and fresh bodies were constantly being brought down from the different floors. Beds had to be obtained —vacant beds. One after another we were lifted up and carried into a musty bathroom. We were thrust — our bandages still on — into lukewarm water with a pungent smell. Three handfuls of a greycoloured ointment were slapped on to each of us beneath the armpits and on the hair on the lower part of our bodies. An

enormous bear-like orderly wrapped me undried in hospital linen and bore me off in his arms into a large ward in which a petroleum lamp burned dimly. I heard Briinninghaus say: “That, gentlemen, is known as a water-cure.” My bed was again half warm and covered with stinking pus. My saturated linen clung to my body, both my bandages were dripping, and my straw mattress was wet through. On my bed was no coverlet, only a dirty sheet. My teeth chattered, my wounds burned, and the clumps of pus on my pillow so disgusted me that my stomach turned in revolt. Yet I could not raise my head, nor even hold it over the side of the bed, and I simply vomited in front of me upon my chest and throat. As my stomach was empty of food, only phlegm and bile were thrown up. Nevertheless it sufficed to conceal the stink of the pus; it was not foreign to me; it was my own — and that was something.

As day dawned, I perceived that Schnarrenberg lay on my left; on my right lay a stranger with a full beard. He must have been shot through the lungs, for he coughed frequently, and flecks of light-red foam appeared on his lips. Briinninghaus and Podbielski lay on the other side of the passage between the beds. They looked better than any of the rest of us. Of the others — Schmidt I, little Blank, and Bahr—there was no trace. “Good morning, gentlemen,” Briinninghaus called across. “ Damnation! That was a shearing. It is to be hoped that now we shall enjoy a well-earned rest, eh? ” And he added, as he turned his head to all sides: “ A fine place, I must say.”

““If there were not such a smell of cabbage! ” snarled Podbielski, who was an awkward giant with the eyes of a dog, a labourer’s hands the size of plates, and a beard that hung over his chest like a brown bearskin. He was already known to all as “ Pod.”

I looked from one to the other. I was so weak and brokendown that I could scarcely speak. My only desire was to tell them with my eyes how glad I was that they at least were near me. “How are you, Junker?” Briinninghaus asked at once. With an effort I smiled, and replied gratfully: “All right, Briinninghaus, all right.” “If I could but crawl,” said Pod, “I would take care of our little one.” “Here, orderly,” he called in his deep voice. An orderly came. (Orderlies are of various natures——some are kind and obliging, others brutal and rude.) Pod threw off his coverlet, pointed towards me, and said: “I feel hot. Take it to him, comrade.” “‘ No, Pod, what for? ” I exclaimed in a low voice. “ Shut up, Junker.”

At eight o’clock came the nurses — gentle creatures with well-kept hands — figures out of fairyland. Entrancing little shoes with high heels, and silk stockings of all shades, showed from beneath their snow-white dresses. A tall, dark-haired nurse took charge of my row of beds. As she passed my bed, she came to a standstill. “‘How old?” she asked. “‘Seventeen,” I answered softly, so that no one should hear. When she bent over my head in order to inscribe my board with a white cross, I experienced a wonderful sensation of pleasure as I caught the smell of hair-water and fresh soap.

Before noon orderlies arrived with stretchers to carry us two by two into the bandaging-room. After a short time a heartrending chorus of shrieks was to be heard. Up till then I had believed that all persons in pain emitted the same sounds; now I know that every nationality screams in a different way; and on that very first morning I could distinguish the German from the Austrian, the Hungarian from the Turk. Moreover, I very soon learnt that the coarse-grained bear-like men roar the loudest, and that the delicate and weak are possessed of great powers of resistance. Together with Schnarrenberg I was borne into the bandaging-room. “ We will not scream, Cornet, will we? ” he muttered at the last moment. “ We will just show these nurses... !” When I was laid upon the table, all the nurses gathered round me. “Look, doctor, a boy!” said a dainty blonde. The doctor gazed at me in surprise. He had

large grey eyes. His left eye regarded me as fixedly as if it were made of glass. “ How old? ” he asked. “ Eighteen,” I replied defiantly, turning my head towards Schnarrenberg, partly through anger, partly to derive encouragement from him, but also because my shirt had been rolled up under my armpits and my trousers drawn down below my knees. If I had had the use of my hands, I would have defended myself; but my arms were bound down with broad straps. Schnarrenberg had practically the same injury —a fracture of the upper thighbone. When his bandage was torn down, his face altered beyond recognition —and yet he did not scream. Then my bandage was torn down, something cold touched my skin, and I heard the clash of a couple of instruments. “ Be careful, please,” said the dainty nurse. I gazed fixedly at Schnarrenberg. Oh, no, I would not be less brave! If it were possible for him.... A pair of cool feminine hands were laid upon my forehead, and pressed my head firmly against the table. I smelt the odour of iodine, and a red-hot flame burned through my thigh. I gurgled noisily. Schnarrenberg’s sardonic face sank rapidly, ever more rapidly, into a black fathomless abyss.

While we were being bandaged, our beds were covered with clean sheets, urine-bottles were laid in them, and when I awoke from my faint, all was quiet around me. The June sun shone brightly in through the windows. The dark nurse was walking swiftly to and fro. “ Well, Junker,” Briinninghaus called across to me, “did they send high electric currents through your nerves? Did they turn off the switch? ” An electrician by calling, he was fond of using technical terms. I smiled in some embarrassment. “ You must scream, Junker,” he went on in a disapproving tone, “screaming is good —all the rest is nonsense. To what end? No! One must scream, one feels half as much.... What need for us to play the hero here? It is heroism enough that we have not hanged ourselves long ago.” “ Cowardly pack! ” snarled Schnarrenberg. But nobody heard him. I turned over on my side and saw four pieces of sugar lying upon my night-table. Each afternoon we got a cup of tea with sugar — but how was it that on the other night-tables only two pieces of sugar were lying? I called the nurse, pointed to my sugar, and asked: “ Why have I four? ” I spoke in German. There was no need for them to know that I spoke their language. Much was to be learnt if they did not suspect it. She pointed smilingly at Pod. “No, Pod, that won’t do,” I called over. Pod only grinned. “ Don’t make a fuss,” he said kindly. :,

After tea I slept for a time. When I awoke, I saw Briinninghaus and Pod sitting on the backs of their beds and peering out of the window on to the street. I learnt afterwards that their window looked out upon the Moskva, and that each afternoon naked men and women bathed there. “Look,” said Briinninghaus, “ she is fine, isn’t she? Round before and behind — like my old woman.” “ You only want to make our mouths water,” a voice called out from a neighbouring bed. Suddenly Pod turned round and saw that I was watching them. “ Fine doings, Junker!” he said. “But just wait a few days longer; then I will carry you over here. An hour of moving pictures every afternoon will do you good.”

I was scarcely able to eat anything, although I made the greatest efforts to swallow the food, for I knew that otherwise I could not get on my feet again. But my efforts were of little use. For one thing, I was too weak to hold a spoon; for another, I found food to be terribly repugnant to me, in a manner I was powerless to get over. My only comfort was that I could give it to Pod, who was always hungry, as a small acknowledgment of his kindness. “ Are you mad? ” he. cried out, as I passed it over to him for the first time. “ Why? ” I asked innocently. “ You should eat it yourself. How the devil do you think that your spindleshanks will heal of themselves? ” “Hold your tongue! ” I called back. Schnarrenberg

spoke only with me. He showed plainly that he felt himself at odds with his fate, and worried me about thirty times a day with the remark: “If we could only know how matters are at the front!” Undoubtedly we should have liked to know; in that sense he was right. But we learnt absolutely nothing. An orderly —a damn fool in any case — once said: “Berlin in ruins! ” Naturally we did not believe him.

Day succeeded day. Pod could already hobble about a little, but he only did so when nobody was looking; for the moment a man could crawl, came the order: “To Siberia! ” and we had agreed among ourselves to remain together as long as possible. The man on my right, who was shot through the lungs, grew paler and paler. Yet each day he spoke of getting well in a short time. Once he told me that he was a traveller for a first-class firm in Possneck, in Thuringia, and that he had a wife and two children——a daughter, Anna, aged nine, a boy of eight, named Francis, Both were doing very well at school.

If it had not been for the daily bandaging, life would have been endurable in this hospital, which was said to be one of the best in Moscow; the so-called “sight-seeing hospital,” as we were told. Each morning, with the appearance of the orderlies and the stretchers, conversation suddenly ceased. It ceased even before the piercing shrieks began that rendered every word inaudible — shrieks that continued until noon came. For some days past, the wound in my right thigh had been suppurating. Although swathed many times round my thigh, the bandage was always a greenish-yellow colour and smeared with pus each morning. My temperature-chart resembled forked lightning; and each morning the line began to shoot upwards anew. I awoke with a clear head, to think: “God be praised! now I have done with it! ” But afternoon had scarcely come before my head became filled with a curious heaviness; and in an hour’s time the heads and beds of my neighbours were swaying around me in a rocking mass. Once more I returned to the front to shoot and stab around me—to be pierced by lances and slashed by swords. Each night I was taken captive anew, died afresh, lay beside the dying officer again, and was spat upon once more from the syphilitic mouths. When, aroused by the dreadful realism of my dreams, I started up and thought: “ Night is over,” the striking of a clock told me that barely thirty minutes had elapsed. I must have experienced all this with terrible reality and sensitiveness, for in the morning Pod’s quiet eyes told me that I had tossed about violently. “Perhaps,” I thought, “my fever-chart will show yet another zigzag. Nearly every day the curve mounts up to forty or forty-one, and if it keeps on long enough, my heart will cease to work for all time.” Nevertheless I had clear moments at night every now and then. It was certainly no fancy due to fever when I felt recently that a woman sat upon my bed, kissed me tenderly upon my burning forehead —her lips were as cool as if touched by ice — and said softly: “Spatsch, spatsch, sleep, sleep!” That was certainly no fancy, for Briinninghaus told me that, when the nurse was on night-duty, she always came and sat upon my bed, and that she had kissed me as I had felt. Was it the dainty blonde from the bandaging-room? Is it to be wondered at that I adored her? And not I alone, but all of us, loved these nurses because they were so sweet and clean, although we were unable to talk much with them, as they did not understand anything we said. Always when they took hold of us, raised us up, or put on fresh sheets, and sought to be really kind, they hurt us. Nevertheless we often called them and put up with a little pain in order amidst that dirt and misery to feel the touch of delicate clean hands and to drink in the smell of perfume and hair-lotion. Yes! we were all filled with a secret love for them all. An ideal, or Platonic, love, which, while it blossomed into fantastic fruit in days of separation, yet sank to
a painful longing for separation in the days when we were together.

On the morning that ushered in our third week in the hospital, Schnarrenberg was cursing with a quite peculiar bitterness. What was the matter with him? Was his strength giving out? Once more we were laid upon the slaughter benches and strapped down like sacrificial lambs. As usual I turned my eyes towards his coarse face to gain courage from his strength. This morning, however, he avoided my gaze and stared up at the ceiling with wide-opened eyes. A nurse was handling red perforated little tubes, which neither he nor I had seen until that morning. The doctor seized one, gave it a brief examination, and thrust it rapidly into Schnarrenberg’s wound. Instantly Schnarrenberg’s limbs became so tense that the leather straps that bound them threatened to break; he drew breath twice like bellows and let out a piercing shriek. Something broke within me. “Keep cool, keep cool,” said the dainty nurse. No, no! I saw another red tube in her hands, a similar tube.... The moment the doctor touched me, I roared like a wild beast.

From that morning onwards, Schnarrenberg never spoke a word to any of us. For four days I saw nothing but his broad back and bull-like neck. If he had not been so naturally ruddy, one might have thought that he was blushing with shame. There was certainly no other reason to account for his stubborn silence; he must have been ashamed. Sometimes nothing could be done with him, poor fellow! If something had not occurred to rouse him suddenly from his sullenness and self-dissatisfaction, he would probably have remained silent for weeks on end. We all suddenly and simultaneously observed that the behaviour of the nurses had strangely altered. Although they continued to do their work as heretofore, they were perceptibly cold and short with us. While we were still pondering over this, the rough and careless conduct of the

orderlies made this change still more evident. Something must certainly have happened at the front. They must have recently sustained a heavy reverse. This dim presentiment was confirmed one afternoon when little Blank, who could now walk on crutches, again turned up amongst us. He was a frail little man, a clerk in civil life, with the eyes of a girl, narrow drooping shoulders, and a contracted, sunken-in chest. “ I am in the next ward,” he said, “ but I could not come before.” He drew a ragged bit of paper from his pocket and slyly pushed it beneath my sheet. “It is a bit of a Russian newspaper — I found it in the lavatory. Perhaps there is something in it about the front.” I almost trembled as I raised the ragged paper to my eyes beneath the twofold shelter of his and Pod’s backs. “We have the devil’s own luck,” I said; “it is a bit of a report from the front. I can just manage to read: ‘ The fortified area of Brest Litovsk had to be evacuated for strategic reasons. We have taken up new positions....’” “Ah! You swine! ” said Briinninghaus. “ Now we know why....” “For strategic reasons,” laughed Pod. Little Blank at once hobbled off to tell the news to his ward. “Ill be back immediately,” he said cheerfully. With a jerk Schnarrenberg turned over. “God!” he said to himself. “ Now we are getting on again! Now we shall have peace in a month!” The news passed from one to another, and a bright spark of hope leapt from bed to bed. All of a sudden the ward was filled with a humming as if a swarm of bees had flown into it. “I shall just be well by the time we can go home,” said the man with the shot lungs, and smiled to himself.

Of the nurses, only the dainty blonde in the bandagingroom continued to be the same as before; all the others covered their bodies with a prickly skin. Some of the male nurses poked fun at our wounds and spat upon us on the least provocation. But the doctor with the glass eye remained unchanged, and we all loved him for it. The orderlies’ conduct grew worse

each day. Not a single one of us was now placed upon a stretcher without being forced to cry out in pain. “There is Brest Litovsk for you, you Huns!” I heard one say. As they came for me one morning, Pod sat down upon my bed. When they nearly let me fall from the stretcher, he was upon them in one bound. “ You have not tasted blood for a long time, you damned carriers of chamber-pots!” he roared aloud, raising his sledge-hammer of an arm. One stretcher-bearer grew pale; the other was about to turn nasty, but a glance at Pod’s wild eyes and herculean body completely silenced him.

One Saturday a great house-cleaning was carried out. We were just thinking that a general was about to inspect the hospital, when a number of ladies came rustling in. The matron —a sour old bird— a couple of old maids who looked like governesses, and two young girls.

“* Now I must show Your Imperial Highnesses our youngest Hun! ” I heard the old bird say. The blood went to my head. They all stepped up to my bed and looked at me with big eyes. ‘Like a caged monkey,” thought I angrily. I clenched my teeth and put on a haughty look, but I saw all the same that both girls were fairy-like creatures, pretty as pictures, with fine narrow noses, large, shining feminine eyes, delicately curved lips.

“That was something ultra fine, if old Briinn is not mistaken,” murmured Briinninghaus, following their scent like a pointer as they passed out. I found out later from the orderly that they were two daughters of the Czar, the Grand Duchesses Olga and Tatiana.

In the afternoon the music from a military band, with resounding brass and clash of kettle-drums, came up from the Moskva. Pod looked round; nobody was in the room; all had run out into the corridor to look at the parade. He groped his way to my bed and turned back my coverlet. “Sit upon my arm, Junker, there is something to look at!” I sat up on his left arm —a child at the breast of a bear. Carrying me cautiously to his bed, he let me down at the window, shoved a pillow behind my back, and sat down next to me, his strong arm round my shoulder.

Opposite the window was a small church, a typical Russian church, with fifteen onion-shaped cupolas, all of them painted sky-blue and studded with gold stars. A newly formed regiment passed down the street, a number of standards at its head, new, rich, beautiful flags. Long-bearded popes walked to the right and left and disappeared with the flags into the church. Singing began, rang out heavily, and was followed by a long and solemn silence. “Now they are consecrating the flags,” I said softly, somewhat moved.

“Indeed? ” said Briinn mockingly. After a while little Blank —the girl —came in and with bright eyes sat down at my other side. Again the blast of trumpets, the dull beating of the kettle-drums. Accompanied by the venerable popes, the flags came back out of the church door. All jubilantly waved their caps, many reverently crossed themselves. The regiment fell into line and to loud music marched down the street to the railway station —to the front.
“If there were no military music, there would only be half as many wars,’ said Briinn suddenly.

“Yes, Briinn....” said Blank, lost in thought, “ and these popes,” he continued, “they are representatives of God, aren’t they? Like our pastors? But how is that now? All are subjects of One, subjects of God, aren’t they? But each one speaks against the other.... ‘Give victory to our flags!’ says the pope. ‘ No, give it to ours,’ says the pastor....”
“It’s a difficult matter,” said Briinn. “Perhaps in the evening, when work is over, the Lord plays heads and tails with St. Peter about it? ”
“Don’t talk rot!” cried Blank angrily, immediately looking helplessly round. “ No, listen, Ensign, all the priests of

the world are appointed to glorify Him, are they not? But that means to serve love, charity, compassion, to avoid pain and violence? How is it possible, therefore, that—-” He broke off, he could not go on. “Oh, bother,” he said suddenly, and went out.

The wound in my thigh suppurated more strongly every day, and my fever did not abate. I was so weak that my comrades had to feed me —I could not carry a full spoon to my lips. Every morning I swam in a puddle of greenish-brown pus; a smell rose from my bed-quilt worse than that from decomposition. Perhaps some poison had come into my wound? Perhaps it had been caused by the wetting at that time? At all events my blood was carrying on a violent combat against a foreign, fatal power, at every moment hurling millions of leucocytes against those destructive powers which from day to day enlarged my wound and which had already transformed it into a white, dead mass twice as large as the palm of the hand.

Since the morning of my arrival in this hospital I had not seriously thought of death. Now I felt darkly and oppressively that I should not be able to endure this daily weakening much longer; that some day my body, unable to withstand the progress of the pestilence, or to overcome the nightly fever, must abandon the struggle.
‘Must it be? ” I asked myself a hundred times. “ Then was all suffering in vain... ?”

One afternoon, just as Pod was feeding me with tea by the spoonful, two strange orderlies came into our ward with a stretcher. They had paper slips in their hands and walked searchingly between the rows of beds. I gave such a start that the contents of my full spoon fell down on my bed. “ What’s the matter, Junker?” asked Pod.
I had felt it; they did want me. “ Nu, pascholl!” said the first one, taking down my fever tablet and laying it at the head of the stretcher.
“‘That is the ward for the amputated,” said the man with the shot lung importantly.
“Nu, pascholl!” repeated the first orderly. The other intimated that he would fetch the surgeon.
““Come on, go with them,” said Pod. “It’s of no use. Be sensible! Besides, they dare not amputate without your consent.”
“My friend Mayer,” the man with the shot through his lung interposed, “was amputated against his will. They simply narcotized him while he slept! ”
*“‘ Hold your tongue, stupid hound! ” cried Pod wildly.
I was trembling all over. Should I submit, or should I rebel? My heart would soon refuse to work. In my condition it would not take long.

“Come, be calm!” Pod repeated, taking my spidery hands between his great paws and stroking them sheepishly. “ You will only be under observation at first—for eight days at least! And then, if you do not want... you can be on the watch now you know what to do! ”
I fell back. “ Yes, Pod,” I said. “ Yes, Pod....”

As they put me on the stretcher, I accidentally encountered Schnarrenberg’s eyes. They were large and round and seemed as if a new light were in them. All looked after me anxiously, and with difficulty Pod accompanied me to the door.
“TI shall come up every day,” he said eagerly. “In three days I shall be up to climbing stairs; I shall begin to practise
today! ” His huge figure remained standing within the frame of the broken-down door, and there was a look on his broad, round face which I had never seen there before.

The ward on the first floor afforded a sight at which cold iron seemed to press against my chest. The man with the shot through his lungs was right; none of its inmates possessed all his limbs. It was to be seen by the faces of those who lay in the beds that they had gone through something terrible. Those who hobbled about between the beds on crutches or sticks had lost arm or leg or both. In the aisle, on a small chest with wheels, sat a man from whom even both legs up to the thigh, and one arm up to the elbow, had been amputated. He was the first to greet me.

I was put in a bed standing by itself at a window from which I had the same view as from Pod’s bed —the gay church with the onion-shaped cupolas, the shore of the Moskva, where hundreds of people were bathing. Opposite me was lying a Bosnian, a dark man with the build of a gladiator, whose brown, Oriental skin had a colour as if white blood were flowing beneath it. Next to him was an old man with the beard of a forester, who reminded me of a Tyrolean wood-chopper.

A hundred eyes looked at me curiously, questioningly. Alas, I knew myself what an event it was for a ward when a *‘new-comer ” is brought in, but it was painful to be such a new-comer. After a while the first one ventured to come near me. He was one of the luckier ones; he had lost only one leg.
“Well, comrade,” he said in a friendly voice. “It is better here than downstairs, eh? To be sure, something will be taken from you, but... what will it be?” he added inquisitively.
“Then we are in the same boat,” he said comfortingly. He sang a little while he talked. He must have been a Viennese. “No, we are better off than all the others,” he continued.
“We shall soon get home, shall be exchanged. Off with the leg — don’t care a snap! The chief thing is to get home! ”
Before the evening meal the dainty nurse came, sat down on the edge of my bed, and took my hand as if to feel my pulse. “ Well, how goes it? ” she asked in a warm tone.
I took her by surprise. “Nurse, why have I come here? Am I as bad as all that? Must I really —”
“No, no,” she laughed. “ They only want to have you under observation... that does not mean anything.... Many have been taken downstairs again after a week.”

But I did not believe it. Her laugh did not sound genuine. And how was I to believe it if nobody confirmed her? For the first time since my captivity I felt indescribably alone. If at least one of my comrades lay near me.... But these were all strangers, Turks and Bosnians, Austrians and Hungarians - « » not a single German.

I turned round and looked out of the window. The evening sun was glittering on the Moskva, and its rays caused the stars on the church to sparkle. What was Pod doing now, I wondered —and Schnarrenberg and Brinn? After all, had they not been strangers to me up to the moment at which the bullets struck us down next to one another? Yes, they tore the badges and buttons from our collars —at one blow wiped out all boundaries between us, filled up every gulf! — made us perfectly equal, perfectly equal!...

If only they could visit me, I thought. But that might not be for days.... Assuredly Pod would come as soon as he could creep up a single stair, and as assuredly little Blank would come; as soon as he found out that I had gone, was lying here alone, and was to be amputated.... He was ahead of them all. He could already manage to walk on crutches.
I started up. Music came to my ears from a weak little jew’s-harp. It was the old man with the forester’s beard and the Defregger face. He blew with full cheeks, and it was easy to

see that he beat the time with legs that had been amputated at both knees. The two stumps moved in lively rhythm against his thin coverlet, and his pale cheeks violently puffed out the Tyrolean wood-cutter song.

The next morning the dainty nurse, strange to say, was in the bandaging-room on the first floor. As they carried me in, she spoke a few rapid words to the new doctor; but I was so excited that I did not understand what she was saying.

The new doctor was a little, oldish man with bushy eyebrows and gold spectacles. He stood bending over my right leg for a long time, and I noticed that his glance was fixed on me with a compassionate expression.

“No, there is no help for it,” he said to the dainty nurse. ‘* The mortified part is already too extensive and is progressing all the time, so that we can, at most, observe for another four days, no longer....”

“There is nothing definite to be said,” the dainty nurse translated. ““We shall observe for a time.... Nevertheless, it would be as well for you to decide whether you would agree to an amputation. As already said, it does not appear necessary for the present — perhaps not at all—but....” I bit my lips until the blood came. I knew they lied. There was a bitter taste in my mouth.

When I got back into my bed, both worked-up and faint, an enema was being administered to the Bosnian opposite. It was a strange liquid that was being let into him, looking like colourless oil and with an overpowering odour. The gladiator-like Oriental lay with his eyes' wide open — but the more that the graduated glass tube emptied, the more fatigued he got, until his eyes closed almost imperceptibly. The surgeon rose, the orderlies brought in a stretcher. “Go ahead, quickly,” I heard him say, “into the operating-room....”

There was a torturing unrest within me. I felt that something had been done that really ought not to have been done, but before I could come to a clear understanding of it, the Viennese came to my bed. “ He did not wish to be amputated,” he reported. “Devil knows if they will not make use of his powerlessness....”
“So he did not want to be amputated? ” I asked hoarsely.
“No, he would rather be dead. What is he to do without a leg in a wilderness where everyone rides? He has already knocked down a few who tried from behind to get a mask over his face....”

I thought hard. Perhaps this strange enema was a new kind of narcotic for those who rebelled. Well, he would soon be back; then I should know; and I should not allow anyone to give me an enema if I did not.... Yes, if I did not... ! I continued to think. But should I not, after all? I raised my coverlet; it was not better. I was swimming again in a soft, greenish mass. The puss was eating me up; it smelt like decomposing matter. A morbidly increasing need for cleanliness awoke in me to help me. Everything would then be clean and dry again, I said to myself, intoxicated with these words.... There would be no smell, no murderous fever, no more vomiting with disgust at my own body.... And I should get home immediately! But... horses rose up before my eyes. They would no longer exist for me; never more could I get into a saddle, never more feel warm life between my thighs. Nothing would be of value to me any more. I was still so young that I had nothing else!

Fields and forests rose before my eyes. I loved to ramble, I loved nature, but I should no longer be able to stoop to a flower, to a lizard. With crutches or from a wheel-chair the world could not be fully appreciated! Before my eyes there also rose sports grounds, gymnastic apparatus, tennis-courts —no, all these would no longer exist for me....
But I suddenly thought, if I didn’t do it, what then? Then all would be at an end, and I should rot in a foreign country!

Then not even what now seemed so vapid, so little to me would remain. No, it was not little, it was not vapid, it was still enough, more than enough. Should I not keep my eyes, should I not keep my ears? Perhaps all in life that now seemed to me most important was really of little importance. I was still so very young — what did I know?

Only a short while ago I had believed that logarithms and cubic roots were the most important things in life. Our professor had told us so — must we not believe it? Then I saw that they were unnecessary, useless, I learnt that shooting and stabbing were far more important and necessary to life... so perhaps a day would come when J should smile at this as I had done at the other.

I was young, I knew nothing of life. I only felt that it must have other things in it than I had hitherto known; that logarithms and the integral calculus, shooting and killing could not be all. No, far greater and more glorious things were waiting for me without doubt — why else did men so love life? Did I not daily see that everyone clung to it with incomprehensible tenacity, that few gave it up voluntarily, that almost all only renounced it after a terrible fight?

No, I had not yet felt what was truly beautiful in it. I had not yet comprehended its mysteries. I had not yet grasped its meaning. I had not yet tasted its sweetest gifts. I... I had not possessed any woman.

After two hours the Bosnian was. brought back. He lay white as chalk on the stretcher, and all waited in suspense for what he would do. Until evening he slept unnaturally heavily; then, gradually becoming restless, he opened his eyes, one ered, and vomited.

For a while he lay breathing heavily; then his eagle-like nose distended and a paralysing terror overspread his face. I distinctly saw him stealthily, like a thief, slip his hand beneath the coverlet as if to seize something — slowly, slowly.
The next moment he uttered a strange, gurgling sound and tugged like a madman at an invisible resistance. “ Nurse, nurse,” I cried.

When at last a sister came eabing up, the death-rattle was already in his throat. The coverlet was pulled back, bandages were brought in in hot haste.... He lay in a glistening puddle, amputated at the upper thigh and with open wound, and was rapidly sinking. The bandage was grasped so convulsively in his hands that the blood-saturated gauze could no longer be loosened from his fingers.
That was still left for me to do, I thought, if.... No one could hinder me from doing it....

Pod came the very next afternoon. He had actually crept up the stairs on all fours like a dog and was cursing because he had not succeeded in doing it in any other way. “ Why must one drag a two-hundredweight body through the world?” he said grimly, “if it does not even give one the strength to go visiting like a decent Christian? ”
Then he looked at me narrowly, passing his hand unostentatiously over the coverlet along my right leg. “ Everything still present, eh? ” he asked, with a sigh of relief.
““T don’t think so, Pod. What do you say? ”
‘IT think so. In fact, we all think so, even Schnarrenberg. What, after all, depends — ”
“You all think, therefore, that otherwise I should go to the beyond, plainly spoken? ”
Pod squirmed. “ Hm,” he said gloomily, “ I don’t know about that. In fact, nobody can know about that. But if it does not get better, it will blow you over some day, that’s what I think.
Already you look confoundedly chalky. Has nobody here a looking-glass? ”

*T'll bring you one next time! ” His kind face had a tortured look. “ Briefly,” he continued, “I think that you should say ‘Yes.’ The amputated are sent home immediately, I have heard; that is worth something too. What should you stay here for? Who knows what we have to expect? Moreover, you need never go into war again. That is still better — damn it | er
“Yes, Pod,” said I, “ that’s so, but — ”

“There are wonderful artificial legs nowadays,” he interposed. “ A regular industry, let me tell you! ” He expatiated on it in detail, his zeal passing all bounds. “I once read an article by a military surgeon about it. In conclusion he said that the artificial legs were as good as the natural ones....”
In spite of everything, I had to laugh. “ Yes, Pod, that is all quite true — but the operation might fail....”
“Fail? ” asked Pod in astonishment. It was plainly to be seen that he had not thought of that.

““T am already very weak; perhaps I cannot stand it, and then.... There are many here from whom at first only a foot had to be taken off, but it did no good. The wound continued to suppurate.... Then they went on to the knee and, when that failed, even to the upper thigh. The Tyrolean over there at first had only his toes frozen in the Carpathians. And now? Supposing the same happened to me? They can try once only in my case... they cannot go on any farther....”
“ Confounded kettle of fish!” Pod muttered. He was at an end, he did not know how to go on.

After a while he got up to leave. “I must be gone now or there will be the devil to pay with my orderlies, but it just occurs to me...” he continued in a relieved voice, “ you might venture to have it done much sooner than any others of us! ”
““Because they will take particular pains with you! I am thinking of the dainty nurse, you know....”

* Just as I say! Now sleep well.... If possible, ’ll come again tomorrow.” He groped his way out cautiously by the beds, looked back once again from the door, and closed it with ostentatious care. A hot lump rose in my throat. “He is getting down on his knees now,” I said helplessly to myself.

The meal came and passed as usual, and the Tyrolean began in the old way with his wood-cutter song. In the bed of the Bosnian a man had been put both of whose testicles had been shattered by a shot. His face wore an expression that seemed to indicate that he had lost all comprehension.

My thoughts began to concentrate around a small nucleus. I was too weak to be tormented by a pronounced thirst for women; I had too little surplus in me to feel a desire for what was physical of them — no, it was not that — but my soul was still strong enough to give birth to a longing for their spirituality, a longing after the solely feminine, the negative pole as opposed to my young manhood. It was indefinable, this longing, it could not be expressed in words, it was simply present, nothing more.

“No,” I said to myself, “I do not want to die; for I have not yet lived! That bright, rosy bit of life of which we read in books and poems, I have not yet learnt to know. It must be indescribably beautiful, this bit, but it must be most beautiful of all to yield for a first time to its mystery, to forget therein all, all of what has fallen on me during the last weeks and nearly caused me to confuse life with war....”
Could it appear otherwise to me? After those months full of
blood and dirt and murder must it not seem like fairyland — like another and brighter side of existence? Hitherto I had only seen the shadows.

No, I went on thinking, what was a horse, what was a field, what was a tennis-court, after all? What were they compared with this? At all events the fairest still remained for me... and in a half-dream I saw before me a maiden who let me forget all this. Her hands knew nothing of blood, her eyes nothing of corpses, her lips nothing of feverish outcries. In her the light of life was embodied for me, the true, glorious light. . - - And I did not even stop at the thought which thrust itself on me in the continuation of these fancies, that in her I saw and recognized the divinity embodied in human shape, the representative of God in this world, in contrast to the earthliness in which I was now living, smothered in dirt and pus.

Night came, but I did not sleep; a burning longing had seized on me — the longing for life and for what in the first place signified chaste juvenility. I felt uncertainly that this train of thought had made me come to a decision, had perhaps saved me from death.
“* Well? ” I suddenly heard somebody ask.
I started up. “ You,” I said happily.
“Yes.... I only wanted to inquire whether you have made up your mind.”

I looked at her with burning eyes. Her white coat fitted tightly across her breast; her knees rounded themselves in oval curves through her skirt. Her hands looked as if they had paradise to give away. All that I had brooded over, all that my young life and longing had cried out for, suddenly stood tangible before me, like a sign from God become a certainty in her body.
“Yes,” I said firmly. “In three days, nurse.”

Again I passed a night of torment. It seemed to me as if the nights were becoming more and more tormenting — perhaps because the old dreams had been joined by others, by gruesome fancies of severed legs and limbless trunks piled up in baskets.

I crouched down and slowly passed my hand along my right leg, testing every inch, I clasped my knee, its round, movable cap, the shin-bone, the ankle, the toes — everything that was actually so altogether healthy that one would grieve to have it simply thrown away like refuse. I remembered with painful clearness many a thing this leg had done with particular excellence. Was it not the lightning-like wedge that had propelled the football, the limb that had rapidly swung itself across the horse’s back when getting into the saddle? Knee, shin, ankle, toes, all were as sound as ever — must | sacrifice it only because a pointed bit of lead had perforated its upper muscle ?
I was just beginning to waver once more, to balance my resolve to and fro, when the door was pushed open and big Pod marched as one coming to effect a rescue, followed by little Blank.
“Well, my boy,” he said, “ here’s a looking-glass! It is only a fragment, to be sure, but it does not deceive....”

I held it before my face and looked timidly into it. The last time I had seen myself in a mirror was at the front, and now I shrank. Pod had not exaggerated. A little death’s-head looked back at me out of the bit of glass. Its skin lay like thin, yellowish parchment on the bones, its lips were bluish, thin and fleshless, chapped all over, its cheeks sank inward like deep pits. Only my eyes still lived — they were three times as large as they used to be, and had a sickly, burning brilliance.
“Tt is, unfortunately, no beauty-mirror to flatter,” said Pod grumpily.
** Anyway, I have made up my mind,” I said slowly. “Even without the looking-glass, Pod.”
Little Blank looked at me admiringly with his girlish eyes. “You will get home then, Ensign,” he said as if he would like to change places with me.

Before tea someone called from the window: “ Look, just look....” All who could rushed to the window benches. “ It is just like three months ago,” the Viennese called to us. “A new pogrom against the Germans — they drowned eight merchants that time! ” |

We looked out in excitement. On the street beside the river eleven persons were running fast with hundreds of pedlars and labourers at their heels. From all sides the fleeing men were being driven towards the Moskva. Nothing was left for them to do but to jump into it, to save their lives by swimming across. We saw the water splash. A little later eleven heads bobbed up —all had jumped in. “That is enough now, by heaven! ” little Blank whispered. No, by the devil, it was not enough. Half a dozen of the pogrom pursuers jumped into empty boats and with rapid strokes rowed after the swimming men.
““My God, surely they will not... ?” whispered little Blank with rigid lips. |
“ They will, these beasts...” muttered Pod.

He was right, he knew them. One after another they were pushed back by the neck into the water, five, six times, till none came up — like young dogs they drowned them. “But over there one has reached the shore! ” Blank cried.
“ He had better have been drowned,” said Pod. “ They told me what they did with the last one....”

It was far to the other shore. Nevertheless, we saw the boats land, and their inmates overtake and surround the fugitive on the open field. All bent down, ten, a hundred times in quick succession.... The German fell on his knees, for a long time pleadingly holding up his hands. At last he fell down powerless on his face.
“They have stoned him,” said Pod in a hard voice.
There was a riot in the ward. Were they not Germans, were they not our brothers in arms? No orderly is to be seen, no nurse. All looked on at this spectacle, seemingly in calmness.

“ And the police tolerate this? ” Blank asked in a low voice. ** Just as soon as a few harmless peasants stand together for a little talk, the Cossacks beat into them with their knouts in order to disperse these prohibited gatherings. And here? ”
“That all comes from the war!” one cried grimly.
“But these Russians are so pious, so good-natured? ” little Blank asked, beside himself. He was a Catholic.
“ Just let someone read a Czarist paper to you,” said Pod; “then you will know what leads them to such things....”
Little Blank got up. His young face was pale, his thin legs trembled. “I must get to bed,” he said. “I can scarcely keep on my feet.”
At the door he stood again. “ And in this land we are to live? ” he added. “Perhaps for months? And as prisoners? Ensign, I would gladly give my leg if I could get out of this hell that way....”

On the day preceding my amputation a tin of preserved peaches, a box of cigarettes, and some matches were standing on my night-table. I had no idea who had brought them, but drew the things with weak hands into my bed and took out a cigarette. I had not smoked for weeks. My God, what a blessing it was!... Looking round, I saw that the wood-cutter was following my smoke with yearning eyes. “ Do you know who brought them? ” I cried as I threw a cigarette over to him.
“Yes,” he said readily, “my Lieutenant. He gave me my jew’s-harp, too.”
Then I remembered having sometimes seen a young Austrian officer in a red hospital-coat at his bed. He had the head of a musician, was of dark complexion, and dragged his left leg behind him.
* Yes,” said the wood-cutter. “I did not know him, but he is of my regiment, that’s why he always comes....”

This I understood. But what led him to take any notice of me? That I could not understand. Nevertheless the little gift made me as happy as the finest attention of Pod or Briinn. Pod and Briinn were of my regiment, and as a little fellow I had grown up between them. That accounted for it. Moreover, they knew me from the front, and that also accounted for it. But this one never saw me before, never spoke to me.

Assuredly Pod and Briinn’s kind ways kept up one’s faith in man — and I should have despaired if I had not had these simple dragoons about me. But this little deed, and that at a moment when I had none of my comrades about me, made me happy in a way in which perhaps nothing else in life 1 «ll ever make me again.

The cigarette almost made me giddy. Or was it only joy? I relapsed into my brooding. How was it possible that only a short time ago these persons were mercilessly committing murder? I had done so myself certainly — but after daily intercourse with these cripples could I ever do so again?

Sometimes I did not understand myself any more. But was it not terribly difficult to understand that all those deplorable cripples were not victims of some dreadful accident? Was it not incredible that men wanted and made all this, that this helpless trunk in a cart on wheels had not been maimed by a brainless machine, but that a thinking man, with his own hand, had made him what he was now?
I was unnerved, that was it. I should have thought otherwise at the front, but here....

I forced myself to think of Schnarrenberg, my brave sergeant major. Was he still the same, or was he already... ? We had all done our duty, nor had we any time for such thoughts so long as we were at the front — it would have been mad to think of such things there, because we had to defend ourselves. Our homes lay behind us. But here, away from the war.... And, moreover, our hospital, the Grudetzki barracks, was one of the best of the Russian military hospitals, an object for exhibition to Russian Grand Dukes, the show-hospital for neutral commissions. Many thousands of others there were in this enormous realm into which no one ever set foot. How would it look there?

I could not go on. I wanted to cry out. What, at such moments, was a box of cigarettes and a tin of fruit placed by unknown hands on the bed of one unknown — for no other reason than that the latter was seen to suffer? In such hours it was a symbol, a witness to a sane belief in humanity — despite everything....

Towards evening uneasiness became noticeable in the ward. A rumour went round of new transports, and something was heard of an order according to which all the prisoners of war were to be treated by their own physicians, because, in consequence of the new transports, there were scarcely enough Russian doctors for their own wounded.

I thought suddenly of my amputation. Then I should be amputated by a German physician; then there was no more danger for me; then I should surely get over it. I inquired everywhere.
