It was possible that it was a fabrication such as one of those many reports with which we were flooded daily — all of them only fancies, bred from desire. No, this time it seemed to be truth.... Oh, it would be the most sensible truth in the world! Could there be anything more bureaucratically insane than that the physicians who were prisoners of war were not allowed to help their own comrades? And could there be anything more natural than to let those captive physicians follow their work and their profession on behalf of their compatriots, instead of keeping them crowded together and allowing them to perish in prison camps, because they were prohibited
from giving such help, and would be sorely punished if they did so?

After the evening meal — as usual there was kascha, a coarse dish of hulled barley, which did not agree with our weakened stomachs — I saw that the man with the wounded testicles, for the first time since he lay in the ward, had raised himself out of bed. He came straightway, and with legs apart, up to me and looked at me as if he had been roused from a terrible dream.
** Come, tell me,” he began, “ you are educated and you must know. Can one do it without? ”
‘What do you mean, comrade? ” I asked, confused.
* They have, you must know — ” he opened his underdrawers and made a short motion as if cutting. “ Nothing any more, is there? ”
Should I tell him the truth? I could not. “Oh yes....” I said. “ I think so, although... no children, I believe....”

“So,” he said hoarsely, “only no children....” He was. silent for a time, drew a few breaths, took a photograph out of his shirt, and held it before my eyes. A buxom, good-naturedlooking girl — just the right kind of a machine to bear children, Briinn would say. “‘ My wife,” he said briefly. “ We could not afford to have any children, we were not rich enough. But she wants to have six some time, six at least. Without children life was worth nothing, so she always said....” He went back into his bed, stretched out his limbs, and spoke to nobody again until he was sent to Siberia.

When I was carried to the bandaging-room the next morning, there was actually an Austrian regimental physician at the table, a solemn gentleman with a little grey in his hair. “ Here comes our youngest,” said the dainty nurse, smiling at me encouragingly.
He turned round and looked at me for a while in silence. “ Well, what is the matter with you? ” he asked.
“IT am to be amputated,” I said feebly.

“‘ Amputated? Nonsense!” he exclaimed. I stared at him wide-eyed. He opened the bandage, drew out the drainage tube,. introduced an instrument into the passage of the shot, shaking his head disapprovingly. “ Incredible! ” he muttered to himself. “‘ What did they treat you with lately? ”
I could see by his look that he would not have withheld a sharp word if the Russian nurse had not been standing next to him. “ An amputation is for the present not to be thought of,” he said curtly.

My wounds were carefully cleansed, and wet poultices laid on them, nothing further. Nothing was nearly so painful as it had been at the hands of the former physicians. I was so agitated that I impulsively grasped his hands. “ All right, all right,”’ he said gruffly, but a smile flitted over his face. “ Next, please....”

I lay in bed as if someone had told me that peace had come. I caressed my leg and sang to myself. Lord, was it possible? Was it not a fever fancy? I pinched my rescued leg, rubbed my eyes, felt my forehead. No, I was in my right senses. Besides, it was morning, and everything, everything was true....
In the afternoon Pod came. “ I am not going to be amputated, Pod! ” I called out to him.
“The Austrian physician... ‘Nonsense,’ said he, only, fancy! ”
“Do you see? ” he said fiercely. “ Are they not hogs, those damned surgeons? ”
“No, Pod, our doctor with the glass eye was a good man.”

“Drat it! What care I for his goodness if it costs me a marching-stick! My God,” he continued, “I ought to have known that sooner! I hardly dared to come up! ‘ Now it is done,’ J kept thinking to myself....”
*¢ Just wait,” I said gaily, “I shall get well as soon as you now! But do not hurry....”

He laughed. “ Ill take good care not to! We shall not be so well off in Siberia, I fear....” He put his hand in the pocket of his hospital-coat and drew out two pieces of sugar. “ Schnarema sends you this,” he said shortly. “ He also peneves that today.... Well, drop it! ”
**Man,” he exclaimed, “whence this wealth? Of course Ido.
““An Austrian Lieutenant brought them to me while I slept! ”
‘“‘ These fellows have a heart, it cannot be denied,” Pod said patronizingly.
We smoked like chimneys. “ What about the man with the shot through his lungs? ” I suddenly asked. Pod shook his head, then said: “ Oh, that is only a corpse on leave! ”
At last he got up. “ Let’s go back to our bower,” he said, his mind now at rest. “ Besides, I need no rOnge creep on all fours,” he added proudly.
I forced a few cigarettes into his hands. “ Give Briinn and Schnarrenberg some, too, Pod.”
“ That’s all right! ” he said briefly. “See to it that you come down again soon.”
The same evening the Austrian Lieutenant came in, went up to the wood-cutter, and sat down on his bed. I waited a bit, then called out: “ Please, Lieutenant...”
He came at once. “ Well,” he said smiling, “ you appear to be better today? ”
“You look almost gay,” he interrupted me. “ A few days ago I was almost afraid for you....”
“Our doctor is clever, isn’t he? ” he again interrupted me.
“ He is a famous professor from Vienna. I have spoken to him about you.”
I gave up thanking him. He did not look as lieutenants usually do. He had the head of an artist and two splendid fiery eyes. “ And what did he say? ” I asked in suspense.

“That it was a great shame. Your wound only became so dangerously extensive because of wrong treatment. He hopes to remove the suppuration in three to four days. It was high time for your frail body....”
I was silent, breathing rapidly. “Then I shall get quite well? ” I asked in a low voice.
“Then,” I continued, “then at least half of these poor wretches have lost their limbs without absolute necessity? ”
“Undoubtedly,” he said firmly, “more than half — twothirds, according to medical judgment.”
Again | was silent. “ Tell me, Lieutenant —”
““ My name is Brehm,” he interposed.
“Lieutenant Brehm, why were our physicians, who were prisoners of war, not allowed to treat us? ”
“No one exactly knows,” he said in a low voice. “ But it is supposed because, in proportion to the Russians, there would not then have been enough cripples among us, and not enough dead....”

Three days afterwards I was carried downstairs. Pod and Briinn saluted in their beds as I joined them again. “ Long life to Austria! ” cried Pod. His good face beamed like the moon. Even Schnarrenberg’s hard features relaxed. “ Nothing in the papers yet about peace? ” he said by way of greeting. “To think of your coming down again! ” said the man with the shot through his lungs. It sounded almost as if it vexed him.
The dainty nurse had kept my old bed free for me. She was a Countess Urusoff, her Christian name being Lida, as I was

informed by Lieutenant Brehm. Now I understood the pretty little shoes, the silk stockings, the perfectly kept hands — and her few accomplishments. All the nurses in this hospital were society ladies, many of them aristocrats. The tall, dark one, who was so curt and energetic, was even said to be a German from the Baltic and was so unkind to us only because otherwise she would have been accused of secret sympathy, and therefore of treason to her country. Be that as it might, my bed was clean and freshly covered, and on the night-table there were even a few pansies. They stood in my empty preserve-tin.

Almost everything about us had changed. The four dragoons from our brother regiment had gone; two had been sent to Siberia, two had died, so Pod reported. Little Blank had been put in our ward; the dainty nurse had managed that. Of the others near by, only the man with the shot through his lungs was an old acquaintance. After a few minutes he told me that he would soon be well.

My wounds made rapid progress. I could already lift up my coverlet without a feeling of horror. No biting odour of decomposition met me. The peaks of my fever-curve fell lower every day; the nights began to be dreamless; the wound above my knee on my left leg had already closed; the rim of the wound on the upper thigh of my right leg was beginning to itch, and consequently to heal.

My new-old surroundings had a great influence on my rapid improvement. The terrible shrieking at bandaging-time had decreased by half since captive physicians officiated there, and although in general the injuries were not lighter, they were more concealed, less visible at a glance, than in the amputation ward. True, if one were observant and looked a little nearer....
One man had been lying for weeks on water-sacks with one leg over his coverlet. Back and seat had long been bereft of skin — every breath must have caused him terrible pain, for

he moaned unceasingly. Another, with a shot through his bladder, had a long tube hanging from under his quilt, a tube from which black and bloody drops oozed out into a bowl. A third had a shot through his stomach. Anything he tried to swallow at once exuded through the passage of the shot — if his wound were not to heal in time, he must surely starve to death.

A shell-splinter had torn the flesh from another man’s kidneys. He would have to lie on his stomach for months, perhaps. His kidneys were exposed, and their corrosive contents ate into his muscles. In our ward were two with eyes shot out, three with terrible abdominal wounds, two with shots in the rectum which could never heal because the physicians had not means at their command to prevent their constant pollution, and one with the entire lower jaw missing, who would have to be fed through tubes all his life.
“ Schnarrenberg,” I asked suddenly, “shall you ever be able to shoot again? ”
He started up in some amazement. | distinctly saw that he was at war with himself, that in him, too, something new was struggling, wanting to get out of him — but that it was too new, too weak.
“‘ Of course,” he snarled angrily. “ What else? ”

Again our days passed on in the old round of bandaging, eating, sleeping. Nevertheless we were surrounded by a new atmosphere. We old inmates had the feeling that what was hardest lay behind us, and we were now getting medicines — stimulating and cleansing remedies. A few of us even got something that the Russians called “ slabo,” only a sort of miserable porridge, to be sure, but better assimilated by our weakened stomachs than the national food, the black kascha.
We occupied ourselves in attempting to walk in the quiet afternoon hours. As a matter of course, we only did this when no one was in the ward, and a slightly wounded man always

stood on watch at the door to detain any unexpected nurse or orderlies with questions until we had reached our beds again. We did not want to get to Siberia any sooner than was necessary, and we very well knew that we should be mercilessly sent there the very minute an ill-disposed orderly saw us run about.

As I was about to make my first attempt at walking, Pod shoved two crutches under my shoulders. J had to learn to walk again like a child, and if Pod and Blank had not carefully supported me, I should have fallen down, despite my crutches, like a drunken man. My legs had lost all power, and also my arms. Notwithstanding this, we all practised daily — because we never knew when they would drive us out, and because we slept so well afterwards.

Oh, God! At home all this would have been professionally supervised and carried out! There they had gymnastic apparatus; enervated muscles were electrified and massaged with strengthening ointments — here there was nothing, nothing but two crutches made of bamboo-cane and covered with oilcloth! And had we not even to borrow those from the amputated or to steal them? We had to try in secret to get on our feet again; but how many never got so far because no one took pity on them? And how many who, after a little assistance, might have been able to walk again as they once did kept stiff or shortened limbs for the rest of their lives because there were not even the most primitive instruments, the simplest remedies, at hand?

Usually Pod summoned us for the Kino hour after these walking tests. All near by collected at his window to watch those hundreds of people bathing naked in the warm waters of the Moskva. They were, for the greater part, older men and women, but there were young and pretty girls among them, too.
“‘Qne ought to have glasses,” said Briinn, the great erotic. ‘““A real telescope....”
Pod reproved him, “ You can never get enough, Briinn.”
‘Man! Just fancy if that were customary with us; without a rag, without a fig-leaf even! ”
“Then you’d put electricity on the shelf and become swimming-master, eh? ” called out a new-comer. All broke into a roar of laughter.

Just then a dark-haired girl let down her skirts and remained standing a moment, brightly illuminated by the summer sun. She had powerful, unspoiled limbs and a brownish skin. Her rump was voluptuousness itself.
“By thunder! ” said Briinn appreciatively. “She is well padded.”
“T like more in front,” said Pod dreamingly.
“That’s because you don’t understand anything,” Briinn retorted. “In front a girl ought to have only so much as one can grasp with one hand. There should be more somewhere else.”

Devout silence followed this dictum. The eyes of all watched the young girl with a peculiar expression as she slowly stepped into the water, bent down, sprinkled her breasts with her outspread hand, and slowly dived into the green of the water.
“Man! just imagine that for once we could have something so soft in our cold bachelor beds!” Brinn called out enthusiastically.
“ It is easily to be seen that you are regaining strength,” said Pod smilingly.
“You will soon be sent to Siberia — to cool off! ” someone added with a sneer.

Our daily afternoon Kino hour passed all too quickly with this badinage. All joined in it, except Schnarrenberg and Blank. While, however, Schnarrenberg secretly listened — to take part in our conversation would, in his opinion, be incompatible with his military rank — little Blank, the girl, lay blushing in his bed. It could clearly be seen that he was desperately trying not to hear our strong expressions.

The nights became quieter and quieter. When the dainty nurse came, she found me in my full senses. She scarcely ever said more than her softly whispered “ Spatsch.” One evening, however, a few days after my return to the lower ward, she sat down in silence at my bed, looking at me with eyes in which subdued pain seemed to linger. Was she ashamed, perhaps, on account of my amputation affair? And because, now that the Russian doctors did not treat us any more, there was not half so much noise in the ward, and convalescence became much quicker ?
** What ails you, nurse? ” I asked in a low voice.

‘I only wanted to ask you not to think badly of our country, of our people! He — the Russian — is not bad; he is only lazy, lazy and encouraged to be indifferent! We are backward in everything, far behind, that’s it...”
I took courage, seized her hand, and kissed it timidly.

“Qh, you cannot believe how hard it is for us,” she exclaimed, “to have to see everything, not to be able to do anything against it! Every friendly act, every humane deed, is reported and may cost us Siberia or our estates, but I do not submit. I work day and night to lessen the shame upon our country...”
At last one morning, despite all wishes to the contrary, the dreaded hour arrived. All the beds were newly covered with clean linen; all bottles and chambers thoroughly cleansed.
“Here, Potemkin is not dead yet,” cried Pod across to me. “ You'll see, the commission will come today! ”

He was right. Pod was always right; he had a nose for such things, the scent of a regular pointer. Shortly after the midday meal the dreaded event came. An orderly stormed in, bellowing like a bull: “ Attention! ” An entire suite appeared at the door — a surgeon-general, three doctors of lesser rank, a group of surgeons, and a couple of nurses. Of our doctors there was nothing to be seen.

Bed after bed was visited. “Get up, get up.” The orderlies placed crutches under the arms of one after another of us. “There, now try! ” said the surgeon-general in his clipped German. He had a sharp, dried-up hawk’s face and spoke as if he were commanding a squadron.
Pod, Briinn, and Blank were ahead of me. When the crutches were handed to Pod, he humbly shook his shaggy bear’s head. “ Nitschewo...” he said in a friendly way. It was his one Russian word.
A couple of nurses laughed. The surgeon-general looked at him as if he would have liked to have him shot. A glance at his herculean frame sufficed him. “ All right,” he cried. “ Next.”

Pod drew his longest face, cast his eyes across to us as if looking for help. I shrugged my shoulders. What could I do? Little Blank’s manner soothed the surgeon-general. Blank accepted the offered crutches and cautiously walked up and down two or three times in the space by his bed, like a good boy. “ All right, next.”” When he got to Briinn, there was trouble again. The very moment that he felt the crutches under his shoulders, and the orderlies withdrew their support, Briinn fell full-length on the floor and screamed pitifully as if he were being burned at the stake. He was lifted up and his wound examined. It was closed. “ When did you come? ” asked the hawk’s head. The dark sister reported that he had been lying there for three months. “ All right,” said the all-powerful one, pleased. “ All right,” Briinn grinned after him.

I was the next. “Get up, get up! ” I rose with difficulty. “ Kastille, Kastille! ” cried the surgeon-general. My arms were lifted, the crutches slipped from under my shoulders, and | was left to stand alone. Everything turned round before my eyes, and my right leg swung like the pendulum of a clock. I could not place it on the floor, try as I might. “ Walk! Walk!”
cried the hawk’s head. Slowly I set my left leg forward and swayed back and forth like a drunkard. “Go on, go on! ”
At this moment the dainty nurse stepped forward. “ He has not left his bed before now, Your Excellency,” she said bravely.
“Qh,” he laughed menacingly. “ At a second trial he will run like a borzoi.”
“ But he is excessively weak, Your Excellency.”

“* Thanks. I can see that for myself. I am a doctor! Anyway, he need not walk; he will ride for weeks — as far as Siberia. Long before he will have recovered! No, no, all right. We need room. Next....”
With a short look he went past the man with a shot through his lungs.
“* Oh, God,” the latter whispered to himself, “Oh, God... and I? What about me? I should like to get out! I shall be well soon.... Why, why does he pass me by... ?”
“Thunder and blazes, ’twill be in a minute now,” said Pod in the afternoon. “ We need not be secret about ‘it any more. I shall go down to the court and sun myself a bit.”

In three or four days I was also able to get down to the court with the help of Pod and Briinn. The stairs, to be sure, were a little hindrance still, but the lure of the sun caused all difficulties to seem light.

From the first landing of the stairs, where I had to wait some time to get my breath, an unexpected view presented itself. The Kremlin lay before our eyes. Gigantic walls enclosed hundreds of cupolas, some of poisonous green, others of pure gold or azure-blue, and of all shapes. I saw them for the first time, and a flood of what I had once heard and read swept over me. But the view did not make anything clearer to, me, Rather, it seemed to me as if the mystery of this country became more impenetrable, the strangeness of this life more incomprehensible.
“So much gold is said to lie in there that all the misery in the world could be done away with by its means,” said Briinn.

I shrugged my shoulders. What should I say to this? I should not become clearer in my mind about what this picture awakened in me if I were to look at it for days; I felt attracted and repelled and knew no reason for either. Did it proceed from the mixture in my blood, from my heritage from my mother? “* Let us go into the sun,” I said at last.
In the court I came at once upon Lieutenant Brehm. A grenade had made a stump of one of his feet. Walking with a stick and dragging his left leg behind him, he came at once to meet me.
“Well,” he said heartily, “for the first time in the sun? That does more to make one well than four weeks of bed. But wait, I’ll get you a chair....”

He came back with a chair, let me slowly down into it, and sat down beside me on a bench. Pod and Briinn were hobbling across the court and, supporting each other, laid their faces together at the railing that enclosed the entire space. It was the boundary to a street in which the life of Moscow pulsated in strong colours, and in which there was incredibly much to be seen for sharpened, starved eyes: coachmen and policemen, workmen and — girls.
‘The commission has visited you? ” asked Brehm.
** Yes, recently. It was a spectacular play.”
* Then you will get away soon.”
“Yes, although it was distinctly agreed that in case of war no prisoners should be sent to Siberia.”
“ So even this is not permitted? ”
“ Of course not, but what does Russia care about agreements? It is, and remains today, as it was three hundred years ago, the realm of arbitrariness.”
“ And why were these agreements made? ”

‘Because the climate of Siberia is unbearable for central Europeans! Fifty degrees of cold in winter, and fifty degrees of heat in summer. Who can stand that? No, let us speak of something else. Why bother yourself about it now? ”

I only nodded. How blessed the sun was! I put out my hands to its rays, spread out my fingers, closed them again. My God, they had become regular spider-legs, white, wrinkled, bloodless. The skin could have been drawn away in long strips.

After a while he left me. A German Guards officer, a long, over-slender man, Klemt by name, addressed me. We exchanged a few sentences, and he inquired in an agreeably sympathetic way how my wound was, how I was feeling.
“You have had the devil’s own luck! But why are you not put with us into the officers’ ward? ” he asked in conclusion.

“No,” I said quickly. “I have comrades — comrades who care for me like brothers! I should like to stay with them as long as possible. With my knowledge of languages I can be useful to them in many a way. And they have no one else who could help them....”

I stretched myself and was lost in dreams. Moscow — Kremlin — Siberia. Was it not really like a dream? Suddenly the barred gates opened and an ambulance rattled in over the gravel. Two splendid Orloffs trotted quickly past me, described an elegant curve, and came to a halt two paces in front of me.

A long-missed smell of sweat and horse’s hair came to me. Could there be a more beautiful symbol for me on the first day of sun, on my first day out? The horses remained standing in front of me for a whole hour. Their bell-like hoofs pawed the gravel now and then. Their gorgeous trappings rang in time to their nodding.

I did not stir. My eyes glided over every part of the noble bodies, from their red, distended nostrils to the curly hair of their tails, which almost touched the ground. I should have liked to lay my fingers on their silk-like faces, but I could not, as yet, stand without help. I would have keeled over at the slightest pressure of their heads. No, I must give that up. But my eyes tried to make up for it and examined their bodies inch by inch, so to speak. They were of that breed made famous by Russia’s sleighing races. They had hooked rams’ noses, low backs, chests of steel, and ankles like a bear’s paws. Their great eyes looked at me fixedly, their fine ears waved listeningly towards me. “ Zelle, old beast of section Z...” I suddenly thought.
I drew in the smell of their sweat like an invigorating elixir. I slowly, slowly felt along my right leg. Yes, it was still there. I had it still. I was rich.

During the following night the man with the shot through his lungs died. He passed away quietly and unnoticed. When I awoke in the morning, I saw that he was lying in bed with open mouth full of red, dried little bubbles. Later I learnt that he had entered a complaint and asked for a bill of health because the commission had passed him by. That he was almost well and that he would like to get out were the reasons he had given.

I took my crutches so that I might go out until they had carried him away. I almost seemed to miss his grumbling, his constant faultfinding. However, I took this walk every morning as soon as I woke up; for I preferred dragging myself painfully | down to the water-closet to using any longer the commode, which was hardly ever cleaned and nearly always so full that it could not be used.

To be sure, that was now a thing of the past. Oh, it was not a trifling matter that was now done with! At first it drove me to despair to sit on this commode, supported by two men and in the presence of all — then I got used to it as one got used to everything. But a new hell had come in its place, this expedition itself. It was difficult and painful, that did not matter. But it was a walk through rows of the dead, that was it....

The great morning cleansing only began about eight o’clock. It was only at eight o'clock that the beds were looked after, the new corpses carried away. When I had to go, they were all still lying as they had died, and no morning went by without my having to go through the long ward past ten or twelve dead to get to the door. Often their arms or legs, convulsed by the death-struggle, were stretched out so far into the aisle that I could scarcely wind my way between them. Some lay naked on the floor, some hung half out of their beds, and many had bloody mouths, rigid in the last cry. Almost all, however, had open eyes, looking at one strangely with their glassy pupils; for from the moment when the orderlies learnt that a man was likely to die, they did not trouble any more about him, but let him die as he must and could — among a thousand human beings, and yet like a beast in the field....

At noon the dark nurse told us that the order for transportation had come. “Tomorrow, very early....” She said it shortly and concisely, but it seemed to me as if her pretty lips were trembling. “ Have you any wish? ” she asked me.

I hesitated a little. There was something I wanted, but I knew that it was forbidden, that she dared not grant my wish. “TI should like to have a knife,” I said timidly, “a tiny little penknife. We cannot even cut our bread....”
“ That is not allowed to prisoners of war!” ” she said curtly, and went away.

Had I been mistaken after all? Well, be it so.... The next moment Pod came across. “ Now the thunderbolt has fallen,” he said gloomily. “ Fortunately we stay together, but I wanted to say,” he continued, “I should like to learn Russian, I shall need it on the way — we meet people, don’t we? Will you teach it to me? ”
“ Certainly, Pod, I will get a couple of copy-books from the officers, perhaps a Russian grammar; then we can soon begin.”

“Grammar?” said Pod astonished. “What do I want a grammar for? And I have enough paper myself....” He drew forth a dirty bit of paper and wet his pencil. “How do you say ‘hunger’? ” he asked dictatorially.
“Golod,” he repeated, taking the pencil and writing: “ hunger — golod.”
“ Mjassa,” he said, writing: “ meat — mjassa.”
“ Chljeb,” he wrote. “ Butter? ” he then ashes
“ Djdngi njetu —no money! ” he wrote in big letters on his paper, folded it up in the old creases very carefully, and got up.
“Thank you,” he said, “that’s enough for me. I shall get along with that. I don’t need to know any more of this confounded language....”

Scarcely was the morning’s clearing of dead bodies over before the orderlies came in with long bags. They looked at the numbers on our tablets and threw a sack down beside the bed of each one of us “ healthy ones.” All our clothes were in them, from boots to cap, just as they had been taken from us the day we were brought in.

“Go ahead! Get up, get up! ” We crept somewhat depressed out of our blankets, but when we had emptied the sacks and spread out our old uniforms before us, we quickly recovered our spirits. It was as if, with our riding-boots and tunics, a bit of the vigorous and manly spirit which we had possessed while

still young and hopeful had entered into us again, a spirit which in the times of crutches and trailing hospital-coats we had often lacked and, perhaps in greater part, lost. Perhaps mixed with this was also the feeling that pain and lying in bed were over for ever, that we were soldiers again, and that, though nothing good was ahead of us, we were again getting out into the world among others than those moaning and dying men. Yes, we should again hear other words than calls for orderlies and nurses, see other things besides wounds and pus and death.
Our underwear was washed, but not mended. Holes torn by bullets still gaped in riding-breeches and coats. “ Never mind,” said little Blank, the girl, “I can sew nicely — Ill darn everything for you.”

Pod helped me to put on my riding-boots. It was a difficult task, because my right leg could not yet bear any pressure or exercise. At last we were sitting on our beds, all ready dressed and looking with surprised eyes from oné to another. Some- ' thing had totally altered us. Briinn’s coarse jokes were left untold, Pod suddenly called me by my title again, Schnarrenberg even moved a little apart. It looked as if the braid and buttons had all at once regained their old distinction.
I called “ Pod ” three times for no other reason than ostentatiously to emphasize his nickname and my familiar address. ..- “Pod,” I said at last, “am I someone else than I was two hours ago? ”
“In those confounded hospital-coats we were all alike, but now....
“But I do not want any change between us, Dragoon Podbielski! ”
“ At your service, Ensign,” he said laughingly, and became his old self again.
We had nothing to carry except what was on our bodies.

I had not even a cap, because I had had on an officer’s helmet, which a Cossack officer had taken from me as a war souvenir, and many had had one or other of their garments stolen out of the bags while they were in storage. A few appeared in underdrawers, a few in shirt-sleeves. No one had thought of giving them fresh garments. In the court a few sentries awaited us with fixed bayonets. “Men, why don’t you have a couple of cannons also? ” cried Briinn.

Lieutenant Brehm was standing at the gate. He pressed both my hands and finally said: “I should like to give you something for the journey! ” It was a bank-note of ten roubles, a fortune for me, for us all. It was doubtful whether there was a single copeck among the entire transport. “To be repaid at home! ” he said smilingly. I could not answer. I could only press his hands more firmly.
When we were just about to march off, the dainty nurse came hurrying down the stairs. “ Where is the Junker? ” I heard her call. “ There, there, here,” roared Pod.

I was standing between Pod and Briinn. She stepped up to us, gave us each a silver rouble, and looked at me for a long time. “JI wish you happiness and health,” she said softly, fumbling at her apron and shoving a small parcel into my pocket. “ It is from your dark nurse! ” she said hastily, her little hand trembling. “ Never forget what I once told you — whatever may come! ” she added with difficulty.

“Po tschetirt —in fours! ” shouted a starschi, a sergeant major. She tore herself away and hastened off. Pod, I, Briinn, and Blank formed a line. In the front row were Schmidt I and Schnarrenberg. None of the rest of our regiment had come with us. We were perhaps parted for ever.
The barred gate opened and we marched out. But the marching soon came to an end. One after another dropped behind. The train became longer and longer, more and more broken. It was

a hot day in autumn; none were accustomed to the heavy boots; many of them, like myself, had hardly walked at all until this morning. Our armpits began to hurt from the crutches, and the long boots pulled like weights at our feet. “ Boys, I must sit down for a bit,” I said at last. I was not the only one. Here and there a few others were sitting on the curb-stone — pale, miserable, panting. We sat down, four in a row. The stones were warm, and it was confoundedly comfortable. In front of us small coaches were hastening by, crowded street-cars rolled past, gaily dressed women promenaded. Briinn was just going to crack a joke about a fat peasant woman when one of the sentinels dug me in the back from behind with the butt-end of his gun. “ Get ahead with you, German devil! ”

Pod jumped up as if he had been stung. “ You haven’t puked any guts for long, have you? ” he roared. “‘ Want to beat poor cripples, eh? ” A mob gathered, and all the women took our part. Pod went on open-heartedly — what did it matter, since he did not know Russian? His pointing to our crutches and wounds, the indignant sound of his voice, was understood by all — and who, for that matter, could withstand the faithful eyes of a St. Bernard?

Then Briinn cleverly remembered the word “ hunger,” the crowning word of the phrase-book, which had in the mean while become famous, and hurled it at the mob. Moreover, he took off his cap and held it out in front of him. Everyone in the crowd put his hand into his pocket, and a rich stream of copecks flowed into the cap. “Forty copecks,” he said, grinning. “ By thunder, we ought to repeat this spectacle at every street-corner.”
All were in high good humour, and Schnarrenberg alone was furious. “I notice that you are forgetting your uniform, Briinninghaus,” he said severely. |

At noon the last houses were passed and the street ended in a potato-field, Beside a peasant’s house we were allowed to rest and sit down in a meadow. I distributed my last cigarettes, and, notwithstanding that we were all tired to death, we were really in a happy frame of mind. At such moments Briinn usually found the right word. “ Let come what may,” he cried, “ at all events it is much nicer than in that great chest of woe! ”

Our stages became shorter and shorter. We did not get anything to eat, and we had to quench our thirst at some pump or other. “I shall soon gnaw at one of these wooden posts,” grumbled Pod. The guards had given up trying to drive us on. Did they themselves see that it was impossible? Our armpits were burning as if red-hot coals lay on top of our crutches. Our feet, unaccustomed to walking on roads, were blistered. * They have always been, and will always be, unmitigated hogs, these Russians! ” said Schnarrenberg in a tone of conviction. “ Could they not at least have requisitioned a few Panje wagons for us? ”
“Or a couple of stylish automobiles? ” added Brinn.

At last, towards evening, as we crossed a railway embankment, we saw in front of us a small barrack, enclosed by a high fence of boards. The yard swarmed with people. “ This is Ugrieschskaja, the great distribution centre,” I said. “ Rather lilliputian,” remarked Briinn. “We shall hardly be able to turn round properly with our crutches in this hole,” nodded Pod.

The gate opened. We were counted off. “ By the Lord — it tallies! None of us has run away!” said Briinn mockingly. We were taken into a shed with room for a hundred men and left to our fate. What did it matter to the Russians that there were two hundred of us?

“The lightly wounded to one side! ” called out Schnarrenberg, the senior in rank in the transport, in his voice of command. He was right; he, at least, desired to leave room for the severely wounded to lie down.
“Shut your mouth! ” some voices cried from the back-

ground. “We are no longer in the barracks-yard — d’ye hear?” I hobbled quickly to his side. “Don’t get excited, Schnarrenberg,” I said hastily. “It will do well enough S80..... He was hanging in his crutches as if about to fall. His hard soldier’s face was as white as chalk. “ What was that, Ensign? ” he panted. “ What did they say? ” “ Nothing, Schnarrenberg, nothing, come with me....” |

In the mean while Pod had lain down on a plank bed in such a way as to make room for us all if we made ourselves as thin as possible. Just as I was coming through the crowd with Schnarrenberg, I heard him say perfectly calmly in his deep voice: “ You haven’t spit out any teeth for a long time, eh? The place here is for my Junker — that settles it.”
I lay down at his side. At the same moment I felt something hard in my pocket. It was the parcel from the dark nurse. I opened it and found a small, brown penknife.

When I woke up, it was broad daylight. Pod was already sitting next to me bending forward. The upper part of his body was naked, and his shirt was on his knees, “ Damn it all,” he greeted me. “‘ Were you able to sleep? ”

“TI could not manage to. In a couple of hours I was being bitten as if I lay among a colony of ants. Now we shall be molested again with those confounded little insects —I have already mobilized an advance guard of ten men.”

Our whole bodies felt bruised. We were not used to lying fully dressed on hard wood without pillows and blankets. Also, on account of our wounds, we could lie only on one side, could never change our position. And what that signified...
I slid slowly down from the bed.... “ Is there water anywhere for washing, Pod? ”
‘*No, my son, we wash with tea-water, I have heard. That replaces the soap. Besides, this camp is not commanded by a man, but by a female, a Czech.”

“Ha ha, because she wears the breeches, not her lord and husband! She is said to be a beast.... She demands that all badges and rank distinctions be dropped; she exchanges German money at the rate of sixty pfennigs for one mark, and she puts half the money for our board into her own pocket! Genuinely Russian, eh? ”

In Ugrieschskaja all nationalities were sorted out, all the Slavs, Roumanians, Italians, and Poles from the Austrian Army, and all the Alsatians and men from Schleswig-Holstein from the German Army. “ Why so? ” we asked. These people went into better camps, we were told. “That would be an opportunity,” Briinn mused. “I am from the Danish coast! ” Cries of “Fie! fie! ” silenced him. “Don’t you know that it would be treason? ” someone called out to him. “ You must vote for Denmark later. Stupid fellow, do you think you will get anything for nothing? ” “I only thought...” muttered Briinn in confusion.

In the mean while I had glanced round the shed. Ugrieschskaja was far too small for the number of those who must often wait there for months until transported to Siberia or Turkestan. The main space was occupied by a dark shed supplied with plank beds, our sleeping-places. In the centre there was an open platform which for some occult reason was called kikeriki by the soldiers. On this there stood a few rows of iron camp-bedsteads with boards, but without mattresses or blankets. Those were the couches for the captive officers.

I strolled about this platform in the hope of discovering a comrade from my regiment, but I was not successful; for they were mostly Austrians and Hungarians. There were two German officers sitting apart in a corner, but no familiar uniform, no familiar face. When I got back to my place,

Blank was just coming with tea, a cloudy, yellowish liquid, which only tasted good because it was hot and we could not get the frost of the night out of our bones without something warming inside. A dense, damp, biting atmosphere prevailed —jit was the odour that had sometimes struck us out of thickly populated gipsy wagons. How could it have been otherwise? Many had already lived for weeks on those wooden beds, unwashed and without having taken off their clothes even for one night. Many still had open wounds, or were covered with vermin up to the neck. Some had bad-smelling bandages on their limbs; for there was no means of changing them even once. Some ran about half naked because during their stay in hospital some of their garments had been stolen. Some were already in the last stage of consumption. The uncertainty of what was to become of us was beginning to lie on us like a great weight. If we could but know....

We drank our tea in haste so that we might get another pot to wash with. “ First of all we must try to get a tea-kettle for ourselves,” said Briinn. “It is the very first thing we must get,” I upheld him by saying. “ Nobody counts for anything in Russia with out a tscheinik! ”

_ “Tf we only had a couple of cigarettes! ” sighed Briinn. “Everything is bearable if one only has a cigarette in the corner of one’s mouth....” “ As soon as we get out, Briinn,” I said, to comfort him. “ Are we not rich? ”

‘A little while ago I saw someone with a good extra cap,” said Pod. “It would just fit you, Junker. Shall I bargain with him for it? You can’t run about all your life without a lousewarmer.” “ All right, Pod.”

He came back with a well-preserved cap having a shield in front. “A silver rouble,” he said radiantly. “It is only from a strand-plover,” he added, thrusting in his fists and widening it until it fitted me.
“I wonder if this existence is meant as a foretaste of our future camp life? ” questioned little Blank. One could distinctly hear that he was depressed.

“No,” I said decidedly. “I don’t believe so. That would really be... No, it is only a transition. To economize in regard to space in such an enormous country — would that not be contrary to all reason? ”
* Moreover, we should be dead in no time,” Pod muttered.
“Yes,” Blank agreed, “yes, it is autumn now, and we can stand it. But I have been told that this serves as central camp in winter also —at fifty degrees below zero! ”
“Then thousands have already frozen to death on these boards,” muttered Pod.

After a while Briinn returned from an exploring expedition. “Boys,” he said, “we are fortunate. The first comers have been waiting here for five weeks. With us the transport is full. In three days we are to go on....”
‘Where to? ” asked Schnarrenberg. It was his first word since the previous evening.

On the fourth morning the higher officers were summoned before the commander. Would we really go? When Schnarrenberg returned, he looked almost gay. “ The Lord be praised! ” he said, drawing a deep breath. “ We are to go on!” He stepped with renewed military bearing into the middle of our platoon and called out in his sharp, commanding voice: “ Get ready for marching! Step forward in two lines! ”

We placed our crutches under our arms and stood up. On the right wing Pod stood like a pillar, his tscheinik dangling from a rope round his waist. We stood unnoticed in the court until noon. Schnarrenberg, pelted with angry cries from all sides, bit his lips as his gaiety rapidly disappeared. He was certainly not responsible, but was there any longer justice in the world?
At last the commander’s wife appeared, a woman with a sharp nose. “ Does anybody want to change his money yet? ” she asked sweetly.
““No, I kiss your hand, madam! ” said Briinn distinctly.
A couple of men in the second line laughed.
“May the devil take you,” said this ladylike person as she walked away.

At three o’clock the great gate was opened and our troop crept out like caterpillars. At the railway station was a train composed of fifty to sixty cattle-cars. “ We must try to get on the parlour floor,” said Briinn, meaning the upper plank beds.

We came to a stop in front of the cars. “ Count off forty,” cried out Schnarrenberg. “Stop, stop, what’s the matter... ?” he called. In an instant the whole troop broke up into a thousand combatants who ruthlessly stormed the cars and tried, by blows and kicks, to gain the upper beds.

We had no need to hurry; we had our Pod. He was the first to sit on the upper plank bed of a car, and as he did so, he called out in his deep voice: ““ Whoever gets up here had better count his bones first! ”

There are four plank beds in a Russian cattle-car, two upper and two lower, to the right and left of the sliding doors. “‘Forty divided by four arithmetically amounts to ten per bed!” proclaimed Briinn. “Damn and blast it! — are we herrings?”

He was right. Such a place was hardly enough for six, but might hold ten if all lay on one side and did not stir. We upper ones had two little windows to the right and left and were able to see something. The dust and vermin dropped through the cracks in our boards on to the eyes of those lying underneath and stayed there half the night. But there was no mercy; in the end all the healthy ones landed on the upper plank beds, while the sick and wounded crept into the dark holes which nobody wanted.

In the evening a troop of guards came marching up. A heavily armed man stepped into each car, selected the best place for himself, and shoved aside those next to him with the butt-end of his gun. “ Don’t make yourselves too comfortable, you hogs! ”

In our car were Hungarians and Austrians, Styrians and Tyrolese, two sturdy Bavarians, one Saxon, one from Berlin, two from Hamburg, besides the men of our regiment. In the corner were four Galicians, small, hook-nosed Jews with cork-screw locks, polite and obliging little persons whose strange language sounded amusing to us.

The sun was already setting when a large naphtha locomotive rattled over the switches. With a few jerks the train moved on. “ Where are we going, anyway?” asked little Blank. “I don’t know,” snarled Schnarrenberg.
“Do you know where we are going to? ” I asked the guard.
* Shut up, I want to sleep! ”
We climbed down from the beds, opened one of the two

sliding doors, and crouched down in front of the opening. Level land went past us, peasants’ farm-houses, from the windows of which shone the mild glow of lamps. The hay had long since been cut, but now and then a heavily loaded Panje wagon came along, drawn by small poor-looking horses. Peasants clad in gay smocks walked beside them, and young girls in white blouses sat on the hay. A chorus of ringing soprano voices, accompanied by deep basses, rose up into the dark evening sky.
We listened in silence. The fingers of a heavy hand seemed to penetrate deep into our hearts.
“At my home,” said Pod slowly, “my wife is most likely sowing the winter wheat....”
I only nodded. My eyes gazed into the distance. How that girl was singing... !
“ At my home,” continued Pod, “my Anna has long since harvested the hay....”
My head fell on my chest. The train rattled on monotonously, Eastward, eastward! the wheels rattled. Who knew whither ? |
At this moment a man behind us began to sing. Three, four, half the car, softly joined in.... Ah! must it not come true one day?
Teure Heimat meiner Lieben, = Denk ich still an dich zuriick....

The country in front of us, the strange, strange country, became darker and darker. We could see only its lights, feel © only the smell of its meadows, perceive only the breath of its wind. At our backs the singing grew louder, in the car the sound grew more and more fervent.
Sei gegriisst in weiter Ferne, Teure Heimat — sei gegriisst.

Little Blank got up softly and crept silently into the dark corner of his wooden bed. Pod suddenly clapped his hands in front of his face. His heavy body shook and I felt him leaning at my side. _“ What is it, Pod? ” I asked softly. “ Are you sick? ”
He drew his head still deeper down between his shoulders. “If they would only stop singing that confounded song! ” he muttered hoarsely.

Night came. I could not sleep. The wound in my left side, which had been bitten by lice, pained me as if I had been stung. I forced my way carefully out between my comrades, Briinn on my right, Pod on my left. Briinn was asleep, with open mouth, looking a little foolish. Pod resembled a sleeping bear. All lay at full length on their left sides; all had their faces turned in one direction.

We changed our position every evening. One day all would be on the left, the next on the right, side. In no other way was it possible for all ten to sleep at the same time. But the nights when we lay on the right side were nights of torture for me, because on the right side was my largest and scarcely healed wound. |

A dim little petroleum lamp flickered in the centre of the car. I sat down on the floor and leaned my back against the sliding door. To the right and left at a height of about half a yard were the lower plank beds, rough boards which, at slightest touch, splintered the skin. From time to time a sleeper uttered a hoarse curse, another drew in his breath with a deep consumptive sound.

I remembered the war. This was its reverse side, I thought. I thought of everything, of severe wounds, even of my own death. But then.... How splendid were our attacks! Each man forgot himself, and all pettiness fell away from him! The individual was lost, the mass took its place, and everyone knew: “I must sacrifice myself — my Fatherland lies at
my back...,” That was not senseless, that was grand and rich! But here...

Someone got up in the Hungarian’s corner. He glided, half awake, to my door, slid it back a little, let his trousers down, knelt down on his knees, and shoved himself along the floor as far as the crack.

A load weighed me down. I lowered my head and tried to go on thinking. In vain.... At times there was a stir on my plank bed. The guard snored loudly, Briinn cursed in a low voice, Pod sighed in his sleep. “Anna...” he said in his deep voice. “Anna...”

I put my fingers into my ears. These journeys often lasted for months, I thought, discouraged. Day after day, night after night. Could it be endured? The dim lamp swayed, the wheels rattled, the guard snored.

Again one of the Hungarians crept out. It was the gipsy, a wild, black rider of the plains. The light fell on him. He saw me plainly, but that did not trouble him.... Was he in pain? After a while he began to pant. His face became fixed and he opened his mouth as if athirst. Suddenly I heard a long-drawn groan, and saw him fall back as if relieved. Must I cover up my eyes also, oh, God?
Pod cursed at the food. “It is not only little, but bad,” he growled. “On my farm at home we give the hogs what we get here! Kascha, kascha— what is that? Grains are bettere
** At home the prisoners must also starve! ” Briinn muttered crossly.

“But only because our own people must starve themselves,” said Schnarrenberg severely. “Why do they blockade us when it is contrary to all international law? Russia is not blockaded. It should not be necessary for Russia to let us starve to death.”
Briinn was silenced. He was still a little afraid of
Schnarrenberg, partly out of a soldier’s respect for a superior rank, partly from a bad conscience because of some unpleasant passages in his military record.

After we had bribed our guard, called konvoi, with fifty copecks, we were allowed to get out at the stations to make purchases. At all railway stations were tables on which peasant women piled up their wares. Everything one wanted was there, and ridiculously cheap. If one understood how to bargain a little, one could get a freshly roasted duck for forty copecks, a chicken for thirty, a fat goose, crisp and dripping, for seventy.
“And these dogs allow us to starve on thin broth! ” Schnarrenberg repeated.

Scarcely had the train stopped at a station when Pod, Briinn, and Blank jumped out. Blank, with his tscheinik, had to get the hot water for the tea which was to be had at every station free of charge. Briinn went his own way, which always led him into the neighbourhood of some peasant girls, but Pod was a faithful purchaser.

I often saw him from my car. He stepped with a look of a connoisseur to each stand, took hold of things, felt them, dug his fingers into them, his nose almost curling up at the variety of odours. Finally he would draw out his paper, that wonderful paper which began with “ hunger” and ended with “no money,” and between these two prisoner symbols — Pod’s most important words — all those things which were the dreams of his ever empty stomach.

After a while he would come back with some titbit. “ Man, Junker,” he said after his first expedition, “if we had more money —I do believe that in this blessed country I could get enough to eat for once....”
At a small station I got out with Schnarrenberg. We hobbled up and down slowly and somehow missed the guard’s signal to get on. Even before we understood in what way we
had sinned, the guard had dug into my side with the butt of his gun so that I almost stopped breathing. I ran hurriedly to our car. “ Come, Schnarrenberg, for God’s sake,” I called out.
He did not heed me. Perhaps he thought that he knew the Russians better. “‘ Confounded scoundrel,” he roared at the konvot. “ What are you thinking of to abuse us so? ”

Putting his finger in his mouth, he whistled, and three guards came up. Four leather nagaikas, torn from their girdles, covered Schnarrenberg with a rain of blows. Bright blood dripped from his forehead and from his cheeks. Without a sound he staggered to our car and fell on both knees almost as soon as we had dragged him into safety from the rain of pattering blows.
“He won't risk any more talk,” said Briinn sarcastically.

In Nizhni Novgorod our trip suddenly came to an end. Nobody knew why. At a spot where ancient granaries of black wood looked down upon us, we had to get out, and there we sat for hours on the hard pavement watching the buzzing life of this old commercial city. At noon twenty peasant wagons rolled up to where we sat. “For the wounded!” said the guard. “ Man,” muttered Briinn, “is it possible that there are really human beings in this town? ”

We climbed up on to the wooden teljagen and made ourselves as comfortable as possible. A troop of Cossacks with clashing sabres surrounded us on all sides. “ Forward, pascholl!” The streets were incredibly full of holes — almost tunnelled. Even though we proceeded very slowly, we were terribly battered and bruised.

We drove for an hour through the city. The streets were lined with houses carved up to the roofs, belonging to rich merchants; and curious churches stood in the squares. Variegated Oriental life passed by us. The people stood and followed the long procession with proud eyes. Some lowered their heads when they saw our rags; others looked at us menacingly. “ As if we were driving about in a paint-box! ” said Pod.

Even after two hours we had not reached our goal. A third hour passed, and still we were driving through the middle of the town. “Have we not already seen this church with the blue cupolas, Briinn? ” “ Either these Russians do not know their own city,” he answered laughing, “or they are making use of us as exhibits, driving us a few times through the whole town in order to make the people believe in a countless number of prisoners! ”

He was right. We saw some streets three or four times and only got out of the city in the evening into a small central camp like that of Ugrieschskaja, a fenced-in court with three already half-filled wooden sheds. “Ill be hanged if the whole business had any other purpose than to show the people their captives! ” said Briinn. “I fear that we shall be driven through many a city before we get to our destination...” nodded Pod.

The same plank beds as in Ugrieschskaja were in the barracks, the floor of which was not even of wood and had been turned into slush by the rain of the past days. Those who were already there crouched opposite us, among them a small group of Germans who looked at us inquisitively, and a Hanoverian dragoon, a large and slender Cornet, who came up to us. “ My name is Seydlitz. Can we help you? ”
“ Thank you, we only need quiet, I think. But have you been captive long? You look so fresh! ”
“ For three weeks. We come directly from the front.”
“How do matters stand? ” Schnarrenberg and I asked simultaneously. He pushed me violently to one side.
The White dragoon reported. Was it possible? Victories, always victories? In Kurland, Poland, Galicia? “We hope for peace before the winter is over,” he finished.

Schnarrenberg stretched himself. His face, covered with blood and still striped from blows, was covered for the first time with a smile. “ Boys,” he said brightly, “we are victorious, that is the main thing! And everything else...” He raised his hand and snapped his fingers contemptuously. “* No, this is the principal thing...”
The next morning I was roused by a slight dispute. “ You must have gone mad! ” I heard Pod say.
I rubbed my eyes. “ What’s the matter, Pod? ”

He pointed to a volunteer with spectacles who crouched with naked upper body on the plank bed next to him, a frail youth with the face of a girl. “This lad cannot kill lice, Junker. Did you ever hear of such a thing! He takes one after another out of his shirt, and sets it down carefully on the ground....”
“You are a pacifist, I suppose, eh? ” Briinn called across. |
We all laughed loudly. “No, lad,” said Pod, angered, lifting his broad paw and waving it lightly. “I advise you to put your friends out of doors—else [ll kill them on your _ own body! ”
All lay in the meadow in the midday sun. We got a little thin soup and a bit of meat on a wooden spike. A few really got a bit of meat, but most got a bundle of muscle and skin mixed with the wood. |
*“*Can’t we buy anything here? ” asked Pod gloomily.
The White dragoon, who, with a little hussar from Wandsbeck, had joined us, shook his head. “ Only kvass,” he said.
“ Kvass? ” said little Blank. “Is that something to eat? ”
“No, to drink — Russian beer made of fermented black bread, I think....”
“Of black bread?” shouted a Bavarian, called by his comrades the “Schwalangscher.” “Holy Lord! — and _ this they call beer? Are these people quite forsaken of God? ”

He went away to look at the beverage more closely. Three of the men were playing cards, another cutting his toe-nails. “IT saw an uhlan on a plank bed a little while ago,” I said to Seydlitz. “ What ails him? ”
“ Dysentery,” said Sedylitz softly, and continued: “ He is a splendid fellow, a war volunteer of forty-five years, a Doctor Sieveking from Hamburg, a lawyer. A pity about him.”
One evening Briinn sat down at my side. “ Junker,” he said, “T should like to learn a little Russian, too. I think we shall soon go on, and then one could use it....”
I did not mention books or any method of teaching —I had grown wiser. “ Well,” I said briefly, “what do you want to know? Have you got a piece of paper? Write it down....”
“ How do you say: ‘I love you’ ?”
He wrote it down. “ Give me a kiss? ” he then asked.
I told him. “I should like to sleep with you? ” he continued, in a matter-of-fact voice. I told him this also, and he wrote it down carefully. “ Anything else? ” I asked.
“No, thank you, that is enough for me...” he said briefly. He then sat down apart, with wrinkled forehead, and learnt it by heart.

Eight days later our wagons again appeared in the yard, and we were ordered to get ready at once. The entire camp was being evacuated, and those who had come before us had to go too. Only some twenty or thirty who were unfit for transport stayed behind.
We stood up, but sat down again immediately on the grass. We were slowly beginning to learn what “at once” — sitschas — meant in Russian. “Now there will be more
blows,” I said in a tired voice. “If we were only in the cars again! I could not stand being on a lower plank bed....”
“No fear, my son,” said Pod. “ I'll take it.”

When we saw the guards coming from far off, I hobbled back with my two new comrades to the shed. Dr. Sieveking was lying on the grass in the sun, his limbs drawn up, his head on a large stone. His riding-breeches were stiff and hard from phlegm and blood, his hair white and tangled, his cheek-bones protruding, his lips dry. He wished to clasp our hands once more, but he was only able to extend his fingers a little.
“ Just go on, my boys,” he said with fixed eyes. “Go on, my dear boys! And do not forget Germany! ”

Pod had taken the two new-comers, Seydlitz and Posek, on to our plank bed. He had realized that I should like it and had invited them.... “So that our Junker may have a couple of people with whom he can converse decently,” he said roughly. “I am only a stupid rascal....”

The train rolled on. Day after day went by. Pod no longer jumped eagerly off the train whenever a station came. I could only send him out to buy things once a day. “ We must be saving, Pod. I have only three roubles left — how much have you?” ;
“Man,” he said gloomily, “I haven’t had a copeck for weeks....”

If we could only have got money somewhere! I must keep Pod in good humour, cost what it might. It was not only to me, but to us all, as if the sun were shining in our gloomy car when he was cheery. But he was only cheery when he had - eaten enough, and he needed a great deal....

Of the five new-comers we had in our car, two were sick with dysentery. They had been too weak to get to an upper plank bed and now lay, feeble and dirty, in a dark corner. They no longer ventured to creep forth by day, but at night they lay, their backsides at the cracks of the sliding doors, for hours at a time. Although they ate hardly anything, they were constantly evacuating, and everything about them was sodden.
“Dirty mess! ” cursed the Schwalangscher. “Throw them out! ”
“And if it were you? ” little Blank called out in excitement. “(Can the poor fellows help it? ”
“IT guess you want a slap in your face,” Pod muttered, meaning the Schwalangscher.
“TI only meant to say that they ought not to have been allowed to come with us,” he said, silenced.

At the stations we now often met long trains of refugees, from the Ukraine and Poland, from Lithuania and the Baltic. For months they had been living with wives and children in the cars, in which they had made themselves as comfortable as possible.
“ Junker,” said Briinn on the evening of a day we had passed in such a station, “do ask the guard whether we could get a girl to come with us.”

“Why? We have collected five roubles; isn’t that enough for him? It is one of the refugees, a pretty girl — young, plump, healthy! She can remain until tomorrow morning with us and then return at once...”
“But I don’t want to ask! Find someone else.”
He looked at me with wide-open eyes. “ But why not? ” he asked amazed.
“ Because I won’t have a hand in sain a shameful thing....”

“ Listen,” he said, “ you may think about it as you choose — we don’t want to know your reason! But if you have so little feeling of comradeship in you... you are young, perhaps you don’t know yet what it means.... We old ones, how-

ever, we married ones.... Do you believe that I bite my fingers till the blood comes every night for nothing? Every night, every night.... No, by the Lord,” he broke forth, “IT beg of you, we all beg of you; nobody but you can speak with him! Oh, God in heaven...”

That night, just as the “turn-in” signal sounded, Briinn drew a robust, buxom girl into the car on the off side. The guard pretended to be asleep, no one spoke a word, only the gipsy whined like a dog.

The girl turned round, shivering with cold, and laughing in an embarrassed way. Briinn seized her violently and drew her by both hands to the lower plank bed which had been cleared for the purpose by the others. I heard his hard breathing, saw his spread hands moving up and down her body. “Lord in heaven! ” he said every moment, “Lord in heaven....”

Thirty starved men looked on stealthily, but only the gipsy crouched openly beside him. Seydlitz and Posek, Blank, Pod, and I lay on our backs looking up at the ceiling with fixed eyes. I felt a savage tenderness towards Pod the giant, Pod the bear. At the same time I was tortured by a dull suspense. Would he also... ?

Suddenly Briinn shouted. It was not a human sound that broke forth from him. It was the sound of an animal that for a few seconds had forgotten its captivity and had dreamed he was in golden freedom. A sound came to my ears as if from a wrestling-match. Was it necessary to wrestle with one another to obtain that which was said to be the fairest in life? Was it painful... ?

What were they doing? I thought horrified. I had never seen it. I had never done it either. It burned in me as if to rend me. I had to bite my lips to keep myself from looking at them openly like the gipsy....

When towards morning I turned round once, I saw the gleaming flesh of the girl. She had hardly anything on her body, nor was it any longer Briinn who knelt beside her. It was already the fourth, sixth, or eighth....

Briinn lay in the open space and slept, his handsome barber’s face smiling, his turned-up little moustache twitching. Little Blank was weeping, his youthful body shaking violently. Pod lay next to me bathed in perspiration. He held his fists pressed over his eyes and incessantly whispered: “ Anna! Anna!...”.
In Samara I sent Pod for the last time to make purchases. “ There is only enough left now for a dozen meat pyroschnis, Pod,” I said smiling. “The last copecks— bring what you can for them.” ;

He came back with twice as much as he should rightfully have got. It was always the way with him. Devil knows how he managed it!. Were the peasant women not able to withstand this begging bear, or did he steal?
For once we até enough to satisfy us. The next day Briinn, with a symbolic motion, drew his leather belt tighter. “ The beautiful days of Aranjuez are over now...” he quoted pathetically. |

I no longer got out at the stations. I could not look at Pod as he stood with open mouth in front of the tables of pyroschnis, the upper part of his body bent a little forward, his eyes hypnotically gazing at the fat and shining brown pasties. He had already been subjected to blows once because he had not heard the signal to get in — Blank now took care of him. All of us had a feeling of misery in the pit of the stomach when we saw geese and ducks. “I can no longer stand the smell of this stuff! ” said Briinn.
It fared worse with the two suffering from dysentery. They lay curled up under the plank bed, and their faces seemed to

be covered with wrinkled parchment. They could no longer drag themselves to the sliding doors in order to evacuate, and around them was a puddle of yellow phlegm and pale blood. Their wet clothes smelt horribly, and when we stepped back from the open air into the car, we felt like vomiting till bile came.
For a third time I spoke with the guard. “Comrade,” I said, “those two will die if they are not taken to a hospital! We shall all be infected. Do report it to the commander of the transport...”
“ Die, and to the devil with you! And if you come to me again about the matter...” He laid his hand on the nagazka. Its switches were still black from Schnarrenberg’s blood.
“‘ What kind of soldiers are these? ” asked Seydlitz hoarsely.

“Qh,” I said, “they are not soldiers, they are transporters of the exiled, that troop of police whose sole task it is to take criminals to Siberia. They can be recognized by their uniform, green rubaschka, black riding-breeches, revolvers with red cord, Cossack sabres, nagaika.”
“Then we are not prisoners of war?” was all he said. “We are only criminals, murderers, thieves, deported? Well, then I understand...”

One morning we heard a long-drawn moaning under our plank bed. Pod got down and drew a sick man by his feet out of the dark. He was very heavy and the other had lain half upon him. Pod took hold of him also and started back frightened. “ He is already cold! ” he said roughly. “ Come, take hold! ” The upper one in dying must have rolled over him, and he was too weak to free himself. Now he moved his eyes pleadingly and gurgled something which we did not understand.

By the time we reached the next station, the second one had also uttered his last sigh. We breathed in relief. “The Lord be praised! ” said the Schwalangscher. “ At last we shall be rid of them!” No one was angry at him this time. All were thinking the same.
When the train stopped, I hastened to the commander of the transport, a bearded N.C.O. “Two men have died of dysentery in our car. Would you please give orders for their bodies to be removed? ”
“ Nitschewo! That would mean a lot of writing. Anyway we are almost at our destination. I must deliver the full number.”
I felt myself growing pale. “ How....2 But that cannot “be.... We shall all be infected.... Some of us still have open wounds....”
“TI must deliver the full number,” he called out brutally. “Tdji! Hun! Pascholl!”
Nobody answered when I told them. Schnarrenberg’s jaws ground violently, little Blank clapped his hands before his face, Seydlitz threw back his head proudly.
“ Throw them under the plank bed,” said the guard, rolling a cigarette and spitting.

Pod and Briinn drew them by their legs into the darkest corner. They glided noiselessly to the floor, leaving a broad track of mucus behind them like snails. “ We must wash the floor at the next station and sprinkle it with chloride from the toilet,” said Schnarrenberg, “or we shall all perish....”

For four days we travelled on in their company. Gradually a biting odour began to penetrate through the cracks of the plank bed under which they were lying, and sometimes it seemed as if the cold of their bodies rose up into our limbs. We no longer spoke or sang. Often at night one or another would start up out of his dreams screaming. Pod’s full face had grown pallid and hollow-cheeked in the last few days. Blank often cried himself asleep, and at such times he sought shelter on Pod’s broad body as a child does on its mother’s.

Upon our arrival at the camp station the first snow was falling, thin as dust, and through its shimmering drizzle we beheld the country spreading out to the horizon in lifeless desolation. We did not yet know that this treeless steppe was one of the most miserable regions of old Russia, that it was the Orenburg sand-steppe, but we felt its desolation at the first glance. “ And is it in this God-forsaken corner of the world that we are to live in retirement? ” asked Briinn.

Again we had to wait for hours drawn up into two lines before the cars. All were badly frozen, but particularly we who were wounded, because we could not stamp our lame legs on the ground to warm ourselves. “Could they not, at least, have left us in the car until they were pleased to take charge of us? ” Schnarrenberg snarled.

At last a couple of Cossack officers came riding up from the nearest village. We were counted off, once, twice, three times —§it would not tally. “ Where the devil are the two missing ones? ” roared the bearded N.C.O. “ In the car,” we all murmured in dull chorus. “Why did they not come out with you? ”
“ Because they died like dogs! ” Seydlitz broke out.

Pod signed to the Schwalangscher. “Tie my handkerchief over my nose!” he said grimly, taking out a second rag and tying it over the Schwalangscher’s mouth. Then, with tightshut lips, they climbed into the car and dragged out the two by their boots.
‘Stop, stop — where to? ” shouted the N.C.O.

*“‘ Where they belong,” muttered Pod, and laid them directly under the hoofs of the commandant’s horse. The animal snorted violently, reared up, and backed. The second officer’s horse, a white one, almost turned a somersault. The faces of the dead were bluish-black. The snow gently and swiftly covered their open eyes.
** All here, Your Excellency,” reported the N.C.O. |
The commandant, a little wizened fellow with the pointed face of a mouse, touched his fur cap lightly with his hand, quite unmoved. “In fours, forward, march!” he growled from his saddle.
Silently we moved off. “This shrew-mouse is a regular skinner, if I am not mistaken,” said Pod, with conviction.

We were brought for the first time since our capture into earthen barracks, horribly unhealthy, much-feared rectangular sheds dug deeply into the ground and covered with a flat roof. They were not even finished, for the walls were only partly covered with thin boards, and in many places the bare earth peeped out. At the ends were the doors, along the sides a couple of little windows, already half covered by the drifting snow; and in the centre was a long aisle leading from door to door. The remaining space was taken up by two tiers of plank beds made of pine boards.
“By thunder,” said Briinn, “the veriest fox-holes, and so dark that a man can’t even read his morning paper! ”

We lay down together as before. Again twice as many were forced into one shed as there was actually room for. If we could only have moved about a little, could have nailed: a few boards together for a table! For weeks we had been eating off the bare floor. In time our backs would become so crooked that we should no longer be able to look up at the sky....
“‘Doesn’t the stove appear to you too small for so large a space? ” asked Blank anxiously. He was anemic and always cold.
“Earthen barracks are said to be very warm,” remarked Seydlitz consolingly.
The first evening Pod came in with an infantryman as thin as a rake. “ This is another who is condemned to be constantly famishing,” he said in his dry way. He seemed to be a

daring fellow. A sharp, hooked nose adorned his leather-skin face, out of which there blinked a pair of black, fiery eyes. “ Is there room for this man in our guild? ” Pod continued. “ He is a much-travelled lad, an artist and a conjurer. I thought he might be able to cheer us up a little now and then by his tricks.”

When, after three days, the first wood for fuel came, large fragrant logs, Pod and the conjurer went out for booty. Pod came back with a black eye, eight logs, and a mocking smile. “Here, boys,” he said, “is a pillow for each —thick and thin ones; choose as you used to do at home with mother! ”

They were all smooth, wedge-shaped pieces. Up to that time I had always used my riding-boots, the soft uppers of which, when rolled round the soles, made a useful head-rest and, when laid on the wedge-shaped log, could be used as a horsehair pillow. If we had only had covers,... When captured, I was fortunately wearing my long cavalry coat, and could use it as a covering, but many had nothing on their bodies except their tunics and froze terribly every night.

Schnarrenberg, the senior in rank in this shed, informed us that the commandant was looking for an interpreter in order to be able to speak with the prisoners of war. “ Report for the post,” urged Seydlitz, Pod, Briinn, and Blank. “ Who knows who else may report and perhaps betray us for some small advantage to himself?... Yes, Junker, do so! Then our complaints will at least come to the right quarter! ” |

I got a guard to take me to the commandant. The Shrewmouse sat in the staff-building smoking one papirossi after another. A German surgeon-major whom I had not yet seen was standing before him, a gentlemanly, erect man. I was just able to hear him say in French that something had to be done.
For no particular reason I suspected that the commandant knew only a few words of French. He always used the same words: Certainement, sans doute....
“It is unprecedented,” continued the surgeon-major in a sharp voice.
** Oui, oui, sans doute.... Well, and you? ” He turned to me, speaking in Russian.
“*T want to report for interpreter. Your Excellency has made known —— 99
“Very good, charascho.... You are very young. Must children be sent to the front in Germany? ”
Always the same silly question, I thought. “I am a war volunteer,” I said for the hundredth time.
He laughed sneeringly. “Indeed?... Well, much pleasure...”
“Has Your Excellency any further commands? ” I asked briefly.
“No, you can go. You are interpreter from today. Nor do I need you any more, doctor. Good morning....”

We remained standing in front of the staff-building. “ Dr. Bockhorn,” said the surgeon-major, shortly. “We shall in a way work together, Ensign,” he added, firmly grasping my hand; “ and it will not be easy for either of us. Incredible conditions prevail in this camp, especially as regards sanitary arrangements. And nothing is done! Yes, he promised everything — certainement, sans doute — and he does not even understand French, this whitewashed Oriental! But what am I to do? He does not know German, I do not know Russian.... It will be better now! ”
When I came back, all looked at me in suspense,
“ Well, my son,” asked Pod, “how was it in the den of the lion? ”
“* Yes, I have become interpreter,” I said joylessly. “ But you were right, Pod, the Shrew-mouse is a skinner. There is a Ger-
man physician in the camp, a man of spirit. He _ take care of us. Dr. Bockhorn is his name....”

Yesterday morning the Shrew-mouse had an Austrian flogged because the famishing man had stolen a bit of meat. Four Cossacks undressed him and threw him down on the frozen ground, his hands and feet tied together with long ropes. At each end two Cossacks stood and stretched his body by means of these ropes until it was nearly torn asunder, while an N.C.O. beat his naked back with all his force with a seven-tailed nagaika. After the very first blows the skin over his lean spine and ribs burst. Dripping with blood, the Austrian shrieked as if he were dying. The Shrew-mouse smoked a cigarette and watched each blow. “ Count out loud! ” he called several times. When the Cossacks stopped after the fortieth blow, he said calmly: “Another ten and this barbarian will not shriek again....”

A short time afterwards the first cold of winter set in. There was only enough wood to get the stove a little warm, and there were daily fights for places near it. Freezing hurt, but so long as all else did not fail... There was not even water in the camp. It had to be fetched in barrels from the river, and no one wanted to go for it in that cold. When I reported to the commandant that two water-carriers had had their hands frozen because they had no gloves, he said they should wrap their foot-rags round them.

I asked for tools so that a pit could be dug for the excrement. There was no definite place — all the prisoners sat down in the corner of the yard, since the cold weather had set in, even in front of the shed doors. “I have no tools,” said the commandant, polishing his nails. I asked for large consignments of wood. When morning came, the clothes of those lying along the outer walls were frozen to the wet plank beds. “ There is no wood in the whole steppe,” answered the commandant, stretching out his legs comfortably in front of the over-heated stove. ‘‘ Moreover, the stoves are in the sheds for ventilation, not for heating. Prisoners of war have to provide their own fuel! ”

When I left the staff-building, a young Cossack officer followed me. He had been standing next to the commandant on our arrival, and his horse had almost turned a somersault when Pod had laid down the two dead men in front of them. He greeted me courteously and took a long look at me. “ Tell me again what it is you wish,” he said in a good-natured voice. “ Pll see whether I can do anything for you. But don’t hope for anything! I am as powerless as you....”

Unusual laughter greeted me as I entered the shed. A tall sapper from the neighbouring plank bed held a paper in his hand from which he was just reading aloud. “ Have you not yet noticed that I love you? ” he read pathetically. “I devour you with my glances, I follow you everywhere. I caress the place where you lie. Come to me tonight. No one in my corner will say anything, each of us has a friend....”
‘* What does this mean? ” I asked Pod.
