* A love-letter,” he said quietly, almost shamefacedly. “ The sapper found it by chance. Someone in his plank bed must have written it.”
“A letter from a man to a man? ” I asked stupidly.
The sapper read on. “ I kiss you, I worship you....” At this moment somebody laughed, not genuinely, but artificially, shrilly.
“Man,” called out another in vexation, “do not pretend. Did you not this very morning write one yourself to the little dragoon? To little Blank next to us? ”
During the second week a German orderly came to fetch me. “You are to come to Dr. Bockhorn, please.”

Dr. Bockhorn lived with five Austrians and two young German doctors in a detached stone house. All greeted me cordially, but were surprisingly silent. “ Ensign,” said Dr. Bockhorn, “I have an unpleasant communication to make to you. Typhus has broken out in shed IV.”

“We must take counsel,” he continued. “ We have nothing, no remedies. What are we to do with empty hands? There is not even a hospital division in this camp. And there are altogether twenty-four thousand men here. There is nothing at hand, neither blankets not bandages, neither linen nor soap, neither water nor wood near at hand. It will lead to a terrible catastrophe if we cannot induce the commandant to do something. Be ready for tomorrow. In the mean while we will draw up a list of what is absolutely necessary! ”
At the door of our shed I came upon Seydlitz. ‘“‘ What is the matter with you? ” he asked. “ You look so miserable! ”
We crept together on to our plank bed, he helping me a little with the climbing. “If only we could get some letters sometimes! ” said Brinn. “I’ve not heard anything from my wife for five months....”
“Yes,” said Pod gloomily, “no news from home, that is the worst! All may be dead long ago. If I but knew whether the harvest was good...” "
“My boy began school at Easter,” said Schnarrenberg. I had never heard him speak in so soft a voice. “I wonder how he looks, the fair-headed little lad in his gay CAs 35"
“My sister was confirmed this year,” said von Poseck, dreamily. “She is so lovely and gentle that I always felt ashamed to be near her....”

“ My brother was to have been an apprentice this year,” said little Blank, “to the same boss that I had. He was gladly taken to replace me. The boss is a large dealer in groceries, bread, butter, eggs, sausage, ham...”
‘Suddenly Pod turned me round to him by the shoulders. “ What’s the matter with you, lad? ” he asked roughly. “ Does anything trouble you? ”
I released myself. “ Let me alone, Pod.”

“Call them all,” I said hoarsely, “but softly —no one is to know as yet.” They crowded close to me. Sixteen eyes were looking at me, wide open, with a presentiment of something dreadful. “ Typhus has broken out, comrades,” I whispered.

We did not achieve anything. First we pleaded, then we stormed. Finally the Shrew-mouse threw us out. The Cossack Captain was standing next to him. His face went white when I translated what Dr. Bockhorn said, and he threw himself between the doctor and the commandant when the latter wanted to go for the doctor with his riding-whip.

In the shed frozen limbs were of daily occurrence. A few from each bed had fever. The Cossacks had to drive out the men with their nagaikas to make them fetch water. Outside, on the right and left of the doorways, mountains of excrement began to form. Some did not go out any more when they wanted to evacuate. The stubborn fight against vermin gradually became purposeless. Sometimes it seemed as if the lice came in multitudes out of the ground, and, in addition, our faces were disfigured and swollen by the bites of bedbugs.
“For God’s sake,” said Schnarrenberg one day, puzzled, “this cannot go on. What will be the result of it... ?”

“These lice,” said Pod comfortingly, putting a fat insect with a black mark on its back on his thumb-nail, “ have received the Iron Cross from the Russians for torturing us to death. Don’t you see it on its back? ”
“Do you know, Pod,” said I roughly, “that they are the transmitters of spotted typhus? ”
His smile died away. “Is that so... ?” he said hoarsely. “Ts that so? ”

The little windows were now completely snowed up. Formerly we had been able to recognize by his legs whether a passer-by was one of us or a Russian. We had already learnt to tell our comrades by their boots and their gait. We knew when Schnarrenberg returned from an official errand and stamped by in heavy riding-boots curved a little outwards, or when the conjurer went out on a raid for booty, by a couple of stork-legs stuck like two sticks in a pair of much too wide infantry boots.

Many busied themselves for hours in guessing from this part of a human body, not only rank and nationality, but age and characteristics. They made a sort of science of it and maintained that more was visible from the boots and gait of a person than from his face. But now we could not even pass the time with this amusement.

Everything seemed gradually to perish in a gloomy twilight. “* We cannot even find our lice now,” said Briinn. There was only enough petroleum to burn for three hours in the evening at each end of the shed. Our faces slowly grew pale as those of prisoners in a cell, our movements heavy and uncertain. All of us had long, tangled beards, and eyes red and inflamed from the dirt. We could not cut our nails and had to bite them so as not to grow claws. “It would be a laughing matter if it were not so like a weeping one,” said Briinn sometimes. ©

The cavalry corner of our shed, once the liveliest and cheeriest, had become disturbingly quiet. Briinn alone now and then made one of his ironical remarks, but more rarely than in our worst times at the front. Contrary to all expectation, Schnarrenberg had grown extremely depressed. Many despised him for it, but I thought I understood him. It was a period of transformation for him. His hard but just soldier’s heart could not yet understand this meaningless suffering. He still regarded it, so to speak, as unreal and temporary. By the time that he, always accustomed to the most exact order, had realized the change and grown used to the new conditions, he would be an old man and would look upon it as a combat equal to the combats at the front or perhaps even superior to them. |

Little Blank was the most downhearted of all. It grieved us to look at him, and because he had lost so much blood, he suffered most of all from the cold. “ But are these not only summer barracks?” he often asked. “Surely human beings cannot be left to pass the winter here, and a Russian winter at that! ”
That day twenty men died in barrack IV, all of spotted typhus.

“ Junker,” said Pod one morning, “two Hungarians are lying at the door. They have not been on their feet since yesterday and have a strange look. Do go and see whether — ” He broke off and looked at me with an expression in his eyes that made me turn away.

At a moment when I was unobserved, I stole over to them. They were two Honved hussars, clad in grey uniforms, and were, apparently, already delirious. A couple of Croats sitting next to them paid them no attention. Pod had not been mistaken. Their hands were covered with red spots, their lips scabby. They had typhus.
When I returned, Pod drew me aside. “ Well? ”
“Yes, Pod,” I said hoarsely, “now it has come into our shed too. All our group must be told of it, so that they may take proper precautions....”
Pod made the round. When Seydlitz was told, he pressed his eyes together with an inimitable movement which gave his face

an indescribably haughty and contemptuous expression. Briinn shivered and collapsed as if from a stroke. “ That is our deathsentence! ” said he, more gravely than anyone would have thought possible from him.
Schnarrenberg started up. “ Nonsense! Nonsense and cowardice! Keep such ideas to yourself at least, won’t you? ”
The tears dropped from little Blank’s eyes. “I shall be the first,” he said, sobbing. “I have no more power of resistance. This constant freezing has taken it all out of me....”

The two Hungarians died that same evening. Lights began to flicker everywhere, like will-o’-the-wisps on poisonous marshes. We suddenly got more food. It was not that we received more, but that many refused the soup because they could no longer eat. That was less of an advantage to us than it appeared to be, © for the soup was so thin that we could drink it by the pailful without deriving any strength from it, and we did not take more than we absolutely needed; for it gave us a tormenting thirst which we had no water to assuage. And in our situation hunger was less felt than thirst.

The feverish no longer left the shed to relieve nature. The sandy ground began to soften from the urine, and heaps of excrement collected under the plank beds. Schnarrenberg had the excrement cleared away by detachments of the healthier men. Schnarrenberg was certainly slowly finding himself again. It had become clear to him that here, in the rear of the war, one could also fight. He had necessarily to learn the new kind of fighting, and that could not be done in a day. It was such as a German could have no conception of. A soldier found it much more difficult to obey here than at the front, and Schnarrenberg’s orders were only obeyed when Pod and the conjurer drove the men to the work by means of a log of wood. The first day Pod was obliged to knock down an Austrian in order to have Schnarrenberg’s command carried out. His conjurer was invaluable, a ju-jutsu champjon who overcame every resistance with a lightning-like mysterious grip.

Our cavalry corner supported the superior in command by setting the best example. Von Seydlitz, with haughty face, and often out of his turn, cleared away the piles of excrement in our vicinity as if it was an ennobling labour. No one from the neighbouring plank beds appreciated this, nor did anyone appreciate Schnarrenberg, who, because he was in command, was daily in danger of his life, so much so that he could no longer pass through the shed without a body-guard, or he might have been strangled. Yet his energetic orders certainly saved the lives of many of us, though it seemed as if all had lost hope and would have preferred to put their hands over their eyes and suffocate in the dirt.
Dr. Bockhorn informed me that the typhus had already spread to all the sheds. Sixty died daily. It would be Christmas in a few days.

Pod had made a good find in the conjurer, who was handy in everything and always willing. He took garments away from the dead in order to provide us with good clothes, and none of us objected. “ Are they the less warm for that? ” said Briinn. We did not freeze so badly, and that was the main thing. We scarcely recognized each other, however, for we sat on the beds shapelessly muffled up in two or three tunics. We wore, chiefly, Austrian uniforms over our old ones. They were rather thin, but, worn in twos or even threes, gave us warmth. At times the conjurer showed us a few of his tricks, and though we could no longer laugh at them, we all liked to see them.

The only one who would not accept any of this weird clothing was little Blank, who needed it most. “No,” he shouted, when the conjurer urged him to have a cloak, and shrank back as if he thought it would burn him. “ No, Hatschek, I’'d rather freeze....”

Last night was Christmas Eve; what more can be. said? Nothing but the words that Dr. Bockhorn had spoken that evening: “ A human being who is not capable of sacrificing himself for an idea, no matter of what kind, is not yet a human being in the higher sense of the word, has not yet exceeded the animal.... We are doing here that which makes the real human being — suffering for an idea....”

One morning the first of the doctors died, the younger of the two Germans, the one with the scarred face. The day before, he had broken down at the side of a sick man and had not regained consciousness. Dr. Bockhorn raged. “ Are we in a madhouse? ” he roared. “ Are we in hell? ” During the past week he had aged ten years.

In front of the sheds the corpses began to accumulate in great heaps. We were not even given a barn to put them in, and the ground was frozen too hard to permit of their being buried, even if there had been anyone strong enough to dig the graves. They were simply thrown out on to the heaps of excrement, where fat rats gnawed at them.

Little Blank entreated us not to make him go out any more. He had found an old tin can somewhere. “ Pardon me,” he said, like a child, “ but I cannot go out of doors. I should die of disgust. The dead are lying about everywhere and staring at me....”

In our barracks we had forty dead up to that time, and we had been able to take them all out. Pod was still strong and - kind. In those days, towards the end of January, one hundred persons died daily in the whole camp.

On the preceding day as many had died in our shed as in the whole camp a fortnight before. Matters went rapidly downhill with us. The doors were scarcely opened even to throw out the dead. Once Pod had to lead a detachment to free the doers. It had not been possible to get out or in on account of the piles of dead. When he came back from this expedition, he looked so different that I scarcely recognized him. “ Junker,” said he, in a new, strange voice, “I liked being a soldier and did not shirk when my country called me. But I went in the belief that I was a soldier and should be treated like a soldier — not like a convict. This here is... is.... And if they should get me again some time without having cared that such a thing could happen once more — ”
** Don’t weaken, Pod,” said I, in a low tone. “ We serve our country here just as at the front! It is only another sort of combat, harder perhaps and more enervating, but...”
He swung his arms about. “ Yes,” he shouted, “but...
* Be calm, Pod,” I begged, “ and be just. Do you believe that the Russian prisoners of war have such treatment with us, too? ”
‘“‘ The Russians are not to blame for our sufferings,” Briinn interposed. His voice sounded cutting and full of hatred. “ His head is not all right! ” I thought, startled. |
“The war! ” he shouted. “The war!” he repeated, yelling hysterically, beside himself. “The war....”

Next morning someone shook me awake. Before me stood the German assistant doctor, a young medical student. He looked alarmed, and his eyes burned out of black sockets. “Get up,” said he; “ we must go to the commandant again. Two Austrian doctors died last night.”

I walked beside him through the dark shed. Sometimes we had to step over strangely distorted bodies that lay in the aisle. They were men attacked by fever who had fallen from the uppermost plank beds.

“ How can you stand this? ” he asked weakly. “ We at least have our quiet room — are alone at least a few hours every night without having to hear shrieks, without having to see dying men. But you...”
“We do not hear or see it any more,” I said. “ We have grown callous.”
“* Yes, there is no other explanation; nevertheless...
‘How is the surgeon-major? ” I asked quickly.

Still well.... But who knows... ? With it all he is consuming himself inwardly. Spotted typhus is not necessary. It can be avoided. Light, food, cleanliness, make it impossible. That’s the worst of it; it is not necessary. Only slovenliness, only laziness, only indifference.... I fear today’s interview. .. » He is no longer master of himself.”
In the doctor’s house Dr. Bockhorn and an Austrian doctor were awaiting us. He greeted me shortly. “Good morning, Ensign. I need not tell you anything, eh? ‘ Either — or’ is the word today! ”

The Cossack Captain was sitting in the ante-room. In the name of the doctors I begged him to take us to the commandant. He made a helpless gesture and looked discouragingly from one to the other. “ Captain, we entreat you for our last fifteen thousand men! ” I said. He bit his lips and went in. There was evidently a violent dispute. “ You must, commandant,” I heard the Captain say. “It is in the regulations.” At last he came out, much agitated. “Please...”
We stood in a half-circle before the commandant. A huge army revolver was lying in readiness on the desk. It was not there the last time, I thought to myself.

Dr. Bockhorn spoke. I translated. “ We request that you put more water at our disposal. We cannot even moisten the lips of the feverish. We beg for military blankets, or at least some straw. All the sick are bedsore from the hard boards, and the danger of contagion is, accordingly, enormous. We beg for wood for the stoves. Besides dysentery and typhus, thirty per cent of the men have inflammation of the lungs and frozen limbs.”
“I cannot work magic,” replied the Shrew-mouse.
Dr. Bockhorn began to shout. I hesitated a little. Then I translated: “ No prisoners’ camp for twenty-five thousand men can be arranged without providing the most needful things.”
“Do you mean to lay down the law for me, an Imperial officer? ” the Shrew-mouse growled. |
“Do you know how many die every day now? One hundred and fifty! ” Dr. Bockhorn raved.
“At the front still more die,” the Shrew-mouse said sarcastically.

Dr. Bockhorn looked as if he wanted to fly at his throat. “We must at least have an empty barn for our dead,” he panted. “Is that asking too much? At the front they at least bury the dead. Here they are left to the rats. In a short time we shall have the plague.” At this the Shrew-mouse started convulsively.
‘Give us tools. Or shall we dig with our finger-nails? ”

Dr. Bockhorn staggered. “‘ Very well,” said he, “ very well. Now tell him the last, Ensign: We need a vacant space for an isolation hospital. Next to the doctor’s house there are empty stone barracks guarded by sentries. We want these barracks. If they are not given to us, they will be taken. You may kill us for it, but we shall be grateful. We entreat for a last time, but then... but then...”
“What was the man saying just now?” interposed the Shrew-mouse suspiciously.
“That the exasperation of the survivors will drive them to the uttermost, and that the fifteen thousand will slay your five hundred Cossacks at one onslaught if you will not —”
“You mean to threaten me? ” he shrieked.
“ Only to inform you,” I said coldly.
“Qut with you! ” he shouted, and gripped his revolver.
“ And the hospital? ” roared Dr. Bockhorn.
*¢ And the hospital? ” I repeated, foaming.
For a second time the Cossack Captain intervened. “I beg of you to a me bas cried entreatingly. “It is folly... I dare not permit.
** See to it that the least possible number of these Huns ever see their homes again! ” the Shrew-mouse yelled at him in a commanding voice. |
The Austrian doctor burst into convulsive weeping. Dr. Bockhorn looked like an insane man. “Everything lost! ” he murmured, “ everything lost....”
I was sitting next to Seydlitz on the plank bed. Opposite to me the long-legged sapper was writhing about, his face and hands spotted. *“‘ Accursed dogs,” he murmured, “ accursed dogs..

“] have been railing at my fate,” said Seydlitz slowly. “I used to think to myself: ‘ Why am I alone condemned to this lazy inaction while my comrades must fight anew for their lives every day? ’” He looked round him and made a comprehensive gesture with his hand. “ Now I am reconciled to it....”
Did he speak the truth? I thought, or did he only say it to give me some firm hold in this chaos, to make us all see some meaning in it and help us to endure what seemed to be meaningless?
“We shall not be ashamed when we do return home,” he continued. “ We shall have no crosses on our breasts, no, not that... but it will be seen by our eyes that we did not flinch

. and perhaps someone will whisper that he was in Totzkoje; for even if we are not at the front, we are none the less here for Germany; and even if it was another kind of combat, still it was a combat for our country, like the other....”

We were silent for a long time. Suddenly he began to speak of Germany, and his hard, somewhat croaking voice became strangely soft — as if he were speaking of a distant beloved, so it seemed to me — as if a lover wished to tell the first one he met of his great happiness and longing. It went to my heart.
“Germany is a meadow in flower,” he said in conclusion. “Germany is a clean, soft, white bed. Germany is limpid water....”
“‘ Lad,“ said Hatschek, the conjurer, “do put on a cloak! We have all been wearing them for weeks and nothing ails us.”
“ Nothing as yet...” whispered little Blank.

“Qh, nonsense! And as for the rest, do you believe that that will save you? Have we not all of us got lice? Are we not all of us sore? There, you see.... No, that is kismet, lad, fate; as one says in German: ‘ Who is to get it will get it though he lay in a room apart.’”
* Hatschek is right, Blank,” I said, coming to his aid. “ You are freezing for nothing. Each louse may bring it, and you have hundreds on you — like all of us.”
“ But I must be doubly careful,” he said obstinately. “I am the weakest of us all.”

In a sudden attack of tenderness I stroked his head. His boyish tuft of hair was matted and the colour of ashes. Alas! I should not have done so; for, with this consoling action, tears streamed from his eyes.
“ Junker,” he asked softly, “have they forgotten us? ”

“Those at home, I mean. Is not Germany a powerful, great empire? How can it be that we are subjected to this? We have done nothing evil; we have only fought for our country, honestly and decently, like the others for their countries. Why are we kept in dungeons? Why are we treated like convicts? No, I cannot explain it otherwise. They have forgotten us....”
‘They must defend the frontier to the last man,” I said, as
to a child. “Perhaps they believe, too, that we are well Offew var

“Yes,” he said, “ yes, certainly.... But someone might nevertheless think of us. We have fathers and mothers and brothers... is there no one there to remind them of us, to say for once: ‘ Do not forget the prisoners of war’ ? ”
“Someone will come in time, my lad, only it is a long time. We are far away, and no news penetrates to them....”

“Yes,” he said passionately, “if we were only permitted to write! Oh, I should tell them about it.... ‘If we were animals, we should long since have perished,’ I should write to them, ‘ but we are human beings....’ There is nothing, no possibility.... Perhaps they think: ‘Oh, our prisoners of war are well off; we need not be anxious about them. For them the war is over....’”
He was right. To receive no news, not to be able to give news! Have we conquered? Have we lost? To know nothing, to hear nothing! That was the worst!

Daily there was more room in the sheds. The incessant struggle for the plank beds had changed its aim. Nobody now wanted the upper places, for fear of not being able to climb up if he should get the fever, since whoever was not able to do so and had no lower bed had to lie in the wet aisle on excrement and urine. ‘a

Dirty icicles hung from the ceiling. The fever-ridden eagerly followed their growth and thrust them, as soon as they were large enough to be broken off, between their crusted lips to cool them. The German doctor came every morning, but his only task was to say who were dead. What else was there for him to do? He did not even need to touch them, so practised had he become. “ Ex,” he said after a glance, “ ex, ex, ex....”

Pod and the conjurer, and often Seydlitz as well, accompanied him on this round. Those designated by “ Ex” were at once piled up in a heap so as to get them out later. No attention was paid now to their names or nationalities. Up till now their identity disks had been taken away from them, but that could be done no longer. :

Were we actually still alive? Or were all of us already dead? Had we been dwelling for years in this den? Or only since yesterday? Blank was right. If we had been animals we had long since perished. But we were human beings... and it is harder to kill a soul than a body....
How much longer was it to last, my God? Two hundred were now dying every day....
I had tried for the last time. I had gone to the Cossack Captain. Had he not human eyes? I went to him in secret.

On the pretence that I had to speak to him officially, a sentry took me into his dwelling. When he saw me, he jumped up from the soft on which he was lying with opened litewka. “ Has something happened? ” he asked in alarm.

“No,” I said, “ not yet, but no one knows how long this can go on—there is latent madness in us all. All know that they have to die —in such a position one shrinks from nothing. What could make it worse? Nothing.... It could only shorten our pains....”
“What can I do? ” he asked in a low tone.

“Everything! Could we not at least get more water? Our men can no longer fetch it, they are too exhausted. But you have soldiers, five hundred men with nothing to do. Or at least a few blankets? Or straw? Even the straw from your horses, which you throw away to rot? Samara is a large town and is not far from here.... A little soap, just for the doctors — a little underwear; our shirts are rotting on our bodies....”
“Oh, please understand me,” he exclaimed. “I am a junior officer. I cannot give such an order, and if I had enough compassion left to die of it, I could not change matters....”

“You must do something, even ever so little,” I almost implored him. “ We must see that there is at least one human being in this land. Show him to us. Fifteen thousand men will curse Russia ifthey do not see him, see him soon, see him tomorrow! ”

Throwing himself on a chair, he laid his head on the table. ** Do you believe that I can ever be at peace again in this life? No, I have had to see too much shame.... Oh, not only here. - «1 have been wounded twice, but I would have reported again long ago for the front if I did not know that here then — ”
“Yes, please, yes, remain here,” I cried. “ Promise me that you will —”
“T shall remain and shall try to soften matters. But that signifies nothing,” he groaned, “ only little drops....”
“Listen,” I interposed, “is there no way by which to give us at least the barracks as an isolation hospital? Could you not, could you not some day forget to post sentries there? ”
He rose. “And what then?” he asked in a smothered voice....
“Then we will move in, and when we are once in... he will not dare to drive us out again.” :
* And another thing. Come over to us once! I vouch for you. No harm will come to you. Hitherto you have only heard how it looks in our shed. You must see it —see it....”
“IT shall come. But now you must go away. No one must know that I spoke to you in secret. I should be degraded and sent to Siberia if he were to discover thatI...” |

He pressed both my hands. “ Here, take this...” giving me a box of cigarettes. “ Now go... I shall do everything, by God...” How warm and clean his hand was! How kind and comforting his voice sounded!...
Briinn was crouching on a vacant plank bed. His hair was matted, his moustache drooped, his eyes were uneasy. He held a large louse between his finger-tips.
“To think that such a beast should carry death in itself, eh? ” he said in a voice that almost sobbed with agitation. “So small and insignificant — one could hardly believe it....”

His eyes were staring and almost looked as if hypnotized by the bright grey dot which was violently trying to free itself from his nails. ‘“‘ Want to bite me, eh? Want to inoculate me? Or have you already done so?...” Suddenly he crushed it, threw it on the plank bed, and trampled like mad on it with both feet. “You beast!” he shrieked. “You beast! Do you want to murder me? Do you want to murder us all?...”
That day the Cossack Captain visited our shed. Pod was the first to see him. “ A Russian officer is standing at the door and wants to speak with you,” he said.
“* He wants to inspect our shed, Pod,” I said hurriedly. “ But he must not be hurt! Take along the conjurer.... Schnarrenberg, you come too.”

The four of us went to the door and received him. “I thank you,” I said in a low tone. He raised his hand to his cap. “ Please be quick,” he exclaimed with difficulty. His face was quite green, and he looked as if he was about to vomit. Did it come from the terrible stench in our den? We did not notice it any more. We hardly went out of doors and knew nothing else.

In the first cross-passage twelve men were lying one upon the other. We were waiting for the arrival of the doctor to carry them out. Slime was dropping down from the second block of plank beds, where four men, sick with dysentery, were lying. We had been waiting eight days for their death, but they were tough. The ground was strewn with half-frozen urine puddles and trampled human excrement. |
“ Kill him, the Russian beast! ” yelled a voice from the rear passage. It was the Schwalangscher’s voice.

A Styrian was on his knees singing a monotonous psalm like a dirge. A Bosnian, his parchment face turned towards Mecca, rose and sank on his plank bed in rhythmic prayer. A man sick with abdominal typhus, who in his fever had rolled down from his plank bed, was trying in vain to get up on it again. Pod assisted him up as we passed.

We arrived at our corner. “ Here is our lodging, Captain! ” He remained standing for a moment, pressing his handkerchief over his mouth. Seydlitz saluted in military fashion without moving a muscle of his face. Blank got up, tired. Briinn did not move, only looked askance into his eyes, pale with hatred. ** Accursed dogs! Accursed dogs!” groaned the sapper next to him. |

When we got back to the first cross-passage, half a dozen cries suddenly rose up. “ Don’t let him out alive, the beast! ” shrieked an Austrian voice. “Keep him as hostage! ” a German said. A Hungarian hussar came running out of the crosspassage, madness in his eyes. The leg of a plank bed, forcibly torn away, hung from his fist. Before he could reach us, the conjurer tripped him up with a lightning-like movement of his foot and hurled him under the plank beds.

** Silence! ” cried Pod in his deep voice. We opened the door. The Captain took the handkerchief from his mouth and looked at us in turn. There were tears in his eyes. Were they from the biting air, or from inward emotion? He shook hands with each of us as if he wanted to say something but could not. Then he turned round and went rapidly away.
“‘ He is weeping now, if I am not mistaken,” said Pod slowly.

Yesterday von Poseck complained of headache and attacks of giddiness. At noon he would not take any soup. “ You must eat, Poseck,” said Seydlitz quietly, taking a bit of meat out of the dish and revolving it enticingly, like a top on its wooden spike. “It is a good piece — proper meat! ”

“I cannot, Hans, don’t be angry....” Within an hour he had a fit of vomiting, and shortly afterwards his whole body was seized with a violent chill. The lines round Seydlitz’s mouth grew a shade deeper. He took off his Austrian cloak and covered his friend with it. Poseck shivered violently all over, and his teeth chattered so that they could be heard at a distance. “ What do you think, Ensign? ” asked Seydlitz in a subdued voice.

It was the usual thing — what could one say? I knew that he had found Poseck on the first day, and that they had suffered everything side by side. “ Perhaps it is only an attack of fever,” I said, but I could not look into his eyes the while.

Briinn was fading away with incredible rapidity, although not actually ill. I suspected that in his despair he committed onanism several times every night. He frequently sat with crossed legs on an empty plank bed and talked to himself.

“There is nothing up here,” he said yesterday. “ Thunder! In the field there were always fine posts. When the air was thick there, Briinn could always manage to get an order for the rear lines.... There is no such thing here, there are no rear lines. .. « Here everyone has his turn! Cursed! Not even covering is here... and throwing oneself down is no good either.... No, here one cannot fritter oneself away, there are no such posts here...” |
“Why do you write everything down, Ensign? * Schnarrenberg asked me.

I looked up from my note-book, a thick writing-pad, which I had fortunately rescued when captured. “In order that for once mankind may learn what was possible in the twentieth century! And be able to avoid it in future wars!” I said severely.
“Then you also believe that there always will be, must be, wars? ”
“*No, I do not believe that. But I fear that in the next hun-
dred years, from one day to another, so to speak, we shall not have progressed far enough to have any other kind of solution for our disputes....”

* At the front I never thought much of such diaries,” said Schnarrenberg after a while. “ What good are they? Good ones are as rare as white ravens — most of them consist of either trimmed-up heroic deeds or private intimacies that interest no one. During the fight itself no one can write anything — no one has time for it — and afterwards everything looks different.... Have you, for example, ever observed ~ how a man fell? I never had time for it — he just fell — done. It is like this with everything that happens in war. Afterwards everything looks different.... Here it is not the same,” he continued. “Here one has enough time, one can photograph each single incident in all quietness, describe every trifle exactly to a hair in perfect leisure. Here life does not fly, here it creeps... here descriptions become genuine — after days one can still compare whether one has been exact, even to the dot over the ‘i.’... |

“It is gradually beginning to seem to me like incessant firing, Ensign,” he said in conclusion. “ We waited for the attack as a relief... but here it is still worse. Here this relief, this freedom from suspense, never comes....”

Pod suddenly broke down. He, too, was not actually ill, but he could no longer take hold of the dead, which was easy to understand. The conjurer could not do it by himself, and Seydlitz did not stir from Poseck’s side. So we were as they had been in the other barracks for over a week. The dead were no longer carried out, but, beyond the mental effect, that could have no consequences. Only the conjurer had strength enough to pull them down into the aisles, and there they froze in a few hours. Sometimes a dying man crept into the corner of an upper plank bed, but he was soon betrayed by the odour of decomposition; and he could also be pulled down. I saw prisoners sitting on dead comrades, or making use of the dying to lean against as supports for their backs. A great number of those dead of typhus lay half naked, some with their feet covered only with foot-rags. Only those dead of dysentery lay in all their clothes, which could not be used, because they were completely saturated with mucus. At night we survivors crept under mountains of uniforms taken from the dead to warm ourselves and wrapped ourselves closely in them on all sides to protect ourselves from the rats, though since there were so many dead in the shed, the rats did not molest us living ones.
Two hundred and fifty died daily....

Then, one day, little Blank became prostrated too. He was immediately attacked by high fever and cried constantly for water. Pod, who had remained kind to the living, went out frequently to get snow for him. It was, to be sure, soiled from the excrement all around, but, nevertheless, less dangerous than the dirty icicles that hung from the beams of the roof, and in which the expectorations of the consumptive and the evaporation of those down with dysentery had crystallized. We had placed Poseck and Blank together so as to nurse them together. Poseck was strangely quiet, Blank greatly excited. “You can give me a cloak now,” he said to the conjurer. “ It’s all the same now; yes, give me two, three, as many as you have. I have frozen long enough....”

“Ensign,” he said once, “ are not the Scriptures the cornerstone of all religions? But how does it say in the Scriptures — “Love your enemies’? I cannot make it out.... Is there, perhaps, a Russian God and a German one? ”
I pressed a foot-rag filled with snow on his burning forehead. “ No, my boy,” I said. “There is only one God.”
In the evening his mind began to wander. “ Another pound of coffee for the lady, Franz,” he cried busily. “ Guatemala, special quality! Certainly, madam....”

It was night. I had taken the petroleum lamp from the door and set it on the bed next to me. A few who were afraid of the dark hurled curses after me, but no one had the strength to prevent me from doing it. My book lay on my knees. A copying-ink pencil was in my hand, which was wrapped round with some kind of rag.

I thought of my native country. I no longer had any hope of seeing it again, but my book, at least, should reach it. There would be many diaries about the war — may the Lord forfend that there should be a more heart-rending one, another document like this! My book would suffice for a millennium..

I had always tried to be cool and matter of fact, to let nothing of my moods and opinions get into it, to describe only what I saw. If I did not carefully conceal what was in me, if I allowed some of it to flow into its pages, nobody would be able to read or understand it! It would be nothing but a single inarticulate shriek.... With what kind of letters could I write this down?

I no longer had hopes of getting out. Therefore I wrote that paragraph and added to it: J’accuse —I accuse! But I did not accuse for myself, no, not even for my fourteen thousand comrades who had perished under my eyes in these dens —I accused for the sake of the shame and disgrace to humanity, which comes from God, as the priests say. The disgrace was not to us— our sufferings were too small for that; the disgrace was to one above us — God!

Perhaps there must be wars, but one so near death as I knew only that this disgrace that follows upon it, this monstrous horror, need not be. That I knew. Was it not worse now than two thousand years ago? If we had been made slaves, as was the custom in those times, we should have fared better, and fourteen thousand, perhaps a hundred thousand in all Russia, would not have had to perish like dogs in their own dirt. No man will allow himself to be offended unpunished —so ye believe: does God? And this sin done to His creatures, those made in His image, is against God.

I was tired. I could not go out. At that moment the sapper on the next bed grew silent. He stopped so quickly in his monotonous cursing, which had lasted for days, that I was struck by it. I raised the lamp a little and saw his face. He was dead. He looked like all the others. His individuality was blotted out. He was no longer the sapper from Harburg, Meier or Miiller by name; he was now only one dead of spotted typhus, number 14,324 in this winter, nothing more.
I placed the lamp next to me again and crept under my tunics. From the next plank bed a young Viennese was constantly calling out: “ Mother, mother, now all is over...”

Schnarrenberg had become our chief support. Since life had been at stake, he was up to the mark like no one else. I never heard a sound of complaint from his lips. He was a coarser edition of Seydlitz, so to speak, the type of common soldier as opposed to that of officer. Both were soldiers to the very marrow.

He had only one weak spot, the war, the great war, which all had agreed to call the world war, which was the cause of our sufferings, but of which, nevertheless, we did not speak much. Schnarrenberg alone lived on in it. Was it, perhaps, for this reason that he was bearing all this more easily?

“If one but knew how matters are at the front? ” was his eternal question. But we heard nothing, no mail was sent to us, no sign of life reached us from the outer. world, probably through fear of the scandal that our reports would arouse in the world. We were to disappear without anyone’s learning in what a cruel and inhuman manner...
“Shut up with your war! ” cried Poseck in one of his lucid moments. He was mostly unconscious. “ If the world has not
yet advanced enough to settle conflicts or differences in a sensible and peaceful way — this world with all its technical and scientific progress — it can go to the devil for me! ”
We were all surprised at this outbreak. Schnarrenberg wanted to retort, but I drew him away. “ Do leave him in peace, for God’s sake,” I said hastily. “Do you not see... ?”

That day the sentries were not posted in front of the empty barracks. I ran at once to Dr. Bockhorn. “ We must move into the barracks at once, doctor!” Bockhorn nodded absently. “Now he has come to his senses, the barbarian!” he said dully. “* Now, when it is almost too late! ” I did not enlighten him.

In the afternoon I went over. The entire place was occupied. The men lay, side by side, on the stone floor, without covering, without straw. Bockhorn ordered empty plank beds to be broken up so that the sick might at least lie on boards. The German assistant doctor and two Austrian doctors were all that remained. They worked from morning till night. It almost made one shriek to look at them.

All those who could creep came full of hope into this hospital, for the tidings of its opening had flown through the shed. What were the doctors to do with them? They divided them into groups of the slightly less ill, such as had still some days to live, and then the severely ill ones, such as would die in a few hours. But there were healthy ones also. These only had dysentery, inflammation of the kidneys, tuberculosis, or abdominal typhus. In short, those who had not spotted typhus or black smallpox were called healthy. Could anything else be done when everything was overfull?

Towards evening an Austrian doctor collapsed. “ We cannot go on! ” cried the German assistant doctor. Dr. Bockhorn was leaning exhausted against the door. “Is it not madness? ” he asked in a hollow voice. “Now they are giving us an isolation hospital for four hundred sick, at a time when three hundred are dying daily.”

I was lying on my heap of rags. Why could I not weep? Perhaps it would have done me good.... Someone tugged at my arm. “ Poseck is dying, Ensign, come,” said Pod. Leaning on Pod, I got up and went to Poseck, who was terribly spotted. He stretched out his thickly crusted tongue, thirstily moving it violently to and fro. Seydlitz was dropping bits of snow on it. The dying man was looking into his eyes with the expression of a faithful, grateful dog. Sometimes he moved his fingers as if he wished to give us his hand.

“My little sister has silvery hair,” he suddenly whispered. Pod shoved his fist into his mouth and bit on it. Seydlitz passed one bit of snow after another over Poseck’s lips. His fingers were trembling a little, but his face was unmoved. Little Blank, who was lying next to him, had raised himself a little. He looked at Poseck with terrified eyes and wept from weakness, like a child. Suddenly Poseck’s tongue was still. Seydlitz, putting the snow aside, pushed the tongue into the cavity of the mouth and pressed the jaws together from above and below. “Finis...” he said slowly, and, pushing by us, went out.

I crept back to my pile of rags. Something was working in me. I slapped my right leg, now wholly healed. “Had I but given thee up! ” I groaned. “ Perhaps I should now be at home — and even if I were dead — would it not be better than here... ?”

In the afternoon we carried von Poseck out. Seydlitz had wet his hair with melted snow and combed it neatly — we could not give our comrade better preparation for his last rest. We had drawn off the handsome brown riding-boots while he was still warm. The conjurer, who was handy at everything and at that time the most vigorous of us all, had helped us. But it was a bad bit of work; for Poseck had not
had them off his feet for months. Pod and I could not look on. But Seydlitz was quite right. If he had taken them to the grave in the spring, they would have cut them off when they buried

“Well, are you ready?” asked Seydlitz softly. He took hold of the shoulders, Hatschek of the legs. Poseck, once so plump, was terribly thin. Schnarrenberg and I walked on the right and left, each of us holding a hand to keep it from dragging along the ground. Pod and Briinn walked behind, while little Blank looked at us with wide-open eyes.

An icy east wind was blowing outside. We walked as quickly as possible, but it cut as with knives, and we no longer had warmth or blood in us. There was only a little snow on the steppe, and at every few paces the shape of a dead man showed beneath it. We stumbled over arms and legs as hard as wood, which, on being knocked against, emitted a ringing sound.

A distant mound seemed to be free of dead. Seydlitz nodded his head in that direction. “Here,” he said turning round until Poseck’s face looked towards the west. Slowly we let him down. Seydlitz laid the dead man’s hands on his breast. We wanted to fold them, but they would no longer keep together. We remained standing for a while in front of him with lowered heads. His young face looked terribly changed and like that of an extremely aged man. A few weeks ago he was still young and fresh, I thought amazed. Would they soon bring me here too? So stiff, so yellow, so aged... ?

Suddenly Seydlitz saluted, soldierlike. We all stood erect, our hands to our caps, and did not stir. “‘ Now come...” said Seydlitz, taking down his hand. The wind bit us to the very bones. “Forty degrees minus,” muttered Briinn. Pod already had white spots on his cheeks. We ran at full speed back to our barracks.
“If we could but conquer! ” said Schnarrenberg.

“We shall conquer!” said Seydlitz. His high-bred face resembled that of a racehorse showing his front teeth. With one movement of his hand he took all in: Poseck out there in ’ the snow above us, Blank in high fever next to us, the plank beds under us, the dead before us. “Can this have been in vain? ” he added.
“Why did they bring us just here? ” Pod asked helplessly. “In all this enormous country, the greatest on earth, was there no other place? ”

‘We were to perish here! ” said Briinn cuttingly. “In this war the fight does not end at the front. In this war they stop at nothing. They dare not kill us outright, so we must starve and perish. No one will ever find it out. Does anyone know where we are? No, to this day.... Would Germany stay away? But before we can give any news, we shall all be dead, and the dead are mute....”
““We must go on living,” said Seydlitz, “if only to bear witness some day. Only the living can testify. The dead are modest....”
** But to be able to hold out we must know how it goes with our Fatherland,” said Schnarrenberg.

No, there should not be any doubt of it, for the Lord’s sake, I thought in fear; for then... oh, he is right; what we are suffering here can be endured for an idea alone. It is too great ever to be repaid with material things....

I had found a bit of wrapping-paper and taken out my copying-ink pencil to draw something, anything. Was it skulls? Was it Poseck’s aged face? Little Blank at my side .was moaning incessantly. I watched over him. We relieved each other every hour. All the others were asleep. I drew, drew.. and suddenly I wrote:
nur noch einmal frei der Bande mit versehntem Aug zu griissen und auf wandermiiden Fissen Deine Erde zu betreten,

I read it. Who wrote this? Since when had IJ been able to write poetry? I read it for a second time, amazed, questioningly. Yes, it was a poem. I looked about me, disturbed. Dying men, dead rats.... I began to write again:
Nur noch einmal Deine Felder, Deine dunkeldichten Walder, wo auf griinen kiefernzweigen spriessend helle Kerzen steigen: Deine Walder zu betreten,

It flowed from me as if someone were whispering it into my ears, and as if these were not the first verses in my life, as if I had already written a hundred poems. How was this possible? I looked round again. Groans and effluvia, stench and dirt.... I continued to write:
die in roten Lichiern glanzen, buntgeschmiickt von Blitenkranzen: Deine Heiden zu betreten,

Little Blank groaned hoarsely. “ Water, water! ”’ I took some snow, pressed it on his lips, and changed the foot-rag on his forehead. A man with fever crept up to me on his knees to get some of our snow. I gave him two handfuls, and, stammering some foreign word of thanks, he crept back. I took up my pencil for the last time:
nur noch einmal vor dem Sterben mit dem durstgen Mund zu kiissen, nur in letzten Scheidegriissen Deine Graber zu betreten
No, it is all up. I shall never be a poet; my first poem would also be my last. Our mortality had risen to three hundred and fifty. Three hundred and fifty per day.... I had seen Dr. Bockhorn weep.

I could not write any more. I had grown too weak and the horror around me too terrible. At times I thought of the dainty nurse. “Come what may,” she had said. But of what use was that? We were living in an inferno. No, we were not living any more; we were still waiting — for what? For death? A madman’s imagination could not picture more horror than was to be seen in our den. And in our abused souls...

Two walls of dead were already lying in front of the barrack doors. We had, as it were, to walk through a tunnel of corpses when we wanted to go out. Between some of our plank beds the soup still stood, cold, frozen. The orderlies had brought it in and put it down among the sick men, more they could not do. It seemed as if everything was about to become extinct. No human voice was heard, only sounds as of animals groaning and gurgling, or here and there a whining, praying, and horrible cursing. Some had black, frozen limbs, and the stench from their wounds mingled with the odour from the corpses. Rats everywhere, rats all over....

One morning two Austrians went mad, one from thirst, and one from horror. They crept about among the dead, howling, and playing with the rats as if they were little dogs. The day before, a German infantryman had gone mad. If he had not been so weak, he would have strangled us survivors in his frenzy, one after the other. We could only sleep when one of us kept watch. How fortunate we were to have the conjurer with us! 7

I now knew why the poem had burst from me. It was the last word J had to say for all—to our country! Germany! Germany! Thou art our last thought.... For thee we have suffered, for thee we have died. Do not forget it! No, we shall not see thee again. All is over, all, all, is over. I staggered as if I were drunk, but I had to stay awake until my time was over. “ Water, water,” moaned Pod, the powerful giant, the brown bear. The day before, it had been only Blank, now it was Pod too. No, I must not sleep. But why not? Was it not all the same? Should I not be carried out on the morrow also?

Since the previous day I had been beset by an insane fear. Whence did it come? Was it my turn now? Did I feel it? Perhaps I had already got the bite that would in a few days put me at Poseck’s side? I was speaking to my mother. Of late I had often been speaking to my mother. “Had I to die in

“your country, mother? ” I asked shrilly. “No, be content, father; I have done my duty, though I was only a prisoner, and though at times I may have appeared downhearted and discouraged, I never forgot that here also I served my country, like you....”

The perspiration broke from my forehead. My eyes pierced through the dim vapour as if they saw someone coming. I had such a strange feeling.... Had I fever already? My pulse flew madly. Cursed, cursed. Would this hell never give us up again?
I should have loved for once in my life to embrace a girl. Once.... Now it was too late. Over, over, everything over. Death devours. I heard his jaws grinding. Is he insatiable? Does he want me also?

I HAD written nothing for a long time; for I had lain for weeks with spotted typhus. Seydlitz and Schnarrenberg pulled me through. Pod, Briinn, and little Blank were among the living also. Only Schmidt I, quiet, modest little Schmidt I, who had never obtruded himself, was dead. Oh, many would have got well if they had had comrades such as mine.

When for the first time I awoke with a clear head, an old, broken-down man was standing beside me. “The epidemic is subsiding, Ensign,” he said. “It has vented its fury. We have now only forty dead daily. If they have the will to hold out, they will get well....”

It was Dr. Bockhorn who spoke. He and an Austrian were the only surviving physicians. But was it possible that the epidemic was really subsiding? It was as if God himself had taken pity on us, when man had a heart of stone.
Eight of us were lying in the vacant house next to Dr. Bockhorn’s room. How had we been allowed there? I wondered.

We had straw under us, and three or four cloaks over us. Seydlitz, Schnarrenberg, and the conjurer were nursing us. We got strengthening food. Where from? I again wondered. “A Russian officer sends it daily,” said Seydlitz briefly..

“* I have succeeded,” said Dr. Bockhorn one day, “in having two hundred convalescents transported in a fortnight to a better climate. Do you eight want to go with them? Here you can never get quite well again; at least, not mentally.”
** Yes,” we all cried in unison. “ Yes, yes, yes! ”

After a fortnight we all managed to walk a little. Pod was the strongest of us, Blank and Briinn were the weakest. We met in the yard of the house. The snow had almost disappeared and the faint sun heralded an early spring. Cossacks were at work everywhere picking up the dead. They threw them, oe ae twenty in a bunch, on to broad wagons, put a rope over them, and drove away. “They have begun to fear the plague and cholera,” said Briinn.
At noon Dr. Bockhorn arrived with convoys from the town.
“There, children,” he said, “now get in.” We laid our cloaks under us and sat down back to back. “ You are not coming with us, doctor? ” I asked.
““No, I must stay. I should like to go, believe me.... But scarcely anyone has been left. Farewell, comrades,” he called out suddenly.
The wagons started. We all had tears in our eyes. “We thank you, thank you,” eight rough voices cried. He did not stir. “By thunder,” muttered Pod, “there’s a man for you....”

Even though we drove slowly and carefully across the yard of the camp, we could not altogether avoid the dead bodies. Seydlitz looked fixedly to the left where was a certain mound. We distinctly saw Poseck, his hands still on his chest, but his feet naked, for the wind had loosened and carried away the wrappings.

At the railway embankment stood eleven cattle-cars with small stoves. The N.C.O.s ordered twenty men to each car. Climbing up, we all got upper plank beds, at least for the day. The straw that was lying on the boards had already served for horses, but what did that matter? “ How is this possible? ” asked Briinn, amazed. “ Has the Shrew-mouse suddenly been turned into a human being? ”

We soon found out. Shortly before our departure an officer rode up to us on a white horse. “ Interpreter,” called the starschi on guard. I climbed down again. The officer had dismounted. The Cossack Captain was standing, very pale, before me. “ The commandant has been ill for two weeks of spotted typhus,” said he softly. “I have been acting commandant of the camp. Have you any other wishes? ”
“No,” I said hoarsely. To think that one had to be tonguetied at such a moment!
“There is wood for burning in the front car; and,” he added, almost as if ashamed, “ here, take this please... for you and your seven comrades from the doctors’ house.”
As he gave me his hand, he slipped something into my pocket. I tried to say something, something very grateful, appreciative....
“ All ready, Your Excellency! ” the starschi reported.

I got in. Totzkoje stayed behind. Faster and faster we rolled away from it — from it and-its seventeen thousand deaths. We all gazed out as one den after another disappeared and sandy steppes followed on right and left....
“ The Captain looked after us as long as we were in sight,” said Pod, in a low tone. “ He was holding his hand to his cap, if I am not mistaken....”

At Samara, the nearest town of any size, our cars remained standing on a side-track. Had they forgotten us? We did not stir. The commander of the transport had his home in Samara, disappeared into the town every evening, and did not return until noon the next day. Perhaps this just suited him. Perhaps he was even the cause of it. It was so difficult to get to the bottom of things in this country.... However, we were quite satisfied with the stop. It was very comfortable in the tjeplushkis when they were heated and padded with straw. “ Absolute mansions,” said Briinn once; “ one could almost await peace here! ”

Samara, the city where we left the cars for the first time, was never to be forgotten. Stands loaded with tempting things were everywhere. “If we had but one tiny rouble,” said Pod plaintively, “in a week we should be on our legs again....”

I kept to one side and, unobserved, bought eight pieces of © soap, a small mirror, and a large bowl. Taking the mirror, I went behind the car and looked at myself again for the first time in half a year. In the name of God, was that I? A convict, a tramp, a burglar? No, no, that was not I! “ Though you were not such — now you are! ” said a voice. “ Thy childface is gone, thy freshness is gone. Thou hast become a severe, haggard man. Six months have wrought what would ordinarily have taken a lifetime.”
I distributed the soap and gave the bowl to the conjurer. ‘There, Hatschek,” I said, “now go and fetch plenty of water.”
“Man,” cried Pod, “ did you have some money left? ”
He turned the soap disdainfully round in his black fingers. “I should have liked something to eat better,” he growled contemptuously.

The conjurer came back and we all washed. For seven months our bodies had not known water. My God, what that meant! It was not washing, but rather the peeling off of a white hide in large strips and crusts which loosened the layers of dirt from face and hands. Gradually, from eight terribly neglected individuals, covered with crusted dirt, there came to light eight pale men; and oh, the freshness of it!... It invigorated us like good food, it made the world worth loving again. “ By thunder,” spluttered Pod into his bowl, “I should not have believed it. By the Lord, it is as if I had for once eaten my fill again! ”

Yes, it was actually as if our greatest weakness had been washed away with this water, and with it the greatest part of what still clung to us of oppressive memories. Our skin, to be sure, was like rank potato shoots in dark cellars, and at first we were almost frightened of one another, but, with the help of God, we should soon become human again.
“There, Pod, and now we will go shopping,” said I at last. “You come along too, Blank, we shall not be able to carry everything alone.”
** Are you crazy? ” asked Pod, without moving.
“Don’t make a fool of me,” he said, offended.
I drew a fifty-rouble note out of my pocket. “ Now will you come along? ”
He became lost in thought. “ Man,” said he at last, “in this country one never knows what to think. One is the Devil in person, another an angel...”

After long bargaining we bought eight heavy, crisply roasted fowls, two large loaves of bread, and a packet of tea. The “ Totzkoje cavalry corner,” as we were now called, became riotous when we entered.

“Lord bless me, this is invalid’s fare,” cried Briinn enthusiastically. The fowls were still warm and dripping with fat. No one spoke. We devoured.... We smacked and crunched, we gulped and dripped. Must we not smack like beasts of prey to get delicious meat down our throats again after seven months? “There will now be two holidays in my life,” said Pod dreamily. “ My wedding-day — and this.”
I took out my cigarettes. No, verily no, our happiness had no end that day. Who else but us knew what a cigarette meant?

To our surprise the sentries were respectful and friendly to us, although they were not green-coated police for the deported, but Cossacks from the Shrew-mouse’s regiment. The Captain must have impressed this behaviour on them at our departure, and I was now convinced of what I had suspected in the first weeks of my captivity, that these people were really good at heart. Yes, they were good at heart, and only bad when incited or ordered to be so by superiors. Example is everything.... Under the Shrew-mouse these soldiers were Asiatics and brutes; under the Captain they were transformed into kind, harmless persons. Once when we were speaking of this among ourselves, Briinn very correctly remarked: “ Like master, like man.” So it is, and because they were still a young people, they needed example more than anything else. But though they were still so young, they were still strong in their love and hate.

Again all nations were represented in our car, Hungarians, Viennese, Tyroleans, Bavarians, Wiirttembergers, north Germans. Since Totzkoje, the Schwalangscher had kept close to our corner and, even though unasked, was of some assistance to us. Since his comrade and brother-in-arms had died in Totzkoje, he had sat alone in the car, but now he had found another compatriot, with whom, to our amusement, he could converse in the broad Bavarian dialect. This was a small, droll fellow, a stableman and, like himself, more broad than tall. On the very first day Briinn had given him the name of “ Tadpole,” a nickname which among soldiers indicated love rather than hatred, and which had to be deserved before it was conferred.

Those were lovely days at the railway station in Samara. We all smiled, we were all gradually looking on the world again with human eyes. Only at times did someone look as if life were still unreal to him, as if he feared that this beautiful dream would suddenly fade away again.

The evenings were our best timc, though we had only a little, rather smoky stove, with a pipe leading through a hole in the roof for chimney, and warm only for those near it — but what did that matter? It was, and remained, a stove, and it was still very cold outside.

Hatschek was stoker. A few talked, but most of us looked mutely into the fire and dreamed. Seydlitz sat silent; Blank smiled to himself; Schnarrenberg brooded; Briinn joked a little; Pod thought of his farm....
“Now, children, let us go to bed,” he said every evening paternally.
The Schwalangscher was standing lost in thought before the

stand of a shop where everything on earth was to be had. He was trying, in vain, to explain something to an old peasant woman by stretching out his fist to her and tapping it several times with his right forefinger. Then he put his left fist to his nose, groaned voluptuously, and sneezed violently.
Pod came up. “ What do you want to say to her? ” he asked, patronizingly. |
“I should like some snuff,” said the Schwalangscher. “ Honduras, Brazil, we say at home....”
Pod reflected for a while, and then, as if suddenly enlightened, drew his paper out of his pocket, his famous dictionary. “We shall have it in a minute,” said he, proudly. “Just a moment...”
He looked and looked. His pride vanished. His bearded face lengthened. “ It is not there; oh, damn,” he said shamefacedly, and crept away.

When, after nearly three weeks, an officer of higher rank found us, he cursed our starschi like a madman and threatened him with purgatory and shooting. We suspected evil — and it came. On the next day we were packed into five cars and on the same evening coupled to a train going east. My protests were of no use.

“To the devil with it,” said Briinn, but we did not take ‘it much to heart. The past three weeks had been a veritable heaven and had strengthened us so much that we had become reconciled to life again and full of confidence. The old life in the cars went on, with its round of purchasing, eating, sleeping. The country was free of snow; spring would soon begin. Pod looked out of the window for hours at a time.
“ Now they are beginning to sow at home,” he would say; or: “ I wonder if Anna is changing the fields correctly.”

New trains of fugitive women and children stood at the railway stations. Briinn, who was about a great deal, would sometimes come back humming, “‘ Therefore, my lassie, do not weep, don’t be so sad, wipe off your tears with sand-paper....”
“* Where is he all the time? ” I asked Pod, who only smiled. “Have you not noticed that he is all right again? Then, too, spring is coming, and thirdly — he scents spring chickens.”
In Ufa, the Tartar city, I succeeded in an unwatched moment in buying a Russian newspaper. I hastened back to the car. ** Children, I have made a catch.”

We sat down close together and I read out in a low voice. Of course, only the victories were spoken of in the paper, but those victories had all been gained at cities and rivers that lay far behind the places we remembered from the last front reports. Undoubtedly since the autumn our troops had captured entire provinces.
The renewed crowding together and the journey towards the East were forgotten. “Did I not say so? ” remarked Seydlitz proudly, shoving out his front teeth.
“Now Russia will soon be whipped, you will see,” cried Schnarrenberg ecstatically. “‘ Just this spring offensive, and our troops will be in Petersburg! ”
I, too, was jubilant at first, but suddenly I grew silent. “ Did not Napoleon get into Moscow? ” ran through my head. “ And

“It is easy for Schnarrenberg to talk,” said Briinn on the following day. “ He is a soldier by profession, war is his calling, and it is all the same to him whether he is here or at the front — he would just be a soldier, nothing else.... I, however, am an electrician, Pod is a farmer, and little Blank is a herring-packer.... No, we have nothing to do with it; this matter does not concern us. Let them break their heads themselves if they are not content.... But they ought to let us go home, to our wives and children and our vocations....”
“You are always thinking of your little self,” I interposed. “From here we cannot see how matters are going.”

“What does it concern us how matters go?” interposed a volunteer opposite. He stepped to our plank bed, and continued: “ And whether it is actually want of space, or competition, or the devil knows what that is the cause of this war, if at the very start all the milliards which are now exploded in powder had been used to settle these disagreements, it would have been the same in the end — only there would have been no dead. And if we should lose, what shall we have then? We should have to live on just the same, without all this money and with the dead....”

I was silent. Ought I to have spoken? Of ideals and history? Of how the fate of an individual signified nothing when the fate of a people was in question? No. Whoever puts self higher than the whole cannot be convinced even by the best words; for he who has the ideal has it, and he who has it not will never attain to it....

The trip through the Urals seemed short to us. Though it lasted three days, it was not tedious for a single moment. With every curve came wonderful views of towering heights and plunging abysses. Often we had a feeling of speeding past valleys which no human foot had ever trodden. For hours at a time the train wound through walls of rocks so near that we could have touched their reddish mass if we had but stretched our hands out of the window.
_ During the night before Tscheljabinsk Pod woke me. “ Some want to flee, Junker,” he said softly. “ Do you hear? ”

I listened. There was whispering under our plank bed, agitated breathing, cording of bundles. “It is madness, Pod,” I whispered back. “Shall I not advise them against it? They might as well go to the next policeman and allow themselves to be re-arrested. Without knowledge of the language, with only three loaves of bread and fifty copecks, they want to cross half the world.”

“You would not succeed in convincing them,” said Pod. ‘* Whoever has got this fixed in his mind.... But perhaps we are going on to a new Totzkoje. No, just let them travel. If you were to keep them from it, then for the rest of your life you would be condemned to hear how they would have been home long ago if you had not at that time — ”

The train panted slowly up a steep ascent. That was what they were waiting for. The door slid back with a creak. Almost without a sound the first one, a German infantryman, jumped out into the steaming snow. Three followed, a Saxon and two from Berlin. “ Shut the door again, Pod,” I said in excitement. Pod closed it carefully. “The guard is sleeping the sleep of the just,” said he. “Tomorrow he will beat us half to death for it....”

I did not fall asleep again. “ They are free now,” thought I. “Free.... In the wilds of the Urals it will not be easy to find them.... And even if so...” Perhaps two or three weeks of freedom were worth anything that might follow.

Next morning there was great screaming. The sentry cursed, the commander of the transport raged. I explained to him many times that we had been asleep, that we had heard nothing. And surely we were permitted to sleep, were we not? He understood. Every other transport would have flogged us with the knout until we succumbed. They did nothing.

I dreamed more and more frequently of girls. They were always undressed, and the sight of them excited me to enfeeblement. Chiefly I lay in bath-houses, hidden under the benches, or on the edge of a people’s bath, concealed behind bushes. At first I was ashamed of these dreams, despising myself for my unbridled imagination, but I soon recognized that they were only reminiscences of the Moskva that tortured me, that they did not spring from a smirched spirit, but were detached impressions from my subconsciousness.
With increasing vigour this greatest torment of all captivities

became more and more torturing, and I often bit into my hands with desire and impotence and wished for the night as if it would bring the most beautiful thing in life.... Gradually I began to understand something that had hitherto been incomprehensible to me. I understood the gipsy in our car, I understood Briinn.... There was only one thing that could make us forget our misery for a few seconds, and it was this. Dreams were still helping me... still! But if one day these dreams should not suffice... ?

No, I would resist, I would not squander myself. I would not darken this first glow for all time with a gloomy memory. “Who will be my first girl? ” I often thought. I feared for myself when thinking of that hour; for I had an insatiable hunger for tenderness in me.... But perhaps I should not be able to bear even the slightest tenderness because I could no longer understand it... for in the years when I might have taken and given it, I had only seen savagery. At the time when others had snatched their first kisses, my lips were bloody from horror; at the time when others had possessed their first girls, I had to comfort the dying.

After the Urals, Siberia’s infinity began. In those spring days it looked much more friendly than we had imagined it. We speeded by whole forests of rhododendrons, passed whole fields of gleaming tulips, snowy narcissus, and rose-coloured cloves. At times the wind carried heavy fragrance into the car, at times our eyes were fixed upon moist spots of large edelweiss and bizarre-looking orchids.... “And this is Siberia? ” asked Pod. “And there is edelweiss here?” asked the Schwalangscher. a
“Yes, in the spring, and for six weeks,” said Seydlitz calmly.

Not far from Omsk I saw Krepost, Dostoievski’s place of banishment, and I suddenly remembered some passages from the Memories of the House of the Dead. Had it not moved me more than any other book in my life? Had it not been with me at night in heavy dreams, horrible nightmares? Had I not thought that no man of our time could live for a month in such a hell?

We had borne it for six months, I thought to myself. And if it had only been Dostoievski’s house of death, none of us would have wept.... What was Krepost compared to Totzkoje? I thought back, allowing a few days from the Memoirs to glide before my eyes and a few hours of the dens of Totzkoje.... No, God in heaven, be calm! It would have appeared a paradise to us, to us of Totzkoje.

Three weeks passed in the old way. Rattatam, rattatam.... Did they want to take us to the end of the world? Fields, steppes, forests, steppes, Omsk, Nikolaevsk, Taiga, Achinsk, Krasnoyarsk, Kansk —all passed by. Mighty rivers, boundless deserts. “‘ Children,” Briinn called out in astonishment, “ does this country never come to an end? ”

At last we halted at Irkutsk. “ Prepare to march! ” We were surprised in spite of all our waiting. So it was here we were to live? A gay bustle prevailed at the railway station. Soldiers knelt with their mothers in front of sacred pictures and sacrificed large candles for their weal and woe. Young women in flowered cotton skirts and short fur coats accompanied them to the train and kissed them, weeping, for the last time. “ There are still enough men,” said Schnarrenberg. “ One could hardly believe it after such losses....”

The prison camp lay outside the city. We were so invigorated by rest and food that we made the march on foot without any difficulty. A half-empty stone barrack was assigned to us. Here. were only Germans, so that we were separated from the Austrians for the first time. Opposite to us was a plank bed with “ intellectuals ” — one-year volunteers, teachers, bank-clerks, merchants, and a professor. We recognized them without introduction by their courteous way of talking to one another. I learnt that there was an officers’ camp near by. It was good

there, much better than here.... Should I go over there? I hesitated a moment.... “ No,” I said. “ Here I have comrades, friends, tested in dark hours. There everything would be new to me....” And should I find such faithful souls there? Civilization did not always mean worth. I did not want to start from the beginning again. What I had, I had....

By order of the German camp-commandant, Schnarrenberg was appointed commandant of the barracks here. His first order was that all rats were to be destroyed. It was necessary; for not even in Totzkoje had so many of these disgusting little beasts run over our feet as in this camp. Schnarrenberg’s organization for the destruction of the rats was model and was based on the fact that there was plenty of water. There were innumerable holes between the stones in the ground. At half of these he posted men with heavy clubs, at the other half men with pails of water. “In with it,” came the order, and with gurgling and spluttering the flood descended from pail after pail. “ Attention! ” he called. There was splashing and squeaking, scampering and running. Angry, pointed, naked heads started up through the holes as one, ten, twenty, fifty shot out through the passage. A hail of blows beat down upon them. Hundreds already lay dead on the battle-field.... “ Water, water, water all the time! ” It drove the last ones dripping out of the passages, and their disgusting bodies accumulated on the wet ground. For my part, I could not deal out blows this time. ... Their curly tails were so loathsome to me since Totzkoje that I would not hit one.

That same evening we were sitting, freed from the pests and in good humour, on our plank beds. “ Yes, I am used to this,” said the conjurer, near whom had been the greatest heap. “ In circus and show-booths rats are our daily companions. Such a great battle-day, therefore, is a pleasure for one of us....”

I had to laugh as I looked at him. He never seemed properly dressed in his uniform. I always thought that he ought to wear a turban and wide, baggy trousers or some other fantastic garment. “ Do tell us something of your life, Hatschek,”’ I said.

“Of my life? Oh,” he laughed, “there is no ending when once I am set loose.... I have worked in the whole world, with Sarrasani, Hagenbeck, Busch, Renz.... Often at fairs, too, of course.... At the last I had a bad year. For a time I worked with Madam Glindfa, the unrivalled sensation of the world. There was a good program besides, first-class street advertising, extra parades. Nevertheless there was not much profit. .. « From her I went to a twelve-yard business, to Professor Jackson’s world-famous dog theatre, a nine-foot caravan.... For a time I was introducer and clown, principally because I could evoke such storms of laughter. When they called upon me to enlist, I was just doing well again. I had joined a firstclass troop of acrobats where I did my trick with a serpent lady. Lord, I could have done great things with that! We intended to get married afterwards, but first we had to — well, you know what I mean.... All vigour for our work was the word with us, and after work, pleasure. Well, deuce take it, the Prussians came, and all was over for us....”

Looking gloomily in front of him, he was silent for a while and then suddenly put his hand in his tunic and drew out a little parcel that was carefully wrapped round with thick paper. He undid it slowly, put it to his hooked nose, and breathed in deeply. “ It is one of her handkerchiefs,” he said dreamingly. “There is something of the odour of her skin in it.... Do you want to smell? ” He passed it round carefully. Eight coarse hands cautiously stroked the cracking cambric, eight noses sniffed longingly for a fragrance that had long since vanished....

The commandant of this camp, who seemed humane, acknowledged our greetings in military fashion when he rode through. That meant a good deal; for most of the Russian officers just tipped their caps with a gesture that was more an

expression of their contempt and their consciousness of their superiority than an acknowledgment of a salute. It required an effort to salute again and again those men who had not yet understood what it meant to be an officer and to observe the obligations attached to the wearing of a uniform, but we should have been severely punished if we had not done so. Here, as elsewhere, the bearing of the commandant inspired respect and confidence in the soldiers. I saw sentries smile at me and they even exchanged words with me as I passed. Abuse and ill-treatment were very rare.

Our guards were mostly old peasants with the waving beards of saints and light-blue, childlike eyes, who felt the war to be a misfortune, because they had never been taught to regard it as an act of punishment towards the Germanic barbarians, the disturbers of the world peace. One soon knew who could read the papers and who could not. The former declared that the Huns had caused the whole war, the latter that they were as little to blame for it as they themselves were.

Although we did not believe that this commandant put half of our food money into his pocket, as was the custom in this country, we could not understand why the food was so bad in a country where roasted chickens could be got for half a mark. “Why does Germany not look into it? ” asked Briinn in a tone of hate. “ Do you believe that they are told how much we actually get? ” I said. “ What was originally allowed for us would probably have been quite enough, but no one in Germany realizes that a part of it is left behind in at least six or eight places? ”
We spoke of food more and more frequently, and here the Tadpole, like Podbielsky, went into action again. For hours they talked of pastries, noodles, dumplings, pancakes, or smoked meat....

** That’s nothing,” said Briinn; “ I could make big dumplings for you in the Kénigsberg manner.
