You take,” he continued hastily, “pork and beef, the former from the leg, the latter from the rump, hash it in a machine, together with anchovies or herrings, mix it with bread-crumbs, salt, pepper, and stewed onions...” He talked unceasingly until Pod gave the plank bed a resounding blow. “ If you are not quiet soon,” he cried in ~vexation, “J shall make hash of you yourself, you confounded tormenter! ”

One day I-heard that the officers in the neighbouring camp fared worse than we. They had had no pay for two months, and when, at the beginning of the third month, a receipt for the | amount due was handed to them, they were told that if they signed that, they would get seventy-five per cent of it. They refused and got nothing for the third month. But what was to be done? They must have food, so at last they agreed; but because they had hesitated for a few days, they only got fifty per cent of what was due.

A shrewd little rifleman from the neighbouring plank bed went every day for a few hours as servant to the Russian officers and, when he came back, always told to the smallest detail what he had seen. All were lost in reverent admiration to think that there was still such manner of living on earth.
“ And they eat at a table, covered with a white table-cloth, eh? ” queried a bank-clerk.
** And afterwards do they sit in arm-chairs and smoke thick cigars, eh? ” further questioned a teacher.
* Of course,” continued the rifleman, “ and one with a bracelet at that. And there is coffee...”
“ Coffee, proper, real coffee? ” three or four called out.
“ Certainly, in cups. They are small to be sure...”
“* Aha,” said the bank-clerk, “ black-coffee cups, I know them
“Yes,” boasted the rifleman, “ they are so thin that I scarcely dare touch them. Besides, I always get dizzy from the smell....”

This rifleman, or the “ Bed-bug,” as he was called, often brought back food. Did the Russian servants give it to him or did he steal it?... He gobbled it all up himself, however much it was, but as his weakened stomach was nof accustomed to the rich stuff, he soon threw it up again. Every evening showed the same picture. He gulped like a wolf and spat out like a heron.
I often saw our Pod looking with moist eyes at the thrown-up remnants and heard him murmur: “ Did you ever see such a stingy dog... ?”
** Listen,” I said to him one day, “can’t you try to buy me a piece of soap and a tooth-brush? ”
“Yes,” said the Bed-bug, “ but they are very dear.”

Though I gave him plenty of money, it was not enough. His were veritable drug-store prices. “ Yes, the war, you know...” he said regretfully. “‘ The prices are rising....” He was a charming rogue, but the chief thing was that I had soap and a tooth-brush and no longer had to rub my teeth daily for half an hour with my bare finger.

Day by day we saw more of those friendships that had begun in the first days at Totzkoje, but had been suppressed by increasing enervation. In the quiet and warmth of this camp . they seemed to grow like mushrooms.

It was no longer particularly strange to see captives walking arm in arm, and they were already beginning to sit on one another’s laps. At night I often heard words and songs from the neighbouring plank bed, curiously like those that I had heard once in the railway wagon, on that night when the fugitive girl was with us.

Some couples passed the whole night out of doors. “ My God,” said Briinn, laughing; “ let those who can, do it. It is warm now and dark out there — as at home.” The day before, two strong men had been fighting over a young infantryman, who looked like a spoiled girl as he watched them with gleaming eyes. “ Do you see him? ” said Seydlitz, contemptuously. “Has he not already become a perfect woman? A primeval woman who is glad and proud when two men fight to gain possession of her? ”

Briinn did not belong to those types. Nevertheless, he grew limper week by week. “ You ought not to do it, Briinn,” I said at one time, “or at least not so frequently.... It may not harm if one is well fed and vigorous, but in our condition...” He laughed mockingly. “No sermon, please...” he said limply. “I know all about it.... Aha! Self-pollution we called it at home, a fine name and not inapt... but, devil take it, what does that concern me? Did I come here myself? They ought not to bring us here if they want us to remain human beings. And if they themselves were here, those high and mighty ee Pll go to hell if they would not do it too.”

One day the cesspits were emptied and sprinkled with chloride of lime, the barracks aired, the yards swept. There was great spring cleaning in the kitchen, and the commandants of the barracks were ordered to see that every part was clean. A couple of Russian physicians went through every division, removed each man that looked ill, and, to our surprise, put them, without any examination, into the hospital where not even the most sick had been admitted before.
“ Potemkin, the immortal one, is haunting,” said Seydlitz, mockingly.
At noon a number of Russian generals appeared in the camp, and, with them, a young, very blonde lady in the garb of a
nurse. “That is Elsa Brandstrom, the Swedish nurse,” somebody called out.

She went through the whole camp and inspected all the barracks. We stood up in military fashion in front of our plank beds. The blonde nurse, in a resolute manner, put questions here and there and wrote down everything. The generals pushed forward, but she took her time. “No hurry, gentlemen, one thing after another....”

As she passed our cavalry corner, Seydlitz stepped forward. “ I beg to report that the cleanliness is only twelve hours old, nurse,” he said calmly. “ And that nine-tenths of the sick in the hospital have only been there since this morning — until then, in spite of numerous appeals, no one was received there. They will probably appear here again tomorrow,” he added.
Our hearts were beating in our throats. She looked at him a long time with her strong, blue eyes. “I thank you,” she said, gave him her hand, wrote for a while, and slowly passed on.

We should all have liked to speak to her, only two words. - Was there not something of home about her... ? But we knew that not all the ten thousand could speak to her, and which of us wanted it most? No, what Seydlitz had said was for
*“ Things will be better now, you will see,” was Schnarrenberg’s first word. “ She comes regularly into the camps now and has all Siberia under her supervision.”
“Yes, if Potemkin did not come from this country...” said Pod deliberately.

After this episode our commandant went on furlough. Was it Elsa Brandstrém’s doing? For she believed she had done some good by coming and had not dreamed what the effect would be. In his stead came a Captain of the same sort as the Shrewmouse, and what Seydlitz had foretold came to pass. The sick came back, and the kitchen soon swam in its own dirt. Instead of the meat to which we were entitled, we again got heads and hoofs and genitals, and no more chloride of lime was given out for the cesspits.

Almost automatically the guards became harsh, rude, full of hatred; in spite of which, or probably just because of it, two of the men in our barracks committed trifling errors, such as incorrect saluting. And there then happened what, up to that time, we had not believed possible.
“Form ranks for running the gauntlet,” was the command. We all knew the real reason: that no one had betrayed the man who had spoken with Elsa Brandstrom....

The three hundred of us fell into line. Fifty Cossacks stood _in two rows with long-tailed nagaikas in their fists, the commandant on horseback in front, and a N.C.O. at every twenty paces. In the background were two squads of our guards with loaded arms and belted cartridge-pouches.

Two or three Cossacks tore the tunics from Schnarrenberg and Seydlitz, the leading men, to show us how it should be done. We did it silently. What else could we do? Three hundred civilized men stood with bare backs in the spring sunshine, as they might have done a hundred years ago.

When the first ones were led in front, Schnarrenberg and Seydlitz started to run, erect and with fixed eyes. I followed them with Pod and Briinn. Resounding blows rained down, shafts of fire burned into our lean backs. I could not run quickly because of my leg, and I was distinctly conscious of the smell of leather and the evaporating sweat of the Cossacks. Indistinctly I heard their savage cries, their guttural screaming; and my ears hummed as once when I was almost drowned. As I could only hobble along slowly, I got more blows than the artist, for instance, who sped through the lane like a greyhound.

I saw the skin break on Pod’s back, just in front of me. I must not tumble, I thought, and I resolved with all my might not to break down. A dull anger rose up within me. If I could only walk slowly, step by step, with proud head and stiff neck, through this butchers’ lane, just to spite them all. But those were cheap thoughts, only meant to keep me steady. In reality. ... Lash came upon lash, like blows from the sharp paws of atiger-cat... like burning knife-cuts.... I raised my head. Seydlitz was already through. Straight and erect he stood in front of Schnarrenberg, his large front teeth thrust forward a little, and his face looking as if in this hour he had been ennobled a second time.

We sat silent on our plank beds without our tunics, because their pressure hurt us. Our shirts stuck to our backs and were here and there striped blackish-red. Little Blank had not properly recovered from the fever he had got in Totzkoje, and now this.... Of our cavalry corner no one spoke. Schnarrenberg’s jaws were grinding, his bushy moustache was quivering, and the folds on his low forehead were deep as furrows. Seydlitz was calmly smoking a cigarette.

‘Yes, their punishments are a particular feature,” said the one-year volunteer from the neighbouring plank bed. “I once got fifty nagaika lashes on my naked back in the presence of the commandant because I had not saluted him properly.... I lay in hospital for four weeks! ”

“ T once got six days’ imprisonment when they simply forgot to bring me food or drink,” another related. “If the hole had not been so damp that the water was constantly dripping from its walls, so that I could moisten my tongue from the drips, I should have died of thirst....” :

“I was once locked up merely through a misunderstanding,” said a third. “ I sat for three months in a den of rats — katorga, they call it — and when I got out and asked the reason for it, neither person nor paper could explain the cause of my punishment, in which I had almost died....”
“‘ Are we, then, completely without redress? ” murmured Schnarrenberg.
“ And all that only a week after our camp had been inspected by the representative of a neutral power? ” Seydlitz added.
I felt that he who had said nothing would least of all forget those blows, perhaps because he had said nothing.

The next day the conjurer unexpectedly came up to me. “Ensign,” he said in a low voice, as if he felt he had to confess to me, “I always hated the army, had to hate it, shall continue to hate it... for my life... you will understand that without being told. But if at Totzkoje we had not had Schnarrenberg with us... and Seydlitz when the blonde sister came
. and yesterday again— did you see it? Our weak ones only held out because they saw both of them standing as firmly and as unfeelingly as in battle.”

A short time before, Schnarrenberg had daily ordered the commandants of the various divisions to see to cleanliness and order. “ If we do not do it ourselves, nobody will,” he said to them. “ We know now that the Russians want us to perish, don’t we? ”

Among others things he ordered every man to take enough exercise, to wash once, to evacuate only at certain places, to be careful of his uniform, and to try to behave decently. “ It is my opinion that we must appear as fresh and erect as possible.” He concluded his order with the words: “ And if not for our sakes, then for the sake of the country for which we suffer.”

He was thereupon informed by the commandant that on one occasion a Russian general who had visited some barracks when the men were taking their exercise had been so enraged by the disgusting sight that he had promptly forbidden all exercise in that camp for all-time.

I met a compatriot from Schleswig-Holstein who had come from the island of Nargin in Murmansk, a desolate rocky island in the Caspian Sea, called in German Schlangeninsel — Snake Island. “ There was no fresh water there,” he said, “ except what was brought from the land, and when it was stormy, we were often left for a week without drink.... Of three thousand men, over two thousand died in six months.... In the end we lived on snakes, which we devoured whole, skin and hair and all. Otherwise we should have starved.”

On the plank bed of the volunteer they were talking of the war. Opinions varied, but none were really in favour of it any longer. One of them very rightly said, however: “ When once it is know that a man is obliged to sell, he never gets the true price for his wares, and it is the same with the war. A nation that has reached the point of wishing for peace at any price will be overcome by a less powerful nation, and a country that is known never to have defended itself will easily be attacked. It is the strong land, not the weak one, which can dictate terms of peace.”

“Yes,” said the professor, “ that is true, but the truth is not always justice.... In my opinion, man is only an animal as long as he uses war as a means of settling disputes. Savages fight when they quarrel, and when a man of culture fights or commits murder, he is despised as savage and uncultured and is punished. Should that which is forbidden to individuals be allowed to nations? ”
“You confuse what is to be achieved with what really is,” said Seydlitz calmly.

I met Pod at the latrine. He was sitting with gloomy face on one of those seats placed at sitting height round a gigantic pit. They were merely narrow boards, which after a time cut into our thighs and were neither comfortable nor safe.
“ T have been sitting here since morning,” said Pod gloomily,
“and nothing comes but clear water.” “It is much the same with me,” said I. “One never gets away in less than an hour....”
“Ought we not to report for work, Junker?” asked Pod. “This confounded hog’s food is simply destroying my bowels. We need good peasant food, bacon, eggs, milk...”
“Yes,” said I, “ that is true — but how can we do it, Pod? ”
“‘Let us simply report as farm-hands, farmers by vocation. You go with me as interpreter —”
“But you are the only one who understands anything about it.”

“That does not matter. I’ll teach all of you in a jiffy. As for the rest...” He drew a deep breath. “I must see grain and cattle and fields again for once, my lad.... I shall be glad to work for you all.”
“Yes,” said I in a low voice as he got up, “ we will try it, Pod. I shall report this very day.”

When we inquired about the condition of the peasants in the country, an Austrian told us that, for the most part, they were well off, but that the conditions on the large estates were terrible. “I was on a prince’s estate, and it was worse there than in the lead-mines,” he said. “ We got only dog’s food and had to work until we broke down, and when we were sent back to the camp, they would not take us in, because they said they had ‘ delivered healthy men.’ The worst of all was the flogging. ' A man who stopped work from sheer exhaustion was lashed until the blood came... and when he fainted, they just waited till he came too, and went on again. But, as I have already said,” he concluded, “ the small peasants are said to be as well off as at home....”
Seven of us reported, Pod, Briinn, Blank, the conjurer, the Schwalangscher, the Tadpole. The two Bavarian sons of farm-
ers were eager to do the same when they heard of it, and I willingly put them on the list; for they really knew how to work.

After a fortnight a favourable answer came. The Zemskaja Uprawa assigned us to Goloustnoje, a village on the western shore of Lake Baikal, north of Irkutsk. We were waiting for transport there when Blank was again seized with high fever, and we had to leave him behind in the care of the one-year volunteers, decent fellows, who promised to attend to him well. Schnarrenberg was not suggested as a substitute, for we knew it was Seydlitz’s wish to have his assistance and protection.

In this dilemma a “ May-bug,” a shrewd man from Berlin, applied to me. “Could I not go with you in place of the sick man? ” he said. “I managed the whole work of a farm once and could help you in many ways. Besides,” he continued, half to himself, “they are looking for me, and it is easy to find me in the camp.”
“¢ What have you done? ” I asked smilingly.

“ Qh,” he said quickly, “ nothing bad, it was only... The farmer’s wife, you know, with whom I was, got a child from me. ... That was nothing bad — we lived as one family, and I was cock of the walk... until one day news came that her husband had been wounded and would come back. Then I quit, preferring to go to a camp.... I am afraid that he will be looking for me some day and find me... Lord knows how they would punish me then.”
“Hm,” I said, “that is dangerous, and may cost you your life if the husband, out of revenge, represents your deed as a crime, as rape. You shall come, of course.”
The little village of Goloustnoje was soon reached. Our guard, Hildebrant by name, a clever Jew who spoke German fluently, was from that region and was heartily greeted in the village.

It was a fishing hamlet and farming village in one.' Nets were hanging from the houses, ploughs were standing in the yards, and from the house one looked out on the blue infinity of Lake Baikal, the Siberian ocean.

The peasant was a blonde, broad-hipped woman of about thirty years. Her husband, a powerful fellow, according to her, had been recruited in the year 1914. Her apparent distrust of us vanished when Hildebrant, provided by us with roubles, explained to her in detail that here was a select group of German peasants, men who would bring the harvest in better than it had ever been done before. “ That is easily possible,” muttered Briinn ironically.

That first night Pod did not close an eye. I heard him incessantly talking to himself. “These ploughs are from the time of the Napoleonic wars.... But that’s no matter.... The scythes are quite usable as far as I could see... not first class, to be sure, but all the same... The wagons are awful, wooden axles; oh, Lord!... All that will go into such a cart my Anna could take on one pitchfork.... Otherwise a good worker, this woman.... A pair of strong arms... quite good food.... If I could but understand her.... The horses regular Cossack-killers.... The cows large goats. ... Not one ever cleaned.... Well, we shall see.... There are cows and horses, wagons and scythes, grain and grass — what more do I need? ”

Early next morning work began, work that would go on in the same way until the autumn. Pod without question took command, the May-bug helping him and giving advice. At first Briinn and I were a week with the cows, so as to curry their neglected hides in Schleswig-Holstein manner for the first time in our lives, while the Schwalangscher and the Tadpole did the same with the horses in Bavarian fashion. Good | Hildebrant, “kindest of men,” as the conjurer said, walked from one couple to the other with a long bayonet which
flashed dangerously. Nevertheless, freedom prevailed — sweet, warm, fragrant freedom....

After a fortnight the harvest began. Pod mowed with a flourish that fairly made his scythe sing. I thought of Hodler’s “Mighty Mowers” when I looked at him. The May-bug mowed with the two Bavarians behind him, while the proprietress, Briinn, Hatschek, and I gathered the corn into sheaves and bound them. For the first few days we were all tired to death, despite our joy, for the heat was almost unbearable, reaching nearly forty degrees when there was no sea breeze.
Pod alone felt nothing of it. Pod was happy. Pod was at home. |
“Man,” he said daily, “and this I have once again, once again. Come now what may, I shall hold out to the end.”

Rest at evening in Goloustnoje. We sat in front of the house on a bench which the conjurer had made, and below us gleamed the blue, gently stirring sea. The good Hildebrant chatted of everything imaginable, while the astonished proprietress, and often a couple of neighbours, listened attentively. How kind all these people were to us when no Shrew-mouse was near....
One day Hildebrant brought an “extra,” which I read aloud. There were accounts in it of terrible horrors, of violation of women and mutilation of children —all ancient and silly gossip.
“ To think that you are so wicked! ” cried the proprietress, amazed.

I explained to her that it was untrue, that such accounts were only written so that the men would go into battle in good faith and not curse the war. “ What do your prisoners write of the war? ” T asked.
“Niko, my nephew, fares well, very well. And my Ivan, too, writes that he cannot complain...”

“Well, you see. And do you know that the letters of your prisoners were destroyed in Petersburg a short time ago because they reported only good of us? In order that, with the help of God, your hatred should not cease... !”
A peasant cursed. “ That is low,” he said.
“Listen, Pod,” I said, “tell me honestly if you have ever seen anything of what this paper speaks.”
“No,” he said quietly. “ And I was in it from the very beginning. But in East Prussia I saw with my own eyes a woman crucified by the Cossacks.”
I translated. “ Yes, the Cossacks...” the proprietress conceded.
“And you, Briinn? ” I asked further. “ No,” he said hesitatingly.
I clenched my fists. “ What is to be done? ” I said angrily.
* Avoid war,” answered Briinn shortly. “ It all comes from the war. The simplest thing is to make no more war.”

The sound of singing rose from the shore of the Baikal. The voices of four girls and two lads, still almost boys, rang out into the ocean. It was the song of “ The Captives,” one of those yearningly sad songs peculiar to this people who have for centuries been oppressed like no other people.
“ However,” said Hildebrant, suddenly, “in the end you will be conquered, you Germans.”
“ Well, yes,” said Pod, “ and no wonder, if the whole world is begged to attack us from all sides....”

The summer was over and the leaves had begun to turn. Briinn had been in high spirits for some days. He no longer slept with us and was growing stouter every day. “Country air seems to agree with you splendidly,” I said. “ Yes,” he said laughingly, “ but chiefly bed! ”
Almost every evening I heard him sing: “ Therefore, lassie, do not weep...”

1917 153 The leaves had fallen and the fields were bare. In Siberia the harvest lasts five months. “ Now it will soon be over, Pod.” I had to prepare him slowly, or he could not bear it, I thought anxiously. He gave me a look that cut me. “What... ?” he stammered. “ What do you mean, lad? ”
‘“‘ That we must soon return to the camp, Pod.”
He turned away and went to the cows and horses. Should I follow him? No. At such times dumb beasts are better friends than human beings.... |

In spite of all his precautions fate overtook the May-bug on the last day but three. I was alone in the yard when a peasant came up, a powerful, gigantic cut-throat, with a notched stick of wood in his right hand. One could see that he had come a long distance. “ I am looking for Kulicke,” he said in a tired voice, “ a German prisoner of war, a man from Berlin. I was told in Irkutsk that he is working on this farm.”
Before I could give Hildebrant a sign, he volunteered: ‘Yes, he is here. What do you want with him? ”

“Oh, nothing....” After a while my comrades came back from the field, the May-bug walking beside Pod and chatting with him, not dreaming of danger. “ Oh God,” I thought, “ this giant of a man will kill him....”
“ That is he, there, the tall dark one,’ said Hildebrant, pointing to him.

The peasant ran towards him with uplifted hands. “It is you,” he said, “ you? For weeks I have been wandering about trying to find you. How shall I thank you for all you did for me and my farm? The cows are full of milk, the pigs have little ones, and four calves have been born.... And do you know, brother — the boy is a prize baby....”
When we returned to the camp, Schnarrenberg greeted me with unusual warmth. “I have been waiting for you,” he said.

“We could not have gone on much longer.” Seydlitz grasped my hand heartily. “ Yes, Schnarrenberg is right,” he said with a weak smile. “ We are too much accustomed to one another. There was a hole in our life while you were away.”

Little Blank was considerably better, though he was still coughing a bit.... “No,” he said gaily, “the one-year volunteers really took good care of me, and I am heartily grateful to them....” “ There is something about him which was not there before,” I thought broodingly. “He is much more shy. What is the reason? ”

Nothing out of the ordinary had happened in the camp, nothing new except that the cesspit was to be cleared out before the winter came. “ Very well, we must travel again,” said Pod, indifferently. For three days there was nothing but story-telling. Everyone knew a story and everyone boasted a little. Only Briinn was silent, strikingly silent. “ Well,” asked Blank at last, “ and what have you to tell us? ”
‘“*Man,” said Briinn sulkily, “ leave me in peace. In spite of roses and narcissus, in life there is generally something that one misses—rhyme the rest for yourself,” he concluded rudely.
When we were washing next morning, I saw that Blank had red spots on his neck and shoulders. “Oh Lord!” I cried, frightened, “ what is the matter with you, boy? ”
I looked at him in astonishment. He had reddened up to his hair. “ No, I really do not understand it...”
“May I speak to you this evening? ” he asked in a low voice..
I went about confused until evening. There must be some
reason for the change in him, I thought. But, whatever he might confess, I would help him as well as I could....
At twilight we went out in front of the barracks and leaned against the wall in the dark. “Well, boy?” I said encouragingly. 7

He swallowed a few times. “Oh,” he said at last, “it is terribly difficult to speak of it, but I have no one to ask but you. Do you know little Funker? He sleeps next to the bed of the one-year volunteers. You see, he nursed me, and once came to me at night...I like him, you know... and I was so helpless.... At first I was horrified.... Now I do not know what to do.... I always make up my mind to turn him off, but cannot do so any more, I fear....” He was silent for a while, breathed loud a few times, and said: “Do you despise me now? ”
I shook my head. My God! What should I say to him? It was not to my credit that I could control my body better
. it was merely that I had no surplus— for such things. ... Perhaps as far as that side of captivity was concerned, my own hour would strike some day....
“No,” I said, “of course not. However, you must fight against it.”
“No,” I said, “not on that account. That does not matter for us here in our condition....”
* But it is very harmful, isn’t it? ”

“No, not that either. It is only... it is dangerous. ... One changes physically without noticing it, I believe, and one day.... Who knows how long we may still have to wait? Here it is only need—pbut if it became a habit, and you went home and never wanted to touch a girl again... ?”

“ Oh,” he said, and I knew by his voice that he was smiling — little, bashful, driven Blank — “I do not fear that, Ensign, for... I only kiss him... only in thought as a girl, and because he looks so much like one.”

Hatschek and Briinn were speaking about military doctors, and Briinn said: “ I am fed up with them — they were all butchers. Did not a surgeon-major say to me, when I was unable to go to the front because of my heart: ‘ Oh, that’s nothing, my dog had it too’? ”
“He may have had his reasons —” Schnarrenberg said.
Such a remark might lead to a quarrel. “Indeed?... I interposed. “ They are all butchers, are they? ”
“Well, I never knew any better ones,” said Briinn obstinately.

I grew angry. “ Indeed? ” I said for the second time. “ And you others? Are you silent? It is not fair to look at one side only. Have you really never come across a doctor who was as kind as the one who tortured you was cruel? ”
“Oh, yes,” said Blank softly. ““ When I remember Dr. Bockhorn...”
“There! ” said I angrily. “ But your brains are like sieves in which only what is coarse remains....”

We had scarcely got used to our surroundings again when we heard that we were to be moved once more. The order to march was only applied to our barracks and the neighbouring one, and before we had regained our composure, the “ Totzkoje cavalry squad ” was again rolling in tjeplushkis beside Lake Baikal. We had joined the one-year volunteer division, and together we just filled one wagon.

For two days we went east, around the southern shore of Lake Baikal. Pod looked with wide-open eyes towards the western shore, where lay “his” farm, with grain and cows and horses. Briinn cursed for two days, even more loudly than usual, Even the mercurial Tadpole was sad.

The Trans-Siberian railway passes through forty-six tunnels in the mouritains that enclose the sea on its south-eastern shore. The ice-covered stones looked like glittering, glassy bells on the shores. Winter was coming again for the second time.....

In Nerchneudinsk our guards were changed. Up till then our board-money — twenty-five copecks per day per head — had been kept from us on the ground that the larger notes must be changed before we could be paid, but when we asked the new leader to change the money for us, he only said: “ Certainly, from tomorrow....” And we understood that with the old leader the large notes had also disappeared!

We cursed dreadfully. No one had any money, and even though we “farm-labourers” still had a few pence of our wages— what was that among forty men? “ Swindled again...” muttered Pod, enraged. “Lord,” Briinn said, “‘they find new tricks every day by which to cheat us and enrich themselves.” “We are always worse off during transport,” said the Tadpole, adding: “ For this reason alone, they send us to a fresh camp every six weeks....”

Everyone agreed to what was said. Gradually evening came, and ever farther towards the east rolled the train. “ Now comes the worst region, as far as I know,” said Seydlitz suddenly. “ Transbaikalia, the land of the deported and of the lead-mines.” As if in confirmation, at this very moment we caught sight of a little group of the deported, who, rattling their heavy chains, were being driven through the desert at the side of our train. |
“This was all that we needed,” said Seydlitz in a hard voice.

We were speaking of leave. We often spoke of things that seemed perfectly senseless. How could we have borne the constantly increasing hunger of our souls if we had not satisfied it now and then with dreams? “What would you do,

Junker, if they suddenly gave you eight weeks: of leave? ” asked Briinn. I smiled. “I cannot tell all in a moment.... I should probably go to the Baltic Sea, but not on account of home. . On account of the water, on account of the bathing.... Eight times in the water daily for eight weeks should make one clean again, I think....’
“I might plough,” said Pod slowly, “or. sow or reap, according to the season....”
Briinn threw back his head souiciastaousl ‘y. “You think only of working!” he said mockingly. “ And you, girlie? ” he continued.

“Oh, my God!” said Blank. “To begin with I should go every evening to a beer-garden, where there is dancing on Sundays. And for a week I should go back to my firm, to my old place behind the counter, without asking for any salary, just for fun....”.

“Stop, man,” cried Briinn. “ During my holiday I shouldn’t want to hear anything about business, that will come soon enough. No, boys, I should do something quite different. For the first four weeks I should not stir out of my feather-bed, but... No, on such a holiday one ought not to be married. On such an occasion one ought to be able to do as a famous man about whom I once read a story did — Vasova, or some such name.”
“‘In former times,” Blank, reddening, interrupted him, evidently just to give the conversation a turn, “ officers were discharged on their word of honour to return after a certain time, so I read.”
“* What! ” cried Briinn. “ Man, that ought to be done still. Do you know what I would do then? I'd whistle at my word of honour and they would not see me again.”

Next day we shall be there! so the rumour ran. My God! In this desert! The land lay before us like a frozen ocean. Thin snow glittered on the wind-protected inclines, but where the wind had scattered it, naked, often rocky, ground showed up. Not a tree or a shrub as far as the eye could see. “ Yes, this is Transbaikalia,” said Seydlitz. “I know it from the book Siberia, by Kennan. This is the margin of the Gobi desert, which begins in this region, and one of the next provinces is Chinese and called Manchuria.” |

We were detrained at a small railway station with a watertower on the right, a miserable hamlet on the left. Towards the north, in a flat depression, we saw sixteen or eighteen stone barracks. “ That is our camp,” somebody cried. The enclosure, a fence of boards higher than a man, with barbed wire and tall sentry-towers at the corners, began just past the railway station, and when the gates were opened for us to go in, we were surprised to see that the lower part was an officer’s camp and that the men’s camp, those very stone barracks, was a short march away.

Some two or three hundred officers standing on the lower yard looked after our procession of beggars with serious eyes as we crossed their camp. They were mostly in grey uniforms, Austrians of every rank, from cadet to colonel. Of German officers I particularly noticed a young aviator, some oldish first-lieutenants, and an artillery ensign. “An ensign? ” thought I, strangely moved. Was that meant as a sign for me? They all looked comparatively well dressed, not nearly so ragged as we, and their faces, though haggard, were not so grey as ours.

After leaving the officers’ camp, which was surrounded only by a fence of barbed wire, we passed for a while through sand as fine as dust, real desert sand, until we came to the stone barracks, where a building on the left wing had been assigned to us. What else was there to say? Here the conditions were as everywhere else. Two rows of plank beds, one above the other, huge, unheated stoves, miserable lamps without oil. But we were glad to drop from our backs the packs of uniforms from Totzkoje. They served many purposes, could be used to lie on, or hung upon cord as partitions. It was so cold that we stood with our hands in our pockets, scarcely daring to move. |
* Well, let us all settle down again,” said Seydlitz calmly, very skilfully and neatly making a mattress out of his Austrian uniforms,
Briinn, discouraged, threw his bundle noisily on the plank bed, sat down on it, and buried his head in his hands. “‘ Man,” he muttered, “ if I had only got a bullet through my head at the front!”
“You might have got it,” cried Schnarrenberg, enraged. Weakness had excited him to unreasonableness, and he knew Briinn from the field. “ You need only have shirked less! ”
“Shut up,” said Brinn, tired. He was too weak now even to quarrel,

During the first nights those stone barracks were so icy that many got bladder trouble. After one night I myself was so bad that I had no time to jump up and run out. It seemed as if all closing muscles had become inactive, so that the urine just ran without control. We had no change of underwear, and what we were wearing had stuck to the skin for the past year. How could healing come if we were wet into the bargain? Nor did it, for we grew worse every day. “ How degrading this is! ” I thought, setting my teeth. At last I found a preserving-can

on a heap of dirt. I placed it on my plank bed, and at least did not have to run out at a temperature of forty-five degrees below zero. But often it was of no use, for the urine ran so quickly that I could not get hold of the can, and at such times I almost wept with rage....
Pod watched me grimly. “ We must have wood, lad,” he said resolutely, “else you will be afflicted for all your life.”

“In the neighbouring barracks I have seen a space that is full of unoccupied plank beds. We will break up a couple of those.” He consulted the conjurer, who was ready to help. I waited anxiously for a few hours in case a sentry should catch them.... At last they came back with empty hands, but Pod with four marks of lashes on his face, and Hatschek dragging one leg after him. “They nabbed us. The wood is lost for all time.” |

One day a volunteer told of Murmansk. “Seventy thousand men were brought to build the ‘death’ railway,” he said. ‘* We had to stand for eighteen hours every day, badly fed, up to our waists in ice and mud. We had neither proper lodging, nor clothing to change into when ours was wet. Once several freight cars were sent with sick men from where we were working to the next town, and not a single man was alive at the end of the journey. All had either starved or frozen to death. Of sixty thousand men, over thirty thousand were driven to death at Murmansk. It has truly been said that every sleeper of that railway lies on a corpse! ”

A few days later, when I went out to get some fresh air, a long-haired dog ran up to me. I stroked him with hands that almost trembled. How long it was since a dog had pressed close against me! It was a powerful animal, a Siberian sledge dog, such as are seen in pictures with Eskimos, famished and longing for affection. Was he from the village? Had he run away? A great feeling of happiness filled me, instantly giving birth to the desire to keep him.

** Will you come with me? ” I asked affectionately. “ Will you stay with me? I’ll manage the food with my cavalry squad.” The dog wagged its tail and looked at me lovingly from brown, almost human eyes. “ Very well,” said I. “ Then let us go. Come, Suschka.” It followed at once, and was greeted with joy by the squad. “This is our regimental dog now,” Blank announced, with shining eyes, while Pod pressed it mutely to his broad breast, and even Seydlitz stroked it once. I got bits from everybody, some muscle from the midday soup, some bread-crust from the day before. When I lay down, the dog stretched himself out beside me as a matter of course. How warming it was! I shoved him a little towards the lower part of my body, against my bladder, and, covering both of us with my cloak, I slept as I had not done for a long time. Even the next day my bladder was a little better, and after three days it was completely cured. “ This is a medicine dog,” said Pod, astonished.

A Swedish pastor came to hold divine service in the barracks and at the end gave communion to all who wished for it. “Shall we go up, Junker? ” asked Pod. We all went, except the Bavarians, Briinn, and the conjurer. About a hundred men, ragged and bloodless, knelt down before the sacred symbol. With fine tact, the young pastor avoided the Bible, giving us in his own words what we needed, enlivening and strengthening messages. The red wine burned our tongues and reached our very hearts. We were invigorated as from an actual meal. When we came back, Briinn was sitting on his plank bed. His eyes were sunken, he looked weak and stupefied, and there
was a contemptuous twitching about the corners of his mouth. ‘* Why did you not go with us, Briinn? ” I asked.
“For me there is no God any more,” he said coldly.
“Tf you must know, since Totzkoje,” said Briinn spitefully.

We were allowed to write home. At last, at last.... Four cards and one letter in a month, so ran the order. Schnarrenberg distributed the printed cards, and there was bustle and talk in our den as if we had won the lucky number in a lottery. Almost all were writing, with boot-soles or pieces of board on their knees for writing-pads. I used my diary, but to whom should I write? To my father, no one else.... The one who would have valued what I had to say was no more. To my father, therefore. And what should I write to him? The truth could not be told in three sentences, and in any case would not pass the censor. So I only wrote that I was alive and hoped to return home some day. I told him I was still wearing the clothes I had on when taken captive, and begged him for underwear, soap, brush, and comb. I added that my wounds were healed, but that I still dragged one leg a little.

When would he receive this first sign of life from one believed to be dead, I thought, smiling? In five, six weeks at the soonest, perhaps not for months — home lay so far away! Perhaps it would never reach him at all; perhaps in some fight at sea he had long since...
“ Junker,” said Pod at this moment, “ write ‘Germany ” on my card in Russian letters, it will be better, eh? You may read it if you like....”
I wrote “ Germania” in large letters and read his last line, which ran: “Don’t forget that this year potatoes must be planted in the rye-field, Anna....”

Our comradeship began to weaken. Though I struggled against this knowledge, what I had to see every day was stronger than my wishing and wanting. In our cavalry corner it was still present in a way, but for how long no one knew. It was crumbling everywhere, and if it was breaking up in our group, which the field and front had welded together, how could it remain in the other groups, which had only drifted together in the camps through some wind of fate.

With us Briinn was the most striking example. He now thought only of himself and grew more spiteful every day. Schnarrenberg, too, by his provocative manner, got into a sort of chronic irritation and appeared harder and more brutal than he really was. Little Blank, who had grown somewhat dolorous and needed a great deal of comfort and support, was becoming ruined morally. The two Bavarians, who had, as it were, belonged to our cavalry corner since Irkutsk, were ruder and more uncontrolled than at first, but still bearable, obliging, and ready to help. Only Pod, Seydlitz, and the conjurer had remained the same. And I myself? Alas, I too was no longer what I ought to be....

God in heaven, it was no wonder! If one could have got out, seen other people, other faces... ! If it had been summer! Besides Briinn and Blank, we of the cavalry corner went out into the yard every day with three tunics on. There were few who still had the energy to go out every day for a walk, few who recognized that tuberculosis attacked everyone who did not daily fill his lungs with fresh air, and who would face forty degrees of cold and the icy blast of a desert wind at fifty degrees in order to avert another evil.

It was lasting too long. Noble sentiments are the fruit of great moments and cannot be preserved, like ripe fruit in cans, to be consumed in larger or smaller portions according to need or demand! In the field there had been comradeship. Was it there still, would it be there up to the last hour, even if the war went on for years? This was no soil for comradeship....

We had been comrades in Totzkoje, for instance, and we should be comrades still if some deed were demanded of us, or in case of sudden danger. But there was nothing sudden here, everything was creeping, was paralysed.... Our forced confinement was malicious and enervating, demoralizing and ~ vile.... The fixed, constant unhappiness, the never-ending, daily recurrence, does not weld together, but rather rends asunder. There was nothing doing here, no hopes; that was probably the reason... the constant idleness, the incessant hunger, the eternal need of being alone... that was no soil for comradeship.
We gradually became spiteful like old dogs, faultfinding and malicious, like withered old men. We were becoming like animals, and if the end did not come soon we should end in hating one another.
“What is it you are always writing? ” asked Pod.
I closed my diary impassively. “ Everything, Pod,” I said confused.
*“ Well,” I said, “everything that happens here. What is spoken, what is done, how everyone feels and acts...”
“Then I am in your book also? ”
““Man,” he laughed outright, “ what for? I am a stupid old fool. Who could ever take an interest in me? ”

I smiled to myself. “ Perhaps more than you think, Pod. You forget that in my book you stand for nine hundred thousand, who all suffered what you suffered, who all resembled you... and Briinn for a hundred thousand like himself, who felt this life as he did....”

“Yes,” said Pod, putting his finger to the side of his nose, “now I understand. And Schnarrenberg and Seydlitz and the conjurer? And Blank and the Bavarians and yourself? And the Turks and Hungarians and Austrians? Do you speak of all, eh? Of all the two and a quarter millions? ”
“Yes,” I said, “and these ten or twelve I describe represent, as it were —”
“ And so you want to publish it some time? ” Pod interrupted me,

After a short silence he said: “ Very well, go on writing, and write of me also. It is quite right for those at home to know how the blood was sucked from our living bodies and what we thought of, spoke of, felt. But it will only be of value if you neither beautify nor conceal anything.”
“ Then it will be prohibited,” he said quickly.
“Because it is so horrible, so hateful, so low.”
“‘ Truth does not need a handsome dress. It is most beautiful when naked, my dear Pod,” I replied. “ Lies cannot help the world and the generations yet to come.”

Briinn had a visitor, an electrician, who spoke, like himself, in professional metaphors and in strangely chopped-up phrases. He was in the transport that came after us, had a black, shaggy beard, a face like a mummy, and a very hoarse voice.

“It was in Stretensk, a miserable Cossack hamlet, east of the Baikal, on the Schilka,” the man related, “‘ and my death’shead look dates from those days. They thrust us into summer barracks through whose cracks we could see the desert. They were on a steep mountain side and we had to carry up the water from the river. Eight hundred of us were put where there was only room for five hundred, and of course typhus fever broke out. We took one of the barracks as an isolation house, but no one wanted to go into it. They preferred to stay
with their comrades. They lay in twos without straw or covering and with logs of wood for pillows.

“We suffered most from thirst,” continued the man, “ but whoever dragged himself out into the snow to try to quench it was driven back by the Cossacks with knouts, for fear of infection. We sometimes drank water from the privies, and at last, when we realized that we should all die, we mutinied.... One can mutiny without weapons when an empty hospital stands locked up near by, when one knows that the Russian physicians have blankets and pillows and medicine in abundance and won’t give them out. Moreover, an American commission in Irkutsk — with doctors and nurses and all possible material — had already been waiting for weeks to help us. It was of no use. We were whipped back like cattle into our dens by mounted persecutors, and when whole groups of our men sought death in the river in order to be relieved of their torments, the commander had it guarded by sentinels. We were not even allowed to take our own lives. On Christmas Day, 1915, Elsa Brandstro6m came to Stretensk and rescued the handful that still remained.
“* Almost like Totzkoje,” said Briinn. “So we were not the only ones who fared so badly.”
“Well,” cried Seydlitz, “ what more do we want? We are in heaven here compared with Totzkoje and Stretensk, so be satisfied.”

Only a few had been able to withstand the gradual weakening of both body and soul, and while they did their best to help the others, the majority had grown too impatient and callous to take advantage of their help.

One day packages came from home for some of those longest in the camp, and, among others, to a young infantry soldier on a neighbouring plank bed, his first package from. home, and at an unobserved moment I saw him patting the new shirts and pressing home the home-knitted stockings to his lips.

“Ensign,” he said towards evening, and I saw his eyes shining as I had seen but few shine, “I have got my first package from home, from my mother. Now I am saved. Should you like to see it? ” As he showed it to me, I felt that though he had already unpacked and packed it three or four times, he could still see his mother’s hands on the little articles....

The next morning I noticed the same boy weeping bitterly and went over to him. Pod came, Pod, who was always at hand when anyone was crying. “ What are you whimpering about, you fool? ” he asked rudely; for he was always rudest when softest at heart.
‘“‘ Ah, hm... there was a can of fish in it, too, you say? ”

“ All right.” Pod started, his nose to the ground, a veritable hunting-dog, and came back, an hour later, with the package under his arm. “ But the fish is gone,” said he. “‘ But mother did not do that up herself, eh? Here, my boy, take better care next time.”
We climbed up on to our plank bed. “‘ Who was it, Pod? ”
“* Meyer, of course, who else could it be? ” Meyer was a bad sort, known to be a thief and a fighter.
“Qh, nothing, only put one, two, three on his thievish face....”
In the evening I learnt that Meyer had been put into the hospital. Pod must have half beaten him to death. I said he would get the knout for it if anyone told on him.
“Qh,” said Pod calmly, “that doesn’t matter. The boy has his package again, which is the principal thing. As for the rest, Meyer will steal no more and I —I have a broad back.”
Briinn gradually turned away from us. He had been making
new friends and was not very particular in his choice. They were usually those who could not contradict what he said.
Once he said: “Our position here and the way we are treated are only the natural consequences of our policy. What is a German soldier? An object, a number, an animal....”

“How so? I will explain. All of us have an open pimple, haven’t we? —those round things that make the most intelligent face look foolish. We are said to be a multitude, indistinguishable from one another because of this thing. Only the higher ones are allowed to look decent — the N.C.O., the regimental sergeant major, the Colonel. They wear caps with shields so that they may be distinguished from us at a distance.”

“Yes, but? Don’t you understand yet, Muschko? It is all a question of command. The German troops in their huckaback and pimples are nothing but convicts, and it is because we look so silly in those things, in such prison-garb, that we are treated so badly. Why do all other armies wear smart head-coverings. Just look at the English caps...”
* Stuff — but!” he roared. “If you are too stupid to understand this, it is your own fault, and that ends it! ”
Yes, full stop,” Pod called over to him. “ And now shut up your big barn-door. We want to sleep.”

The winter dragged slowly on. Our one and only wish was for the spring. Many died in this, my second, winter of captivity. We alone did not notice it so much, because our doctors, with the help of Elsa Brandstrém, had established a model hospital for the sick. All we noticed in spring was that some of the plank beds were empty, and we had much more room than we had had during the winter.

In our disconsolate position it made us very happy to know that there was a refuge in a hospital with physicians. As was inevitable in a pen where the windows were sealed up, consumption made rapid progress among us. Scurvy and nyctalopia, well-known symptoms of famine, increased fourfold. So far fever had passed us by, but even without that there was quite enough to break our tired bodies. We were already between Scylla and Charybdis. When we couldn’t sleep for cold, the lice didn’t trouble us, and when we were warm, we couldn’t sleep for lice, so what were we to do?

One day there was a violent fight, which would certainly have spread over the whole barracks if it had not been for Pod, who sprang with a sudden bound on to a plank bed and in his thunderous voice shouted above the noise: “ Two men to stir the blood!” Everyone laughed, and the crowd dispersed. He who laughs does not fight. Our Pod was still a pillar of strength, the same in spite of torture.... Afterwards I learnt that the fight was for possession of a photograph of a naked girl, which was shown round secretly that evening by its owner. But he got no more good from it than we did— only exciting dreams of passion, but it seemed to gratify him to show his precious possession.

Conditions rapidly grew worse. No consideration was shown to those either writing or sleeping. Wanting to write again to my father, I loosened a couple of leaves from my diary and sat down on my plank bed.
“It is so difficult to say the right thing, father,” I wrote. “ And it is equally difficult not to complain. We do not want to be unjust or to ask for anything that cannot be given but...”

They were playing cards on the next plank bed. “ Trumps,” roared a powerful gunner, as he slapped his flat hand down on the boards and made them shake. I put one finger to my ear and went on writing. “ What tortures us most is that we

cannot see an end to this. You may not know, but perhaps you can see it, very small, like a distant star. We only see a night that is always growing blacker and more torturing and threatens to engulf us...”

“Good Lord, man, leave my boots alone, you confounded thief,” somebody shrieked. A log of wood flew through the air, came down on the corner of my plank bed, and grazed my head. The boot-thief stole away as if he heard nothing.

“There are only a few among us who are still strong and uncontaminated, whose marrow has not been frozen by these years, father. But if it lasts much longer, not one will come out of it without a canker in his flesh or in his soul. We are all brave, and the weakest are perhaps os bravest, but what 1 is demanded of us is beyond our strength.’

A shout indicated that someone had cheated at cards. A circle of onlookers filled the corridor. Unfortunately Pod was absent just then. The black-haired electrician had someone by the collar, shaking him as a dog does a rat. At last the man tore himself loose and doubled up his fists. “ Give it to him,” shouted Briinn, egging him on. I heard the sound of a couple of blows struck on naked flesh. Blood flowed.... “I'll choke the breath out of you, you thieving dog,” panted the electrician. “ And if I myself shall survive these years with a pure soul, father, I do not know...” I wrote slowly, and my hand resembled a famished spider crawling slowly over yellowed leaves.
As soon as the cold lessened and was only thirty degrees, according to the doctor, Seydlitz and I walked silently three times round the camp every day. “A fight against tuberculosis,” we called it.
As we were passing for the third time the white fence that separated us from the officers, we met an Austrian Lieutenant.

When we saluted him, he thanked us and walked on a little, then suddenly stood still. “I have noticed you taking this walk for a couple of weeks past,” he said, smiling. “It is terrible in there, I suppose? ”
I was silent and Seydlitz pressed his lips together. “It is endurable,” he said coldly.
“How long have you been captive? ” he then asked.
“That is two years. I have been here since 1914....”
“Are there good reports from the front? ” asked Seydlitz curtly.
“Yes,” he said. “ But what’s the use of that? Victory upon victory and still not peace! What is your rank? ” he asked, interested.
“TI am a N.C.O.,” said Seydlitz, “ Cornet.”
“Ensign,” said I in a low voice.
“Ensign? ” he cried. “ What are you doing in the soldiers’ camp? You belong to us.”
““T have good comrades,” I said, “ from the field, from my regiment, from the hospital...”
“TI can understand that. Nevertheless... You could visit them from here also, would even be able to help them better from here. You would get fifty roubles a month....”
“ Yes,” I said weakly. “ I know all that, but — ”
“ Listen,” he interrupted, “come to visit me and bring your friend with you. I am a good deal with an Ensign of the artillery who would be mighty glad, I think...”
“Yes,” said I, “ we should like to do that very much, but the sentries wouldn’t let us pass —”
He laughed. “ That is simple. Do you know any French or English? Then report to the commandant for giving lessons. As a teacher of a language you will get a propusk, a pass.”
“Yes,” we said, “ we will try it.”
“All right,” he said, and held out his hand through the
barbed wire. “ You need only ask for me. My name is Saltin. They all know me....” | |
We went home. “Shall we do it, Seydlitz?” I asked thoughtfully, for something within me had sounded a warning.
* I don’t know, Ensign. You can do it easily enough. Go over for good when you can no longer bear it here. As for me — ”
“ That is just what I fear,” I said in a low voice.
He walked on in silence, the furrows deepening in his lean face. “ Three days later I should have been captured as ensign,” he said at last. “ Well, better ones than I have had to bear it, so I can.”

I have had my father’s first card, and he is alive and well. What more did I want? I felt happier, although one line ran: “Qur lot is harder than yours, yet we do not complain.” “Oh, father, father, if you but knew! ” I thought bitterly. .. » But he is not to blame, how could he know? No one knew. “ But they shall know,” thought I, as I pressed my treasured book to my heart and tried to forget that line. I wanted only the happiness from that card. There was such need of it, such need.... The longer the winter lasted, the more terrible it seemed. Would spring never come this year ?

One day Briinn had irritated Schnarrenberg so much by one of his sarcastic lectures that he fell upon him without further ado. By his sensible way of living Schnarrenberg had kept himself in better form physically than any of us, but Briinn was just like a limp piece of rubber. In his excitement Schnarrenberg had beaten him so badly that he was unconscious for some time. Some were pleased, but the majority hated Schnarrenberg now more than ever, partly because of his bodily strength, and partly because he was protected by the Russians as head of the barracks. But this event was significant of the mood we were in, a mood of increasing hate of man for man, which often, at the slightest cause, led to an almost insane outbreak.

On passing No. 3 barracks one day, I met an old acquaintance from the Grudetzki barracks, the man from the amputation ward who had been hit in the testicles. “‘ Have we not already seen each other? ” he asked. “ Yes,” I said, “in the hospital at Moscow. How are you? ” “Qh,” said he, “I don’t know what to say, but I learnt long ago that all is up. You lied to me that time. I know why, and it was better that I should find out gradually. Now I don’t care. I have an easier life. For here... When I see what some have to go through just on account of what was taken from me... And I should not have been cold-blooded myself... sometimes I am almost glad of it. I often think that everything in this world is made up for in some way.... Because of what I had to suffer I need not now writhe like a brute.... It will only become difficult when I am at home again. For my wife without children — But that is not to be thought of for the present,” he added, saluting as he went off.

Seydlitz had just been with me. I had never seen him so cheerful. “ Just think, Ensign,” he said, as he gave me a letter from his mother, “my first letter, and it says that the order for my promotion was already out when I was captured.”
“You see! ” said I gaily. “ And now you want to go over, don’t you? ” ;

“Yes,” he said firmly, as he laid both hands on my shoulders. “Ensign,” he continued, “ you must understand me rightly, you above all. I could do no one any good by staying here. It is different for you in some ways, but I am alone. I have no one here to whom I am really attached and am probably not much liked. Perhaps I did not deserve anything else;
and, finally, I want to take care of myself so that I may be able to serve our country after this is over.”
“You are perfectly right,” I said frankly. “ And no one will think ill of you, if you—”
“You must come with me, or you will die. I can see it, and if it does not have to be — ” |

“Very well, Seydlitz,” I said smilingly. “Let us go and look at it first, and if we find a couple of human beings — you know what I mean by that — and if what Saltin said was true, we shall be able to help our men better.... Yes, we will go together.”

We got our propusk without difficulty. We had been trying since midday, with the aid of a borrowed brush and my washbowl, to scrape at least the outer dirt from our uniforms. We made a raid against the lice and combed our soft, Christlike beards. “ Are you going to the court ball?” asked Briinn sneeringly.

At the officers’ camp we were directed to the stone barracks on the left, and, mounting a few steps, we found a door bearing a card: “Captain Schank, Lieutenant Saltin. Lieutenant Kovacs. Lieutenant Sineth.”

Lieutenant Saltin was alone with a dark-skinned officer. He jumped up, took our cloaks from us, and called out: “ Balinth ” twice into the corridor. A Honved infantryman appeared and stood at attention. “Go to the mess, Balinth, ‘and bring something to eat for three.” The other man, a Hungarian Honved Lieutenant, courteously took his leave.

“There, my young friends,” Saltin said. He had a long, blond face, nervous hands which he kept putting up to his mouth, warm blue eyes, and dark eyebrows. “The worst of it is behind us now, eh? In a month it will be spring.... ”

He nodded, smilingly. Here was a human being we could speak to, if only by exchanging glances. Everything was almost touching. We sat on chairs — roughly made, to be sure — at a narrow table made of boards from boxes... and when the soldier came back with coffee and rolls, I couldn’t resist crying: ‘ You are gloriously off here.”

Saltin shook his head. “It only looks so.... Of course, I understand it must seem like paradise to you, but after living like this for three years... You see, if one wants to go to bed, the other three must get up. We can only wash by turn and go to bed one after the other... and one is never alone. There are hardly any books, much quarrelling, still more nervousness, and every minute some affair of honour. .. - In four weeks this existence would torment you as much as yours has done. One gets used to it quickly, and, taking our former life into consideration, and remembering how we were spoiled and privileged... we certainly do not suffer less than our soldiers....”

He brought cigarettes, placed them on the table within easy reach, and we smoked happily. The cleanliness and comfort of this room almost intoxicated us. Saltin won our hearts from the first— would he have done so at home under normal conditions?

Time flew by. He spoke of a thousand things, and we drank in every word. How humble we had grown, like old slaves! The only thing that tormented us was the lice that now and then bit us ferociously, but, because we did not want him to notice, we restrained ourselves from the scratching that had become a habit.

It grew dark and we had to go home. “ Soon again, my German friends,” said Saltin cordially, as he shook hands and accompanied us to the barbed-wire fence. “ And think it over, Ensign, whether you would not, after all...”
“ A splendid fellow,” murmured Seydlitz on our way home.
“Yes, we have found one, haven’t we? ”
** Are the Germans also like that? ” he asked.

We went on in silence. Were we not a little horrified at the thought of our plank beds? Seydlitz suddenly stood still. “ Ensign,” he said, “weren’t you struck by the fact that Saltin never seemed to be itchy? ”

“Yes,” I said eagerly, and he continued: “Do you think they have no lice there? ” I doubted it. “It is only because of his fine bringing up,” I said. But he didn’t seem to understand. “I don’t think that the best bringing up would be of any good when lice bite you, my good fellow,” he said dryly. So this difficult problem was left unsolved until next time.

The day before, an order had come from the Russian commandant that threw our cavalry corner into the greatest excitement. “ Since the number of dogs kept by the prisoners is constantly increasing, all animals must be sent to be destroyed. Disobedience of this order will be severely punished,” Schnarrenberg read aloud.

We spent half the night talking over what was to be done with Suschka. All agreed that we would not give her up, that we would not be parted from her. Even Schnarrenberg, the only one who had taken no notice of the dog, was of the same mind. “ But suppose someone in the barracks betrayed us? ” was all he said. “ You know that I have more enemies than friends....”

“No fear of that,” said Pod in his deep voice. “I'll take care of that....” So we trained Suschka for a whole day to stay quiet, under a bundle of old uniforms, whatever noise went on. She understood very quickly and would slip at once on the order into her safe hiding-place and not stir. When she was perfect, Pod lifted Suschka on his arm like a child, walked with his most sailor-like gait into the middle of the barracks, mounted a plank bed, and loudly demanded a hearing.

“Listen, boys,” he said with emphasis, “ you have heard the order. You know we have a dog that belongs to us all, and we are resolved not to give her up. I am certain that none of you is rogue enough to betray an innocent creature, so we have decided to take you into our confidence. But if there should be a Judas among you,” he continued, in a voice of thunder, “ I will afterwards make life such a burden to him that he will have to follow this dog before four weeks are over.” There was applause, Suschka barking in sympathy. “ Three cheers for our Pod,” called out little Blank in his high voice, and a hundred voices shouted: “ Hurrah, hurrah! ” Pod got down and came back. “ They are all right, my Suschka,” he said slowly, as he ran his fingers affectionately through her long hair.

Next day came the guards, led by a starschi, and carrying ropes and a couple of sacks. Schnarrenberg went quietly up to them. “I am barracks-commandant,” he said firmly. “ There is no dog in our room.”
I translated. “ Man,” muttered Briinn, “he is not even lying! It is a bitch....”
The guards sniffed and walked slowly through, while Suschka lay quiet as a mouse. My heart beat violently, and Pod scratched his head from nervousness. They made straight for our plank bed....

At that moment there came a dreadful noise at the door like the sound of two men fighting. “ Guards, guards, come and separate them! ” cried some of the men. The guards, half afraid, ran towards the door. Nothing was the matter, only a couple of men flinging curses across to each other in every tone of the register, and smiling at the same time.
The sentries only came back as far as the door. All danger was over. “ Didn’t we do that well? ” the two combatants cried.
They were answered with rousing applause and carried in shoulder-high.

There was little real comradeship among us now, only the companionship of fellow convicts. We seemed to have become detached inwardly, but outwardly, towards our common enemy, the Russians, we were welded together into a strong, indestructible wall.

I kept on stroking Suschka, who was again lying on my lap. “Do you see, my dog?” I said happily; “even the roughest among us helped you. They are good, our boys, as we have just seen once more, good and kind of heart; but they are sick at times, sick and confused.”

I made my first visit to the German officers and resolved to move over to them. The highest in rank among us was a man named Mittelberg, a grey-haired infantry Captain, short of speech and very resolute. When I explained our position to him, he said that he was keenly anxious to see us with him as soon as possible. “No need to perish if it can be avoided,” he said. “We are sorry enough not to be able to make life easier for our soldiers. It is not our fault, but the result of reciprocal international agreements.”

I told him of the life our men led, and begged him to order a few things. “ We give a certain percentage of our boardmoney every month to assist our soldiers, and do all we can with it,” he said, “ but I hope that Miss Brandstrém will soon. come again to look after things. As you know, our hands are tied. All intercourse with the troops is prohibited, and further rendered impossible by the sentries.”
“No one knows. It is supposed from fear of an organization on our part—they apparently fear the German devils even. without arms,” he concluded, as he dismissed me.

From him I went to Seydlitz and Schnarrenberg. “ Sergeant major,” I said cheerfully, “we report ourselves as leaving. Tomorrow we go into the officers’ camp.” He went almost white. “ What! ” he asked, “ both of you, or just you? Then I shall resign my position.”

“Because I will have no one whose advice I can take about my orders. I know I do many things wrong. I got my training in a barrack-yard, not in a prison, and I shall never get quite used to the position here. Until now it did not matter. You helped me, smoothed over my difficulties, often dulled the edge of my commands, adapting them to our state, our mood, our company.... That I shall never learn. I am a soldier, not a negotiator. Very well, let someone else do it now....”
“No, Schnarrenberg,” said Seydlitz, “ you ought not to do that. Though we shall be away... you still have Pod.”

“ Podbielski? Dragoon Podbielski? ” he asked, in an indescribable tone. “Surely I cannot ask advice from that man about my orders. No,” he concluded violently. “ But in any case I shall not do it alone.”
“Sometimes it is almost impossible to help our good Schnarrenberg,” muttered Seydlitz, as he lay down. “Not a trace of elasticity...”
I sat down next to Pod. “I am going over to the officers’ camp tomorrow,” I said in a low voice.
“Well for you, my lad,” he said, with great self-control. “You deserved it long ago.”
“Pod,” I continued, “don’t be angry with me for it. Look — ”

“You need not excuse yourself for it,” he interposed. “ It is quite clear.... Men are not equal and will never be. For the rest, I, with my strong body and nerves, suffer less by this life than you, for instance. And why you should suffer more than I—”
“Yes, Pod, that is all right. Nevertheless... if I did not
feel that I can’t hold out much longer, that I must get out as quickly as possible if I ever want to get home again, I should not leave you.”
“Ensign,” he broke forth, falling into his brusque manner in order to conceal his feelings, “please hold your tongue, or you will get one over the head, do you understand? ”

I did not know whether to laugh or cry. “I shall often come to see you, Pod,” I said quickly. “ And another thing: if you want my dog, Suschka, I’ll give her to you....” He coughed suspiciously. “Hm,” he said, “ gladly. I have one at home, you know, who looks like Suschka. I once brought it back with me from leave,” he continued, with striking eagerness, “ Nikolaievitsch, we called him at the front. But that was too complicated for Anna. She called him Niko for short.”

We were ready for marching, our bundles on our backs. Seydlitz wore Poseck’s fine boots. “ Well, Blank,” said I, “head up and remember sometimes what I once told you.” He cast down his eyes and swallowed a little. “ Yes,” he said weakly, “I will, Ensign. But will you come sometimes? ” he continued pleadingly.
“¢ As often as I can,” I said.

Briinn scarcely stirred when I came to his bed. “ Briinn,” I said cordially, “do try to make a man of yourself. It will only harm you in the end if you give way so much. Remember your wife, your country. It is for our country that we are enduring all these sufferings. You will get home some time and will get your reward. But you will never get into orderly ways again if you continue to go downhill. Grit your teeth for once....”

“Words are cheap, Junker,” he said mockingly. “But of all the pack I liked you the best. I know that you mean well, and so I put up with it, but save yourself the trouble in future. I shall go to the dogs here anyway, with or without music....

** Now you will be with fine gentlemen again,” he continued, after a pause. “ Well, I wish you joy of it. Send me an officer’s wench sometimes, when you have one to spare. In four weeks you will not know us any more. God, what are we worth, anyway? We are going to die—with or without a priest....” I bit my lips. How this man had changed, I thought, how this last year had weakened him! I was about to say something else when Pod signed to me with his eyes to leave him alone.

The leave-taking from the conjurer was short and pleasant. “TI wish you everything good,” he said in a lively way. “ And don’t forget the juggling tricks and the three best ju-jutsu motions. One never knows when they may be needed.” |
The two Bavarians stood with heels together in military fashion. “ Why, what has taken you? ” I laughed.
“ Excuse us,” the Tadpole began. “ We often did not behave to you as we ought to have done —”
“Qh... because you were quite different from what an ensign usually is....”
“Well,” the Schwalangscher added, “ we now wish the Ensign everything good, and ask that he will not forget the two Bavarians! ”

When we first entered the room inhabited by the officers of lower rank in the German barracks, we saw nothing but a dozen iron bedsteads and as many people in field uniforms. A gunner officer, who was sitting on the bed at the door, got up at once. “ You are the two new-comers from the soldiers’ camp? ” he asked. It was the Ensign whom I had seen when we came before, and he was evidently glad to see us. “ Saltin told me about you. My name is Olfert, Ensign....” He was a small but broad and heavy man with quiet movements... nothing young, nothing ensign-like about him. He was more like a lieutenant.

He led us to the officer of highest rank in the room, a Lieutenant from the reserve officers called Berger, who was teaching German to a tall Turk. He cordially bade us welcome, made us put down our bundles near him, and led us from bed to bed. Eighteen men in field-grey got up and gave their names, eighteen different faces glided past us, young and old, hard and cheerful, discontented and indifferent.

“* Now, gentlemen, it would be best for you to bathe first and then put on new things from head to foot,” said Berger, as he called the one and only batman and told him to bring hot water from the kitchen. “ Lieutenants Windt and Opitz, will you lend — the gentlemen your buckets? ” “ Certainly...” said a small, thickset infantry officer with very fine hair, who we could tell was from Berlin by his accent.

The only vacant corner was near Berger, and there the servant put two large buckets of water, while Berger himself brought soap, another a hard brush, and a third a towel. The question “ Who has any spare parts of uniforms? ” produced stockings from one, a pair of trousers from a second, a tunic from a third, and a threadbare litewka from a fourth. “ We will have your things boiled and frozen,” said Berger. “ Until then you will have to wear these. You must know,” he added, smiling, “ we have no lice here....”

We both reddened. “ Do you see? ” said Seydlitz by a look. But we were greatly relieved. My God and Father in heaven, no more lice! Our hands almost trembled with joy as we drew the warm garments from our bodies.... The shirts could be thrown into the fire at once, as they were mere rags, brown and stiff as boards. The light of day showed that our underdrawers had neither knees nor seat—-what had become of them? All the bashfulness we had lost with our old comrades awoke again among these strange, inquisitive faces. “ Well, man,” growled Seydlitz, “what must be, must....” For heaven’s sake, how our bodies looked! They were spotted brown from lying on hard boards, dotted red from lice bites, and covered with dirt and grey scales. The water was in a short time transformed into dingy broth.

“Boys,” said fat Windt, “you will have to repeat that. Polmutzki, water! Once more....” He sat down on the nearest bed and watched us cleansing ourselves as if it were a long-missed entertainment. “ By thunder,” he continued, “ it is long since I saw such lamentable figures. By comparison, those in Germany were only wax-figure shows. Just look here, boys,” he called to the room in a loud voice, “ are not these a regular couple of spiders? Regular daddy-longlegs, I should call ’em....”

There was no spare bedstead in the whole camp. Olfert searched for a whole day and returned at last with two Cossack sacks, “J have asked the commandant for two bedsteads for you. In the mean while you must put up with these grainsacks. Come along now into the coffiin-making shop. There are shavings there.” He led us into a room where a dozen German and Austrian soldiers were carpentering. Along the wall were piled up hundreds and hundreds of coffins, plain, roughly finished boxes of eight boards, fairly smooth on the outside, quite rough within.

“We shall need them all in the spring,” he said. “ As no one can be buried in winter, we pile up the dead in large earthen barracks, which you may have seen at the eastern gate of our camp. Almost every day several are taken in there to be buried in the spring, as soon as the ground thaws.”

We stuffed our sacks with fragrant pine-shavings and carried them back into our room. There was so little space that we could not lie down on the floor during the day and had to sleep in the passage-way at night. Though they only reached from hip to shoulder, yet for us who had lain for nearly two years on hard wooden boards, they were like spring mattresses

upholstered with horse-hair. We had soft pillows and slept wonderfully, in spite of the scanty mattresses, and when we remembered that there were no lice to disturb our rest, we gladly put up with the half-dozen beg-bug bites which are inevitable in Russia.

Olfert advanced us a couple of roubles from our first Russian allowance, and with them we purchased a small table from the carpenters. My God, that we should own a table... and a couple of bedsteads on which to put our sacks... ! And that we should no longer need to eat off the floor or write on our knees... !
Was the worst behind us? I suddenly began to feel that I might hold out.

On our first walk I asked about a Colonel, a small Honved Hungarian with a typical hussar moustache, whom I had noticed. “ That is Tobady,” said Olfert, “a full-blooded Hungarian, a clever man. He was captured as early as 1914 and has been betting ever since, and for any amount, that we shall still be in Siberia in 1920! ”
“On the contrary — one of the brainiest in our camp.”
“Yes, but...” I protested. “‘ Why, then all of us will be done for, of no more use. Who can stand lying about idle for six years? We should go home perfect ruins, aged men.”

Our room-mates were men of all classes and callings. Near the door was a small rifleman, Jungmann, an acting sergeant _major waiting for an officer’s commission. “ A war volunteer also,” said Olfert when we asked about him.
