He was a polite, modest lad with the red mouth of a child, who always made us think of his mother when we looked at him. Olfert’s place was next to him, and Berger’s opposite.
Berger’s and the Turk’s beds, with a table and a space between them, made, as it were, a small private compartment.

Berger, a Doctor of Law, was a thin, fair, esthetic fellow with the fine, nervous head of a philosopher, feminine hands, and a pleasant and tactful disposition. Over his head there hung the picture of his wife and of a very fair boy. The Turk was a tall, hot-headed fellow, called “ Highness” by some because of the word which he was entitled to use after his long foreign name, which meant Prince in Turkish.

On the opposite side lived Proschow, a young aviator, the brother of a well-known ace who had been shot down on the western front. He wore his short, aviator fur coat with inimitable chic and was known only by the name of “ the Rapid Flyer.” His cap had two small dents that entranced all the youngsters, and no one else could set a cap aslant on his head so enticingly. His mouth seemed to be a few millimetres larger than his brain.

Next to him came Windt, “the Berlin athlete. After three _ days I realized that I did not like neighbours who often spoke to one ‘another in foul language. Neither of them had any delicacy of feeling, and the sharpness of the Berliner was returned with rudeness by the tall East Prussian.

Two or three cadet officers and sergeants followed this Don Quixote and Sancho Panza. They were, with one exception, quiet and kindly fathers of families who disturbed no one as long as they were not disturbed themselves. Punctually, at stated hours, they played their game of skat three times a day, and only on these occasions were they peard: to quarrel violently.

The left corner was occupied by a young Lieutenant called Merkel, a regular officer, who seemed to copy the grey-haired Captain, the commandant of the camp, but without his qualities. With him we younger ones always felt that he would like to practise saluting with us for an hour every day for his own
entertainment and our education. For this reason he was usually alone, and seemed to be more disliked than anyone else in the room. Behind his back he was called the “ Button.”

Along the short wall up to the corner were a few lieutenants in the Reserve, a teacher, two office clerks, an East Prussian farmer with an impossible name, two manufacturers, Miller, “Stone Floors,” Hansen, “ Paints and Varnish.” In this corner controversy was incessant, and pan-German war aims clashed with democratic ideas of a world peace. The office clerks envied the merchants their possibilities of gain, and the merchants envied the clerks their life-insurance pensions. “ What do you actually want?” I heard the man Hansen, known as “Paints and Varnish,” say recently. © “You get your money in paper bags.” He frequently used this last word, though no one seemed to know exactly what it meant.

Next this corner lived two lieutenants, one of whom, Thurn, was a dark, handsome, southern-looking infantryman of an extremely amiable and obliging disposition. “A pity,” remarked Seydlitz, “that in puncto sexus he is said to be rather objectionable.” The other, Schulenburg, likewise an infantry officer from north Germany, was a fine, erect man, whom we liked best next to Berger, who seemed to be of an unusually kind disposition. He was very calm and reserved, and led this monotonous, nerve-destroying life among these different people, strictly in accordance with duty, and yet in such a way that not only his subordinates but everyone else looked up to him and respected him here as at home. Seydlitz became greatly attached to him, while I preferred Dr. Berger.

When out walking, Olfert showed me a “type” almost every day. By this name we designated the queer fellows of our camp, whose number increased every week. The barriers set up by education and culture fell with constantly increasing rapidity, people of rude and animal-like character associating with those of upright and pleasant dispositions.

“Look there, that is Lieutenant Stolle,” he said, pointing to an Austrian whose nose looked like the beak of a vulture. ‘He is a gifted pianist, but he had no piano to play on, and to live three years without playing would have put an end to his art. So he made a silent piano from the boards of boxes, and now he plays from six to eight hours daily on this box. If you look at him you can see how wonderfully beautiful his face becomes at some passages. He declares that he hears every sound, having long since lost all sensation of muteness.”

One morning, when I was taking a walk in the court with Olfert, I had an amusing experience. He pointed to a sentry near the gate, a real Siberian with a waving saint’s beard. “* Look here,” he said with a laugh, “ vodka is at hand in spite of all prohibitions.” At this moment there stepped through a small side-door a Russian Praportschik, Vereniki, the adjutant of the camp-commandant, a man much feared on account of his sharp manner. We saluted smartly, he merely touching his cap. A little farther on he noticed the drinking sentry. At one bound he was in front of the petrified man, with his right hand had wrested the bottle from his mouth, and with his left the fur cap from his head. The next moment he had brought down the heavy flask with a crashing blow upon the sentry’s bare head. There was a noise of crashing, liquid spurted forth, and a smell of drink arose as with a dull groan the sentry sank on his knees and lay motionless. Vereniki looked at us furiously and, with his small, exceedingly springy footsteps, went past us into the soldiers’ camp. Woe to us if we had laughed!
We stood transfixed. “Did he kill him?” I at last cried. “With what? ” Olfert smiled calmly. “ You don’t know these skulls yet, it seems....”
A few minutes passed before the sentry stirred again. When

we went up to him, he opened his eyes confusedly, breathed heavily, sniffed and grunted and rolled round on his belly, and with his long tongue easily lapped up the liquor that had dropped out of the bottle and that smelt strongly as it mingled with the desert sand....

One day I met Holcking, actually Count Holcking, a Captain in my own regiment. He was in the same camp, but because he was obliged to walk with a cane and rarely went out, I had not met him before. I looked at once for his sword — it was gone, or did he perhaps not carry it out of consideration for the others? I suddenly remembered the details. Had it not been for me the most wonderful moment in the war when the old gentleman returned him his sword with a knightly bow?
“ Captain,” I asked hesitatingly, “Captain, do you still know me? ”
He thought a little. “ Yes,” he said, “ you were an Ensign with us, eh?” A terrible weariness made itself apparent in his words, and when he held out his hand limply, 1 knew that it was paralysed.

“ Captain, I saw you last in the Russian divisional staff. I lay wounded in a Panje wagon when a couple of Cossack officers brought you up in a troika. An old General gave you back your sword. I heard what he said to you, Captain. It was a moment that reconciled me to many things....”
“Indeed?...” he said in a curious tone, adding with a sneer: “It did not last long, that famous moment....”
“So you have not your sword any more, Captain? ” I asked quickly.
“No,” he said in a low tone. “ At the very next stoppingplace a Cossack officer seized it, beat me twice over the head with it, and took it away with him as a war memento.”
He hobbled helplessly on while I remained standing, transfixed. “So it was only a farce?” ran through my head. “A fine gesture? Nothing more? ”

I felt suddenly as if a chord had broken within me. The most secret and beautiful thing that had hitherto drowned all discords, and alone had made it possible that my experiences, in spite of all the terrible things, were resolved into a pure harmony within me.... Now that was gone too! Now only shrill discords vibrated in my soul — remnants of a chord that could no longer produce a full sound in me. I had no more harmony in me, I no longer rang true....

A few days before, the stout Forest Commissioner, whom I had once met at Saltin’s, had died. I went with a detachment of Germans to the funeral, at which an Austrian padre spoke some appropriate words. When we came away, I heard somebody ask: “ And no one really knows of what the good old matt actually died? ” “He died because he had no forest. somebody answered in a low tone, and, on turning ound, I saw the pale Captain Behnke — a Forest Commissioner like the dead man.

A sort of “ reprisal ” had prevailed in our camp for a short time. On the ground that the Russian officers in Germany fared worse than we, for a fortnight we had been forbidden to leave the room after eight o'clock in the evening.

I was sitting with Saltin one night when immediately after eight I remembered the order and tried to get into my barracks in time, but was just too late. Vereniki had just ridden through the gate with a squad of Cossacks, whom a had already placed as guards at all the doors.

“ That is stupid,” said Saltin, “that is very stupid. It may cost you two months katorga, or even worse. Vereniki is a brute....” “Can’t I hide somewhere? ” I asked. He went out, but came back at once. “ He has even posted guards in the corridors. No, it is of no use and will only make matters worse....”
In such cases there was nothing to be done but wait and

trust to luck. Captain Schank did not conceal his anger. “Who knows but that all four of us will be punished? ” he muttered. Saltin was vexed at this remark. “If anyone is to blame, it is I,” he said, not without severity. “I will be responsible for him.”

At this moment Vereniki’s well-known shouting was heard in the room of the Turkish majors next door. “ I’1l shoot you,” he said savagely, and from the words of the Turkish Major I gathered that Vereniki was, as usual, holding a pistol at his temple, finger on trigger. “I am not to blame,” someone asserted solemnly. “ Starschi, off with him! Katorga!” roared Vereniki.

The noise of a rumpus in the passage came nearer. The latch was hit down with the butt of a pistol, and the door was opened wide with a kick, which was Vereniki’s manner of announcing his visit. He entered the room like a foaming lion — broad, massive, rocking, while three trembling soldiers stood behind him. I have never seen a Russian soldier near him who did not tremble.
** One, two, three, four — beds! ” he counted shortly. “ One, two, three, four, five — persons! ” he roared. “ Who is it that belongs somewhere else? ” I stepped forward.
“Why do you disobey my orders? ” he thundered at me.
“Inferiority complex” ran through my head. “I do not disobey them,” I answered in Russian. “I was just leaving when your guards were stationed at the door. It was two minutes past eight.”

He wanted to flame up. I stood stiffly, looking at him — perhaps not quite without fear — but looking openly into his evil face. “ Cadet? ” he asked suddenly in a strange tone. “ Cadet? ” he repeated resoundingly.
“Yes, volunteer on the very first day.”

What was he thinking of? I could not believe my eyes when he thrust the mighty pistol with a jerk into his belt-pocket and, with a splendid gesture, held out his hand to me, a hand of steel covered with hard skin. I shook it warmly. “Come,” he said brusquely.

I followed him out, and we went down the stairs side by side. In front of the barracks he paced up and down twice, silently brooding. “ You have other eyes than the Germans? ” he suddenly asked. “ You speak a different Russian from the Germans. Whence?...”
*‘ T had a Russian mother,” I said in a low tone.
“I have a German father.” He laid his hands heavily on my shoulders, looked into my eyes with the expression of an animal, then turned away and roared in his old manner: “ Starschi.” |
The starschi hurried up, hand to cap. “ Take this gentleman to his quarters. See to it that nothing happens to him. Be courteous to him. Take care of the Cossacks, do you understand? ”
“At your service, Your Excellency,” and the saluting hand trembled like a leaf.
“ ] thank you,” said I in a low tone.

I went through the camp at the side of the starschi, who chased off with a curse a couple of Cossacks ready to receive me with their nagaikas. In front of my room he saluted me respectfully and hurried back with jingling spurs.

Lost in thought, I stood for a while looking after him, confusedly. “ How is this possible? ” I thought. “He is the first to understand my peculiar position.... No one else has realized that I have a special burden to carry besides a general one... only this man....” Was this race incapable of being understood?

One evening, when we were standing in front of our barracks, two young lieutenants passed us arm in arm. “ Two lieutenants, rose-red and brown...” Olfert quoted. “ That is a special couple,” he then said mockingly. “Some of you know what that means. They are really a couple of sweethearts and blind to everything excepting themselves. They live like two turtle-doves, and neither will eat anything until he has pressed it upon the other with words as sweet as sugar. Their existence is based upon the strictest matrimonial rights and laws....”

I looked after them. They were two good-looking, healthy men. “ Here too? ” I thought. “And not only in the upper camp? ” “ And when they get home? ” I asked Olfert. “ These two? ” he laughed. “ Oh, they are lost. They will never touch a woman again as long as they live. Ugh! they say even now ‘a woman? How can one... ?’”

One day an incredible rumour ran through the camp to the effect that the Revolution had broken out in St. Petersburg. A man called Kerenski had seized the reins of government and a General of the name of Russki had forced the Czar to abdicate.

We could hardly believe it, but suppose it were true. It could not be, it was impossible. Had it not been reported a thousand times that peace was come? Was that not why we already said: “Peace has broken out again today”? But if it _ were actually true, would not that mean peace with Russia, and an immediate return home? Above all, would it not mean victory? Must we not conquer if the Russian front fell? If we could keep two fronts without being beaten, we must win, when one has collapsed....
My God, I was quite confused. I felt I must go down and hear if any more particulars were known. In the barrack-yard men were standing around in groups. Would it be like this in case of peace?...
A Jewish apothecary, who in some way always managed to get Russian newspapers, showed it to me in black and white. On the 11th of March the Government was overthrown, on the 15th the Czar abdicated.

That morning I accidentally ran into the good Saltin’s arms. He drew me to him when he saw me, and his eyes, though bright, were full of tears. “Ensign,” he cried, “ you must come to us this evening; we are giving a mulatschak in the cadet-room in celebration of the Revolution. Bring Olfert and Seydlitz with you.”

We went. The centre of the cadet-room, which was just like ours, had been cleared and converted into a banqueting-hall, - with tables placed end to end. A Hungarian gipsy band was sitting by the wall. Their fiddles were made for the most part of box-boards, but they played them as if they were at home, sobbing and dancing at the same time. They were all Hungarian soldiers from the upper camp, but they always found a way to come down when there was a mulatschak — or maydan, as Dostoievski calls it in his House of the Dead.

The room began to fill. Each brought his own particular drink, which was usually mixed with Russian vodka. When Saltin saw us, he led us to seats near him and pressed a full bottle into each of our hands. “ Hush, no refusal, you are my guests. Drink to our home-coming, boys....”

A wild carousal followed, the gipsies played like a dozen virtuosi, and the liquor was strong and biting. When they played a csdrdds, the Hungarian officers all began to dance. Seydlitz followed the joyous crowd with his big eyes, while Olfert only smiled, for he had seen it several times before.

The officers drank to us from all sides. Saltin had made us acquainted with some of the nicest men among them. “ Home again” was the motto at this mulatschak. Was it any wonder that things were madder than ever before? Which of us could remain unmoved by such a motto? My bottle also was emptied before midnight; a dozen of the superior officers were already

reeling, and obscene words were heard on all sides. An old Colonel at the head of the board was weeping aloud, and nearly all the others had tears in their eyes. Was it the news, the tremendous news in black and white which Saltin had fastened to a lamp in the centre of a board as a symbol of the feast? Or was it the music, the long-missed gipsy fiddle? God in heaven, it was both....

At four o’clock in the morning the national anthems were played — first the German, then the Turkish, and lastly the Austrian. All stood to join hoarsely in the choruses. By chance I looked at Seydlitz. His face was cold and disdainful, his nostrils distended; and he was not joining in the singing.
Soon afterwards we dragged ourselves home, Olfert walking at my right, a little tipsy, Seydlitz at my left, unmoved. “ Why do you look so grim, Seydlitz? ” I asked gaily.
“ Because our national anthem is sung by men in a drunken condition ninety-five times out of a hundred,” he said in a hard tone.,

The Russian officers seemed to grow younger all the time. — Sometimes they were almost infants, but we saw that they did not come voluntarily. At the inspection, called powjerka, when we had to march by them, we were compared twice daily with a photograph that they took of us. These officers were mostly courteous and nice.

A close inspection of all rooms was held almost every month and was carried out by a very different kind of officer. They took away everything they found, books, writings, newspapers, money. For this reason everyone had some hiding-place or other, hollow legs of tables, trunks with double bottoms, small bags hung between our legs beneath our trousers. My diary was my greatest anxiety. Hitherto I had always been able to hide it, but lately an officer had discovered all the hollow places in our furniture by almost clairvoyant tapping, and he made great booty of secret writings and plans for escape.... I rescued my diary by a trick as simple as it was daring. I merely hung
it out of the window on a ‘nail below the window-sill, and when he looked out, the projecting sill prevented him from noticing that a bag swung beneath it....

I went for the first time to visit my comrades. The steppe was brilliant in its first and only green, its spring of four weeks. The way to the upper camp led past the so-called “ Home-hill,” which rose up like a small peak in the middle of the camp, and one could look from it across the board fence into the steppe. Behind the fence, to the east, Chinese Manchuria began. And westward...

It was always crowded, this small mound, from spring till autumn, from morning till night. Some stood lost in thought, leaning on sticks, others crouched with crossed legs on the warm sand. Others, again, lay on their stomachs, holding their heads in their hands, and still others on their backs, looking with unmoved eyes into the clear sky. Seldom was talking to be heard on this mound, and all, excepting the skygazers, looked in the same direction, towards the west.

The wind swelled out their uniforms, old, shabby uniforms of German field-grey, Austrian bluish-grey, Turkish sandybrown. Their hair waved in the wind, their lips were pressed tightly together, and the sun played on shining worn-out buttons and epaulettes, or shone on grey, haggard faces and was reflected in half a hundred eyes, wide open and full of longing.

I knew some who lived on this mound instead of in their rooms. One could see a long way beyond the fence and was less of a prisoner up there. That was probably the reason. One felt the wind that came from the west, or smelt the dellicate odour of the grass that stretched out towards the west. One saw the railway tracks that led to the west, and at times a train rolling quickly towards the west....
We were nearer home when we stood on this mound, and

that is why it was called “ Home-hill.” From there we could imagine for a moment that we were free and alone in the middle of a wide steppe, perhaps on an exploring expedition, perhaps on a trip to the flower-houses of Nippon.... We saw the glittering iron ribbons which, in spite of everything, connected our desolate colony with the world, the iron rails on which we should some day roll homeward....

The Cossack sentry allowed me to pass without further question on my teacher’s propusk. In front of the soldiers’ barracks were swarms of grey ants, captive men moving hither and thither, tired and limp. I went into my old home. The sour, stuffy air of the dark space almost suffocated me, although the place was empty and all the windows open. And there I had lived for six months!

From afar I could already see Schnarrenberg’s resting-place, pedantically clean, and Briinn’s place, disorderly and dirty. The Tadpole sat in the middle, with Suschka next to him. The other plank beds were empty. Suschka whined with joy at sight of me, and the Tadpole himself climbed down quickly with a cry of “ Ensign, is it you? Now our bear will be glad.”
I shook hands with him. “ Where are the others, Tadpole? ”
“In front of the barracks, all lying in the sun. But someone must stay here to keep watch, else our last bit would be stolen! I shall be relieved in an hour by little Blank....”
Before going on I played a little with Suschka, who, to my delight, had recognized me at once. Her long hair was cleag and shining and carefully curried like a horse’s Coals, <5.

I found all the cavalry corner at the south wall. Pod sat in the sun with nude upper body, allowing his hairy muscles to brown, and leaning his broad back against the wall between little Blank and the conjurer. Briinn and the Schwalangscher were stretched at his feet. Schnarrenberg, the only one with tightly buttoned-up tunic, was sitting stiffly apart.

“Lad,” cried Pod joyfully, and his hands gripped my shoulders like bears’ paws. His good-natured rustic face was bright and shining as I drew cigarettes from my packet and distributed them. Briinn snatched at them as one addicfed to morphia snatches at the poison. “ You are a good fellow, Junker,” he muttered. “Not yet spoiled by the fine gentlemen over there; still the same, it seems to me....”

“Well, Ensign,” began Schnarrenberg, “all will be over soon, eh? Revolution! That is all that was wanting! ” He remained silent awhile and dropped his bulldog head on his chest. “ And I have to stand here aside while you go into the final fight...” he murmured, forgetting everything around him.
“What’s in the papers? ” asked Briinn. “Have they murdered all their officers? ” |
“No,” I said. “Everything seems to have gone off practically without bloodshed.”
“ Pity. These torturers ought all to have been butchered, as under Robespierre, and hung up on the lamp-posts....”
“Do you think that I shall be home in time for the harvest? ” Pod asked in a low tone.
“T hope so, Pod. It is only May now. We are counting on our Government proposing a separate peace this very month.”
“ Certainly,” said the conjurer. “ One does not make a revolution during war if one wants to continue the war.”
“Yes, now we have won,” said Schnarrenberg contentedly, adding: “Could you imagine such a thing happening with us?...”
Little Blank burst out laughing, and he laughed so violently that he choked and coughed for a long time. “ No,” he said finally, “how could we imagine our Emperor...”
After an hour I got up. “ Will you walk with me a bit, Pod? ”

* At once.” He moved to my side, big and brown. We went our old way, the full round that we once had named “ fight against the tuberculosis.” “ Well, Pod —tell me something. How are matters with you all? ”

He moved his head from side to side. “ Since the Revolution it is better again,” he said. “ Everything is a little freshened up. But before that it was very bad, fights, fornication, thieving. This damned winter... it would have spoiled the most decent fellows! I don’t believe that we could endure a third winter....”

“How? About the same, and doing the same as he always did.... But sometimes he is quite crazy.... For instance, when you left us, you were scarcely out of the door when he threw himself full length on his plank bed and whined like a lag-dog....”
I was silent for a long time. “And Schnarrenberg? ” I asked at last.

““My God, he hardly speaks to anyone now that you are gone. It is only since the Revolution that he has found his tongue again. On the first day he cried that all would soon be over and the final battle fought. It was only after someone had said that the stupid fool had better go there himself, as we had had enough of his talk, that he became tame again. However, he has resigned from his post.”

“ Don’t ask so many questions.... He has become a regular little prostitute, but he fares much better because he gets cigarettes and presents from all sides. But he will not be able to stand it much longer, I fear. I think that he coughs too much...”
* Ah,” I thought, “so his confession that time was only the beginning! That was the typical way; and the end... ?”’ “ And the conjurer? ” I asked with an effort.

“* He is still the same. He helps everybody, but does not want help from anyone. He keeps quite fresh, does his tricks and contortions for exercise every morning — business he calls it. The Bavarians are also fine fellows....”
“ And you yourself? ” I asked at last.

“ Ah, my lad —I? If I only had a letter, I should ask for nothing more. Everyone has had something except me. Why? And then... I should like to do some work again, do you know... couldn’t that be managed? ”

“ I have already thought of it, Pod, but I don’t believe it can be done. This camp consists mostly of wounded men and such as are not fit for work. Besides, there is no farm at all about here. No labourers’ trains are dispatched from here, it is too far away. But we shall soon get home now, Pod.”
“Yes,” he said in a low tone, “ that’s what keeps me up.... And if we got home this month, I could help Anna with the autumn sowing....” |
I slipped ten roubles into his pocket.

Once a month every officer in turn was allowed a steam bath. Whosoever’s turn it was went down to the village with a guard from headquarters. The bath was a miserable structure of wood. and pieces of rock... just a little room with a large stove — and two or three slippery wooden steps, but excellent in effect. Water was poured out of a ladle on to the stones of the stove, which were always red-hot, and it at once atomized into steam. Two ladlefuls were endurable, three scalded one’s skin and took away one’s breath. One sat for a while on the first or second step until the whole body was as scarlet. as a boiled lobster.

It was not necessary to wash, for the perspiration drove every grain of dirt out of the pores. “ It is called a ‘ Russian bath’ because it saves washing and soap and work,” Seydlitz once said. Old peasant women were often sitting there, and we had to wait with the guard until they went away. Notwithstanding all its advantages, it was a two-sided affair. True, we got home clean, but often brought a family of lice with us.

The best part of it was, undoubtedly, the walk. Often, a: as we went home, a Trans-Siberian express train rolled into the railway station and stopped to water the engine at the tower. At such times a couple of copecks and a few persuasive words usually induced my guard to accompany me to the platform to wait there until the train moved off. I generally sat on a bench and, with a peculiar pressure at my heart, silently watched the train, which in another week would be almost where my comrades were standing and where our country began....

While three of us were standing in front of the barracks talking about the mentality of the Russian people, an Austrian Captain _told this tale: “In my former camp we had a camp-comman- "dant who, by order of the General, had to erect a wooden fence higher than a man round the entire camp. As soon as the inspection was over, he had it broken down again and sold all the wood — it filled several trains and was worth three hundred thousand roubles to him —to the owner of an estate. For six months all went well, but when the General came unexpectedly for a second inspection...

“° Where has the fence gone to, Commandant? ’ ‘ Oh, Your Excellency,’ replied the gentleman, ‘in spite of all my efforts, a new bit disappeared every night. The prisoners of war broke it up and gradually used it as fuel.’ Denial was of no use. The whole camp was locked up in the barracks for two months, and as an extra punishment, the Commandant deducted twenty roubles from each of us for three months — amounting to another hundred and eighty thousand — and put them with the others into his pocket! ”

Once when I stopped at the railway station on one of my expeditions to the bath, a first-class compartment of the great Trans-Siberian express stopped just in front of my bench. A servant in livery opened the door and jumped out to make purchases. Beside the open door and behind the window sat a beautiful woman. I smelt the perfume about her from the platform and saw through the open door her crossed legs, long and white as columns. She had a rather long, genuine Russian aristocratic face and a skin of ivory whiteness. Her white throat rose like a flower from her low-cut dress, and I could faintly see the narrow groove to the right and left of which her breasts rose. “My God in heaven!” I thought, trembling, “ are there still such things? This perfume, this whiteness, this cleanliness...”
I did not know how it came about, but without intending to do so I suddenly took off my cap and said pleadingly: “ Just one cigarette please....”

She rose and stepped slowly to the open door. “ Now,” I thought, “ she will call the guard to the miserable prisoner who not only stared shamefacedly at her, but even begged her for cigarettes. What a state of affairs!...” No, nothing of the kind. She put her hand into a box beside her, and, with a wonderfully dignified gesture signing me to approach, threw a handful of papirossi into my cap. I took them mutely and bowed before this strange woman, as a beggar bows—low and humbly. She did not speak a word — only looked at me softly, with unfathomable velvet eyes.

At the shrill sound of a whistle the servant hastened back, the door banged to, and the great Trans-Siberian express sped on. I stood still until the steppe had swallowed it up. In my hands were six cigarettes—lLa Ferme, Petrograd, the
best brand.... A sudden pride shot up in me, and I went white and red in turns. “ What have you done? ” I railed at myself.

Then I smiled. No, I had not bowed down before an enemy. I was not a soldier, an officer, at that moment — I was only a man, a captive, and I had bowed down only to the woman as such — and to beauty. In short, to all that she meant to me....
“Give me one of those cigarettes,” croaked the voice of my guard. |
I started violently. “ No,” I cried hastily, and added: “ Here are others, come...” I put my beggar’s alms carefully into my pocket and gave him four out of my own box.

Our spirits began to droop as it gradually became clearer from the apothecary’s newspapers that the new Government was dependent on the Entente. Sometimes it almost seemed as if the Revolution had been instigated by the Entente solely for its own purposes. Alas! all had turned out differently from what we had wished and believed. It was not the Czarist Government that wanted to continue the war. On the contrary, the Government was tired of it and had been oterthrown for that reason alone. There was no longer talk of a separate peace, since the new régime came into power.

So-called “meetings” of our guards took place daily. A civilian spoke to them on these occasions, and the guards told us afterwards that a peace was no longer to be thought of. Hold out! A new offensive! That was the motto....

At Czernowitz they had actually succeeded in breaking through the German-Austrian front. We were seized by a gnawing fear of a victorious offensive instead of the expected separate peace. Dr. Berger consoled us. “ This is only a prestige offensive,” he said, “the last flicker. In four weeks this retreat will be made up for....”
That was certain. But our Roped: our hopes? It was well that
I had been so recently in the upper camp. I could not have faced either Pod or Schnarrenberg now.
I slept very little those nights, in spite of the fact that I now had a bedstead with two stuffed sacks, which I could spread almost like a real mattress over the entire length of the boards.

Night after night it was the same. The moon shone in through the window and made the haggard faces around me look ever more angular than they were. Even Seydlitz had been uneasily rolling from side to side the last few nights. The “ Warrior ” with the child-mouth prattled in his sleep. Lieutenant Windt snored in spasms like an excited bull. All slept restlessly because all brains were feverish.

“Now the cannons are rolling at the front,” I thought im torment, “ and hundreds of thousands are making attacks, and thousands are dying at this very moment. For what? For their belief? For what belief? That wrong has been done us, that we were not barbarians, that we must defend and sacrifice ourselves! The foe is at all the frontiers, the earth is enveloped in lies in order to submerge us. I, however...”

I started up. A train was just running again through the station. Not a Trans-Siberian express in whose berths beautiful women were sleeping — there is fire within me when I think of my last experience — but a troop train, or one of those large American trains, which for a short time past had almost uninterruptedly been racing through from the east, from Vladivostok over Manchuria towards the west. Their cars were three times as large as the Russian ones and were travelling at high speed to the front, loaded with cannons, ammunition, arms, gas....

It was not the bad reports which kept us from sleeping now, it was chiefly those trains which rumbled into our dreams, and which we had to see at every hour of the day. I was surely not the only one to lie awake, to hear the constant, monotonous
rumbling that began again in the east almost before the last sound had died away in the west....

“They ought to be told,” I thought in my half-sleep, “ they ought to be told. Our country ought to be told and make an end of it. You under-estimated the strength of America. She cannot be vanquished. Look at these transports by day and night, by night and day! You are no longer able to withstand it, it is in vain, it is madness!

To continue making entries in my diary became increasingly difficult. At times my head seemed emptied of all thought and of the power to distinguish the association of ideas and events. Of certain events I could not write at all; to describe others the right words failed me. When I read through my diary, I see that the entries became gradually briefer and more concise. My writing takes on the semblance of the words uttered by a ‘man who is becoming increasingly embittered and weaker — a man who in a short time will be too weary for speech. Indeed, the utterance of a man who not only says with difficulty and. briefly what he has to say, but who has lost all pleasure in words for their own sake and in the art of conversation.

Nor was that all. My writing daily became more crabbed and illegible. I no longer had the energy to write fifty lines in succession. Moreover, by the time I had written the third line, I could no longer read the first. It was as though I were constructing a mosaic to which I could only add a tiny piece each day, and on which for four weeks at a stretch I was incapable of working. If the tiny pieces formed themselves into pictures — well and good. If not, I was incapable of altering them. I was too exhausted and hopeless. The cruel disappointment that had come to blight our hopes of peace had struck one and all of us as an ax bites into the trunk of a tree. Although the tree continues to remain green for a time, it has been mortally injured.

Is it not possible, however, that the growing infrequence and increasing brevity of the entries in my diary witness more clearly than detailed entries could have done to the extent of our degradation and depression? Is not silence at times more eloquent than speech?

Frequently we used to say among ourselves: “ If an ordinary human being were placed among us for eight days, he would certainly think he was in an asylum!” If our life did not utterly destroy us, it was only because we were already completely blunted by all that had gone before. We no longer lived in the true sense of the word; we only waited.... We could best of all have been compared with the hibernant animals. Like them we were only conscious of one thing: the expectation of spring! For us spring meant —the return home.

In truth, our condition was such as to baffle description to one who had himself never experienced our lot. We became more restless and irritable with the passing of each day. The majority of us walked hourly in the barrack-yard — crossing it again and again, now lengthwise, now around the sides, forming circles, triangles, ellipses — in short, making a hundred different figures with the sole object of being tired out by evening in order to win the much-hoped-for sleep. Others sat about all day long in silence. A chance remark sufficed to arouse their fury; the paltriest occurrence to earn their frantic enmity. Former friends no longer recognized each other. Sharp-tongued criticism was rampant. No matter whether one laughed or cried, slept or awoke, whatever one did was always wrong, and.no one _ was any longer capable of putting things to rights. Every moraing a couple of officers wearing their decorations went from. one house to another — all these affairs of honour were eventually to be fought out at home with deadly weapons. If that had really taken place, not a single one of us would have been left alive; for each had been challenged at least once to a duel with pistols or heavy sabres.

Days of furious irritability were succeeded by days of deathly apathy. Hopes for the future, longings for wives, children, sweethearts, the call of one’s profession or work, and homesickness at times disappeared wholly and ceased to trouble us as much as the buzzing of a fly. Here and there among us a life sank into the depths, a spirit broke beneath the strain, destroyed —

by anger and the conflict with fate, eaten up with doubts about life and a gnawing fury —sank down beyond the help of all medical skill. Before one had time to be conscious of its approach, madness came to destroy in silence or in laughing, foaming frenzy all that was human in a man.

The Turkish majors invited us to visit them yesterday. Threequarters Germanophil, one-quarter Francophil, they are decent, rather naive men. They take their brotherhood-in-arms very seriously and ceremoniously, and they dispense hospitality in a generous and Oriental fashion. Owing to their relationship to the Mohammedan Russian Tartars, many things are open to them that are closed to us. Their religion is most certainly a permanent bond between them. Saltin informed us at the door that, in accordance with their customs, we must keep our caps on as a sign of special honour. The Turkish officers laid their hands on their hearts, mouths, and foreheads before leading us into their room. The table was laid with a strange dinner of stuffed fruits, pasties, and uncommon sweets. Afterwards we smoked cigarettes and drank Turkish coffee in which the grounds still remained. The conversation presently changed from the subject of eating and drinking to that of the war. The offensive had been brought to a standstill. Confidence reigned once more. “ In a month Russia will be finished ” —such was the spirit of the evening. I ventured to suggest that the Kerenski Government, as the creature of the Entente, would never dare to conclude a separate peace. “ And don’t forget America,” I said. “‘ Have we not heard for months past the unceasing rumble _ of their transport trains? I consider that the entry of America into the war is a factor of the utmost gravity....”
“Since when did you belong to the manufacturers of rumours? ” Lieutenant Merkel, who, as representative of the fit members of our room, had also been invited by the Turks, at once inquired.
“TI fail to understand you. When our youths are already hanging their heads...”

** I was a volunteer, Lieutenant! ” was the answer I wished to return. But I made no reply. My God! It was now the same in every conversation. If anyone made a sensible observation or gave utterance to a sober thought, he was at once classed by men of this sort as a manufacturer of rumours, a moper, a defeatist.... | q?

Captain Mustapha loudly clapped his hands. A real Bedouin from the desert, Mahut by name, who was his servant, brought the little camp newspaper, compiled by Austrian officers, hectographed, and purchasable at a subscription rate of a few copecks. The main portion was taken up with news from the front and extracts from newspapers, while the remainder was filled with the orders of the senior officers. Mustapha read it aloud word for word slowly in order to practise himself in German —a language already known to Captain Salem. At the end came a brief report of a speech delivered amidst much applause in Petrograd by a certain Lenin.
“Lenin, Lenin?” Salem exclaimed questioningly. “Have you ever heard the name, Ensign? ”
At this moment Captain Rogelli entered the room bearing a lute beneath his arm. “ At your service, boys! ” he exclaimed, as we all greeted him heartily.

“Stop! Enough of the communiqué. V’ll sing you something.” Mahut brought schnapps, and we seated ourselves. Ah! nobody in the whole of Siberia could sing more beautiful songs than this Roselli, with his dark-haired artist’s head....

Every Saturday we held a great bug-hunt in our room. Everything was minutely searched and dusted over with insectpowder. The wooden laths of our beds were soaked in petrol, set on fire, and left to burn until the surface was blackened,

when water was poured over them. Up to the present that had proved the most successful of all methods, and if the fissures were then filled with liquid stearin, one had peace for practically a week. Apart from thfis general method of treatment, each of us had his own special way of dealing with the common enemy; methods that in addition to the destruction of the tormentors served also'as a means of satisfying our stored-up hatred. “ As you treat me, so will I'treat you,” said Windt, as he pricked the leaping bugs with one of his needles until — their bodies perforated with holes — they died an excruciating death. The Turk always kept ready a small glass dish filled with water, in the belief that in this manner they died most painfully of all. Sometimes it took two days — so he declared, as the result of experiments. The “ Playful Warrior,” on the other hand, set light to each bug separately. “It is so nice,” he said, as a smile spread over his childish lips, “to see them slowly swell in the heat. And it sounds so pleasant when they explode....”

Saltin was right. After a few weeks this life disgusted one no less than the former. Habit kills everything. Yet what else had we here? Only perhaps that we had no lice. It was no quieter in our room than in the soldiers’ barracks. If indeed we had been two or three in a room, perhaps staff officers.... But twenty? And, in addition, to be one of the lowest in rank? A walk availed little to ease this state of things. For one was forced to salute and salute and salute, until one’s arm dropped helplessly to one’s side; and one left the barrack-yard through sheer inability to salute any longer. At every turn one encountered superior officers — several thousand superior officers —one almost walked upon them and knocked up against them. Worst of all was the fact that many of them were so embittered and so devitalized that no other interest in life remained to them except to watch that they were saluted by their inferiors in rank in strict accordance with the regulations. “I am a soldier through and through,” Seydlitz once remarked, “ but this is sheer folly. Is not walking thereby rendered a thing of horror for everyone? Yet nobody has the energy to abolish it....” Certainly our sense of discipline was often severely tried. A few had indeed already ceased to salute. When questioned, they became sullen. In higher officer circles they were already counted among the revolutionaries — among Kerenski’s “ Reds” — and it so happened that among them I had a friend.

Our room received a box of newspapers and books from a Frau von Hannecken in Tientsin, and these were carefully distributed among us by Dr. Berger. I was given a couple of old newspapers, and a thick book that had been published about twenty years previously. In the newspapers I found a couple of pictures that I tore out and stuck upon the wall above my bed. One was the reproduction of a painting, “ Youthful Dreams,” in which a naked youth is depicted leaning against the foot of a gigantic wall of rock. Sky and water mingle before his gaze into an inseparable whole. A puny particle against the towering mass of rock, his eyes gazing far out into the unknown, he thinks and dreams. The second picture was a photograph of Rodin’s statue “The Kiss.” When he caught sight of the nude figures, Windt gave voice to an obscene joke. The “ Playful Warrior,” often spent long minutes standing before the picture; his childish mouth became still softer, and his lips opened ever so slightly. The third and last picture was of a horse, “ Holsteinerin,” a five-year-old Holstein brood mare out of Ceres No. 228 by Holderness III, and each time I gazed upon it I thought of my own mare Zelle, an old remount from the Z group. Beneath these pictures I sat and read. What a sensation it was to have a book in one’s hand again after two years! If only it had been some other book! It was a book of
Mantegazza’s entitled The Psychology of Pleasure. Was not that irony?

In one corner of the barackward stood a pair of home-made © parallel bars. Seydlitz and I very often did exercises together on these bars. “‘ Otherwise we should become completely rusty,” he used to say, “ and it is to be hoped that we shall not end our lives here.”

Undoubtedly one had to think of one’s body, one had to do physical jerks, but it was not wise to overdo it. Since the Revolution our-food had noticeably deteriorated in quality and quan+ tity. The rouble fell in value; the price of food rose. As we were forced to feed ourselves, and had organized ourselves for this purpose into messes of twenty men apiece, we immediately became conscious of each rise in prices. If it went further at the present rate of going... The Russians gave us each fifty roubles a month for everything. This sum had certainly sufficed in the previous year to purchase the chief necessities of life. But gradually... What did it matter to the Russian Government if ultimately one could only purchase a box of matches with the fifty roubles? Fifty roubles was the amount laid down in international agreement for captive officers — that’s enough! ““Buy combs, children,” said Lieutenant Oehler, a broadshouldered East Prussian, who was in charge of our kitchen, “ for lousy days are ahead.”

Summer had come. But the Siberian summer is as terrible as the Siberian winter. The green of the steppes had long since been burned brown, and yesterday our medical officers found the temperature in the hospital to be 48 degrees. Everyone lay exhausted on bags of shavings, the majority clothed only in a linen handkerchief. If one moved, the perspiration poured down one’s body; while, to cap it all, we were weak and undernourished. “A difference of a hundred degrees —the Devil himself could not hold out against that!” growled Windt, who for weeks past had gone about entirely naked. When questioned, he made an obscene reply.
‘Leave him alone! ” said Hansen, Lacke, and Farben. “ His is the liberty of a fool.”

For obvious reasons we could only drink water that had been boiled. When, however, water itself is costly and wood for the fire still more costly ——-? A great many began to drink schnapps in large quantities. What could one say? If it did not avail to quench thirst or to moderate the heat, at least it sent the brain to sleep for a while; also the thoughts — those damned thoughts of home — that were often far worse to bear than thirst. For several months I still possessed the moral courage to despise the “ red-noses” to be seen in our camp. Today I can understand any man who drank in Siberia. I think that if I had had more money, I should also have been found among their number.

One day, as I went to the lafka, a sort of canteen that stood on the boundary between the upper and lower camps, and in which many things could be purchased at outrageous prices, I caught sight of little Blank in the distance. He stood on the far side of the wire fence and gazed with wide-open eyes into the window, behind which were bread and sugar, tea and flour. When spoken to, he paid no attention. Not that he wished to buy anything, not that it was physical hunger that had turned him to stone, but the spiritual longing to handle these things once more. The past and the future had become blended together within him. I watched him for a long time without his © being conscious of it. Had he not once cried out in delirium in Totzkoje: “ Another pound of coffee for theolady, Frank. Certainly, madam — Guatemala, special quality? ”
The thought crossed my mind that each of us was possessed by a different kind of longing. Blank’s was small and paltry

and exceedingly modest — just to be once more behind a counter was all he desired — yet no matter of what sort our desires, whether great or small, all were alike in the way in which they ravaged and consumed us. At times little Blank coughed, and each time he did so, he passed his hand across his pale lips and stole a glance at his fingers. The idea crossed my mind that Blank would never again weigh out flour and sugar.

For several days Turkish troop trains kept arriving at our camp. From one wagon six still living men were dragged forth from a heap of thirty corpses. Twelve were carried out of another, while many wagons contained only corpses. Ague.

“ That’s nothing new,” said Dr. Berger. “In 1914 two hundred Turkish cholera cases were dispatched to a destination in closed wagons. After three weeks they reached Pensa, and only sixty men remained alive.”

Miiller confirmed his story: “ When in 715 I lay on the station platform in Samara, two wagons arrived with their doors and windows boarded up. Everyone thought they contained food-supplies and left them standing about without troubling to investigate. When at last they were opened, they were found to contain sixty-eight Turks, of whom only eight were still alive. The wagons were run on to a siding outside the town. The frozen bodies were hacked loose with spades and thrown into a hole filled with lime.”

A Slovakian Captain, who was what the Austrians call a genuine Woijak, notwithstanding the shortage of space, had been successful up to this in remaining the only man in the whole camp with a room to himself alone. So impossible was he that not a single man would voluntarily share a room with him. “The world belongs to the shameless,” might with truth have been said of him. As a punishment for some complaint that had been made of him, a youthful Ensign was ordered to share his room. In some way or other one must listen to complaints. And if those “ above” have not the energy, then those “below ” have to snatch the chestnuts out of the fire.

Saltin learnt of this punishment. “ Just think of it, Ensign,” he said. “ The poor devil knocked upon the door. ‘ Come in. What do you want? ’ asked Captain Kosim. ‘I have to report that’ I have been ordered by the camp-commandant to share your room, sir.’ ‘ Indeed,’ said Kosim. ‘ Indeed? First of all, then, open the door wide.’ As the Ensign did so, Kosim rose up and struck him such a blow that he went head over heels out of the room.”
“ Once in a way this fellow should be given a sound thrashing,” cried Windt angrily.
“Yes,” answered Windt quietly, “and also everyone who defends such an ‘ officer’! ”

One morning in autumn we saw a small train standing on the rails without an engine. In the front was a second-class carriage, and behind were six or seven cattle-trucks. Glittering in the sunlight beside the door of the compartment stood a large samovar from which the smoke rose in long columns. Close beside it a tiny flag fluttered in the breeze — a red cross on a white ground.
“That is the ‘ Fair Angel,’” said Dr. Berger, as he turned around. “ Put everything in order, boys, and clean yourselves. The ‘Fair Angel’ is coming!” -
“ Who is she, Lieutenant? ” I inquired.
“Have you never heard the name before? ” answered Dr. Berger. “ Through the whole of Siberia she is known by this name. She is the Swedish delegate, Elsa Brandstrom.”
“Oh! ” I said hurriedly, “ I know her.”
About midday she arrived in our midst. We all stood before our beds; the customarily unshaven, shaven; those who usually

went about half naked, properly attired in their uniforms. There was no sign of dirty water; nowhere was a pair of pants to be seen hanging up to dry. Our room was so clean and orderly that it took on an unfriendly and cold atmosphere in our eyes. Accompanied by our Captain, she made the round of the room, speaking a few words with each of us and asking each what he stood in need of. The Russian officers, whose demeanour was greatly altered from what it had formerly been, remained standing by the door. As she shook Seydlitz by the hand, she said suddenly: “ Haven’t we met before? ”
“ Certainly, Sister. In Irkutsk,” he replied, with a gentle laugh. “‘ We exchanged a few kind words.”
“Yes, now I remember. I was worried about you then. Hadn’t you to pay for it? ”
“No, Sister, not I — perhaps the lot of us. A few days later they compelled us on some threadbare excuse to run the gauntlet.”
“So I heard,” she said softly. “ Were you the whole time in Irkutsk? ”
“No,” replied Seydlitz, pointing to me. “ Before that we were six months in Totzkoje.”
“ Totzkoje! ” she exclaimed. “My God!” Involuntarily she shut her eyes, and her face grew white.

“Sister,” said Seydlitz, “in the upper camp there are two hundred from Totzkoje. Could not one manage to do something special for them? I don’t think one of them has recovered from it. They are all still suffering as a result of having been there.” :

As she went from one to the other, each had a different request to make of her. Dr. Berger gave her a thick letter for his wife, whom — as we all knew — he deeply loved. Windt wanted to borrow money — repayable at home, if possible. Merkel asked her how things were going on the French front. “ Well, s 220 PRISONER OF WAR very well,” she answered. “More than that I cannot say.”
Hansen, Lacke, and Farben asked whether the war would not soon be ended. “ Yes,” she replied, laughing, “I think this will be my last trip.”
When she stood before Schulenburg and inquired what requests he had to make of her, that thin, silent man with the typical officer’s profile answered briefly: ‘“‘ Many thanks, Sister, I have none.”

As she moved round, I followed each of her steps with my eyes. How fair she was! Hope and courage returned to us all. We were undoubtedly in safe keeping, and for her there could have been no better title: the Fair Angel.

In Saltin’s room hung a great map of the war-zone — a map of Europe on which tiny flags marked the fronts and positions of the troops. Black and white flags showed the German lines, black and gold the Austrian, red and white the Turks, and green and white the Bulgarians. The whole was the work of Captain Schanks, who spent days in moving the flags about in accordance with the latest communiqués. He was immensely proud of his work and delighted to be regarded as a strategist. Not for an instant did he ever doubt that we should win the war: Was he not in the right? If one stood before his map, there seemed to be no other possibility. How could an army that occupied vast stretches of the enemy’s territory be defeated ?

When an offensive was in progress, the room became a rendezvous of old soldiers weighing and arguing over the chances and wallowing in strategy and tactics. Among them was one who since 1914 had kept a record of all the prisoners reported by the Russians, and who maintained from the knowledge he had thus acquired that the Russian communiqués were filled with lies; thus, for example, he had calculated that the total of the prisoners reported as taken by the Russians exceeded

the entire strength of our army. He was inordinately proud of his discovery and invariably carried the list of prisoners about with him wherever he went. Once I earned for myself the disapproval of Captain Schank by asking him, as he was in the middle of delivering a long lecture to prove that we must unquestionably be the victors in the war, whether he had ever heard of Pyrrhus’ victory.

With the coming of winter another exciting rumour flew round the camp. Kerenski’s Government had been overthrown. A duumvirate under Lenin and Trotski had seized the reins of power. In contradiction to Kerenski’s Menshevik — that is, minority — party, the new-comers called themselves Bolsheviks —the party of the majority. Eight days later the rumour proved to have been well founded. Kerenski and his Cabinet had taken to flight. At the front the soldiers were fraternizing with one another, while the new Government was suing for peace. Their motto was: “Bread, Peace, Freedom.” Everyone in our room went mad, and in the barrack-yard men embraced who had hitherto never exchanged a word. The guards threw away their rifles and went singing out of the camp arm-in-arm with our soldiers. It was said that some of the officers had already packed their kits. Although I was no church-goer, | should have liked to go that day to church.
Three days later I visited my men. In the men’s barracks several had already packed up their belongings.
“Well, men, what have you got to say to this? ”
Briinn asked: “In that case we shall be able to depart in a few weeks? ” New life had entered into him and no trace was left of his violent hate for his fellow-men.
“Certainly,” declared Pod, “immediately after the conclusion of peace. That is the custom by international law.”
“True,” I replied. “ But first of all peace must be signed.”
“What! ” cried Schnarrenberg. “ What can these Panjes do? They'll have to sign whatever is dictated to them — that is all.”

I inquired about Elsa Brandstrém. “ That’s a woman,” said Pod. “ They say that she has already saved hundreds of thousands of lives. We’ve got boots — proper leather boots, underclothes, soap, books, blankets, and Chinese coats. Here, have a look.” He pulled off from his plank bed a thickly padded grey coat — far too long for him — that could serve equally well as under blanket or winter overcoat. “ At last we can once more go out in winter into the fresh air.”

“Tf only no one stole! ” interrupted the girlish Blank. He coughed frequently, and beneath his eyes were blue-black rings. “ That will certainly begin again. With us it is still all right, but with the others, where even clothes are stolen...”
“* Yes,” murmured Briinn, “ if one were not grown up, they’d steal one’s rump to make German beefsteaks! ”
“What is still more,” said the Tadpole, “we men from Totzkoje have all received three roubles. Perhaps, Ensign, you have a notion who was responsible for that? ”
“What —the aristocrat?” exclaimed Briinn. “Are there also white ravens? ”

“ Have you noticed our café beside the door? ” interrupted Pod. “Gradually we'll get everything —a ninepins alley, a beer-shop, even a theatre will be built. A tailor has set up in our district for whom the Fair Angel fitted up his shop, and yesterday he festively opened his business with the aid of a bottle of schnapps. A cobbler will be the next to come. We have already three barbers. Yet what’s the use of it all as long as we have no money? ”
“Let’s go and have a look at the pub and drink a beer, Pod? ” I asked suddenly.

The “ pub ” was an unused plank bed that had been converted into a table. Round about stood roughly hewn benches, while in the corner on a small stove stood an old kettle from which came an appetizing odour. A tubby sergeant, formerly a cook’s boy, came forward in a white-grey apron.
* What can one have, mine host? ”
“Splendid! Hopphopphopp? ” cried Pod, as his face brightened. “ And even a bow-wow, eh? ”

“Shut your ears, Pod,” I said, taking the innkeeper on one side and whispering in his ear. “ Give this man a portion of goulash every second evening, do you understand? I'll pay for a month in advance. How much is it? ”
“What are you doing, youngster? ” asked Pod suspiciously.
“Nothing, nothing. I am only composing our menu. Tell me — has the post not yet arrived? ”
**No, devil take it. And I am sure that Anna has written....”

We chatteréd until twilight fell. “There is no longer any boundary between the camps, Pod,” I said in conclusion. “ For the Bolsheviks everything and everyone is equal. If you should happen to want anything from me...?” |
“Man alive! What should I do down there? ” he replied anxiously. “In these clothes? If a button is missing from my uniform, I must pay for it with an hour’s drill. No, you come along up here! ”
Our commandant, Vereniki, refused to recognize the new Government. Together with the officers and some of the troopers of our former convoy, he resolved to offer armed resistance..

From early dawn one day we heard the rumble of cannon. Everyone stood at the windows and gazed in anxiety toward the west. Windt, who had just come in, reported: “ He has taken up his position with his troops behind the cemetery hill.”

The first train load of Bolsheviks arrived at ten o’clock, only to be followed quickly by a second and third — all throwing menacing clouds of thick smoke behind them. While the cattletrucks were filled with troops, the muzzles of cannon peered out from the uncovered wagons. Almost simultaneously with the arrival of the train, three hundred cavalry trotted on the right and left of the railway lines into the village. They were mounted on tall, lively horses, armed to the teeth, and red stars blazed from out their high woollen caps. The place was soon alive with soldiers, who sprang from the wagons and, directed by a couple of cavalrymen, ran quickly across the rails to the camp carrying spades and axes, with which, with resounding blows, they levelled the fence in front of the centre barracks and then formed themselves into a thin line in its place.
“It looks as if they want to dig their trenches right in front of our windows,” remarked Dr. Berger.
“ Ah well, that’ll be lively, damn it!” said the airman, Proschow.

I went into the village with Seydlitz. Guns were being unloaded and limbered up. Teams of four horses were then attached to the limbers, and the guns galloped off amidst much noise towards the east. There was no trace of any real authority, and they seemed more like a band of freebooters than a body of troops. Nearly everyone yelled and cursed and quarrelled. Their leaders — young men with clever faces — addressed them in friendly fashion, although at the same time they gazed far beyond them as if they saw a goal ahead in the far distance with which all this had nothing whatever to do.

For a time we remained standing, while Seydlitz watched the passing troops with cold and contemptuous eyes. Some of them were drunk; their fur caps were stuck on the backs of their heads and suddenly, to the accompaniment of a loud singsong, they began to dance madly. “ A band of robbers! ” said Seydlitz at last. “ A squadron under Holcking would drive them into the Baikal.”

Three middle-aged officers stood in front of our barracks. They appeared to be former non-commissioned officers of artillery and acted as if there were no prisoners of war present, argued at length, and finally, although still only half agreed among themselves, gave orders to a battery to take up its position. The guns dashed noisily past the houses and turned and twisted in the barracks-squares. The long gun-carriages were concealed behind the protection and shadow of the red walls, the guns cleared for action.
That afternoon our Captain, accompanied by Colonel von Strann, the senior of the Austrian officers, walked through the camp. Beside them walked two Bolshevik officers.
“Halt, Ensign!” he called to me from a distance.
“‘ The interpreter is ill. I understand you know Russian. The new commandant wants to give us his orders. Here is some paper. Please write down whatever he says.”

“You understand Russian? ” asked the commandant, a young stripling with a clever but wild face. “Good. Write as follows: ‘Whoever supports the White troops will be shot.’ Have you got that? ‘ Whoever gives information to the White troops will be shot.’ Have you got that? “Whoever among the prisoners of war will enter our ranks at once becomes a free Russian citizen and will be given pay and arms’—have you also got that? —‘like our soldiers. Commandant Pastuchow.’ Finished? ”

At this moment a couple of cavalrymen came in with their first prisoner—a young officer of Vereniki’s who had been caught on reconnaissance. He was brought before the commandant, and the two men eyed each other. For several seconds a stream of hatred passed from one pair of eyes to the other as the current passes between two poles overcharged with electricity.
“If you will tell us all, you will only be shot,” I heard the commandant say. “If not —tortured until you speak! ”
“What do you want to know? ” asked the officer, a young Cossack Ensign. The yellow stripes on his trousers seemed like flames, so bright were they.
“Who is your commander? ” asked the commandant.
“God! ” replied the Ensign in a voice filled with reverence.

“Are you scoffing at me, dog? ” foamed the commandant, raising his hand, between the fingers of which the butt of a heavy pistol peeped forth, and striking the Ensign between the eyes in a fit of terrible fury. We crept away.
“ And those are brothers? ” murmured Seydlitz. “The sons of one race?...” |
Two new words were firmly fixed in our minds —two new ideas: White and Red. For the first time we experienced a foretaste of the terror that was about to burst forth over Russia.

Another day I met Schnarrenberg once more filled with optimism. He said the Russian swine were done for; that now it was the turn of the French poilus; and that we should yet march in triumph through the Brandenburger Tor. As we conversed, it happened that we were standing by the mortuary; a pure chance-—and yet...A certain undertone in his voice aroused my anger, and I said: “I have also met Holcking.”
“ Count Holcking — to whom the Russian General returned his sword? Damnation! That was a deed! And still people say that war lacks nobility. War — ”
“Yes,” I interrupted, “ just behind the front another officer

took away his sword again and with it hit the almost dying man several blows across the head.” Schnarrenberg bit his lips, and his stern face worked convulsively. “ If I were you, Schnarrenberg,” I said coldly, “I shouldn’t tell that story quite so frequently. There was nothing noble about it. It was only a farce, a fine gesture, nothing more....”

For a while we were well treated by our new rulers. Sentries disappeared, and officers and men were no longer separated from each other. In the eyes of the Bolsheviks, all were equal — so it was said throughout the camp. We could go wherever we liked, with the solitary exception of the railway station, but that sufficed to render us prisoners as before. To take to flight across the steppes would have been sheer madness. Before the first night had passed away, one would have been frozen to death or devoured by wolves. Ah! these Bolsheviks were cleverer than their Czarist or Kerenskian predecessors. For they achieved the same result by their orders, only at a lesser cost to themselves. Not, indeed, that we regarded them with enmity. All that we had heard of them — their intellectual views, Oriental ideology, boundless brutality — made them appear strange and incomprehensible to our eyes; yet they had given us more liberty and so caused us to regard them with tolerance.

The hill on which the camp stood rose up solitary in the midst of the plain. We walked in all directions across the steppe, or down into the village. It was a joy to walk across the steppe — to walk with light, free paces across a plain over which eyes that had for years past been hemmed in by high fences could once more gaze into far distances. The village was an even greater joy. Our starved gaze surfeited itself on the exiles who had settled there, on the Chinese coolies with their slit-eyes, and on the Burjaten nomads and Manchurian teacaravans with their pompous camels.
At the entrance to the village stood the inn. After the

November Revolution it was always full. A small and dirty Chinese boy served as waiter. Tea and fish and meat were to be had, and we frequently ate baranina — mutton roasted on a spit. For weeks past our mess had no longer been able to serve us with meat. On my first visit to the inn I gobbled up half a leg of mutton, and, as I ate, I thought: “I must come here once with Pod! ”

At the farthest end of the village, in the poor Chinese quarter, an opium den was to be found. Now and again one of us was to be seen vanishing through its dark entrance. I was told that Lieutenant Thurn recently spent a whole day there, and that he returned with dull and vacant eyes, but for two days his face bore the impress of an indescribable beauty. “‘ A _ new and even greater danger for us,” said Dr. Berger, “than the old dangers.”

Women were also to be found in the homesteads higher up. “They’re only peasant girls,” said Windt shortly, “ but they know what copulation means.” On his small and bald head, which could be descried from afar, and which was filled with impudent thoughts, were several suspicious scratches.
“‘They’ve already sent a Russian to Tschita,” said Merkel, as though he were relating a matter of daily occurrence, “ for the purpose of bringing back something worth while.”
“Do you know, Ensign,” said Dr. Berger in an aside, “ that Asiatic syphilis is the most terrible of all venereal diseases? ”
“It is said to be specially common in Transbaikalia,” he added lightly. |
I looked at him. He was once more plunged in his book. He looked as though he had not opened his lips. I understood.
A number of officers with artistic leanings, influenced and aided by our newly won freedom, turned a barrack unsuited for living purposes into a theatre. As the result of an appeal, it be-

came evident that we possessed among us the necessary artists — singers, stage managers, actors, and scene-painters. For a month everyone worked with feverish energy. Costumes were prepared from old uniforms, unused sheets, and sandbags and painted and decorated with colours obtained from multi-coloured papers. Newspapers fastened one above another and painted with paint made out of all possible substances furnished the scenery. The female roles were assigned to young lieutenants and ensigns of an especially girlish and seductive appearance. The opening night was a very special occasion. Our officers’ orchestra — whose instruments came for the most part from the “Fair Angel” and a charming German sister, Fraulein von Walsleben— conducted by a Viennese conductor — little Lieutenant Hollisch — performed an operetta. The actors were overwhelmed with unending applause, while the principal “ girl ” — ravishing in his woman’s clothes — became the centre of a furious fight.
‘“‘ She has received so many offers,” said Windt, “that she has been forced to ask for military protection.”
Greatly encouraged by this success, our actor-manager proposed to stage a well-known operetta. Lieutenant Blau, who was a genius in a small way, was ready to write down the score from memory.

_As we sat at mess on the following evening, a small Austrian Lieutenant unexpectedly appeared in the doorway. At once I noticed his peculiar appearance, as of one who walked in his sleep. He used to stand for hours in one place in the barrackyard as though listening to something. I had often seen him standing thus and had never been able to explain his conduct to myself. Dr. Berger rose and went towards him.
“What do you want, Lieutenant? ” he asked in a friendly way.

“I beg your pardon,” said the stranger, “ but I heard voices here. Is my wife here? I heard her speak to my daughter — most certainly in this room. There! she calls me by name. Don’t you hear anything? ”
Dr. Berger grew pale. “ You are mistaken,” he said wearily. *T hear nothing.”

“There!” cried the Lieutenant. “ There — just now! Keep quiet! Listen! You must put your hands to your ears — thus — do you see? ” Suddenly he laughed. “‘ There! she has just called ‘George,’ don’t you hear? It was quite clear — ‘George.’” His hands dropped from his ears, and he looked inquiringly around the room. “Only I can’t find her, I can’t find her! ” he said helplessly. “ You have good sight, Lieutenant, you cannot deny it. Tell me! Everyone hides her from me — naturally, they are envious; that I can easily understand. Nobody has a wife here except myself. But I won’t be played with any longer — won’t look about any longer.”

Windt came forward. A few, fearing his tactlessness, sought to intervene. He motioned them away. “ Yes,” he said cheerfully, placing his hands to his ears in the same manner as the Austrian Lieutenant, “I hear it also. But it is not here. It must be in the next room among your own fellows.”
“Am I really mistaken? ” asked the little Lieutenant with -a note in his voice that pierced our hearts like a knife.

“No! ” he cried out. “ You only want to send me into the next room again. Oh, I know it! You always play the same game with me. I am always forced to wander about — wander about. But it’s no longer a game.” Once more he suddenly became silent, his head slightly on one side, and his hands held funnel-shape to his ears. After a pause he whispered: “ Or—or did I really deceive myself? Is it perhaps in the next room? ”
“Wait a moment! ” said Windt quickly. “I hear something. Aren’t you called George? ” |

“Yes,” he murmured. “I’m George. Yes, I am.” A laugh spread over his good-natured countenance, and a flicker began _ to show in his eyes that looked through and beyond men and buildings. With his hands held to his ears, he hurried out into -the passage. The door stood open behind him, and we heard him ask the same question in the next room that he had addressed to us on entering ours. Nobody spoke.
“IT have no appetite left,” said Proschow loudly. “ Damnation! ”

“Don’t you know him, Doctor? ” asked Windt quietly. “Have you not heard about him? His name is Kohler, and for months past he does nothing but wander from one room to another. One can only get him out of a room in the same way that I did. It is the only way, even if it is not nice.”

At the beginning of winter our “ university” once more opened its doors. With our camp-stools in our hands, Dr. Berger and I went almost daily to the “ lecture-room,” which was always full — mainly with the younger men — and contained a table and reading-stand. Almost every subject could be studied, and, as the bald-headed Windt remarked, “ only a chemical laboratory was missing.” Since there were representatives of nearly all the faculties among those from the Reserve officers who had been taken prisoners, it was actually possible to learn the same subjects as were at that time being learnt by students at home. The lecturers were mainly university professors and lecturers. Professor Dr. Kowarcsik, for example, lectured on natural history; Professor Dr. Melzer on the history of art and on ancient languages; Professor Dr. Hillberg on modern languages and philosophy; Dr. Bauer on literature; Dr. Dofat on journalism; Dr. Blau on anatomy; Dr. Schmidt on political economy; and Staff-Captain Mohring on tactics and strategy.

In the “ university,” however, there happened what had so often happened before in our camp in other directions. The spirit was indeed willing, but the flesh often proved weak. Too often the words of the lecturer rang in our ears like empty sounds, only occasionally did they clothe themselves in the guise of actual and recognizable ideas. We were too blunted, too tired, too used up to take in what they were intended to convey to our brains. Nevertheless we refused to give in. Each day the contest was resumed anew. If Dr. Berger had not invariably taken me with him, I should much sooner have ceased to attend. Each time he exercised anew a compulsion that could scarcely be felt, while through weakness I was incapable of resisting him.

“Down below, Ensign,” said Lieutenant Merkel, “a frightful fellow, lousy and dirty as a Russian, asked me about you. He’d lost absolutely all idea of how an officer should be addressed. Just take this opportunity to teach him once for all.”

“ Certainly, Lieutenant,” I said aloud. Then I added in an undertone: “ God help me! ” I went outside. Could it be anyone else except Pod? It was Pod. With his long beard and flowing Chinese robe, he looked like a modern Wandering Jew.
“Hello, Pod, old boy,” I called out. “ What’s up? ”
“T’ve got a letter! My first! From Anna! ”

“Splendid! My best plough-horse, Blesse, has foaled twice —each time a filly. That means there’s more to come! At the time she wrote, potatoes were coming up in the rye-fields. Little George is already old enough to drive the cows in from pasture — and is a proper scamp, like his father! But...”
“Yes,” he went on, “there’s nothing to be done — this damned war! They’ve commandeered our best. horse, Ajax, the one we always drove to church with on Sundays. The dragoons have got him.”

I gave a sigh of relief. “ That’s not so bad, Pod,” I said consolingly. “He'll be kept at the base, won’t he? But we must celebrate this letter and also your Anna, mustn’t we? There’s a pub in the village where one gets other things besides horse goulash.”
He shook his head. “ If on our return you don’t come immediately to my farm, my boy,” he said sadly, “to fatten yourself up for half a year on bacon and sausages — ”
We went off together, but after we had taken a couple of steps, he suddenly stood still. “ Junker,” he said timidly, “ Id like to see what sort of quarters you’ve got. Can I? ”

We turned about and went back to my room. Nearly everyone was there. Fifteen pairs of eyes gazed upon us with curiosity. For a time Pod stood with heels well apart. “ Dragoon Podbielski asks leave to enter,” he said in a soldierly tone.
“Yes, yes,” said Dr. Berger. “ Come along in.”
“This is Pod, Doctor,” I said, as I pushed him forward. ** He wants to see for himself how I am housed.”
