Berger laughed. “ By all means. Make yourself at home,” he said. “Here are three cigarettes, Pod. The Ensign has already told me about you.”
We sat for a while on the bed. Pod smoked hard. “ Man,” he finally said, “I had never thought it could be so clean! And the good air.... You've certainly got no lice here, eh? Not a single one? ”
“Is it possible? And pictures, boy? And a table...”

His big doglike eyes remained fixed on my largest picture. “ Desire — of — Youth! ” he spelled out the title slowly letter by letter. “ Yes, boy,” he said softly, “that’s something for you... and for our time.” Suddenly his gaze passed to the second picture. He drew himself up and read: “The Kiss.” For a while he remained silent before he started to speak very softly, and as if to himself: “ You don’t yet know what a woman is, boy.... I know, although I had almost forgotten. Oh! a woman is everything and can be everything. She ruffles your hair — and all is well again. She draws your head to rest between her breasts — and everything is forgotten. She’s soft and warm — all that is not to be found here. Worry is at an end if you have got a true woman — and all despondency. When she lies contented in your arms, life holds nothing more. Nothing more can happen to you — nothing. You know once again who you are, where you are, and where you belong.”

An hour later we went into the village. Baranina was to be had, and Pod devoured a whole leg of mutton. “ Ah, boy,” he suddenly said in his old voice, “this food and that letter — God knows there are good days even in Siberia! ”

I had hardly got back before Lieutenant Merkel — the “ Button” — came up to my bed. “I want to draw your attention to the fact that it is not desired that soldiers should visit your room,” he said softly, but sharply. A sudden fury arose in me at the sight of his empty face and cold fish’s eyes.

“Why not?” he replied stiffly. “Since when has it been customary for a lieutenant to have to give his reasons to an ensign for making a demand of him? Are you quite mad, sir? I refuse to be treated as a civilian! Moreover, it is enough to make anyone angry that you should permit yourself to be on such terms of friendship with common soldiers. It is intolerable, sir! We do not desire to see your friends any more. Nor to hear any more of them! ”
I gazed at him with fury in my eyes. Something boiled up
in me. But I was a soldier — and I knew the futility of argument. “ Damned brute! ” I thought quietly. He went off to bed.

Scarcely had he reached his own bed again before Dr. Berger came over to me. “ Don’t let this give you any grey hairs, Ensign,” he said laughingly. “ And let your friends come as often as they want to. Lieutenant Merkel doesn’t speak for all of us. He speaks only in pluralis majestatis! ”
“Yes, Lieutenant,” I said — and a lump rose in my throat. “No,” I thought to myself, “he doesn’t speak for everybody. Are there not many who think like Berger? ”

“Tf one’s going mad,” said little Windt in a loud voice directed towards Merkel’s corner, “it begins in the head — especially when there’s not much in it! ” It seemed as though he wanted to emphasize my very thoughts. No sooner had he finished speaking than Lieutenant Schulenburg — a thin, silent regular officer —raised his voice. “Lieutenant Merkel,” he said bitingly, “I am the senior regular officer here, and I am glad that the Ensign, in the special circumstances now prevailing, maintains so splendid a relationship with the men from his regiment. In future, follow his example! I particularly desire it.”

As I lay down in bed, I saw a fat louse crawling across my blanket. I captured him and, in order that nobody should hear it, I pressed the breath out of him beneath my bed-clothes. ** Ah! ” thought I, “ Pod left behind a small remembrance of himself.”

In November the Bolshevik Government appealed to the Central Empires for an armistice. An armistice is the first step towards the conclusion of peace, is it not? Or was this announcement in the newspapers only fabricated by the new Government for the purpose of currying favour with the war-sick Russian nation? When three weeks later a telegram. reached the commandant with the news that the armistice had been signed, we could not but believe it. It is difficult not to believe that which one has desired ardently for many years. Dr. Berger delivered a short speech that evening in which he exhorted us as follows: “‘ Now let’s hold out. Let’s never forget that we are here in the service of the Fatherland. And let’s bear our cruel fate bravely and honourably and silently to the end out of love for our Fatherland and our nation.” As his voice ceased, a couple of officers began to sing Deutschland, Deutschland iiber alles. Seydlitz joined in and sang with all his might and main. Morning had dawned before we separated. Everyone believed that it could only be a matter of weeks. A Te Deum was arranged for the following day. I went.

Windt said: “ War and deceit are alike. One must never let oneself be caught out in a deception, and one must never lose a war. When all goes well, everything is well and well done. When things go wrong, then everybody starts to talk until the crash comes.” _ The Emperor’s birthday was due to come round in a few days’ time. It was resolved to celebrate it this year with quite exceptional solemnity. Captain Mittelberg came to discuss the program with the senior officers in our room. The officers’ choir was to sing, the officers’ orchestra to play. Dr. Berger was detailed to preach the sermon, read the service, and give the absolution. Our Captain was to propose the Emperor’s health. “ Well, gentlemen,” he said finally. “ We must now levy another small tax in order to be able to give our guests a more or less suitable dinner.”
“ And tomorrow there will be kascha!” murmured Windt.
“* What did you say, Lieutenant Windt? ”
The tiny incident served to recall what had occurred at a meeting held by the Austrian officers to make preparations for celebrating the birthday of the Emperor Karl. Among them

were many who were plastered with decorations, although they had never once heard the whistling of a bullet, and when the Colonel reminded the assembled officers that as a matter of course all decorations must be worn, a Captain called out sharply: “ Naturally. But in that case I beg to propose that all decorations acquired behind the lines should be worn on the back of the recipient! ”

The banquet began. Our beds were piled up in the passage, and ensigns were detailed to act as sentries. The tables of the German officers were placed together to form one long table. Our Captain was seated at the head of the table and was far too conscious of his own importance. On his right and left were seated the officers of the allied armies — Austrian and Hungarian colonels and Turkish majors. The menu consisted of a vegetable soup, beef served with dumplings, and bilberry tarts. “For this,” said Windt gruffly, as he ate enough for three, “we shall have to take in our trouser-buckles for a month to come, like a woman without corsets! ” Schnapps followed in rivers. An East Prussian, Proschow, who had Russian blood in his veins, had succeeded after many experiments in concocting an “ Emperor’s liqueur ” that was not at all bad.

When on the. evening before the banquet Seydlitz came past his “ distillery,” he said contemptuously: “Schnapps here, my friends! We want once in a way to be patriotic! ” Cheeks gradually grew redder and eyes became glazed as glass followed glass of this powerful vodka. As ten o’clock struck, silence fell upon the noisy company. Our Captain rose and cast a piercing glance at Proschow, who continued to yell without taking any notice of him.

“Gentlemen! ” said Mittelberg, as though he commanded a battalion, “although we stand today in a strange land twelve thousand kilometres distant from our own and from the places in which is being celebrated the greatest of our national commemorations, nevertheless our hearts are no less filled than are hearts at home with the same emotion: loyalty to our country and our Emperor — loyalty unto death! ” He weht on to add that, although we no longer fought with weapons, yet our sacrifices were no less worthy of admiration than those of our comrades at the front; and in his peroration he spoke of speedy victory and a triumphal return - home beneath the eyes of the Emperor. “ And now, gentlemen,” he ended, “rise, lift your glasses, and join with me as one man in the toast: Our supreme war-lord, His Majesty —”

At this very moment the door was timidly thrown open, and on the threshold stood — Lieutenant Kohler! “ Ah! ” he said nervously, in the midst of a deathly silence. “ Pardon me, gentlemen! You are holding a celebration? I only want to ask: Is my wife here? And my little daughter? I distinctly heard their voices.”

The best hated of all were men of the “Button” type who, on the occasion of each victory, opened their mouths to give vent to tactless remarks about “a damned good licking.” The majority of us had suffered too much to be able to comprehend this sort of warlike enthusiasm. A nation must certainly be valiant and capable of defending itself; we should be ready to do our duty once again and would not forget it even here. One thing, however, had become too deeply impressed upon us for us ever to forget it: that war is something far too terrible to be talked about in a boasting and light-hearted manner. For us it seemed only natural that every civilized man should regard it as his first duty to do everything in his power to prevent war. When one of these “ Buttons” once spoke to Dr. Berger in this boastful way, the Doctor replied: “I believe we are living in the twentieth century, Captain? Besides, I am a lawyer — a servant of Right and not of Might! ”

When it was barely light, we were awakened one morning by a wild thundering of hoofs. We dashed to the windows to behold patrols riding in from every side. The broad trench before our door in a few minutes resembled a seething nest of scorpions.

Half an hour later the first line of infantry appeared in very open formation, only to be followed at brief intervals by a second, third, fourth, fifth.... The Red sentries seemed to have lost confidence; their boastfulness disappeared like snow before the south wind. Their officers gazed through their field-
.glasses with anxious expressions and close-shut lips.

“The seventh, eighth, now the ninth — devil take it!” I overheard a couple of Red sentries cursing. A window broke with a sharp crack. The first shell from the field-batteries came ‘whining between the barracks, to burst in a high geyser of flame in the sand directly in front of the first line of trenches, * Open fire! ” called a non-commissioned officer, as he ran down to the battery. Volley after volley rang out; the spaces between the houses resembled mouths belching forth flames, heat, and brimstone. The barracks trembled ceaselessly, the floors of the rooms swayed, furniture and bedsteads creaked and shook, and the smoke of the artillery bombardment swirled acridly in through the broken window. The champion mare “ Holsteinerin ” fell from the wall and broke a leg.

The mass of attacking troops in the distance came nearer and — ably officered — dashed through the fire zone. They continued to advance in a series of dashes, which tended to become shorter and shorter; and they opened up a cool and well-directed covering fire. One after another the bullets came flying through our window. For a while we lay flat upon the floor, then soon afterwards sprang up once more to keep a look-out. The stone breastworks of the trenches in which the defenders stood proved far more dangerous to them than did lying out upon the open steppe to the attackers. Nearly every bullet ripped knife-like splinters from the blocks of stone and sent them showering into the air like swirls of shrapnel, and so each found two and three targets instead of one. Every man that fell looked as though he had been slashed with knives..

Directly beneath our window an officer stood beside a machine-gun which blazed unceasingly, jumped backwards and forwards and sideways, and barked like a mad dog. After a time the gunner sank down over his gun, which then ceased to fire. At the same instant the commandant seized him and threw him with inconceivable strength upon the parapet to act as a sand-bag to stop bullets. He shrieked for a while. All the corpSes were thrown up to form a parapet to shelter the firing line. Presently the storm of projectiles died away. Only here and there did a heavy body quiver. Heads and arms that had been torn away by shells lay scattered around.
“‘ Why are they still lying there, the attackers? ” whispered Seydlitz. “‘ Two big dashes would land them in the trenches.”
It certainly seemed as though the attacking swarms were unwilling to leave their covering to make an attack. Or were they perhaps waiting for the arrival of a prearranged moment?

At this instant a fiendish Cossack “Hurrah” burst forth from behind the barracks, to the accompaniment of the clatter of innumerable horses’ hoofs. I noticed that the commandant sprang backwards and gazed towards the rear with fury in his eyes. Half a dozen of us dashed into the passage in order to be able to take a look in the direction from which the hurrahs were coming.

“Good heavens! What a picture! ” cried Olfert. Two, three, four regiments of Cossacks galloped out of the village, standing in their stirrups, led by a surprising number of officers, and swept with phantom-like swiftness over the intervening space, to pour like a brown flood between the barracks. Two

teams were able to turn their guns upon the oncoming Cossacks. Their first shots cracked plaintively forth, aimed far too high, and the very next instant the Cossacks were upon them. They cut down the gunners, rode on, and reached the trenches from behind at the same moment as the infantry, who, on hearing the sound of the first hurrah of the oncoming attack, had abandoned their position, advanced at a rush, and sprung over the parapet from in front. Not a single man of the defenders escaped. A few defended themselves to the death. A number surrendered their arms with loud entreaties for mercy.

Against the wall beneath our window they placed seven disarmed and severely wounded officers. In their midst stood ‘the commandant. A tall handsome officer approached him. In his right hand he carried a heavy whip on the end of which dangled small leaden balls. A short and sharp interrogatory began. Six of the prisoners listlessly answered his questions, but the youthful commandant made a contemptuous gesture and spat upon the ground at his feet.

“Drag him to death!” said the officer, in a relentless and level voice, bringing as he spoke his heavy whip twice and thrice down across his face. The commandant doubled up and shrieked. Six Transbaikal Cossacks tied his legs with long straps to the tails of two prancing Cossack horses. The officer watched their work critically. “ Well done, boys! ” he laughed. “Now away with you for an hour.” They sprang into their saddles and rode with loud cries out across the steppe. The slender body of the commandant bumped up and down, tore itself to pieces on the jagged stones, and left behind a broad trail of blood.

Two hours later the Captain’s adjutant came and said: ‘‘ The interpreter is still ill. You must come along with me at once. The new commandant wishes to give orders to our senior officers.” We hastened off together to find all the senior officers gathered around Colonel von Strann. Nobody spoke. We had barely reported ourselves and saluted when somebody pressed down the latch from without and kicked the door wide open with his foot. Did we not know him? Of course. It was Vereniki, dusty, perspiring, and carrying his pistol as always with the butt projecting from his hand.
“We know each other, gentlemen, do-we not?” he asked gruffly. I stepped forward.
* Ah! ” he exclaimed, “ you, Ensign? ” I saluted him stiffly. He held. out his hand. “ Have you paper and a pen? ” A second officer entered. It was the officer who had interrogated the prisoners.

-“ Attention! The Ataman Semjonoff is coming! ” he called out, and he took up his position by the door with his hand at the salute. Everyone stood to attention. The Ataman of the Siberian Cossacks, Lieutenant-General Semjonoff, entered the room with long and ponderous strides. A tall and powerful man, muscular and imposing appearance, he was clad in the Mongolian-Burjatischer uniform. A fur-trimmed cloak hung from his broad shoulders, and from the back of his head rose a low, broad Cossack papacha.

I regarded him with curiosity, thinking excitedly to myself: ‘So that is the world-famous Ataman! ” His face was smooth, and each muscle looked as though it were carved out of stone; his forehead was high, his chin powerful and prominent, and his nose of the true Russian type — broad and thick. A black moustache covered his upper lip; the lower protruded ever so slightly. Two large grey, piercing eyes, set in deep cavities, combined with his stiff and heavy bearing to give the impression of inexhaustible strength, calmness, decision, and selfconfidence. “ Gentlemen,” be said in a deep and resonant voice, after he had briefly acknowledged our salute, “ it is necessary for me to inform you that with my arrival this camp comes once more under the administration of the old Russian

Government. Hence all concessions that have been made to you by the Red usurpers are removed, and precisely the same state of things is restored that existed here before the Revolution. Since I do not recognize the peace negotiations at Brest Litovsk and therefore consider myself to be still at war with your countries, you are once more my prisoners of war. In your own interest I advise you to pay particular attention to these facts.”
Again Semjonoff raised his broad hand — and went.

Thus we began to live under the rule of the Whites —a régime almost indistinguishable from that of the Czarist Government. Indeed, the only difference was that we had no longer anything to eat. Famine had broken out in some districts as a result of the fighting and consequent destruction. With whom does one first begin to economize? With prisoners of war. An animal is valuable; an animal can work; and, in dire necessity, it can be slaughtered. Hence an animal must be fed as long as possible. A prisoner of war has less worth than an animal.... The Kerenski currency daily fell in value. Finally we could only buy black kascha without fat, or meat that had been cooked in water. Sentries stood once more before the village. Sentries stood once more before the steppe. The old life had returned. The Home-hill regained its importance. Spring came — and the news that the peace of Brest Litovsk | had been signed. What about us? Had we not awaited this day for years? Had we not through all these years pictured its coming? Painted it in lively and joyous colours? And now we hesitated to say that peace had really been concluded.... How differently everything had turned out! Our depression baffled description. My God! What had we done? All who were in European Russia were going home. But we in
“We must make a longer stay,” said Windt sarcastically, “ because we have had a better time! ”
Seydlitz asked me to teach him Russian. “ This counterrevolution can last for years! ” he said in his common-sense way.

No! No! How could we survive that? Were not all conventions already disappearing from our room? What about the soldiers? What about Pod? We lived in an atmosphere that baffled description. Have men ever experienced anything more terrifying? Peace.... Peace.... Butforusno peace?...

Since the funerals started again, we have made a habit of accompanying each to the cemetery; for this was the sole way in which we could get out from behind the barbed wire. Attendance at funerals was officially permitted. Pleasant it was certainly not, but at the least one felt a few yards of open steppe beneath one’s feet and sniffed a fresh breeze. During the spring days of 1918 the funerals continued daily from early morning until dusk in consequence of the ever-increasing mortality arising from tuberculosis. If one wanted to accompany a funeral, one simply went to the morgue and waited until a new procession started.

One day Dr. Berger and I went together. Fifty to sixty wooden coffins lay about in front of the barracks while weary, stoical soldiers hauled down one body after another from the two or three thousand naked corpses which had been laid throughout the winter on separate shelves in a storehouse, and laid them with careless hands in the rough coffins. Twenty Cossaeks rode up at a trot. Each coffin was borne upon the shoulders of four men, and at the tail of the long procession of fifty corpses were grouped the officers who had come to accompany them to the cemetery. The procession wound its way along a narrow, well-trodden path that led over the saddle between the hills. A path that could be traced all the year

round by the shavings and sawdust — last pillows of the dead — that continually fell out from between the joints in the coffins. On fine days the path stretched out yellow and endless as far as the Home-hill. First came a tiny Russian graveyard with slanting double crosses and an iron railing as a defence against the wolves. Next a Chinese cemetery of tiny mounds from which thin sticks stood up bearing strips of paper with little wavy drawings in Indian ink that fluttered in the breeze. Beside each grave tiny bowls of rice and water had been set down — for the feeding of the dead.

Slowly a vast block of rock rose up before our eyes —a monument raised by the prisoners of war. A few commemoratory lines had been inscribed on the west side of the monument, which was surmounted by an eagle ready to take flight, whose gaze was directed towards Europe. On all sides of the monument the steppe stretched out like a dead forest. Line after line could be seen from the crest of the hill — silent, unending, gruesome — Maltese crosses for the most part, and often bearing no name. Here and there a gravestone stood out from amidst the crosses, a hexagonal block, polished and engraved by the hands of officers. At the eastern end of the cemetery a hundred men worked at digging graves in ground that had not yet thawed from the winter’s frost. The graves were scarcely more than shallow depressions in which the coffins lay covered with a bare handful of earth. Whilst the grave-diggers worked apace, we wandered for a time through the rows of graves. An elderly Captain came and attached himself to us and pointed out the resting-places of those we knew.

“There lies Baranny,” he said. “I lived with him. Because he attempted to escape he was thrown into katorga, and when he was let out, he died. There lies a Nostitz. He hanged himself because he was whipped publicly for having given a careless salute. There’s Bergner, who starved whilst under arrest....”

We seated ourselves upon a smooth rock. The sky was brilliantly blue, the horizon flat as a pancake. The steppe stretched out into infinity like a glassy, light-green sea. Away in the distance a train rolled towards Europe, leaving behind it a trail of white smoke.
“A mother waits at home for each of them,” said Dr. Berger, with his eyes fixed upon the crosses as if in an attempt to count them.

A short while ago I was once more invited by that good fellow Saltin. His room was filled with a number of young officers, and he declared laughingly that in a fury Captain Schank had fled to a bridge club. A Hungarian Lieutenant, Teleky by name, related his experiences on attempting for the first time to escape. “For months I collected the manure from the commandant’s horse,” he said. “For this purpose I often waited for hours. Whenever I saw a Russian riding past, I never let him out of my sight and followed the track of his horse’s hoofs. My comrades soon noticed that I always went about with Russians, but I did it solely for the purpose of collecting the droppings from their horses. Alongside the fence I made a small garden and planted potatoes round the edges. Everything depended upon their growing tall enough. Thanks to the manure, they grew magnificently and soon became so thick and tall that, lying upon my stomach, I could begin to dig a tunnel beneath the shelter of their leaves. As I had only a table-spoon to dig with, it took me many nights; and all the time I worked under the very noses of the sentries.”
At midnight came Roselli, with his dark-haired artist’s head, and sang for us a few songs to the accompaniment of his lute. Everyone became silent when he sang:
In deinen Augen glimmt ein Licht So grau in griin,
Wie dort die Nacht den Stern umflicht.
Wann kommst du? — Meine Fackeln lohn! Lass glihn! Lass gliithn! Schmiick mir dein Haar mit wildem Mohn!
Auf einem jungen Rosenblatt Mein Liebster mir geblasen hat Wohl eine Melodei.
Das Rosenblatt am roten Mund, Und war kein Wort dabei!
Wie dein Ohr brennt, wie dein Mieder drickt! Rasch, reiss auf, du atmest mit Beschwerde... Oh, wie hiipf{t dein Herzchen nun begliickt! Komm, ich trage dich, du wildes Wunder:
Wie dich Gott gemacht hat! Weg den Plunder! Und dein Brautbett ist die ganze Erde....
When he stopped, a Lieutenant seated next to me, a fairhaired, silent man, took a photograph from his pocket and handed it to me.
“No,” he replied cheerfully. “I don’t even know her. She was the wife of a man who died of typhus. But when I reach home, J’ll marry her. For two whole years I have dreamed of her....”

I paid a visit to Pod. On my way to the upper barracks I passed the carpenters’ shop. Nearly all the corpses had gone, and the carpenters were once more cutting out new planks. “Listen to me,” I said to the sapper who had made my table; “couldn’t you make another table? It need only be a small one.” He scratched the back of his head. “ That’s difficult,” he said. ““ We have again got an order for three thousand coffins. Our whole stock is finished, and the commandant says that next spring we'll need more than we did this year! Ill have to make it after hours.”
“Try. It’s for a man in the upper barracks. Podbielski — a dragoon. When can he come for it? ”
As I entered my old barracks, I saw Pod on sentry-go. Suschka jumped delightedly about me. Pod drew his Chinese cloak around him and motioned me with his hand to take a seat. Not a word was spoken.
“What about our return home, boy? ” he finally asked.
A lump rose in my throat. “I don’t know, Pod,” I said sadly.
He cleared his throat. “ Yes. But...” he began.
I turned and looked him in the face. His great doglike eyes were sad and lustreless. His beard around his mouth was thin and chewed up. “Pod...” I said consolingly. “Don’t lose courage! ” |

He shook his head. “ No,” he said roughly, “it’s no good — this getting up and down and walking round about.... I think we all feel the same. No! ” he suddenly broke forth, “ it’s _ no longer any good. For God’s sake! Cold —hot! Cold — hot! Going out —staying in! War— peace! War— peace! God in heaven!... At last we’ve got clothes and boots, and now they give us nothing more to eat! One after another goes down with consumption. Yesterday someone went mad. ‘ Castrate me!’ he suddenly yelled out. ‘ Castrate me! ’ Every week someone goes like that. We'd all been too sure. We'd all pictured ourselves as already at home, do you understand? That’s what’s the matter.”
“T don’t believe that Semjonoff will hold out for long,” I observed, without thinking. But Pod understands too much.
* ‘You only say that to comfort me,” he said. “In reality. Plenty of them here say that it can last for years.”
‘* How are the others? ” I finally asked.
“ Briinn is done for since this change came about. He is slowly masturbating himself to death. Like a baboon. When he did it a short time ago near me, I hit him so hard that he lay upon the floor.”
“‘Shouldn’t have done it? All of them would have caught it from him! Are we living in a monkey-house? ”
“ He’s also done for. For half a rouble he’l] do anything you want with you.”
I bent my head and stroked Suschka. Always the same old story — always the same.

“Yesterday I caught one of them just as he was at Suschka,” Pod went on. “It was the black-haired electrician. If the dog hadn’t howled so... Before I had finished with him, dirty swine, he was only fit to be carried into hospital.”

He fell into a silence. “I suppose I shouldn’t have done that, eh? ” he asked presently. “Let ’em do what they like, eh? Let the whole filthy madhouse go where it’s going, eh? You can afford to talk like that! This doesn’t happen in your room.”
“Oh,” I answered softly, “ don’t be so sure of that. It’s only done in secret, one doesn’t see it so openly... but at bottom it’s just the same.”
“Yes, we’re only men,” said Pod, and added: “ Schnarrenberg is down in the mouth.”
Presently little Blank came along to relieve Pod. His chest had fallen in, red spots stood out upon his cheeks, and dreadful rings encircled his eyes.
“I saw you standing in front of the canteen,” I said. “ Should you have liked to buy something? ”
“No,” he said in a tired voice. “I only stand there... justso...”

I went along with Pod to visit the others, who were lying languidly about: A couple were playing cards. Briinn sat crouching against the wall with eyes that had sunk deep into their sockets. As soon as I sat down beside him, he said to me: “My wife has a child, Junker.”
“‘ How has she managed that? ” I asked thoughtlessly.
“ He’s had a letter from his wife telling him so,” interrupted the artist. |

The Tadpole laughed. “That’s not so bad!” he said sneeringly. “The same thing has happened to a woman in our village. Two years after the death of her husband she bore a child. But she firmly declares that she got it from him.” |

“ ‘What! And? Why, when someone said to her that her husband had been dead for two years, she replied: ‘ What’s that to do with me? It’s history and that’s an end of the matter. I can keep my child so long as I want to! ’”
A couple of men laughed—a mirthless laughter, empty and hollow. |
** Don’t be angry about it, Briinn,” I said consolingly.
* Tl kill her when I get home! ” he foamed.
“ Then kill yourself first! ” cried Pod angrily.
“What do you want? ” roared Briinn. (Had he gone mad?) “You miserable cowherd! You starving windbag! You niggardly driver of a dung-cart! ”
“Must I knock you down again? ” Pod roared back at him. “You stallion! You ram! You beast!...”
I sprang up. “Steady, Pod! My God! What’s this for a new way of behaving? Shame on you both! Weren’t you once
the best of friends? Isn’t it enough that the Russians are doing us to death? Must you a quarrel among yourecives’ Be sensible, for God’s sake...
Pod stood up and went out.

‘* Nevertheless Pod was right, Briinn,” I said quietly. “ One shouldn’t throw stones in a glass-house. What is one man’s meat is another man’s poison. Your wife has done nothing more than you yourself have done a hundred times in thought and deed....”
“ But I’m a man! ” he whimpered. “ A man, a man...”
“Shut your mouth, you yelping puppy!” growled the Schwalangscher.
I got up. What was I to do? Stamp out these ideas? That was hopeless. Or answer him like a clergyman by saying that it was only an eye for an eye inasmuch as he himself... No, that irritated me.
“Good-bye, men! ” I said in a dejected tone as I left the room. It had gone so far: the best of friends hated one another....
“This afternoon an Austrian was here,” said Olfert to me on my return. “ You are to go to him up to five o’clock — Bergmann, Barrack IV, first floor.”

I went. As I went, I asked myself: “ What does he want? ”. In the barracks a stout cayaley officer was pointed out to me. “ Listen, Ensign,” he began, “ our interpreter is still ill. Hence we should like to ask you’... A sentry has offered us a girl or two— good, young things = from an officers’ brothel in Tschita. We couldn’t understand each other very well, so I told him to return at five o’clock....”

I bit my lips. Should I? Should I not? If I refused, my life would be a little hell. He told me all. Price, number of intending customers, length of stay. Oh, he was not in the least bit shy — didn’t try to disguise anything!
“In return,” he said, “ I’ve set your name down as second on the list.”
“ Why? You know I really can’t put you first. After all, we've had the most work — ”
“J should rather not in any case, Captain,” I said, breaking him off short.
“Not at all? Man alive! Think of it— as second! ”
I had great trouble in persuading him that I had other grounds for my refusal. Fortunately the sentry arrived punctually.

I have received my first parcel! Everything I wanted was in it, although it was half empty; the other half must have been stolen. My father wrote that it was the third parcel that had been sent to me with the same contents. And I received only one, and that half empty! On the cover was written in his handwriting: “ We will bring the ideal Fatherland into being and ‘set less store by our lives than by our ideals.”

Almost at the same time my first remittance came to hand: five hundred roubles. Through Vereniki’s intervention I was successful in having it all paid out at once; as a rule large sums were only doled out in monthly payments of fifty roubles. At last I could once more buy cigarettes! Only English cigarettes, made up in China, were to be obtained: Swallow, Honey-bee, Golden Helmet. Still, the chief thing was that there were any to be had. I gave fifty roubles to Schnarrenberg to be distributed among my squad.

Today the sentry must have brought the women. After supper several men disappeared from the room — quietly and slinkingly. First Merkel, then Windt, and finally a cadet as the third. Suddenly the thought came to me: “ Where is Olfert? ” I grew
uneasy. Had he also... ? Supposing he were ruined for life... ? A decent, straight, healthy man.... I got up.

“‘ Where are you off to, Ensign? ” asked Dr. Berger, laying his hand upon my shoulder. I felt limp. The way he looked at me... I swallowed hastily. “I’m only going to look for Olfert, Lieutenant,” I finally managed to say.
“Good! Then go. And if he won’t come, tell him I desire to speak to him — immediately and on duty.”

Once I had crossed the threshold, I began to hurry. Perhaps it was already too late? The sentry had brought them into an empty room in Barrack II. As I mounted the steps, I could see that the passage was already filled with officers. They stood waiting in threes, one behind the other — majors, ensigns, captains, lieutenants — all mixed up together. I descried Merkel — and Windt a few paces behind him. A voice called sarcastically: “Hello! Look at him! He’s in a hurry.” I pushed my way through and entered the room. A small table on which a lamp was burning stood beside the door. At the table sat the fat Captain with a long list spread out before him. The room was divided into two by sheets hung from the ceiling, and behind the sheets could be seen three beds.

A grey-haired Major and a young Lieutenant stood before the Captain. I overheard them quarrelling with each other. “ Rank makes no difference here, Major,” said the Lieutenant coldly. “ The order of entry is the only thing that counts. Rank doesn’t exist any longer here. Here we're all alike — only men! ”

“Terribly sorry,” interrupted the Captain, “ but Bender is right, Major. It was the only possible way.... And I see from the list that your name undoubtedly comes after that of the Lieutenant.” The Major turned angrily away. An unseen hand drew back the centre curtain. A young Lieutenant, whom I knew well, came forth half dressed.
“Your turn, Lieutenant Bender,” said the Captain in a matter-of-fact voice.
I approached the table in confusion. “Ha!” laughed the Captain. “ Have you thought better of it? ”
‘**No,” I managed to ejaculate, “I only want to know if an Ensign Olfert is on the list.”

“Wait a moment....” He ran his eyes over the names. The . Lieutenant went out with a terribly white face. Behind the curtains a muffled scream rang out. The perspiration stood out on my forehead, and my legs began to shake. “I’ve never known a woman — not a single woman,” | thought to myself. ** Never had a woman. Have always thought of it as something beautiful — magnificent — great...” I thought and thought. “To hell with it! Now everything is spoiled! Everything, everything! ”
“Yes, Olfert’s name is here,” said the fat Captain finally. I rushed out without answering him or saluting him and pushed my way again through the waiting ranks.
“Heavens! That was quickly done!” a voice called out enviously.
Olfert stood in the last rank. I seized him by the arm and took him outside with me. “ Olfert,” I said, “come with me.”
His eyes were fixed upon the ground. “I’ve already paid,” he replied restively.

“Tf I—if you—” I burst forth, and ceased. “ Will you come or not? ” I asked coldly. He fidgeted. “ Have you never heard of Asiatic syphilis? ” I asked in a whisper. “ Mouth, nose, eyes — everything eaten up? Will you— In any case, Dr. Berger wishes to speak with you,” I said decisively. “ At once, and on duty.”
He wrenched himself free. “Come along! To hell! ” he foamed.
I went ahead, and he followed me like a dog. I opened the
door and thrust him inside. “ Here he is, Doctor,” I said, in a careless tone. Berger gave us a long and penetrating glance. His lips trembled. “ Go and sleep, boys,” he said. And not another word.

After four days the brothel was closed down by the commandant, to whom its existence had been betrayed out of envy and spite by an officer who had been too late in applying to have his name put down on the already overfilled list. I was standing amidst a crowd in the barrack-yard as the girls were brought out. Cossacks escorted them on both sides and suggestively rolled their tongues across their lips. Three pretty, childlike prostitutes, two dark and slender and catlike, and the third a broad-shouldered, full-bosomed blonde. Their faces were chalky-white beneath the powder, and the fear of death shone in their eyes.

“ They’re done for,” Windt said dryly. “ Vereniki has handed them over to the guard — six hundred men —so I am told. They can do what they like with them — that’s his form of punishment. Awful, isn’t it?” For a while he kept silence. Still, when one looks at it squarely — it was dear enough. And big business involves big risks. What didn’t they earn! Thousands of roubles each, I tell you. Vereniki has collared it all.”
“ That would have been punishment enough,” said Miiller. “But to hand ’em over to the Cossacks, of whom two-thirds are syphilitic.... No, Vereniki always was and will be a brute.”
“ Neither of the dark-haired girls will survive it,” said Merkel, in his matter-of-fact way. “ At the most the blonde...”

“TI simply can’t understand that,” said Seydlitz next day, with the expression of the greatest contempt J had ever seen pass across his face. “ One after the other. Does a woman mean nothing more to them? Perhaps if one got peace for six months. But in eight days one’s just as bad as ever. Often I shiver at the thought of our masculinity, and this everlasting sex business irritates me more and more.”
“Me also,” said Olfert. “But what will you do? It’s the preblem of all prisoners.”
“ Besides, Seydlitz,” I remarked, “ only three from our room were there. Three out of twenty is only a small percentage. All the rest think as we do.”
“Only three? ” queried Seydlitz. “Really only three? ” Olfert seized his cap and hurriedly went off.
Yesterday the small and.slender Hungarian, ‘Lieutenant Teleky, paid me a visit. He asked if he could speak to me for a time alone..
“ Certainly,” I answered, “ at once,” and left the room with him. We went as. far as the mortuary, where nobody was about.
“T am going to escape again,” he said excitedly. “ I’m going to be in at the death! I ask you: will you come along? ”
I hastily lit a cigarette. My hands shook as J raised them to my lips. “ At once? ” I asked.
“‘T have been working for six months on the plan. Yesterday I finally succeeded in getting into touch with someone. In the baths — ”

“A Chinese. A straight man in as far as one can ever judge the straightness of one of these sliteyed men.” He groped in the pocket of his hussar’s cloak and drew forth a tiny, dirty piece of paper. “He can write and speak Russian well,” he said. I read: “I am prepared to lead four men by a secret route to Tientsin. J am in possession of horses and weapons. In three days’ time come to the baths outside.”
I returned him the paper. He paced to and fro. “ God! Good God! ” he whispered three or four times.
“Yes,” I said finally, “ we'll go. But how? ”
Teleky gripped my hand, and asked: ‘Whom shall we
choose? ” For a couple of hours we debated the matter between us. I thought of Pod. I thought of Saltin. Finally I chose Seydlitz.

“What do you say to Lieutenant Hassan?” he asked. I laughed and shut my eyes. I knew him well and he seemed to stand before me: lanky and sinewy; a sharp, bird-like head; the bent legs of a cavalryman; eyes of fire that blazed up upon the very slightest proyocanon:
“Good,” I said. “ You, Seydlitz, Hassan, and I — the complete Triple Alliance! ”
“Very well. You'll be responsible for the rest of the negotiations? ”
“Yes. Only one thing more: to what limit can I go in my offer? I myself have four hundred.”
He wrinkled his forehead. “I’ve only got three,” he said. ** But Hassan will have more....”
“Then he must lend some to Seydlitz. Pll offer him three at the most for each of us. Chinese cloaks we can buy cheaply in the men’s store.” He placed his hand across his mouth and ran off.
“ Of course, Teleky,” I said reassuringly.

Seydlitz was all excitement. “ That you should have thought of me! ” he kept repeating unceasingly. “ Now we’ll certainly be in in time for the death! ” He went off determined to raise money everywhere, nor did he experience much difficulty in doing so, since for this purpose he was capable of anything. I myself lived in a fever of excitement. Should I have chosen Pod? Certainly not. He would have at once let the cat out of the bag. Or that splendid Austrian Saltin? No. Seydlitz could speak Russian fairly, and he possessed the greatest strength of will. He was certainly the only one to be seriously considered.

Three days later, through Vereniki’s intermediary, I was given a guard. I walked ahead with long steps, while my Cossack came with clatering sabre at my heels. When we reached the bath, I gave him half a rouble. “Go and have a drink of schnapps,” I said laughingly. “ll not run away.”
“* Spassivo, Gospodin,” he replied, and went.

In the outer room an old Chinaman was seated. He wore a black-laced jacket. His face was oily and repulsive. I noticed that his cat’s-eyes broadened in amazement when he saw me approach in place of the Hungarian. I greeted him, took the paper out of my pocket, and unfolded it in such a way that he could not fail to recognize it.
“Were you sent by the dark-haired young officer? ” he inquired, in the nasal Russian spoken by the Chinese living on the borders of the Gobi desert.
“Yes. He doesn’t know enough Russian. Here’s your paper.”
** Do you also want to come? ”

“Tl give you each a horse, food and drink, a revolver and cartridges. There’ll be a pack-horse for every two. I'll lead you to Tientsin by a smuggler’s route that is unknown to a single Cossack. We'll ride by night only, and by day we sleep in hiding-places that I have already prepared. I’ve been a smuggler since my boyhood, yet never a Cossack has set eyes on my horse. You'll undoubtedly reach there in safety — ”
“How much do you want? ” I asked, interruping his flow of words.
* Five hundred a head,” he whispered.
“Ha ha! ” I laughed. “ You’re a fool! I can’t give you more than two hundred.”
“No,” he answered firmly. “For such a sum I’m not prepared to sell my head.”
“'You’ve just said that there was no danger? ” I interrupted.
“* No, no.” He raised his hands and stepped backwards. “ You
don’t realize how much everything costs — horses, ammunition, food.”
‘That doesn’t cost anything,” I said calmly, and laughed into his slanting eyes. “ You’ve got to go back in any case to get fresh supplies of tea— or opium! ”
He regarded me evilly. “ You are too clever,” he said. “ But if you can’t pay it, I must find wealthier officers...”
“You can spare yourself the trouble,” I said, seizing my cap and walking towards the door. “You won't find anybody in the whole camp with more than one hundred roubles.”
“Who is the third? ” he began again, holding me by the button of my tunic.
“A young Turk,” I said. “ A Kurd.”
* Ah! ” he cried out. “ Will he pay in gold? ”
“ T think that he has still got some.”
‘“‘ Three hundred in that case,” he said hoarsely.
“In seven days there will be no moon. At eleven-thirty I'll be waiting behind the hill before the centre gate. Do you know the hill? ”
“ We'll come clad like your own people.”

“ Eleven-thirty at night,” he said once more. The door closed. My heart pounded as I thought: “In seven days... God in heaven!... Frau von Hannecken is in Tientsin.... From there as stoker by way of India...” I undressed myself feverishly, jumped into the steam bath, and poured water over the glowing stones. Almost immediately came the thud of a sabre upon the door. “ Sitschas!”’ I cried out. When I came out, the Cossack was sitting upon my clothes and humming a tune. I dressed quickly and went with long steps through the yellow sand towards the camp. I never even honoured the station with a glance, only I suddenly caught myself singing softly — like the Cossack.

It was impossible to say good-bye to anyone. Since one was no longer certain of one’s companions, it would have meant incurring the risk of betrayal to have done so. Not that anyone would have deliberately betrayed the secret — a careless word, and... What was to be done with my diary? Everything else might go, execpt that — that had to be preserved. I resolved to place it, together with a letter in which I took leave of him and requested him to give the diary to the next delegate or the Fair Angel, under Dr. Berger’s pillow immediately before I left. It cost me a severe pang to leave it behind. But there was nothing else to be done. If I were shot or taken prisoner, it would certainly be lost; and that was not to be thought of.

Another hour and I must cease writing. The majority are already asleep. Teleky will wait for us by the morgue with the Chinese cloaks. Shall I ever again hold you in my hands, diary of mine? I want to write so much more. I’m like a man in love, unable to separate himself from the beloved and always finding something more to say. Outside, somebody is hooting like a brown owl. Seydlitz looks at me. The hour has come.
I am back. Everything went wrong. I cannot write. I am too upset —in too great despair. Perhaps tomorrow. Or the next day.

Eight days today since we made our attempt to escape. I can now set down the events in the order of their occurrence. I left the room unnoticed by anyone. Dr. Berger was still reading and did not notice that I pushed the diary beneath his pillow. On arriving at the mortuary we found Hassan and Teleky already there. We hastily clad ourselves in our Chinese cloaks,

and Hassan led the way with a small spade in his hand. He glided noiselessly ahead like a puma. We followed behind him in extended order and halted — each some twenty paces from the fence — listening while he dug out a hole beneath the fence to crawl] through. The night was still. The sky black and starless. From the watch-towers in the corners came at times the sound of the tread of heavy riding-boots. Now and then the clear howl of a wolf could be heard out of the dark expanse of desert. Nothing stirred. Once more an owl hooted. I started and began to move along with my outstretched arms touching the wire, until after going some eighteen paces I knocked against Teleky. ** Get through! ” he said softly. I dropped down, swung myself through, and stood up again.
“ Forward!” said Hassan in his perfect German. “ Half is accomplished!”

Four minutes later we heard two horses snorting. “ Are you there? ” whispered Hassan, and his guttural voice grew hoarser. He was there, hidden behind the hill, and silently and hastily indicated our horses to us — rough Mongolian horses, incapable of being worn out. The pack-horses were attached to two of them by means of long straps tied to their tails. Lieutenant Hassan was the first into the saddle. He sprang into it with a violence that made it appear as though he were. intoxicated by his newly won freedom.

“The pistols,” I said to the Chinaman. He made a short backward movement of the head. “ Later, later...” I heard him whispering. The tiny horses moved at a machine-like trot, the clatter of their hoofs silenced by the desert sand, and the only sound to be heard was the jangling of the harness. Five or six minutes passed away. Then there came again the hoot of an owl — a real owl this time, and not Hassan — that brushed my face as it flew past. “Come with! Come with!” it hooted. The next second a shot cracked out behind us. A second and a third followed in swift succession. Alarm shots rang out from all the watch-towers. Someone cried out in the camp. I galloped forward and drew up with Hassan.

‘“ Halt! ” I cried in low tones. “ About turn, Hassan, about turn! We’ve been seen, we’re pursued, perhaps we’ve been betrayed! It’s useless unless one has a start. About turn, Hassan! ” He raised the whip that lay across his saddle-bow, hissed through his teeth: “I... never will turn back... never, oh, never...” and beat his horse across the head.
“ And you, Teleky? ” I called out.

“No!” he cried through his clenched lips. “No!” He raised himself in his stirrups, laid himself along the horse’s neck and began to flog his flanks. Seydlitz drew up beside me. He was more cautious. “ Are you coming back with me, Seydlitz? ”
“Yes,” he said in a dazed voice.

We galloped in great curves back to the camp. Cossacks rode past us in the distance, shrieking and shooting, and I deceived them by giving vent to Russian cries. So great was their wild excitement that we got through them safely — unrecognized by anyone in the darkness — and reached our place of exit from the camp. Giving our horses a couple of lashes that caused them to tear away into the distance, we dashed to our tunnel, crawled through, and filled it up from the inner side.
Everybody in our room was out of bed. As we had left our cloaks outside, no one realized that we were the cause of all the noise and excitement.
“God in heaven! ” said Windt. “Several must have got out! ” Dr. Berger had already placed my diary in his box. He said nothing. He only silently stroked my hair.

Next day roll was called. We were all numbered off and at ten o'clock marched into the well-nigh empty morgue. Each was forced to stand for three minutes in a small, light room on the floor of which lay two men in Chinese cloaks. As a warning,

it was said! Young Hassan lay partly on his side, and his beautiful, proud forehead had been pierced by one of the countless shots that had been fired. A tiny piece of brain hung like a white worm on the opening of the wound. Lieutenant Teleky had been placed in a sitting position against the wall. His handsome and insolent boy’s face was distorted as if the thin lips had been frozen in the act of uttering the proud “ No! ” that had been his last word to me. His throat was hacked by sabrecuts, and his eyes were fixed upon us in a dull and glassy stare.

Yesterday our interpreter died of tuberculosis—a pucka Austrian Captain. Shortly before he took to his bed Colonel von Strann had once more asked him why it was that he had not sought to escape. “ With your knowledge of the language, it would be easy for you,” said the Colonel, “and think what a career would then be open to you! ”

‘Many thanks, Colonel!” replied Bettenberg. “I should prefer being a live captain to being a dead major! ” He too had been unnerved, bereft of idealism, by Siberia. Like so many others, his own life had become dearer to him than the welfare of the majority, yet in the end it also had failed him....

Vereniki, who always salutes me politely whenever we meet, told me one day that the Ataman Semjonoff had conquered the whole of Transbaikalia and had raised Tschita to the dignity of capital of the new State. The revolution that had broken out in May in Central Siberia on the part of the Czech Legionaries — “‘ Your former Austrian comrade-in-arms,” he said laughingly — had acted like a bugle-call to arouse the whole middle class. All Siberia had fallen into the hands of the Whites. For next spring a great offensive under a unified command had been planned that should drive the Reds to hell in a few months.

He patted me on the shoulder. “ You must wait until we have made a fresh peace with Germany,” he said laughingly. “‘ The Peace of Brest Litovsk cannot be discussed by a good Russian. But I know of something better for you to do: join our army! On my recommendation Semjonoff will at once give you a lieutenancy! Besides, the latest news from the front is bad.”

“Your offensive has failed. The Americans and the French are advancing.” He turned the subject lightly. “Think it over, Ensign,” was his final advice. I was stunned. Was it true? Impossible! After the collapse of the Russian front? “He’s only trying to damp my courage in order to get me to go over to his army,” I said to myself in an endeavour to raise my spirits. God and Father! — if I had not this consolation...

Since it became obvious that the rule of the Whites in Siberia was more enduring than had at first seemed possible, our discipline perceptibly deteriorated. The condition of things in our camp became the same as it was among the men in the upper camp. The disappointment of all our hopes broke our power of endurance. The hours that had been set apart, as the result of conferences and agreement among us, for sleep and work, rest and exercise, were no longer observed. Gambling and cardplaying gradually increased until they lasted till morning, to the accompaniment of noise and quarrelling. Drinking-bouts turned certain corners of our room into something resembling a madhouse. Dr. Berger was powerless. He who had been able to do what he wished with quiet and normal men lost all influence over this crowd of overstrained men rendered abnormal by the long duration of their imprisonment. Each day serious complaints were presented to him for his investigation. Lately the two business men complained of Windt, the athlete — that he was in the habit of doing gymnastics stark naked, making or PT een eer eee
much noise — at whatever hour of the day or night he chose. — What could the doctor do? He was bound to follow up the complaint by speaking to Windt.

“ What? ” laughed Windt. “ What is there remarkable to be seen on me? Let me go on doing gymnastics! I’ve got a wife at home who will expect much from me after her long abstinence, don’t you know? And if I don’t train properly...” I noticed that Berger blushed like a girl. He was helpless to deal with such things and could only keep silence. He picked up his cap and went hastily out of the room.
“Yes,” said Olfert sarcastically, “Siberia is not the land where mimosa flourishes! ”

A few days later a Lieutenant spoke with me about my attempted escape. “ You should be glad that it failed! ” he said. “ T escaped in 1916, and now I am here in Siberia for a second time! As I was making preparations to escape, my Captain said to me: ‘Man alive! If you’re successful, you’ll certainly be given the Pour le mérite!’ I was successful — and do you know how I was received? An officer said to me: ‘ Damnation! I thought you were cleverer, Scholz! If one is nice and safe, how can anybody sacrifice that? Who demanded of you that you should abandon your lovely camp, your regular food, and your good bed? In the name of God, whoever made you do that?’ My Colonel said: ‘ Well, it’s good to see you again! Now get after the enemy! You've been resting long enough, lying for years on bearskins, while we...’ Distinctions? Pour le mérite? Of that I never heard a word. You all live here in the mistaken idea that everything at home is just as it was when you left it in 1914 or 1915. Good God! that’s long past. All our great enthusiasms and great moments are forgotten — now one uses the word ‘swindle’ to describe the war. There are still a few idealists, but the majority... And at bottom it’s no wonder.... It’s only natural.... What’s too much is too much. In any case, no second attempts for me! I can now keep control of myself! ”

Last night I could not sleep. “Is what he said the truth? ” I asked myself incessantly. “Can it really be?... No! it simply cannot be so. With such men one does not conquer half the world! Only his bitterness caused him to speak like that, eh? He really thinks quite differently! And yeta grain... ?”

We discovered a new method of getting firewood. At a time when the thermometer stood at fourty-five degrees below zero, the camp authorities allowed us four pieces of wood weekly for our room; and we had no proper food, not a single real bed!

“Do as we do,” said Saltin, a good father to us all, as we poured out our griefs to him. “ Once a week we climb upon the roof of our barracks and, under the direction of an architect, saw away everything that is not absolutely necessary for the support of the roof.”

I told this to Dr. Berger, who refused to countenance it. “All right! ” I said quietly. “If you choose to let us freeze, we have the right to look after ourselves.” Five or six of us made ready a couple of strong saws, while I asked Saltin for a loan of the architect. The roof of our barracks had never been touched before. What a nest of worms! The architect, who was a lieutenant from Transylvania, went with blue chalk from prop to prop, cross-beam to cross-beam. “ The Russians are so lavish with wood in the building of their houses,” he said laughingly, “ that two-thirds can be removed without risk. Only one must know what must remain, and not make a mistake! ” He moved about marking beams here and there. At times he stopped to calculate stress and strain. We sawed away busily, and the sawn supports steadily went to swell an ever-increasing pile.
“Boys!” said Windt, “there’s warmth for you! I have always envied our fellows in Turkestan....”
“ Don’t trouble to, Lieutenant! ” said the architect. “I was there myself! ”
“Tell us about it! ” called one or two voices.

** Ah! there’s not much to tell. Hot as a furnace day and night, and not a drop of water. I’ve come to hate heat to such a degree that I’d rather freeze for the rest of my life than sweat once more as we did in Turkestan! ”
“‘ Were you treated better than here? ” inquired the Warrior.

The Lieutenant laughed. “ Listen! ” he said. “When four officers escaped in Astrakhan, they punished the remaining 296 by fencing up all windows and forbidding them to enter the barrack-yard, with the thermometer standing at fifty degrees! For a month we lived like that —can you imagine it? Moreover, in Troizki, out of seventeen thousand men, nine thousand died in three months....”

Yesterday evening Hansen, Lacke, and Farben invited me to have a drink with them in their corner. I don’t know what they found in me, but as I took my departure, they all said that I must visit them oftener. Our conversation stuck in my mind for a long time. Was that because they opened their hearts to me? “ Qh, if we were only at the front! ” said Hansen finally. “ There’s fighting there. Good. I understand that, if necessary. But here... What I want to know is: why must war also dominate things here in Siberia? Isn’t that the very limit? Is a defender of his country a criminal? We prisoners of war are protected by treaties — by a convention. It’s all very well to say that we are lucky in that nothing more can happen to us! Aren’t tuberculosis and typhus bacilli flying about here more thickly than the densest hail of bullets? Every bullet is not deadly, but when one of these ‘ bullets’ here scratches ever so slightly one of our worn-out bodies, that’s an end to it! No, é 268 PRISONER OF WAR give me a lead bullet! Apd that’s not all, there’s a lot more at the front — for example ' leave! And even if you never got any leave, the time went morz quickly; they’ve got work, something to occupy them, a safe’y-valve! We’ve got nothing. They can defend themselves; weve got to remain quiet. Out of every four of us, one is alrgady dead — out of every four men at the front is one always killed? Not at all! And when one must die, which is the worst: to fall, sword in hand, in the thick of the fight, or expose oneself helplessly, and inactively await the coming of death? ”

The news from the front has become increasingly worse. Vereniki certainly had not deceived me. We are all confronted by a dilemma. “I cannot understand it when we had just attained to numerical equality with the troops that had been set free,” said Dr. Berger yesterday. “ And now we are forced to retreat as never before in the whole course of the war. America’s material resources must have come into play....” Everyone walked about dejectedly in the barrack-yard. Despondency was writ large upon each face. I often went for walks with the Warrior, since nobody else bothered about him.
“Ensign!” he said to me. “One can ask you a question. Is it possible that we overrated ourselves? ”

I shrugged my shoulders. “ To answer such a question here is quite impossible,” I replied. ““ And, besides, could we have done anything else? ” I felt annoyed with myself for avoiding his question. “ If we win the war, we've certainly not done so,” I said. “ If we lose it, then undoubtedly! ”
A Russian officer passed us by and returned our salute carelessly and with hatred in his eyes.
“Why do these men hate us so? ” asked the little man beside me. “I don’t hate them! Never have hated them! I simply fought because I believed the Fatherland had been attacked.”
I only nodded. My God! Of what use were such questions in
Siberia? Was he not right? Didn’t we all go because we were attacked ?
“ That’s true,” I said wearily. “ We'd never have volunteered for a war of conquest — you wouldn’t have and I shouldn’t have.”

We walked on, saluting all the time, always saluting. A young Austrian Lieutenant, whom I knew well, came and joined us. I noticed suddenly that he no longer saluted, although he had formerly invariably done so. “Look, young man,” I said, “ there goes another fellow who kicks against the pricks! ” Three paces farther on a Captain stopped him — one of the popular kind who knew of nothing better to do than to busy themselves in watching over the deportment of their inferiors in rank.
** Why don’t you salute? ” he growled out.
‘‘ Because I have already done so six hundred times this morning! ” answered the Lieutenant coolly.
The Captain stormed at him! “ Are you mad? Do you want to be an officer? To give an example worthy of being followed? Retire, three paces...”
The young Lieutenant did not move. “ I’ be damned first! ” he said in a clear and calm voice. And walked on.

No one was any longer able to shake off the nervousness and irritation that seized upon all simultaneously. Yesterday, for example, J had my first quarrel with Dr. Berger. That was symptomatic. One had to be almost at the end of one’s tether before one could quarrel with so reserved and fine a man. In a discussion over some trifling and laughable matter I gave him a rough and unpremeditated answer. He started, gave me a long look, and, laying his hand upon my shoulder, said softly: “You too, Ensign? No, I am mistaken — not you! ” Tears rushed into my eyes. I could have kissed his hand. Ah! we were only unlucky, unlucky unto death — nothing more....
Collapse of Germany! Was I mad! Did I see ghosts? A

regular Lieutenant stood ‘in the barrack-yard without tunic and cap. He had put on all fis decorations and kept striking his breast so that they rattled while he called out unceasingly: “ All for nothing... all fo} nothing... all for nothing....”

It was true. I could not set it upon paper. I could no longer distinguish white from black. Only: Vereniki had not lied. Ever since the summer we had been in full retreat. Saltin came from the chemist who had received the newspapers. “ It’s true, Ensign,” he said. “ But we weren’t beaten by soldiers! It was the American trains day and night—day and night! Guns, ammunition, rifles, gas...” He was quite beside himself and repeated his words three times in succession. As he went away, he was crying.

The Russian officers were triumphant. One could see from their eyes, and from the way in which they saluted, that they were saying to themselves: “ Now you've got it at last!” We could make no reply. We dragged ourselves around like criminals whose term of imprisonment has suddenly been lengthened into a life-sentence. How could we return home now? As sons of a powerless, defeated land? Nothing more? We thought the worst was behind us? Yet the worst was only just beginning. ... Dr. Berger no longer spoke. Olfert went about silently. Seydlitz’s thin face had become a mask to conceal the thoughts behind, while the Warrior went about with eyes swollen from crying. Merkel shrank up, and put on a resigned air. For three days Proschow lay silent, without moving — dead drunk. The cadet ceased his card-playing, and the business men stopped disputing amongst themselves in their corner. My God! what had happened to us? Had we all been condemned to death?

I went into the men’s camp. Before I did so, I took down the picture of Holsteinerin, the champion mare, from the wall. I felt I needed it no longer. I should never again ride an old remount from the Z class. My intention was to take it to Pod,

who was a peasant and would find pleasure in it. Besides, I felt I must take something for him with me each time I went to visit him. My old squad greeted me in silence. I silently seated myself between Pod and Suschka.
“Well, youngster? ” he said softly. (“ He’s going to try to comfort me, this fellow,” was the thought that passed through his mind.) “ Pod,” I said, by way of a beginning.

“Hold your tongue. You don’t need to console me. I’m strong enough. But you... you are losing more than I. Pll return to my farm, as before. Perhaps Ill have to work harder in order to live — that’s all. Good. Finished. But you
. you who have had nothing from life, you who have given up everything — youth and health—” He paused. “ You’ve got to meet the bill! ” he ended roughly.
“Enough of that, Pod.” I held out the picture. “I have brought you something. I don’t want it any longer, do you understand?...”

He cleared his throat. “Good God! Once more,..” He covered his eyes with his hands and suddenly rushed from the room. I looked around me. The artist was sitting behind me, and the rest were gathered around him —all muffled up to the eyes. In their flowing cloaks they resembled a regiment of famished Chinamen. Little Blank — the “ girl ” — lay in their midst. He looked like a dying man and coughed incessantly.

“‘ Where is Schnarrenberg? ” I asked Hatschek. He shrugged his shoulders. “ Don’t know, Ensign. Since the Revolution he has been living in the large room with the non-commissioned officers. He’s afraid of us, can you understand? At first he behaved like a madman —shrieked, foamed, struggled. But ever since yesterday he has suddenly become quite as though he had been struck dumb....”
“ What’s up with you, Blank? ” I asked hoarsely.
‘IT don’t know, Ensign,” he answered limply. “I’ve always fever, am always in a cold sweat — deathly cold.... This coughing takes all the strength out of me.... And sometimes blood...”
“ You must go about more! You’ve got a warm cloak! What you need is fresh air! Do go out more often, please! Pod will take you along with him....”

“‘ What are you talking about! I’m so weak that a breath of air would blow me away! Still, it’ll soon be spring, eh? ” A fit of coughing tore him. His glance fell upon his thin, childlike hands. On his thumbs were bright-red spots.

Later on came Schnarrenberg. His appearance gave me a shock. Unwashed and uncombed, clad in a dirty and unbrushed tunic, his whole figure was drawn up and pinched in; and his bull neck had become thin and bent. Never before had I seen him in such a state. He seated himself in front of me, stared into my eyes with a look that pierced into me like a knife, and asked in a hollow voice: “Is it true, Ensign? ”
I could not reply. I thought of Seydlitz — not an inch of elasticity. “ What, Schnarrenberg? ” I asked.
“I must know! ” he said obstinately. “I must know it for certain! ” |

Fear crept into my heart. “ Don’t do anything silly, Schnarrenberg,” I said, in an effort at light-heartedness. He continued to gaze at me unblinkingly and as if he had not heard me. His eyes seemed to be gazing away into the distance behind me. “ Do you think,” he said slowly as though he were wrenching each word out of himself, “that I could... now... wait quietly... another three years? ” He fell into a brooding silence. “ You know very well why I have been able to stand it! Only because... because I hoped, believed... I’m too old for anything new... grown too old here in Siberia! You can do that — you who are the youth of Germany.” He laughed insanely. “So it is true, eh? ” he suddenly asked in his old,
rough tone of command. “Advance, Ensign! Answer! Answer! ”

He stood up. “ That means yes,” he said calmly. “ Otherwise you'd have said: ‘ No!’ And not only said ‘No’; you’d have yelled it aloud! Ah well! Ah well! It’s only what I’ve expected....” Once more he looked me up and down from head to toe —a long, penetrating glance. “ You, boy... last ensign of my regiment...” he suddenly whispered, made a stiff right-about turn, and left the room.

Pod came back with red eyes. “ For weeks I’ve had diarrhea,” he said. “ Hence I’ve got to go out so often, do you understand ? Confounded nuisance! It would be a case of vomiting if there were anything to eat! I’ve got to go every hour. It pulls one properly to pieces. It gripes all the time, all the time. And there’s nothing there, do you understand? At times it feels as if one’s very bowels would be pulled out of one....”
*“T'll bring you something to eat, Pod! ”
“‘That’s not why I said it!” he answered roughly. “ Eat what you've got yourself. You’re not much better....”

He walked across to his new table and picked up the picture. “In her colouring and lines she’s a bit like my Blesse,” he said, with his head sunk upon his chest. He borrowed some nails from Hatschek and fixed the picture above his bed. Plunged in thought, I continued to watch him, until a noise outside the door aroused me. The door was kicked open, and six or eight men bore a heavy body into the room.

“There in that corner are his friends,” a voice called out loudly. I caught sight between the bearers of two cavalryman’s legs, a German dragoon uniform, a swollen blue face, a bushy moustache. “He’d been hanging for a time before we found him,” said an Austrian. “ By his braces.”

It was Schnarrenberg — our sergeant major. His face was unrecognizable. His eyes were wide open. His moustache, which had formerly bristled so fiercely, hung limply from his lip. “So he is finished! ” The thought was like a stab in the heart. “ He thought it was the right way! He was true to himself....”

All conventions and bonds of decency disappeared from our midst. Could anything else have happened? The thought of victory had hitherto held us up and given us strength — what was to hold us any longer? We were not weak nor evil; we were just as much and as little as we’d been before. If anyone frowns at our behaviour.... For my part I refrain from judgment and accusation. I have simply set down events — nothing more. And I’ve not sought to exonerate myself.

The pilot Proschow had another fight with the Turk yesterday. He ridiculed his religious beliefs, despite the warnings of some of the older men, until Abdulla, in a state of frenzy, sprang at him like a cat and sought to throttle him. Seized by a like frenzy, Proschow bit, scratched, fought.... From all sides we sprang to separate them. Thinking that we only meant to aid our comrade, the Turk turned upon us all, and it was only after a fierce fight that we were able to tie him down. Many of us were hurt and streaming with blood. Dr. Berger seated himself beside Abdulla in an endeavour to bring him to reason.
“‘ They'd have killed each other if we hadn’t been too much for them,” said Windt.
“If this winter goes on much longer,” said Seydlitz, “ this sort of thing will happen every day.”
Omsk had been made capital of the White State of Siberia and Admiral Kolchak had been chosen as its President.
“Now, then, Ensign? ” asked Vereniki. “‘ What about it? Your Emperor is in exile, and you are no longer bound by your oath of fealty —”
“ Good God! Look here! I'll bring you the newspapers tomorrow. Then you come along with us. Done! What a chance for a young man like you! Besides, you are a soldier in every inch of you? ”

“ What does that mean? Rubbish! For, in fact, you were one once! That the military spirit has gone out of you here, I can well understand; I’d have been the same in your place. But under a man like Kolchak you'll soon recover it again. He’s a hero, a gentleman! Nobody better could have been found! Tomorrow then...” Away he went with a light tread — free, happy, full of hope — just as I was once! When? When? It seemed to me as if it had been many, many years ago....

One evening at Saltin’s an officer told us that he had spent a long time in Dostoievski’s Krepost. “The upper bunks were ten and a half feet above the ground,” he said. “ Many who fell out of bed in their sleep got concussion of the brain. The place looks today just as it did in the middle of the last century! And we were treated in the same manner.... Only in Russia do they still crowd together men belonging to the highest order of European culture, as they used a century ago to crowd together the worst criminals! Sixteen thousand men died there then. Nevertheless it was better than the Kirchhof Barracks in Nikolaevsk, where I was before that! Only seventy men out of every thousand survived. The Russian guards used to press their dead bodies into coffins with their heels and the butts of their rifles. When the coffins were exhausted, they dug great pits in which they tipped the naked bodies by the dozen from the same cart that they used to bring the meat for our kitchen. These pits were left open until they were filled to the brim, and the uppermost bodies were always halfeaten by wolves before fresh corpses were thrown in to cover them....”

Last night, when everyone was asleep, Lieutenant Thurn seated himself upon my bed. I laid aside the book by Mantegazza and stared at him in astonishment. Excitement lit up his handsome, olive-skinned face; and his dark, almond-shaped eyes, whose whites had a bluish tint that one often sees in those of children, flickered unsteadily. “ What’s the matter with him? ” I thought sympathetically.
“You have such a fine, clear skin...” he suddenly began.
My God! What did he mean? I laughed unwillingly as I said: “ Indeed? ” He came nearer to me. I felt his arm upon my leg.
“You are handsome,” he went on. “I often dream of you. . -. You have a small, delicate mouth.... When you laugh, you show your teeth....”

**T am a man, Lieutenant! ” I interrupted him. He raised his hand as much as to say: “ What does that matter? ” and, as he dropped it again, he laid it upon my hip. “ That’s just it,” he whispered. J took his hand in mine and placed it beside me on the bed-clothes.
“Lieutenant,” I said firmly, “ go to bed. It’s time. I want to sleep.”
“ But why? ” he asked in a weak voice, as his whole body trembled. “ Let me sit a little longer on your bed.... It is so nice.... I love looking at you!... Look! I’ve brought you some cigarettes....”
“Why do you always call me Lieutenant? ” he interrupted me. “ My name is Willmuth — just for once call me Willmuth.”
“‘ Thanks, Lieutenant,” I continued my sentence, “I have my own cigarettes.” He twisted himself about, and his lips trembled. He whispered something.
“What do you mean? ” I said sharply. He bent over me and laid his hands upon my shoulders.
I jumped up as if someone had struck me, and roughly
pushed away his hands. “If you don’t go away at once,” I said brusquely, “I'll call Dr. Berger.”
He rose limply. Were there tears in his eyes? “ Do be nice ...” he begged.

“Get away! Get away! ” I said aloud. Was it because I felt myself to be in danger? All of a sudden I became furious with anger. “‘ That is absolutely beastly, do you understand? If you ever come near me again...” He gave me a look that pierced me through and through. Like a sick dog! I thought with a shiver. Finally he slunk off like a whipped cur. I remained awake for more than half the night. This also? I thought to myself, After a time I threw away the cigarettes that were the last remaining traces of my late visitor, the very same cigarettes that I had purchased myself for special occasions — La Ferme, Petrograd, best quality. A faint feminine scent still clung to the mouthpieces....
I told Seydlitz about Vereniki and his proposal. “He won’t leave me alone,” I said. “ I can’t think why he wants to make a fool of me.”
‘Because you have Russian blood, I should think.”

“Because I’m no longer a soldier, Seydlitz. To be a soldier means to be a man such as you — or Schnarrenberg. For me it is quite impossible to go shooting and murdering any more. At the very utmost I might do it in case of necessity, and for our country. This, however, is a civil war.”
He remained silent for a time. Then he suddenly asked: “ Do you think he would take me? ”
“You? ” I said, taken completely by surprise. “ Would you go over, Seydlitz? ”

“Yes. I am an officer. Nothing else. My father and my grandfather were also officers. It’s my whole life and soul. A new age is beginning for Germany — in one sense or another — and of that there can no longer be the least doubt. J cannot unlearn all that I have learnt. All I know about is war — nothing else. I grew up in the army, in an atmosphere of war, and Ill remain in it. Further, the Whites are fighting for my own ideals: government and tradition. That’s good enough for me. Perhaps one could just as easily join the Reds, who also declare that they are fighting for ideals, and these new ideals of theirs are not bad and are certainly more in accord with the times than our old ideals. But they are an undisciplined horde that won't tolerate a leader, as far as I could judge. Also I belong to the middle class. Why should I foul my own nest by fighting against it? ”

He pondered for a while. “ I’ve heard it said that Kolchak is the most honourable soldier in Russia. A man with clean hands. That’s saying a lot in this country — perhaps the greatest thing that could be said. What more do I want? Above everything else, I must get away from here, do you understand? Only get away and do something, do anything.... Otherwise Pll go mad.”
“ And if you are killed? ” I said in a depressed voice.
“ Well, I shall at least have tasted freedom first! ” he answered cheerily.

“ How do you know that you'll remain alive? One of these days either typhus or consumption or ” — he sighed deeply — “something worse still will get hold of us here.... For it may be years before we get home.” _
