“Undoubetedly. They need every man they can get. Besides, Semjonoff certainly knows the name of your famous ancestor.”

I was sheltering from the wind in a corner of the barracks when Lieutenant Kohler came timidly up to me. “ Ensign,” he began nervously, and his eyes rolled excitedly, “I am still looking in vain for my wife. I’d like to ask you, don’t you know, something very special: If she comes again to your room... and calls me... and I don’t come at once —then please hold on to her... don’t let her go... lock her in... put a guard over her....” He suddenly ceased speaking and began to laugh. Then he bent over my ear as if he wished to communicate a very sacred mystery to me. “ Until —I— come! ” he whispered, and hastened away with short, childlike strides. What he must have suffered! Day by day, hour by hour, he was plunged anew from the heights of heaven into the depths of the blackest hell. But, as he was already exhaused and light-headed, he would not have to endure it much longer. Such was our condition that in order to render ourselves better able to endure the unendurable, we consoled ourselves with the hope that in the near future death would remove from our midst one or other of the most terrifying faces.

There were those who declared that under the Whites conditions were better than they had been under the Reds. As a result of Bolshevik propaganda a party of so-called “ Internationalists ” had grown up among the prisoners of war, composed of German, Austrian, and Hungarian communists, who terrorized all those who refused to join their ranks. The Bolsheviks had placed them in command of the camp, and they had subjected the officers to the most abominable torture. I remember that pamphlets were distributed in the men’s camp calling upon them to join the “ Internationalists.” Some hundreds, mostly Hungarians, did join them; but before they had time to exercise their murderous propensities to the full, the Red Régime had collapsed in Transbaikalia.
When we arose one morning there stood on a siding a long, very long, saloon-carriage, painted white. “ Another delegate? ” I asked.
Dr. Berger looked out and gave a start. “My God!” he exclaimed.
“‘ What is the matter, Lieutenant? What is it? ”
“ That is a plague-carriage,” he gasped out.
“What? Why? What for? ” six or seven voices called out.
“They are only to be seen when the plague is round about.”

Saltin, who had experienced an outbreak of plague, told us all about it. A couple of such saloon-carriages were held ready in every large town, and the instant an outbreak of plague was reported from a village, one was attached to the next train travelling in that direction. The carriages were stocked with disinfectants, contained a tiny hospital with a dozen beds — and in each were two nurses and a doctor. The suspected cases were put into the hospital and so isolated, while their dwellings, together with everything they contained, were set on fire. Not a single object was permitted to survive the flames.
For four days we lived in a state of extreme anxiety. Each night another house went up in flames. “ Damnation! That’s quick work! ” said Windt.
On the fifth day the carriage had vanished. The whole camp breathed again. “If it had come into our barracks or the men’s,” said Dr. Berger, “everything would have been at an end.”

For a few more days we continued to live in a state of gloomy foreboding. Might not one of the countless rats have brought the germs into the barracks? We were in luck. Not a single case was reported throughout the whole camp.
We began to receive books, newspapers, instruments. Slowly a tiny camp library grew up. Gradually, quite gradually, we

came to realize that they had been doing much for us at home; but for the majority of us it was already too late. Bit by bit we got what we needed, although some — indeed, the most — of it was of no use any more. If we had only got these things three years sooner... We had become too listless and worn out to be able to execute even the slightest tasks, and our spirits had become so dejected that no seed of any kind could find nourishment on so parched a soil.

Seydlitz left today. To join Semjonoff’s staff in Tschita. He left secretly without anyone being aware of his departure. “ Ordered to report in another camp,” was the official announcement. Vereniki welcomed him with open arms. He preferred his cool and resolute character to my softer nature. “ You are a fool not to go with him! ” he said again and again. “ You'll repent it later! He will make a great career for himself, this young Seydlitz! ” When he said good-bye to me, he pressed my hand until it hurt: “ We'll never see each other again,” he said calmly, “ but don’t let us forget each other! ”

The first day without him seemed oddly empty. Although we had never spoken a great deal with each other and had not understood each other very well, yet the daily sight of his disciplined and quiet demeanour had often endowed me with moral courage. In the end we were even more cut off from the others than we were from each other. With them we merely lived through the miserable daily round, the everlasting, torturing monotony, which did not form any bond of union and only resulted in making men hate the sight of each other. Seydlitz, on the other hand, belonged to the days of Nizhni Novgorod and the long months in the railway wagons — and to Totzkoje!
“Hello! ” said Olfert; “ you are feeling a bit lonely, aren’t you?”
He put his arm round my shoulders and leaned lightly against me. “ Then you'll take me as a substitute, won’t you? ”
he said in a strange voice. “Very gladly, Olfert,” I said.

The other day I noticed the soldiers in the men’s barracks hunting dogs. They lured all the dogs that were running about to come to them, strangled them with bits of string, and then cut their throats....

I was furious. Then I thought: Has one the right to condemn them? Had I not seen myself that only a short time ago they had dearly loved these dogs and done everything for them? Unceasing famine had destroyed those gentler feelings. Something more had been brought to an end.... I decided to tell Pod to keep a careful watch upon Suschka.

Captain Kosim, who was always quarrelsome, attacked a sentry in a fit of rage. Before anyone could prevent him the Cossack had drawn his sabre. Kosim lay in hospital in a dying condition. The doctors disagreed as to the cause of his break-down. Some called it delirium tremens, but, whatever it was, it was the twelfth case this year.

A short time ago a young Lieutenant made his appearance in the barrack-yard stark naked and annoyed the passers-by in the most incredible manner. He could only be brought back to barracks by the employment of force. He was ordered to be sent to the asylum in Omsk in a few days’ time, and Captain Kosim was to follow as soon as he could be transported. The asylum was said to be filled for the most part with prisoners of war. Frequently one encountered men in the barrack-yard who suddenly performed some mad action. After the news of the German collapse had become known, an Ensign was to be seen running about for days accusing all the superior officers of saluting incorrectly. “Put your heels together, sir!” he
roared out every minute. “Salute me! I am the unknown soldier....” Little by little things grew worse and worse. Gradually one came to fear for one’s best friends.

“Ensign,” said Olfert, “a Bavarian dragoon spoke to me at the fence. He’s been walking up and down for hours waiting to see someone from our room. He asked me to tell you to come as quickly as possible to the barracks. Your old comrade is ill — has been ill for a week.”

“Pod,” I thought in terror. “ Are you calling for me— Pod? ” I slipped on my overcoat, head-protector, and felt boots. “If he asks for me, my God!... If he asks for me! ” I kept thinking. As I entered the room, I saw that his eyes were fixed upon the passage along which I must come. But his eyes were . no longer the good old St. Bernard eyes. He was no longer my Pod — my old brown bear.
“ He’s looked like that since yesterday,” whispered the artist. ** Keeps on looking over there unblinkingly.”
I sat down beside him. “Pod...” I said softly. He did not stir, and only his eyelids flickered slightly.
“ At times he is unconscious,” murmured the artist. “ Notwithstanding his open eyes.”
“Why didn’t you send for.me sooner? ” I asked irritably.
“He wouldn’t permit it. He threatened to kill anyone who did so. He said he would be all right in three days....”
“Full up!” said the artist. “Spotted typhus has broken out again, and only those suffering from it are admitted.”
“What does the doctor say? What’s the matter with him? ”
A volunteer stepped forward. “There was nothing wrong with him organically, Ensign,” he said politely. “The cause of the trouble, according to the doctor, lay far more in his mental condition.”

I started up. “And I knew nothing about it?” was the thought that arose within me. Knew nothing, felt nothing, suspected nothing?... I turned round. Briinn was cowering behind me. “My God! What is the matter with him, Hatschek? ” I cried out in horrified astonishment. He looked like a corpse — pale, hollow, a breathing ruin of a man.

Hatschek touched his forehead with his forefinger. “ For the last four days, ever since Pod has been lying ill... Day and night he cries continually the same old thing.... But they won’t take him away. They simply say he will soon be sent to Omsk, and that we can stand him better than the sick; at least so the doctor said.”

Briinn looked at me like a stupid, dirty beast. “ I must have a woman again, Junker! Young, supple...” he stammered out amid giggles. I suddenly shivered. “ Where is little Blank? ” I asked quickly in an effort to think of other things.
“‘ Dead. Yesterday evening. Consumption,” said the Tadpole. “He suffered terribly. At the last he always talked about a shop. He was full of blood when he died.”
“And they have eaten our Suschka as well,” said the Schwalangscher.
After a time Pod stirred. I quickly bent over him. “ Pod, old man, dear old boy — do you know me? ”
“Yes, boy...” he breathed. What was the matter with his voice? Where had the old deep, rumbling tone disappeared to? I seized my coat. “I’ve brought you something to eat, Pod! Good things —”
“ But you must eat, old boy! ” I said loudly.

A cold shiver passed through my body. I shook myself in an attempt to get rid of it. “ Pod,” I said swiftly, “you must not throw up the sponge. [ll talk to the doctor. You must be brought to hospital. Then you'll get better again. And spring is coming — ”
“] want to stay with my comrades,” he said in a tired voice. “ With the artist and the Bavarians and... Briinn. They need me. - - Pie |

I took his hand in mine— a hard, thick-skinned peasant hand. Tears came into my eyes. If | had bent my head, they would have poured forth in a burning stream. | needed all my strength to enable me to hold my head erect. “Tl come every day now, Pod,” I said cheerily.
“Tt was good of you to come at all,” he murmured.

“ At all? What do you mean, Pod? I’ll come very often,” I said excitedly, almost laughingly. “ Ab! we'll put you on your legs again. And in the spring we g° home! And then you'll plough again, Pod. With the brown one, Pod, about whom you told me, and with Blesse, who is so like the Holsteinerin! You'll give her a good wallop if she tries to hang back in the traces! But perhaps she’s forgotten that trick by now — what do you think, Pod? Yes, and then you'll sing her praises, leaning against your plough, so that it crunches...” He only smiled. Oh! that knowing smile — it smothered up my words like a black shroud.
“ You must will it, Pod! ” I said helplessly.

“Look up Anna,” was all he said. “ She must see you... - - I have written to her about you, often.... Tell her about me... In the evening, on the seat before the door, from where one sees — all — my — fields...”

1 heard nothing more. For a long time he went on whispering, but I could not understand a word. If Briinn had not continued to scream incessantly: “ I want to have a woman again, a young, supple...” I might have caught something of what he was whispering. I remained seated beside his bed between the Schwalangscher and the artist until dawn came. As the sun rose, he ceased to breathe. Up to the last we heard him murmuring and whispering. “It sounded like ‘Anna’? ” queried the artist in amazement. “ Was that his wife’s name? ”

I realized that he had told nobody,.only me— and now there was no longer any need for anyone else to know. I shrugged my shoulders, removed all his papers and letters from his tunic, and took down Holsteinerin, the champion mare, from the wall. In the pocket of his trousers I found an old, chewed-up pencil on which the letter “A” had been carved. I took that also.

As I left the barracks, an icy east wind blew in my face, Nowhere was anyone to be seen. I leaned up against the wall of the barracks and suddenly became conscious that I was crying like a child. A fit of shivering came over me, striking into my very heart, but it did not come from the ice-cold wind which froze the tears as they ran down my cheeks. It came from within — despite the company of many thousands of men I was shivering from loneliness. “ Pod! ” I called out helplessly. “ Pod, my friend...”

Pod’s death laid me in bed. What hunger and heat, cold and illness, had not been able to accomplish throughout the space of three years, it accomplished overnight. I lay for fourteen days, although the doctor declared that I was organically sound — “ Just like Pod!” I thought to myself. For hours at a time Dr. Berger sat by my bedside in order to help me pass the time. Olfert looked after me with an assiduity that became almost embarrassing. When lain upon for any length of time my sacks of shavings became hard, yet what would it have been like if I had had to lie upon bare boards — as Pod and Blank had had to do! These Cossack corn-sacks undoubtedly

had their good points as well; for, above all, they reeked of horses and of resin and of forests. Every time I smelt this odour my thoughts unwillingly flew homewards. What would it be like to stand, after all these years in this desolate steppe, for the first time again in a wood? I thought that I should probably embrace the very trees and kiss their bark. I should like to live in a wood on my return home; seeing nothing, hearing nothing, only breathing and dreaming and gazing upon the trees.... But I should never be able to do that — who would and should who has passed twenty? And in a conquered land? At this stage I always found that my thoughts became involved — my brooding lost in darkness. What should I do on my return home? I should certainly have to adopt a profession. But what? What?

For many of us — indeed, for the majority — this life here was no more than an episode. On their return home it would be laid away in a drawer in their cupboard, and the lock well turned upon it. They would go back to their old life and take it up just where they had left off — and forget! But we — we youths? Seydlitz once said: “I grew to manhood in war. I cannot unlearn what I have learnt! ” Great Moloch had swallowed him up — living. What was I to do to prevent his seizing upon me, alive or dead?

It had lasted too long and had been too much for our years — that was it. It could have been a great and valuable experience for us: its duration and overwhelmingness had turned it into a destroying martyrdom. My God! I could not do as Seydlitz had done — nor could the great majority of us. What were we to do? We who could not change our inner misery into a strengthening virtue? I let all professions pass in review before my eyes. If one only had had one already! We boys would have to begin to learn all over again.... And how can a man begin again to learn who has passed the best years of his life lying on a bed doing nothing, scarcely ever holding a pen, scarcely ever taking a book in his hand? Ah well! they’d understand that, they’d give us privileges. But then... ? Should I become a lawyer? Like Dr. Berger? “In accordance with paragraph so-and-so you are charged with a breach of the peace inasmuch as you made a libellous remark to the appellant...” Would that not be irony? Could one of us still grasp such an idea, after all we had lived through? Should I not suddenly burst out laughing like a madman? In a loud chorus of laughter in company with all those from Totzkoje?
The best thing would be to enter a monastery. In a green, quiet forest among silent, pious monks.

I started up. Olfert had entered the room. He looked round quickly. Nobody was in the room. “ Alone at last...” he said with a forced laugh, coming towards my corner and seating himself upon my bed. I looked up at him in astonishment. He turned his head and looked strangely at me. “ What’s the matter with you, Olfert? ” I asked in some anxiety.

He took my hand, laid it upon his knee, and stroked it diffidently. “Ill tell you,” he began. “But perhaps you know already, perhaps you have already suspected it? I am... No, naturally it is not love — that would be absurd.... But something like it....” He sighed deeply. “ Why didn’t you let me go to the women? ” he burst out. “Then perhaps it would never have happened....”
“What would not have happened, Olfert? ” I asked helplessly.
“* Haven’t you noticed it?... I cannot stand it any longer! I cannot sleep, I am mad, certainly, but I cannot help it... unless...” |

I went hot and cold. Everything within me rose in defiance. Nevertheless... It was not the same as with Thurn. In the name of God! How had it come about? Had I also got to the same stage? “I shall not be able to defend myself if he...”
I thought to myself, partly in anxiety, partly with a new, hitherto unknown, and exciting sense of anticipation....

‘Edwin! ” Olfert called out. For years I have not heard my Christian name, which is not very common among soldiers, and on the last occasion had not a girl used it? This thought failed to be of assistance. I was utterly powerless. I saw his large eyes gleaming; they were wet and dark and the eyelids were very slightly reddened..

A trembling sense of expectation took hold of me. “ What will it be like? ” I thought with curiosity. Never before was a man so near me.... “Perhaps I shall forget everything if he does it,” I thought. Perhaps they all forget about it, when they do it? Perhaps it affects one like morphia? Ah! it would — have been a good thing to have had some morphia just then! All of us in Siberia would have been drug-fiends, if we had been able to obtain any.... “ And,” I thought, “and. supposing I close my eyes and think of a girl... a peasant girl... a strong, solid, broad-shouldered... ? Perhaps then I could — bear it? ” I also remembered how good he had been to me — this fellow Olfert; that he had guarded me like a dog; that it was possible that he suffered inhumanly; that it was only his begging eyes that had taken the resistance out of me....
I lay for a moment paralysed before something unexpected occurred: I suddenly became conscious of something strange, unpleasant, upon my face, a slight prickling or scratching.

. “He is badly shaved! ” was the thought that at once flew to my head. At the same instant the broad country girl whom I had sought to call to mind at the moment of his kiss disappeared, vanished.... “ No! No! No!” I threw myself about, struck at his chest, turned and twisted to all sides, and pressed my thumbs into his eyes. “Let me go! I won't... cannot...” I groaned. At the same instant steps echoed down the corridor. Olfert sprang up, walked rapidly across to the window, and stood gazing into the barrack-yard with his back turned towards the door.
“ Boys! ” said Windt, coming into the room, “have you heard? In the men’s barracks someone has castrated himself — a fellow called Briinninghaus! ”

The next day I got up. I should have stayed longer in bed, but I wanted to avoid another similar occurrence. When I was up and about, I could defend myself better; for Olfert seized every opportunity when we were alone in the room to overcome my resistance. He almost whined. “ No! ” I yelled at him. Once I was forced to strike him in order to defend myself. How would it end? I felt incapable of putting up a defence for much longer.... On the sixth evening I went to Lieutenant Schulenburg. I saw no other way of escape. In such things Dr. Berger was as helpless as I was, but this small, quiet man with the smooth, typical officer’s head and the firm, projecting chin...
“Lieutenant,” I said nervously, “may I ask you to be so kind as to go for an hour’s walk with me now and then? ”
He looked at me until I grew red in the face.
*‘ Lieutenant,” I continued haltingly, “even if you do not like me, or for any other reason, nevertheless please do it for an hour a day.”
** Please do not ask me to give my reasons,” I said in a low voice. He bent his head slightly. “ All right, Ensign, I understand. An hour every day, and tomorrow at ten o’clock.”

The young doctor, who had attended me when I was sick told me that during the first years in Russia their complaints regarding want of cleanliness, instruments, and bandages were invariably replied to with arrest and confinement in the katorga. He had often had to operate with his pen-knife. When
later on he was permitted the use of instruments, he was only allowed to operate with four guards with fixed bayonets standing beside the operating-table.
“Have you any idea,” I asked, “how many prisoners of war have died up to the present in Siberia? ”
“Yes,” he answered. “The last time I met Elsa Brandstrom I asked oe and she told me five hundred Eionane up to the present....”

Spring had come. I spent the spring days in Schulenburg’s company; for our daily hour had imperceptibly increased to two and three. Peace had also come to me. When Olfert saw that I sought refuge from him in Schulenburg’s company, he left me alone; it was undoubtedly true that he felt I would - reveal everything to Schulenburg in the last resort — and it is even possible that he believed I had already done so. Moreover, he began to seek the company of the Warrior. Was it so long since he himself had hurled words of abuse at such “* couples ”?

Schulenburg and I seldom spoke to one another. We walked silently, determinedly, and at a measured pace. At times it seemed to me as if I were being filled with a healing strength in the society of this quiet and strong man. Only once did he break forth into speech, when I grumbled and declared that I did not know what I should do in the future.
“Rot! ” he said curtly. “That’s pure slackness! Probantur tem pestate fortes! as the Romans said.”
** And what will you do, Lieutenant? ” I asked.

“Oh,” he said confidently, “something! Perhaps I'll become a merchant, perhaps a farmer — I'll certainly find something to do! I am not going to allow myself to be beaten. I’m done with the past. Moreover, a time has come again when honest men will be wanted more than ever. I’m not going to belong to the everlasting yesterday. We've been destroying for long enough. It’s time we began to start building again! ”

His words made a deep impression on me. That was the true path! I thought. And my more particular path would be to be a— peasant. Like old Pod....I suddenly felt that unwittingly I had found the right man at the moment when I most needed him—in the days that followed upon Olfert’s ‘break-down and Pod’s death. I rejoiced to think that my instinct still remained sound....

From one point of view it was not a bad thing that our food got worse from day to day: one slept better undernourished. Then there is no superfluity of vitality to go to the brain and to poison the blood. Formerly I had thought that the principal care of a prisoner must be to guard against bodily weakness; but now I know that spiritual degeneracy can be not only more dangerous but much more difficult to fight against. What was left to us? Fantasy... that became for us as a green wood, a city of refuge, a sanctuary. But a wood that was populated with maidens. We talked and we dreamed; and invariably our dreams and our conversation became centred in the thing for which we were all hungering: woman. Our fantasies became more and more inflamed, relief was no longer to be naturally obtained, nor did it suffice to quench the fire that burned ever more hotly. Our brains played ever more and more madly with fancies about that very thing from which we must abstain at all costs to ourselves. Some told of dreams of murders committed out of sheer lust, others of disgusting abnormalities. If the first woman we possessed, after this long period of abstinence, were not clever enough lovingly to heal us and cool our passions, then we were likely to remain abnormal for the rest of our lives and to spread abroad a plague of perversion over our old Fatherland.

I walked up to the Home-hill. For a short time past nobody had gone up there, for a young Captain had there cut his throat with a razor. When he was discovered, he lay upon his stomach with his face turned westwards as though he would gaze towards home until his last breath left him. Since that event the hill had been deserted, but nevertheless I went up to the top. The funerals had once more begun, but this spring we were forbidden to accompany them. Only from the summit of this hill could one follow their path towards the cemetery — why was I there? On the spot where the Captain had lain, I strewed sand over the dried blood so that it could no longer be seen.

Once again the narrow path leading to the cemetery gleamed yellow with sawdust and shavings. How many long caravans passed daily up and down that path! I watched one with an intentness so great that it seemed as though I would pierce through the very coffins. Such a procession had brought my comrades to their last resting-place: Schnarrenberg, my sergeant major; the childlike grocer, Blank; the simple peasant, Pod. I had thought of waiting beside the morgue until their bodies were brought out; then I remembered that I should have to examine perhaps two thousand naked corpses, searchingly, minutely, before I recognized the loved faces. And that would have exceeded my powers of endurance.

As I thought of these things, I became filled once more with a new sense of loneliness and hopelessness. I threw myself upon the ground, spotted with the blood of a man in despair, and in a desperation akin to his I bit into the sand in my agony. In front of my very eyes my comrades were being borne one after the other — two or three thousand of them — to the cemetery; and one of them had been as dear to me as a brother — Dragoon Podbielski. “I am the last! ” I groaned. What was I to do? I could never again be a quiet, happy normal man. What had become of the Totzkoje squad? I'd é never be able to forget, always be forced to remember that masturbation had reduced that jolly fellow Briinn to an idiot; that consumption had eaten up the girlish Blank; that our defeat in the war had broken down the resistance of the determined Schnarrenberg; that the war had swallowed up alive the proud Seydlitz; that sexual desire had ruined the willpower of Olfert; that home-sickness had carried away the strong body of Pod.... What would be the use of my returning home? Would it not be better if I followed them? Here — on this hill where someone had already paved the way for me? Would it not be wiser to surrender a life in which it was possible to suffer what we had suffered? Perhaps it would go on for another two years? And even if it did not — what could I do at home? Had not the war made a Siberia of the whole world for me? For us was it not everywhere Siberia? Because we could never hope to forget? I threw myself about and beat upon my temples. “ And shall I live as if nothing had happened? ” I shrieked into the ground.

Once more I was plunged into the depths of despondency, until a tiny incident occurred to pull my feet out of the slough and set them on firm ground again. It was almost nothing — and it was so tremendous as to baffle description. I was standing at the window and saw Lieutenant Schulenburg — that small, rodlike regular officer — walking past. Erect, austere, silent, he went his way — honourable, independent, far-seeing. “ What would he do if he had your knowledge of languages? ” I said to myself in reproach. Escape—the word flew through my

head. In the same instant I suddenly took a resolve, and with it all slackness vanished. I would escape. I would once more take up life again— wash away from me in facing peril all that had adhered to me here, and drown remembrance in the flowing stream of life.

I was too young to overcome Siberia as Schulenburg could overcome it; I suffered more than he did. I could only overcome it if I threw myself, like a mortally diseased person, into some health-giving stream. That alone could remove the stains from my spirit and give me new strength! If I had luck, I should emerge to shake the drops from my head — and to find myself whole again.

_ Did not our Fair Angel say on the occasion of her last visit: (“My friends, I know of a warfare crueller and harder than any other — prison life! Nevertheless, the victory can be won. And in the end you will attain to a maturity and stature that cannot be achieved by those who experience only the daily round of everyday life! ’” She was right! That was to be the recompense for all these years —that was the harvest they would yield. But I could not wait until all should return home together. In my condition I could not hold out. Va banque — that was the only game for me. I resolved to undergo a drastic cure —one of those cures that either kill or cure. And if I died? I must, in any case, have died slowly without the cure.

As I went away, filled with new hopes, and meditating a thousand plans, that good fellow Saltin called me over to him. He was standing in front of the morgue and pointing to a tiny green plant that had quietly and determinedly thrust its way up through the barren soil.
“It’s the only one in Siberia! ” he said: laughingly. “ For eight days I have watched it growing. Four days ago it spread out its first leaves, and today the first flowers have appeared.”
“Truly, the worst rubbish-heap can bear fruit!” I said with conviction.

I stood at the window and gazed out. Everyone was asleep; only Dr. Berger was still reading. The Warrior sighed in his sleep, and Seydlitz’s place was empty. The desert before my eyes stretched out coldly — white, like a moonlit landscape. “Tt won’t be long now! ” I thought. “ Where there is a will, there is a way.”

I'd find a second smuggler. One night I would break out at the same place where we had crept out before, but this time I would go west and not east. And this time I would be successful.... Two Mongolian horses would be waiting behind the hill. The smuggler would be there with a Russian uniform for me. With a low cry I would hurl myself into the saddle. The new grass would silence the beating of the horses’ hoofs; blowing through their nostrils, the horses would trot away, and their heads would be turned towards the west....

As dawn broke, we made a brief halt. I threw myself upon the steppe and held my head in my hands. Nothing more was to be seen of our camp, with its red barracks and barbed-wire fence. Alone the cemetery on the hill stood up in the distance to take farewell of me. It seemed as if all the crosses nodded approvingly to me — as if all the dead gazed after me.

A NOTE ON THE TYPE WHICH THIS BOOK

This book is composed on the Linotype in Bodoni, so-called after its designer, Giambattista Bodoni (1740-1813) a celebrated Italian scholar and printer. Bodoni planned his type especially for use on the more smoothly finished papers that came into vogue late in the eighteenth century and drew his letters with a mechanical regularity that is readily apparent on comparison with the less formal old style. Other characteristics that will be noted are the square serifs without fillet and the marked contrast between the light and heavy strokes.
